📶 OSI Model — 7 Layers REFERENCE MODEL ▶
Reference Model — OSI / DoD
Open Systems Interconnection — 7-Layer Stack & Functions
Divides network communication into 7 abstraction layers. Mnemonic ↑: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Phy→App) · Mnemonic ↓: All People Seem To Need Data Processing (App→Phy).
▸ LAYER STACK — PDU & PROTOCOLS
7
Application
Data  |  HTTP/S, FTP, DNS, SMTP, SNMP, SSH
6
Presentation
Data  |  TLS/SSL, JPEG, ASCII, MPEG
5
Session
Data  |  NetBIOS, RPC, SMB
4
Transport
Segment/Datagram  |  TCP · UDP · SCTP
3
Network
Packet  |  IP · ICMP · OSPF · BGP · RIP
2
Data Link
Frame  |  Ethernet · 802.11 · PPP · ARP
1

Bits  |  Coax · Fiber · UTP · Hubs
▸ LAYER REFERENCE TABLE
# Layer PDU Key Protocols / Devices Function
7 Application Data HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, SSH User-facing services, application APIs
6 Presentation Data TLS/SSL, JPEG, MPEG, ASCII, encryption Encoding, encryption, compression
5 Session Data NetBIOS, RPC, SQL sessions, NFS Establish, manage, terminate sessions
4 Transport Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) TCP, UDP, TLS (also L5–L7) End-to-end delivery, flow control, ports
3 Network Packet IP, ICMP, OSPF, BGP, routers Logical addressing, routing between networks
2 Data Link Frame Ethernet, ARP, MAC, switches, bridges Physical addressing (MAC), error detection
1 Physical Bits CAT5/6, fiber, hubs, repeaters, RJ45 Raw bit transmission over physical medium

🤝 TCP vs UDP — Transport Layer NETWORK+ ▶
Reference — RFC 793 (TCP) · RFC 768 (UDP)
Connection Types · 3-Way Handshake · Flags · Use Cases
TCP — connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, error-checked. UDP — connectionless, low-overhead, best-effort. Choose based on need for reliability vs speed.
▸ COMPARISON
Feature TCP UDP
Connection 3-way handshake (SYN→SYN-ACK→ACK) None — send and forget
Reliability ACK, retransmission, ordering No guarantees
Speed Slower (overhead) Faster (low overhead)
Header size 20–60 bytes 8 bytes
Flow control Yes (sliding window) No
Use cases HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SSH, SMTP, databases DNS, VoIP, video streaming, DHCP, gaming
▸ TCP 3-WAY HANDSHAKE & FLAGS
# 3-Way Handshake (connection establishment) Client → Server SYN seq=100 Server → Client SYN-ACK seq=200, ack=101 Client → Server ACK seq=101, ack=201 # Connection established ────────────────────────────── # 4-Way Teardown (graceful close) Client → Server FIN Server → Client ACK Server → Client FIN Client → Server ACK # TIME_WAIT state follows # TCP Flags (URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN) SYN - Synchronize (start connection) ACK - Acknowledge FIN - Finish (graceful close) RST - Reset (abrupt close / port closed) PSH - Push (flush buffer immediately) URG - Urgent pointer valid ECE - ECN echo (congestion notification) CWR - Congestion window reduced # SYN scan (Nmap -sS) — half-open, sends SYN, reads SYN-ACK/RST # SYN-ACK = open port; RST = closed; no reply = filtered
🗺️ Network Topologies VISUAL MODELS ▶
Diagram
Physical & Logical Topology Types
Star
Central switch. Easy isolation. SPF at hub.
Bus
Shared backbone. Single failure = full outage.
Ring
Token passing. One break = outage (unless dual-ring).
Full Mesh
All-to-all. Max redundancy. n(n-1)/2 links.
Hybrid
Mixed types (star-bus). Most enterprise nets.
🔢 Subnetting & CIDR NETWORK+ · A+ ▶
Reference — IPv4 Subnetting & CIDR Notation
CIDR Table · Private Ranges · Subnet Math · IPv6 Basics
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) expresses a subnet as address/prefix where prefix = number of network bits. Hosts per subnet = 2^(32−prefix) − 2 (subtract network + broadcast addresses).
▸ CIDR QUICK REFERENCE
CIDR Subnet Mask Hosts Subnets from /24 Common Use
/8 255.0.0.0 16,777,214 — Class A (10.0.0.0/8)
/16 255.255.0.0 65,534 — Class B (172.16.0.0/16)
/24 255.255.255.0 254 1 Common LAN segment
/25 255.255.255.128 126 2 Split /24 in half
/26 255.255.255.192 62 4 Smaller segments
/27 255.255.255.224 30 8 Point-to-point + small
/28 255.255.255.240 14 16 Small DMZ
/29 255.255.255.248 6 32 Point-to-point links
/30 255.255.255.252 2 64 WAN point-to-point
/31 255.255.255.254 2* 128 P2P no broadcast (RFC 3021)
/32 255.255.255.255 1 (host) — Single host route / loopback
▸ PRIVATE & SPECIAL RANGES (RFC 1918 / RFC 5735)
Range CIDR Class Use
10.0.0.0–10.255.255.255 /8 A Private (large enterprise)
172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 /12 B Private (medium enterprise)
192.168.0.0–192.168.255.255 /16 C Private (home / small office)
127.0.0.0–127.255.255.255 /8 — Loopback (localhost)
169.254.0.0–169.254.255.255 /16 — APIPA / link-local (no DHCP)
100.64.0.0–100.127.255.255 /10 — Shared address space (ISP NAT)
0.0.0.0 /32 — Default route / unspecified
255.255.255.255 /32 — Broadcast (all hosts)
▸ SUBNET MATH
# Given: 192.168.10.200/26 — find network, broadcast, range Prefix = /26 → 26 network bits, 6 host bits Hosts = 2^6 − 2 = 62 Block size = 2^6 = 64 (256 − 192 = 64) Subnets = 2^2 = 4 (26 − 24 borrowed bits) # Blocks: .0, .64, .128, .192 # .200 falls in block .192 Network = 192.168.10.192 Broadcast = 192.168.10.255 Host range = 192.168.10.193 – 192.168.10.254 # Subnet mask from CIDR /26 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000 = 255.255.255.192
▸ IPv6 ESSENTIALS
Feature Detail
Address length 128-bit, written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334
Abbreviation Leading zeros dropped per group; consecutive zero groups → :: (once only)
::1 Loopback (≡ 127.0.0.1)
fe80::/10 Link-local (auto-configured; not routable)
fc00::/7 Unique-local (≡ RFC 1918 private)
ff00::/8 Multicast (replaces IPv4 broadcast)
2000::/3 Global unicast (public internet)
NDP Neighbor Discovery Protocol — replaces ARP
SLAAC Stateless Address Autoconfiguration — no DHCP needed
🗺️ Routing, VLANs & Network Devices NETWORK+ ▶
Reference — Routing Protocols · Switching · Network Hardware
Dynamic Routing · VLANs · Spanning Tree · Device Comparison
Routing operates at L3 (IP). Routers select paths using routing tables. Dynamic protocols automate table updates. VLANs segment a single physical switch into logical L2 networks.
▸ ROUTING PROTOCOLS
Protocol Type Metric Scope Notes
RIP v2 Distance vector Hop count (max 15) IGP Legacy; slow convergence
OSPF Link-state Cost (bandwidth) IGP Dijkstra SPF; fast convergence; enterprise standard
EIGRP Hybrid Bandwidth + delay IGP Cisco proprietary; DUAL algorithm
BGP Path vector AS path, policy EGP Internet backbone; connects ASes; complex policy
IS-IS Link-state Cost IGP Used by ISPs; similar to OSPF
Static route Manual Admin distance 1 Any Predictable; no overhead; no failover
▸ VLANS & TRUNKING
# VLAN — logical L2 segmentation on a switch # Access port — carries 1 VLAN (end devices) # Trunk port — carries multiple VLANs (switch-to-switch, switch-to-router) # 802.1Q tag — 4-byte VLAN tag added to Ethernet frame on trunk links # Common VLAN design VLAN 1 = Default (avoid using for production) VLAN 10 = Data / Users VLAN 20 = Voice (VoIP — QoS priority) VLAN 30 = Management (network devices) VLAN 40 = DMZ / Guest VLAN 99 = Native VLAN (untagged traffic on trunk) # Inter-VLAN routing: "router-on-a-stick" OR L3 switch SVIs # Spanning Tree Protocol (STP 802.1D) — prevents L2 loops # RSTP (802.1w) — rapid convergence (<1s vs 30-50s STP)
▸ NETWORK DEVICE COMPARISON
Device OSI Layer Function Forwards by
Hub L1 Repeats signal to all ports — collision domain Broadcasts bits
Bridge L2 Connects two segments; learns MACs MAC address
Switch L2 (L3 if managed) Learns MACs; forwards frames to correct port only MAC address
Router L3 Routes packets between networks; enforces ACLs IP address
Firewall L3–L7 Inspects and filters traffic by rule set IP/port/state/DPI
WAP L1–L2 Wireless access point; bridges Wi-Fi to wired LAN MAC / radio
Proxy L7 Intermediary for client requests; caching, filtering Application data
Load Balancer L4 / L7 Distributes traffic across servers Port / content

Wi-Fi Standards · Frequency Bands · Authentication · Attack Vectors
Wi-Fi generations use IEEE 802.11 standards. Frequency band affects range vs speed: 2.4 GHz = longer range, more interference; 5 GHz = shorter range, faster throughput; 6 GHz = Wi-Fi 6E/7, minimal interference.

▸ WIRELESS SECURITY PROTOCOLS
Protocol Encryption Auth Status
WEP RC4 (40/104-bit) Shared key Broken — do not use
WPA TKIP (RC4) PSK / 802.1X Deprecated
WPA2 AES-CCMP PSK / 802.1X Current standard — use AES mode
WPA3 AES-GCMP-256 SAE / 802.1X Recommended; SAE replaces PSK handshake
802.1X EAP variants RADIUS + certs Enterprise auth; required for WPA2/3-Enterprise
📡 DHCP — DORA Process 4-STEP SEQUENCE ▶
Sequence
Dynamic Host Configuration — Discover · Offer · Request · Acknowledge
DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically. All 4 messages use UDP (client port 68, server port 67). Client uses broadcast because it has no IP yet. Relay agents (ip helper-address) forward DHCP across subnets.
D
Discover
Broadcast — find DHCP servers
→
O
Offer
Server offers available IP
→
R
Request
Client requests offered IP
→
A
Acknowledge
Server confirms lease
APIPA fallback: 169.254.x.x · Lease renewal at 50% & 87.5% of lease time · DHCP snooping prevents rogue servers

Well-Known Ports 0–1023 · Registered 1024–49151
TCP/UDP Port Numbers — Services, Protocols & Security Notes
Well-known ports (0–1023) require root/admin to bind. Memorize all ports below for CompTIA exams — they appear across A+, Net+, Sec+, CySA+.
Port(s) Protocol Transport Security Notes
20 / 21 FTP (data/control) TCP Cleartext — use SFTP (22) or FTPS (990)
22 SSH / SFTP / SCP TCP Encrypted; replaces Telnet (23)
23 Telnet TCP Cleartext — avoid; legacy only
25 SMTP (send email) TCP Cleartext; SMTPS = 465, SMTP+STARTTLS = 587
53 DNS UDP (queries) / TCP (zone transfers) Zone transfers (TCP 53) must be restricted
67 / 68 DHCP (server/client) UDP DHCP snooping prevents rogue servers
69 TFTP UDP No auth, no encryption — internal only
80 HTTP TCP Cleartext — prefer HTTPS (443)
110 POP3 TCP Email retrieval; POP3S = 995
119 NNTP (Usenet) TCP Legacy; rarely used
123 NTP UDP Time sync; NTP amplification DDoS vector
135 RPC / MSRPC TCP Windows; block at perimeter
137–139 NetBIOS TCP/UDP Legacy Windows; block externally
143 IMAP TCP Email; IMAPS = 993
161 / 162 SNMP (poll/trap) UDP v1/v2 cleartext; use SNMPv3
389 LDAP TCP Directory; LDAPS = 636
443 HTTPS / TLS TCP Encrypted HTTP; standard secure web
445 SMB / CIFS TCP Windows file shares; EternalBlue target
465 / 587 SMTPS / Submission TCP 587 = authenticated submission (preferred)
514 Syslog UDP UDP — no delivery guarantee; TCP syslog = 6514
636 LDAPS TCP LDAP over TLS
993 / 995 IMAPS / POP3S TCP Encrypted email retrieval
1433 MS SQL Server TCP Block external access; requires auth
1521 Oracle DB TCP Block external; strong auth required
3306 MySQL / MariaDB TCP Bind to localhost; use SSL in transit
3389 RDP TCP Brute-force target; restrict with NLA + MFA
5060 / 5061 SIP (VoIP) UDP/TCP 5061 = TLS-encrypted SIP
5432 PostgreSQL TCP Bind to localhost; SSL in transit

🌐 DNS Record Types REFERENCE TABLE ▶
Reference — Source: CEH + Net+
DNS Record Types & Zone Transfer
DNS uses UDP port 53 for queries and TCP port 53 for zone transfers >512 bytes. Tools: nslookup, dig, whois.
Record Full Name Purpose
A Address Maps hostname → IPv4 address (forward DNS lookup)
AAAA IPv6 Address Maps hostname → IPv6 address
CNAME Canonical Name Alias pointing to another hostname (e.g., www → host)
MX Mail Exchange Mail servers for the domain; has priority value
PTR Pointer Maps IP → hostname (reverse DNS lookup)
NS Name Server Authoritative name servers for the domain
SOA Start of Authority Primary name server + zone metadata (serial, TTL)
SRV Service Hostname and port number of services (SIP, XMPP, LDAP)
TXT Text Arbitrary text; used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC email auth
DNS FOOTPRINTING COMMANDS
# Forward lookup nslookup example.com dig example.com A # Reverse lookup (PTR record) dig -x 93.184.216.34 # Zone transfer attempt (TCP 53) — reveals all records dig axfr @ns1.example.com example.com # All record types dig example.com ANY # Domain/IP ownership whois example.com

🔭 NMAP Scan Types Reference PENTEST TOOL ▶
Reference — Source: CEH Cheat Sheet
NMAP — Scan Flags, Responses & Common Options
Nmap is the de-facto tool for network discovery and port scanning. Use nmap <SCAN> <TARGET> syntax. Requires root/administrator for raw socket scans (SYN, FIN, XMAS, etc.).
▸ SCAN TYPES
Flag Scan Type Open Response Closed Response Notes
-sT TCP Connect SYN/ACK RST/ACK Full 3-way handshake; logged by target
-sS SYN (Stealth) SYN/ACK RST/ACK Half-open; doesn't complete handshake; less logged
-sF FIN No response RST Works on Linux/Unix; bypasses some firewalls
-sX XMAS Tree No response RST Sets FIN+URG+PSH flags; binary 00101001
-sN NULL No response Varies by OS No flags set; designed for Linux/Unix
-sA ACK RST No response Maps firewall rules; determines filtered/unfiltered
-sI IDLE (Zombie) SYN/ACK RST/ACK Uses spoofed IP; maximum stealth scan
-sU UDP UDP response ICMP unreachable Slower; needed for DNS/DHCP/SNMP discovery
-sn Ping Sweep — — Host discovery only; no port scan
▸ USEFUL NMAP OPTIONS
# Speed / Timing: -T0 (paranoid) → -T5 (insane) nmap -T4 -A 10.5.23.0/24 # Aggressive: OS detect + version + scripts nmap -sS -p 22,80,443 10.5.23.1 # SYN scan specific ports nmap -sV --top-ports 100 target # Version detection on top 100 ports nmap -sC -sV target # Default scripts + version detection nmap -n -Pn -p- target # All 65535 ports, skip DNS/ping nmap --script vuln target # Run vulnerability scripts nmap --script "vuln and safe" target # Safe vuln scripts only nmap -oX scan.xml target # XML output for import to tools nmap -oN scan.txt target # Normal text output nmap -6 target # IPv6 scan

⌨️ Network Device CLI — Show Commands CLI REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: Net+ Cheat Sheet
Switch & Router Verification Commands
These read-only verification commands work on Cisco IOS-based switches and routers. Use them to diagnose connectivity, review configs, and troubleshoot network issues.
SWITCH COMMANDS
show mac-address-table # CAM table: MAC → port mappings show vlan brief # All VLANs, ports assigned to each show interfaces # All interfaces: status, errors, counters show interfaces trunk # Trunk port info and allowed VLANs show spanning-tree # STP topology, root bridge, port states show arp # ARP table: IP → MAC mappings show power inline # PoE status and power draw per port show cdp neighbors detail # Connected Cisco devices, IP, platform
ROUTER COMMANDS
show ip route # Routing table: all known routes show ip interface brief # All interfaces: IP, status, protocol show running-config # Current active configuration show startup-config # Saved config (in NVRAM) show ip protocols # Routing protocols running, timers show ip ospf neighbor # OSPF neighbor adjacencies show ip bgp summary # BGP peer summary and state show access-lists # All ACLs and match counts show version # IOS version, uptime, hardware info
TROUBLESHOOTING TOOLS (LINUX / WINDOWS)
# Connectivity testing ping 8.8.8.8 # ICMP echo test traceroute 8.8.8.8 # Linux: path tracing (UDP by default) tracert 8.8.8.8 # Windows equivalent # Interface and routing ip addr show # Linux: IP addresses on all interfaces ip route show # Linux: routing table netstat -rn # Routing table (cross-platform) # Name resolution nslookup google.com # Quick DNS lookup dig google.com # Detailed DNS query # Packet capture tcpdump -i eth0 -n # Capture on interface, no DNS resolve tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 # Filter by port tcpdump -w capture.pcap # Write to file for Wireshark
📡 TCPDump — Packet Capture Reference COMPLETE REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: TCPDump Cheat Sheet
Capture · Filter · Display · Output — Full Command Reference
TCPDump is the standard CLI packet analyzer on Linux/Unix. Requires root or CAP_NET_RAW. Use which tcpdump to locate. Write to .pcap files to open in Wireshark.
CAPTURE FLAGS
tcpdump -i any # Capture on ALL interfaces (needs root) tcpdump -i eth0 # Capture on specific interface tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 # Stop after 100 packets tcpdump -i eth0 tcp # TCP packets only tcpdump -i eth0 udp # UDP packets only tcpdump -i eth0 icmp # ICMP only (ping traffic) tcpdump -i eth0 arp # ARP packets only tcpdump -I eth0 # Monitor mode (Wi-Fi sniffing) tcpdump -r capture.pcap # Read & analyze saved capture file
FILTER EXPRESSIONS
# Host filters tcpdump host 192.168.1.1 # Any traffic to/from IP tcpdump src host 10.0.0.5 # Source IP only tcpdump dst host 10.0.0.5 # Destination IP only tcpdump net 192.168.0.0/24 # Entire subnet # Port filters tcpdump port 443 # Any traffic on port 443 tcpdump src port 80 # Source port 80 tcpdump portrange 1000-2000 # Port range tcpdump tcp dst port 22 # TCP to port 22 (SSH) # MAC/Layer 2 filters tcpdump ether host 00:11:22:33:44:55 tcpdump ether broadcast # Ethernet broadcast frames # Logical operators tcpdump src 10.0.0.1 and port 443 # AND tcpdump dst 10.0.0.1 or src port 22 # OR tcpdump port 80 and not host 192.168.1.5 # NOT tcpdump dst host 10.0.0.1 and greater 128 # Packet > 128 bytes
DISPLAY & OUTPUT FLAGS
tcpdump -n # Don't resolve IPs to hostnames (faster) tcpdump -nn # Also don't resolve port names tcpdump -v # Verbose output (TTL, checksum, etc.) tcpdump -vv # More verbose tcpdump -A # Print payload in ASCII (HTTP inspection) tcpdump -X # Print payload in hex + ASCII tcpdump -XX # Include link-layer header in hex tcpdump -e # Print link-layer header (MAC addresses) tcpdump -q # Quick/quiet — shorter output lines tcpdump -t # Suppress timestamp tcpdump -tttt # Full date+time timestamp # Write/read pcap files tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # Write to file (for Wireshark) tcpdump -i eth0 -U -w capture.pcap # -U: write packets immediately (no buffer) tcpdump -r capture.pcap port 443 # Read file with filter
PRACTICAL EXAMPLES
# Capture all HTTP traffic (show payload in ASCII) tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 # Capture SSH attempts to this host (no DNS resolution) tcpdump -nn -i eth0 tcp dst port 22 # Capture all traffic EXCEPT SSH (avoid capturing your own session) tcpdump -i eth0 not port 22 # Save 30 large packets to file, no DNS resolution tcpdump -i eth0 -n greater 32 -w out.pcap -c 30 # Pipe remote traffic to local Wireshark in real time ssh user@router "tcpdump -U -s 65535 -w - 'not port 22'" | wireshark -k -i - # Find all HTTP GET requests (show source IP + URL) tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80 and (tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] = 0x47455420)'
🧒Networking for Absolute BeginnersNet+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is a Network?
A network is just two or more computers that can talk to each other. Your home Wi-Fi is a small network; the Internet is the giant network that connects all the small ones together. If computers are houses, the network is the system of roads between them.
ANALOGY
IP Address = Mailing Address
Every device on a network has an IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.10) so data knows where to go — exactly like a street address tells the mail carrier which house. No address, no delivery.
ANALOGY
Packets = Envelopes
Big files are chopped into small chunks called packets. Each packet is an envelope with a from-address, a to-address, and a piece of the message. They travel separately and get reassembled at the other end.
ANALOGY
Ports = Apartment Numbers
One device (one IP) runs many programs at once. A port number says which program the data is for — like an apartment number after the street address. Web pages use port 80/443, email and other services use their own.
ROLES
Client vs. Server
The client asks (your phone opening a website); the server answers (the computer that stores that website). Most of what you do online is a polite back-and-forth of requests and responses.
HARDWARE
Router vs. Switch
A switch connects devices inside one network (like hallways in a building). A router connects different networks together and finds the path between them (like roads between cities). Your home box is usually both in one.
ANALOGY
DNS = The Phonebook
Humans remember names (google.com); computers need numbers (an IP). DNS is the phonebook that looks up the name and returns the number, automatically, every time you click a link.
Beginner TermPlain-English Meaning
BandwidthHow wide the pipe is — how much data fits per second
LatencyHow long one trip takes — the delay / 'lag'
LANLocal network — your home or office
WANWide network — connects distant sites; the Internet is the biggest
Wi-FiA network with no cables — radio instead of wires
FirewallA guard that decides which traffic is allowed in or out
🔢IP Addresses & Subnets (Gently)Net+ • Start Here▶
READ IT
What an IPv4 Address Looks Like
IPv4 is four numbers 0–255 separated by dots, like 192.168.1.50. Each device on a network needs one. We’re slowly running out of them, which is why IPv6 (much longer, with letters) was invented.
TWO WORLDS
Public vs. Private
Private addresses (like 192.168.x.x and 10.x.x.x) are reused inside homes and offices — like apartment numbers that only mean something in your building. Public addresses are unique on the whole Internet, like a full street address.
NEIGHBORHOODS
What a Subnet Is
A subnet groups nearby addresses into one neighborhood so traffic stays local and organized. The subnet mask (e.g., 255.255.255.0) is just the line that says “these addresses are neighbors; everything else is out of town.”
TermPlain-English Meaning
DHCPHands out IP addresses automatically so you don’t have to
Default gatewayThe exit door to other networks / the Internet
Subnet maskMarks which part of the address is the neighborhood
IPv6The newer, much larger address system
NATLets many private devices share one public address
📖 DNS — The Internet's Phone Book NET • Start Here ▶
THE PROBLEM DNS SOLVES
Humans Hate Numbers
Computers talk to each other using IP addresses like 142.250.80.46. Humans want to type google.com. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into numbers — like a phone book that covers the whole internet.
THE DNS LOOKUP JOURNEY
8 Steps From Name to IP
1. You type google.com in your browser.
2. Browser checks its own cache. If found → done.
3. OS checks its cache. If found → done.
4. OS asks your recursive resolver (your ISP or 8.8.8.8).
5. Resolver asks a root nameserver (13 clusters worldwide) — "who handles .com?"
6. Root points to the .com TLD nameserver (Verisign).
7. TLD server points to Google's authoritative nameserver.
8. Authoritative server returns the IP. Resolver caches it and gives it to you.
DNS Record TypePurposeExample
ADomain → IPv4 addressgoogle.com → 142.250.80.46
AAAADomain → IPv6 addressgoogle.com → 2607:f8b0:…
CNAMEAlias → another domainwww.example.com → example.com
MXMail server for domainexample.com → mail.example.com
TXTArbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, verification)v=spf1 include:… ~all
NSNameservers for domainns1.google.com
PTRReverse lookup: IP → domain46.80.250.142.in-addr.arpa → google.com
SOAStart of Authority; zone metadataSerial, refresh, retry, expire
USEFUL DNS TOOLS
Dig, nslookup, host
# Query A record for a domain dig google.com A # Query MX records (mail servers) dig google.com MX # Reverse lookup dig -x 142.250.80.46 # Use a specific resolver (8.8.8.8 = Google DNS) dig @8.8.8.8 google.com # Windows equivalent nslookup google.com nslookup -type=MX google.com
TTL
Time to Live — DNS Caching Timer
Every DNS record has a TTL (Time To Live) in seconds. After TTL expires, resolvers re-query for fresh results. Low TTL = fast changes but more queries. High TTL = slow propagation but less load. When migrating a website, lower the TTL 24 hours before the switch.
🔢 DHCP — How Devices Get Their IP Address NET • Foundation ▶
DORA PROCESS
Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
Discover — new device broadcasts "I need an IP!" to 255.255.255.255.
Offer — DHCP server says "How about 192.168.1.25? Here's a lease offer."
Request — client says "Yes, I'll take 192.168.1.25" (broadcast, so other servers know).
Acknowledge — server confirms: "192.168.1.25 is yours for 24 hours. Here's gateway and DNS too."
WHAT DHCP HANDS OUT
More Than Just an IP
A DHCP lease typically includes:
• IP address — unique on the local network
• Subnet mask — defines network boundary (e.g., 255.255.255.0)
• Default gateway — the router's IP (traffic leaving the network goes here)
• DNS server(s) — where to resolve names
• Lease duration — how long before re-requesting
STATIC vs DYNAMIC
Manual vs Automatic Assignment
Dynamic — DHCP assigns from a pool; good for laptops and phones. IP may change on reconnect.
Static — manually set; never changes. Required for servers, printers, network gear (you don't want DNS records breaking because the server got a new IP).
DHCP Reservation — best of both worlds: DHCP assigns based on MAC address, so the device always gets the same IP automatically.
TROUBLESHOOTING
When DHCP Fails — APIPA
If a device can't reach a DHCP server, Windows auto-assigns an APIPA address: 169.254.x.x. This is a red flag — the device only has link-local connectivity and cannot reach the internet. Check: cable unplugged? DHCP server down? VLAN misconfigured?
📡 Wi-Fi Basics — 802.11, Bands, and Security NET • Practical ▶
802.11 STANDARDS
The Evolution of Wi-Fi
The 802.11 family are the IEEE wireless LAN standards. Each letter suffix means a different generation:
StandardWi-Fi NameMax SpeedBandYear
802.11b—11 Mbps2.4 GHz1999
802.11g—54 Mbps2.4 GHz2003
802.11nWi-Fi 4600 Mbps2.4/5 GHz2009
802.11acWi-Fi 53.5 Gbps5 GHz2013
802.11axWi-Fi 6/6E9.6 Gbps2.4/5/6 GHz2019
802.11beWi-Fi 746 Gbps2.4/5/6 GHz2024
2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz
Range vs Speed Trade-off
2.4 GHz — longer range, penetrates walls better, more congestion (microwaves, Bluetooth, neighbors all compete), slower. Good for: IoT devices, devices far from router.
5 GHz — shorter range, struggles through walls, less congested, faster. Good for: laptops and phones close to router, streaming, gaming.
6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) — even faster, very short range, nearly empty spectrum. Best for: dense environments (offices, stadiums).
WIRELESS SECURITY
WEP → WPA → WPA2 → WPA3
WEP — broken in minutes; do not use.
WPA — better but still has vulnerabilities; phase out.
WPA2-Personal (PSK) — current standard for home; uses AES-CCMP; strong if you use a long passphrase.
WPA2-Enterprise — uses RADIUS authentication; each user has their own credentials. Used in corporate environments.
WPA3 — latest; uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of PSK handshake; resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
🔀 Switching & VLANs — Dividing Your Network Logically NET • Foundation ▶
SWITCH vs HUB vs ROUTER
Three Different Devices, Three Layers
Hub — Layer 1; dumb repeater. Sends every frame to every port. Creates collisions. Legacy/obsolete.
Switch — Layer 2; intelligent. Learns which MAC addresses are on which ports using a MAC address table. Sends frames only to the correct port. Creates collision domains per port.
Router — Layer 3; connects different networks. Uses IP addresses and routing tables to forward packets between subnets and out to the internet.
HOW A SWITCH WORKS
MAC Address Table Learning
1. Frame arrives with source MAC AA:BB on port 1 → switch records AA:BB → Port 1 in table.
2. Destination MAC CC:DD — not in table yet → switch floods to all ports except source.
3. Device CC:DD responds → its MAC gets recorded.
4. Next frame to CC:DD → switch delivers it only to the correct port.
This is why switches are efficient — after learning, minimal unnecessary traffic.
VLANS
Virtual LANs — Logical Network Segmentation
A VLAN divides one physical switch into multiple logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate directly even if they're plugged into the same switch — they need a router (Layer 3) to cross VLAN boundaries. Benefits:
• Security: production servers on VLAN 10, guest WiFi on VLAN 99 — guests can't see servers
• Performance: reduce broadcast domain size
• Organization: group devices by function, not location
TRUNK vs ACCESS PORTS
Single VLAN vs Multiple VLANs
Access port — carries traffic for exactly ONE VLAN. Used for end devices (PCs, printers). Device doesn't know it's on a VLAN.
Trunk port — carries traffic for MULTIPLE VLANs simultaneously. Used between switches, or switch-to-router. Uses 802.1Q tags to label which VLAN each frame belongs to.
FeatureAccess PortTrunk Port
VLANs carriedOneMultiple
802.1Q tagNo (stripped)Yes (tagged)
Connected toEnd devicesSwitches, routers, uplinks
Native VLANN/AUntagged VLAN (usually VLAN 1)
🗺️ Routing Protocols — How Routers Find the Best Path NET • Intermediate ▶
STATIC vs DYNAMIC ROUTING
Manual Routes vs Self-Learning
Static routes — an admin manually configures each route. Simple, predictable, no overhead. Works for small networks. Fails when the network changes (adding a link, a failure) because you have to manually update every router.
Dynamic routing protocols — routers talk to each other and automatically discover routes. Self-healing when links fail. Required for large networks.
ProtocolTypeAlgorithmUse Case
RIPDistance VectorHop count (max 15)Legacy / tiny networks
OSPFLink StateDijkstra (cost)Enterprise interior routing
EIGRPHybrid (Cisco)Bandwidth + delayCisco enterprise networks
BGPPath VectorPolicy-basedInternet backbone; ISP routing
BGP
The Protocol That Runs the Internet
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is used between ISPs and large organizations to exchange routing information across the internet. Every major network has an ASN (Autonomous System Number). BGP is policy-driven — companies can influence which paths their traffic takes. A BGP misconfiguration can accidentally route the internet's traffic through your network (BGP hijacking).
DEFAULT ROUTE
The Fallback Route (0.0.0.0/0)
The default route (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0) matches ANY destination. It's the "if nothing else matches, send it here" rule — usually pointing to the upstream router or internet gateway. Every end device has a default gateway for this reason.
🧱 Firewalls — The Network's Bouncer NET • Foundation ▶
WHAT A FIREWALL DOES
Permit or Deny Based on Rules
A firewall inspects network traffic and decides whether to allow or block it based on rules. Think of it as a bouncer with a list: traffic that matches an allow rule gets in; everything else is dropped or rejected. The implicit deny rule: if nothing matches, deny.
FIREWALL TYPES
Packet Filter → Stateful → NGFW
Packet filter (L3/L4) — examines individual packets: source/dest IP, port, protocol. No context (doesn't know if it's a new connection or response). Fast but dumb.
Stateful inspection — tracks connection state. Knows if a packet is part of an established session. Much smarter — allows response traffic automatically.
NGFW (Next-Gen Firewall) — adds application awareness (block YouTube regardless of port), IPS, deep packet inspection, user identity, SSL inspection. Most enterprise firewalls today.
IPTABLES BASICS
Linux Built-In Firewall
# View current rules sudo iptables -L -v -n # Allow established connections (critical — add first) sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT # Allow SSH (before blocking everything else!) sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT # Allow web traffic sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT # Drop everything else sudo iptables -A INPUT -j DROP # Modern replacement: nftables / ufw sudo ufw enable sudo ufw allow 22/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp sudo ufw status verbose
DMZ
De-Militarized Zone — Public-Facing Servers
A DMZ is a network segment between the internet and your internal network. Public-facing servers (web servers, mail servers) go in the DMZ. If they're compromised, the attacker is in the DMZ — not directly on your internal network. Two firewalls: one between internet and DMZ, another between DMZ and internal. Defense in depth.
⚖️ Load Balancers & High Availability — Never Go Down NET • Intermediate ▶
THE PROBLEM
One Server = Single Point of Failure
If your entire service runs on one server and it crashes, everyone is down. High availability (HA) architectures spread load across multiple servers so that if one fails, others continue serving traffic seamlessly. HA goal: no single component failure takes down the service.
LOAD BALANCER
Distributes Traffic Across Backend Servers
A load balancer sits in front of your servers and routes each incoming request to one of the backends. Algorithms:
Round-robin — server 1, server 2, server 3, server 1… Even distribution.
Least connections — sends to whichever server has the fewest active connections.
IP hash — same client IP always goes to the same server (sticky sessions).
Weighted — big server gets more traffic than small server.
HEALTH CHECKS
Automatically Remove Failing Servers
A load balancer periodically pings each backend (HTTP GET /health, TCP connect, etc.). If a backend fails N consecutive checks, it's removed from the pool. No human intervention needed — traffic automatically shifts to healthy servers. When it recovers, it re-enters the pool.
ConceptMeaningCommon SLA
High Availability (HA)System stays up despite component failures99.9% = 8.7 hrs/yr downtime
99.99% ("four nines")Enterprise HA target52 min/yr downtime
99.999% ("five nines")Telco/critical systems5.25 min/yr downtime
RTORecovery Time Objective — max acceptable downtimeDefined in DR plan
RPORecovery Point Objective — max acceptable data lossDefined in DR plan
☁️ Cloud Networking — VPC, Subnets & CDNs NET • Cloud ▶
CLOUD MODELS
IaaS · PaaS · SaaS
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — rent VMs, storage, networking. You manage OS and above. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine. Most control, most responsibility.
PaaS (Platform as a Service) — deploy your app code; provider manages OS, runtime, scaling. Examples: Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine.
SaaS (Software as a Service) — use the finished product. Salesforce, Office 365, Gmail. No infrastructure concern at all.
VPC
Virtual Private Cloud — Your Private Network in the Cloud
A VPC is a logically isolated section of the cloud where you launch resources in a network you define. You control IP ranges, subnets, routing tables, and gateways — just like a physical data center, but virtualized.
ComponentPurpose
VPC CIDRIP range for the entire VPC (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16)
SubnetSub-range within VPC; public (internet) or private
Internet GatewayAllows public subnets to reach the internet
NAT GatewayLets private subnets initiate outbound internet; no inbound
Route TableDefines where traffic goes (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW for public)
Security GroupStateful firewall at instance level
NACLStateless firewall at subnet level
CDN
Content Delivery Network — Cache at the Edge
A CDN stores copies of your static content (images, JS, CSS, videos) at servers (PoPs — Points of Presence) close to users worldwide. When a user in Tokyo requests your image, it comes from a Tokyo edge node, not your origin server in Virginia. Result: dramatically lower latency and reduced origin server load. Examples: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai.
SHARED RESPONSIBILITY MODEL
Who Is Responsible for What in Cloud?
AWS/Azure/GCP secure the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, network). You secure in the cloud (your VMs, data, IAM config, encryption, application code). Misconfigurations (public S3 buckets, overly permissive security groups, no encryption) are YOUR responsibility, not the cloud provider's. This is the source of most cloud breaches.
🔍 Network Troubleshooting — A Systematic Approach NET • Practical ▶
OSI TROUBLESHOOTING
Bottom-Up or Top-Down
Two strategies for network problems:
Bottom-up (most common for no-connectivity): Physical (cable/light?) → Data Link (ARP, MAC?) → Network (ping, IP?) → Transport (port open?) → Application (service running?).
Top-down: Start at the application ("the web page is slow") and work down to find where the degradation is.
THE DIAGNOSTIC TOOLKIT
Commands Every Network Person Uses
# Layer 1-2: Physical / Link ip link show # interface status, MAC ethtool eth0 # speed, duplex, link detected # Layer 3: IP connectivity ip addr show # IP addresses ip route show # routing table ping 8.8.8.8 # basic reachability ping -c 4 google.com # DNS + ICMP check # Path tracing traceroute 8.8.8.8 # hops to destination mtr google.com # live traceroute with packet loss # Layer 4: Transport / Ports ss -tlnp # listening TCP ports ss -ulnp # listening UDP ports nc -zv 192.168.1.1 22 # test TCP port connectivity telnet 192.168.1.1 80 # old-school port test # DNS dig google.com # DNS lookup nslookup google.com # Windows/Linux resolvectl query google.com # systemd-resolved
PACKET CAPTURE
See What's Actually on the Wire
# Capture on interface eth0 sudo tcpdump -i eth0 # Capture HTTP traffic sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 -w capture.pcap # Capture DNS queries sudo tcpdump -i any port 53 -n # Show packet contents in ASCII sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A # Read saved capture tcpdump -r capture.pcap
Open .pcap files in Wireshark for graphical analysis. Wireshark's "Follow TCP Stream" shows entire conversations. Filter: http.request, tcp.flags.syn==1, dns, ip.addr==192.168.1.5
COMMON SYMPTOMS
Problem → Most Likely Cause
SymptomCheck First
No connectivity at allIP address assigned? (169.254.x.x = DHCP failed)
Can ping IP, not hostnameDNS — wrong resolver, DHCP giving bad DNS
Can ping gateway, not internetISP issue, default route, firewall blocking outbound
Intermittent packet lossBad cable, duplex mismatch, overloaded link
High latency only to one siteRouting issue, CDN problem, that site's servers
App works internally, not externallyFirewall port not open, NAT not configured
🌐 IPv6 — The Internet's Upgrade NET • Essential ▶
WHY IPv6
IPv4 Ran Out of Addresses
IPv4 has 4.3 billion addresses. That sounds like a lot — until you realize there are 8 billion people, each with multiple devices, plus billions of IoT gadgets. IPv4 officially ran out in 2011. IPv6 solves this with 340 undecillion addresses (3.4 × 10³⁸) — roughly one address per atom on Earth's surface. You'll encounter IPv6 constantly in modern networks.
ADDRESS FORMAT
Reading and Writing IPv6 Addresses
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits separated by colons. Two simplification rules reduce the ugliness.
# Full form — 8 groups of 4 hex digits 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 # Rule 1: Drop leading zeros in each group 2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329 # Rule 2: Replace ONE run of consecutive all-zero groups with :: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329 # :: replaces :0:0:0: # Loopback (equivalent to 127.0.0.1) ::1 # Unspecified address (equivalent to 0.0.0.0) :: # IPv6 in URLs — brackets required to avoid port confusion http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/path
ADDRESS TYPES
IPv6 Address Categories
TypePrefixScopeIPv4 Equivalent
Global Unicast2000::/3Public internet-routablePublic IP
Link-Localfe80::/10This link only (not routed)169.254.x.x (APIPA)
Unique Localfc00::/7Private org networkRFC 1918 (10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x)
Loopback::1/128This device only127.0.0.1
Multicastff00::/8Group of devices224.0.0.0/4
AnycastFrom unicast rangeNearest of a groupNo direct equivalent
KEY DIFFERENCES
IPv6 vs IPv4 — What Changed
FeatureIPv4IPv6
Address size32 bits (~4.3B addresses)128 bits (340 undecillion)
NAT required?Yes (address exhaustion)No (enough for all devices)
Header sizeVariable (20-60 bytes)Fixed (40 bytes) — faster routing
BroadcastYes (network noise)No — replaced by multicast
Auto-configurationNeeds DHCPSLAAC (stateless, no server needed)
IPsecOptionalBuilt into spec
FragmentationRouters can fragmentEnd hosts only (routers don't)
DUAL-STACK & TRANSITION
Running IPv4 and IPv6 Together
Most networks today run dual-stack — both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. When a client connects, it prefers IPv6 (via "Happy Eyeballs" algorithm). This lets networks migrate gradually without a hard cutover.
# Check your IPv6 addresses (Linux) ip -6 addr show # Ping using IPv6 ping6 ::1 # loopback ping6 -I eth0 fe80::1%eth0 # link-local requires interface # Traceroute IPv6 traceroute6 2001:4860:4860::8888 # Google's IPv6 DNS # Check if site has IPv6 (AAAA record) dig AAAA google.com nslookup -type=AAAA google.com # Curl over IPv6 curl -6 https://ipv6.google.com
🔌 Common Protocols — What's Actually Happening on the Wire NET • Reference ▶
APPLICATION LAYER PROTOCOLS
Protocols You'll Use Every Day
ProtocolPortPurposeSecure Version
HTTP80/tcpWeb trafficHTTPS (443)
HTTPS443/tcpEncrypted webAlready secure
DNS53/udp+tcpName resolutionDoH (443), DoT (853)
SSH22/tcpEncrypted remote shellAlready secure
FTP21/tcpFile transfer (insecure)SFTP (22), FTPS (990)
SMTP25/tcpSend email (server-to-server)SMTPS (465/587)
IMAP143/tcpRead email (syncs)IMAPS (993)
POP3110/tcpRead email (downloads)POP3S (995)
SNMP161/udpNetwork device managementSNMPv3
NTP123/udpTime synchronizationNTPsec
RDP3389/tcpWindows remote desktopTLS-wrapped RDP
LDAP389/tcpDirectory services (AD)LDAPS (636)
TCP VS UDP
Choosing the Right Transport Protocol
FeatureTCPUDP
ConnectionConnection-oriented (3-way handshake)Connectionless — fire and forget
ReliabilityGuaranteed delivery, retransmits lost packetsNo guarantee — packets can be lost
OrderingDelivers in orderOut-of-order possible
SpeedSlower (overhead)Faster (minimal overhead)
