Header size20+ bytes8 bytes
🔐 VPNs & Tunneling — Secure Connections Over Untrusted Networks NET • Essential ▶
WHAT A VPN ACTUALLY DOES
An Encrypted Tunnel Through a Hostile Network
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server. Everything inside the tunnel is encrypted, so even on untrusted networks (coffee shop Wi-Fi), nobody can read your traffic. There are two distinct use cases that people confuse:
TypePurposeExample
Remote Access VPNConnect a remote user to a private corporate networkWorking from home, accessing internal apps
Site-to-Site VPNConnect two networks (offices) over the internetBranch office ↔ HQ network
Commercial VPNPrivacy/geo-unblocking for consumersNordVPN, hiding traffic from ISP
VPN PROTOCOLS
How the Tunnel Is Built
ProtocolNotes
WireGuardModern, fast, simple, ~4000 lines of code. Increasingly the default.
OpenVPNMature, flexible, widely supported. SSL/TLS-based.
IPsec/IKEv2Built into most OSes, great for mobile (reconnects fast). Common for site-to-site.
L2TP/IPsecOlder; L2TP provides tunnel, IPsec provides encryption.
PPTPObsolete — broken encryption. Never use.
PROXIES VS VPNs
Related But Different
FeatureProxyVPN
ScopePer-application (e.g., just the browser)Entire device (all traffic)
EncryptionOften none (just relays)Always encrypted
LayerApplication layer (L7)Network layer (L3)
Common useWeb filtering, caching, hiding origin IPSecure remote access, privacy
A forward proxy sits between users and the internet (corporate web filtering). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers (load balancing, TLS termination, hiding backend — e.g., nginx, Cloudflare).
SSH TUNNELING
The Poor Man's VPN
SSH can forward ports through its encrypted connection — a quick way to securely reach services without a full VPN. Essential for accessing internal services through a jump host.
# Local port forward — reach a remote DB through SSH # "Make my localhost:5432 → db.internal:5432 via jumphost" ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@jumphost # Now connect to localhost:5432 → actually hits db.internal # Remote port forward — expose YOUR local service to remote ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 user@remote # remote's :8080 → your local :3000 # Dynamic forward — SOCKS proxy (route browser through SSH) ssh -D 1080 user@jumphost # Set browser SOCKS proxy to localhost:1080 # Jump through a bastion to reach an internal host ssh -J bastion.example.com user@internal-host
ZERO TRUST NETWORK ACCESS
The VPN Replacement
Traditional VPNs give you access to the whole network once connected (overly trusting). Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) flips this: "never trust, always verify." Every request is authenticated and authorized individually, granting access only to specific applications — not the whole network. Tools like Cloudflare Access, Tailscale, and Zscaler implement this. Increasingly replacing legacy VPNs.
🧮 Subnetting — The Math That Scares Beginners (It Shouldn't) NET • Foundation ▶
WHAT IS SUBNETTING
Dividing a Network Into Smaller Networks
An IP address has two parts: a network portion (which network you're on) and a host portion (which specific device). Subnetting is the art of deciding where to draw that line — splitting a big address block into smaller, organized chunks. Why? Security (isolate departments), efficiency (reduce broadcast traffic), and organization. It intimidates beginners, but it's just binary math you can learn in an afternoon.
CIDR NOTATION
The /24 Explained
An IPv4 address is 32 bits. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation like 192.168.1.0/24 means "the first 24 bits are the network portion." The remaining bits (32 − 24 = 8) are for hosts. More network bits = smaller subnet = fewer hosts.
# 192.168.1.0/24 in binary 192.168.1.0 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000 └──────── 24 network bits ────────┘└8 host┘ # The /24 tells you the subnet mask /24 = 255.255.255.0 # (24 ones, then 8 zeros) 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
THE KEY FORMULAS
Hosts and Subnets — Memorize These
# Number of usable hosts per subnet usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2 # (subtract 2: network address + broadcast address) # Example: /24 has 8 host bits 2^8 − 2 = 256 − 2 = 254 usable hosts # Example: /26 has 6 host bits 2^6 − 2 = 64 − 2 = 62 usable hosts # Number of subnets when you "borrow" bits subnets = 2^(borrowed bits)
CIDR CHEAT SHEET
Common Prefixes at a Glance
CIDRSubnet MaskHost BitsUsable HostsBlock Size
/30255.255.255.252224 (point-to-point links)
/29255.255.255.248368
/28255.255.255.24041416
/27255.255.255.22453032
/26255.255.255.19266264
/25255.255.255.1287126128
/24255.255.255.08254256
/23255.255.254.09510512
/16255.255.0.01665,53465,536
WORKED EXAMPLE
Finding Network, Broadcast, and Range
Given an IP and CIDR, here's how to find the key addresses. This is the most common subnetting question on exams and the job.
# Given: 192.168.1.100/26 — what subnet is it in? # Step 1: /26 → block size. Host bits = 32-26 = 6. Block = 2^6 = 64 # Step 2: subnets start at multiples of the block size (64): # 192.168.1.0, .64, .128, .192 # Step 3: .100 falls between .64 and .128 → subnet is .64 Network address: 192.168.1.64 # first address (not usable) First usable host: 192.168.1.65 Last usable host: 192.168.1.126 Broadcast address: 192.168.1.127 # last address (not usable) Next subnet: 192.168.1.128 # Shortcut: "block size" trick — count by 64s. Done.
LET THE COMPUTER DO IT
Tools That Calculate Subnets For You
# Linux: ipcalc shows everything ipcalc 192.168.1.100/26 # Address, Netmask, Network, Broadcast, HostMin, HostMax, Hosts/Net # sipcalc (more detailed) sipcalc 10.0.0.0/22 # Python — the ipaddress module is built in python3 -c "import ipaddress; n=ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.1.0/26'); \ print(n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses)" # Python interactive — useful for automation import ipaddress net = ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.1.0/26') print(net.netmask) # 255.255.255.192 print(list(net.hosts())[0]) # first usable host print(net.num_addresses) # 64
🗺️ Network Design — How Networks Are Structured NET • Foundation ▶
TOPOLOGIES
The Shapes Networks Take
TopologyStructurePros / Cons
StarAll devices connect to a central switch+ Easy to manage; − central point of failure (most common LAN)
MeshDevices interconnect (full or partial)+ Highly redundant; − expensive, complex (used in WANs, Wi-Fi mesh)
BusAll on a single backbone cable− Obsolete; one break kills all
RingEach device connects to two neighborsUsed in some fiber/MAN setups (with redundant ring)
HybridCombination (e.g., star-of-stars)Real-world networks are hybrids
THE THREE-TIER MODEL
How Enterprise Networks Are Layered
Classic enterprise network design uses three hierarchical layers. This separation makes networks scalable, manageable, and resilient.
LayerRoleDevices
AccessWhere end devices connect (PCs, phones, APs)Access switches, wall ports
DistributionAggregates access layer; policy, routing between VLANsL3 switches, routers
CoreHigh-speed backbone; moves traffic fastHigh-capacity core switches/routers
In modern data centers, this is often replaced by a spine-leaf architecture: every leaf (access) switch connects to every spine switch, giving predictable low latency and easy horizontal scaling — ideal for east-west (server-to-server) traffic.
DESIGNING FOR RESILIENCE
No Single Point of Failure
TechniqueWhat It Provides
Redundant links + STPBackup paths; Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops
Link aggregation (LACP)Bundle multiple links for bandwidth + failover
Redundant gateways (HSRP/VRRP)Two routers share a virtual IP; one takes over if the other fails
Dual power supplies / UPSSurvive power failures
Multiple ISPs (multihoming)Survive an internet provider outage
Out-of-band managementManage gear even when the production network is down
QUALITY OF SERVICE
QoS — Not All Traffic Is Equal
When the network is congested, QoS decides what gets priority. A dropped video-call packet is far worse than a delayed email — voice and video are real-time and sensitive to latency/jitter, while file downloads can wait. QoS classifies and prioritizes traffic so critical, time-sensitive flows (VoIP, video conferencing) get served first. Without it, a big backup job could ruin everyone's video calls.
🌍 DNS Deep Dive — Records, Resolution & Security NET • Essential ▶
RECORD TYPES
The DNS Records You'll Actually Touch
RecordMapsExample / Use
AName → IPv4example.com → 93.184.216.34
AAAAName → IPv6example.com → 2606:2800:...
CNAMEName → another name (alias)www → example.com
MXMail servers for a domainRoutes email; has priority values
TXTArbitrary textSPF, DKIM, domain verification
NSAuthoritative nameserversWho's in charge of this zone
SOAZone metadataSerial, refresh, TTL defaults
PTRIP → name (reverse DNS)Mail server reputation, logging
SRVService location (host+port)SIP, LDAP, Microsoft AD
CAAWhich CAs may issue certsPrevents rogue certificate issuance
DIG — THE DNS SWISS ARMY KNIFE
Query DNS Like a Pro
dig example.com # A record (default) dig example.com +short # just the answer dig AAAA example.com # IPv6 dig MX example.com # mail servers dig TXT example.com # SPF/DKIM/verification dig NS example.com # nameservers dig +trace example.com # follow the full resolution path dig @8.8.8.8 example.com # query a specific resolver dig -x 93.184.216.34 # reverse lookup (PTR) dig example.com ANY # all records (often restricted) # Troubleshooting: is it a DNS problem or not? # If dig resolves but the app fails → not DNS # If dig fails → check resolver (/etc/resolv.conf)
DNS SECURITY
DNS Was Not Built Securely
Classic DNS is unauthenticated and unencrypted — attackers can forge responses (cache poisoning, spoofing) or snoop on your lookups. Several technologies address this:
TechProtectsHow
DNSSECIntegrity / authenticityCryptographically signs records — detects forgery (doesn't encrypt)
DoH (DNS over HTTPS)PrivacyEncrypts queries inside HTTPS (port 443)
DoT (DNS over TLS)PrivacyEncrypts DNS in TLS (port 853)
DNS filteringBlockingResolver blocks malicious/known-bad domains (e.g., Pi-hole, Quad9)
DNS-BASED ATTACKS
Why Defenders Watch DNS Closely
AttackWhat It Does
Cache poisoningInject false records so victims go to attacker's site
DNS tunnelingSmuggle data/C2 traffic inside DNS queries (evades firewalls)
Domain hijackingTake over a domain's registration or nameservers
Fast fluxRapidly rotate IPs to keep malicious infra alive
TyposquattingRegister lookalike domains (gooogle.com) for phishing
DNS logs are gold for threat hunting — unusual domains, high-entropy subdomains (tunneling), and newly-registered domains are strong indicators of compromise.
🔀 NAT & Port Forwarding — How Private Networks Reach the Internet NET • Essential ▶
WHY NAT EXISTS
Many Private Devices, One Public IP
There aren't enough IPv4 addresses for every device. NAT (Network Address Translation) lets a whole network of devices with private IPs (192.168.x.x) share a single public IP. Your home router does this: it translates internal addresses to its one public address on the way out, and remembers which internal device each connection belongs to so replies come back correctly.
TYPES OF NAT
Static, Dynamic, and PAT
TypeHow It WorksUse
Static NATOne private IP ↔ one public IP (fixed)Exposing a specific internal server
Dynamic NATPrivate IPs map to a pool of public IPsLess common; needs many public IPs
PAT / NAT overloadMany private IPs → one public IP, distinguished by portThe home router model — by far the most common
PAT (Port Address Translation) is what "NAT" almost always means in practice. The router tracks connections by (internal IP:port ↔ public IP:port) so dozens of devices share one address.
PORT FORWARDING
Letting the Outside Reach In
By default, NAT blocks unsolicited inbound connections (a nice side-effect: a basic firewall). But sometimes you WANT external access to an internal service — a game server, a web server, SSH to your home lab. Port forwarding tells the router: "traffic arriving on public port X → send to internal host:port Y."
# Example port-forward rules on a router Public :443 → 192.168.1.10:443 # web server Public :2222 → 192.168.1.20:22 # SSH to lab box # ⚠️ Security: every forwarded port is exposed to the internet. # Forward only what you must; prefer a VPN for remote access. # Linux iptables DNAT (what routers do under the hood) iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 \ -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.10:443
NAT CHALLENGES
Why Some Apps Struggle Behind NAT
IssueSolution
Two peers both behind NAT (VoIP, P2P, gaming)STUN/TURN/ICE — NAT traversal protocols
App needs a stable inbound portPort forwarding or UPnP (convenient but risky)
Tracking which device did what (logging)CGNAT complicates attribution at ISP scale
Reaching home services remotelyVPN, reverse tunnel, or ZTNA (Tailscale/Cloudflare)
Note: IPv6 largely removes the need for NAT — there are enough addresses for every device to have a public one (with firewalls, not NAT, providing the security boundary).
🚪 802.1X & NAC — Who Gets On the Network? NET • Enterprise ▶
THE PROBLEM
An Open Network Port Is an Open Door
In a basic network, anyone who plugs into a wall jack or knows the Wi-Fi password is on the network. In an enterprise, that's a serious risk — an attacker in the lobby, a rogue device, a compromised laptop. 802.1X and NAC enforce authentication before access: prove who/what you are before the network lets you communicate.
802.1X
Port-Based Authentication
802.1X authenticates a device at the port level before granting network access. It involves three roles working together via the EAP protocol.
RoleWhoJob
SupplicantThe device wanting access (laptop)Provides credentials/certificate
AuthenticatorThe switch or wireless APGatekeeper — blocks traffic until authorized
Authentication ServerRADIUS serverVerifies credentials, says yes/no
Until authentication succeeds, the port only passes authentication traffic — everything else is blocked. Enterprise Wi-Fi (WPA2/3-Enterprise) uses exactly this model, which is why you log in with your own username/password instead of a shared Wi-Fi key.
NAC
Network Access Control — Beyond Just Identity
NAC extends the idea: it doesn't just check who you are, but whether your device is healthy and compliant before allowing full access — and what it's allowed to reach.
NAC CapabilityExample
Posture assessmentIs AV running? OS patched? Disk encrypted?
Quarantine / remediationNon-compliant device → restricted VLAN to fix itself
Role-based accessGuest → internet only; employee → full; IoT → isolated
Dynamic VLAN assignmentPut devices on the right segment automatically
Guest onboardingCaptive portal, sponsored access
RADIUS
The AAA Workhorse
RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the protocol behind most network authentication. It provides AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what may you do?), and Accounting (what did you do? — logging/billing). It centralizes credentials so every switch and AP checks against one source (often tied to Active Directory). TACACS+ is a Cisco-oriented alternative more focused on device administration.
🌐 HTTP — The Protocol That Runs the Web NET • Essential ▶
ANATOMY OF A REQUEST
What Actually Goes Over the Wire
# An HTTP request is plain text (in HTTP/1.1) GET /api/users?page=2 HTTP/1.1 # method, path, version Host: example.com # required header User-Agent: curl/8.0 Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer eyJ... # blank line = end of headers # (body goes here for POST/PUT) # The response HTTP/1.1 200 OK # version, status code, reason Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: 142 {"users": [...]} # body
METHODS (VERBS)
What You Want to Do
MethodPurposeSafe?Idempotent?
GETRetrieve dataYes (no change)Yes
POSTCreate / submitNoNo (repeats create dups)
PUTReplace entirelyNoYes
PATCHPartial updateNoUsually no
DELETERemoveNoYes
HEADLike GET, headers onlyYesYes
OPTIONSAsk what's allowed (CORS preflight)YesYes
Idempotent = doing it twice has the same effect as once. Matters for retries: safely retry a PUT/DELETE, but a retried POST might create duplicates.
STATUS CODES
The Server's Answer, by Category
RangeMeaningCommon Examples
1xxInformational100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols
2xxSuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xxRedirection301 Moved, 304 Not Modified, 307 Temp Redirect
4xxClient error (YOUR fault)400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests
5xxServer error (THEIR fault)500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Timeout
Quick memory aid: 4xx = you messed up (bad request, not allowed); 5xx = the server messed up. 401 = "who are you?" (not authenticated); 403 = "I know who you are, but no" (not authorized).
HTTP VERSIONS
1.1 → 2 → 3
VersionKey ChangeBenefit
HTTP/1.1Text-based, one request at a time per connectionSimple; suffers head-of-line blocking
HTTP/2Binary, multiplexed streams over one connectionMany parallel requests, header compression — faster
HTTP/3Runs over QUIC (UDP) instead of TCPNo TCP head-of-line blocking; faster on lossy/mobile networks
Statelessness: HTTP itself is stateless — each request is independent. "Sessions" are layered on top via cookies/tokens, because the protocol doesn't remember you between requests.
📡 Network Monitoring — Seeing What Flows Through NET • Operations ▶
WHY MONITOR
You Can't Manage What You Can't See
Network monitoring tells you device health, bandwidth use, errors, and unusual traffic — essential for both operations (is the link saturated? is a switch down?) and security (is data being exfiltrated? is there C2 traffic?). Different techniques answer different questions, from device health to per-flow detail.
SNMP
Polling Device Health
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets a monitoring system query devices (switches, routers, servers, printers) for metrics — interface status, CPU, temperature, traffic counters. Devices expose values in a hierarchical database (MIB) addressed by OIDs. Tools like Zabbix, LibreNMS, and PRTG poll via SNMP and graph/alert on the results.
VersionNote
SNMPv1 / v2cUses a plaintext "community string" — insecure; avoid on untrusted networks
SNMPv3Adds authentication + encryption — use this
FLOW DATA
NetFlow / IPFIX / sFlow — Who Talked to Whom
Flow data records metadata about conversations (source/dest IP, ports, protocol, bytes) without capturing full packet contents. It answers "who is talking to whom, how much?" — invaluable for capacity planning, billing, and security (spotting exfiltration, scanning, or C2 beaconing) at scale, far more cheaply than full packet capture.
TechOriginNote
NetFlowCiscoThe original; widely supported
IPFIXIETF standardVendor-neutral "NetFlow v10"
sFlowMulti-vendorPacket sampling, lower overhead
PACKET CAPTURE
The Full Truth on the Wire
When you need to see exactly what was sent — debugging an app, analyzing an attack — capture full packets. tcpdump on the CLI, Wireshark for deep GUI analysis. The most detailed (and storage-heavy) option; usually targeted at a specific problem, not always-on.
# tcpdump basics sudo tcpdump -i eth0 # live capture sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 # filter by port sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.0.5 # filter by host sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # save to file sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' # SYN packets # Then open capture.pcap in Wireshark for deep analysis # Wireshark display filters: http, dns, ip.addr==10.0.0.5, tcp.port==22
Beginner Active Directory & LDAP – Enterprise Identity 101
Core Concept
What Is Active Directory?
Active Directory (AD) is Microsoft's directory service — the central phonebook of every Windows enterprise. It stores users, computers, groups, and policies in a tree of Organizational Units (OUs). When you log in at work, your laptop asks a Domain Controller (DC) to verify your password.

Key vocabulary:
• Domain – a boundary of administration (e.g. corp.example.com).
• Forest – one or more domains that trust each other.
• OU – a folder inside AD used to organise objects.
• GPO – Group Policy Object; rules pushed to computers/users.
• DC – Domain Controller; the server that runs AD.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if you are not the AD admin, do not make changes in AD. Escalate to the team that owns it.
Protocol
LDAP – How Applications Talk to AD
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is the language software uses to query AD. Every object has a Distinguished Name (DN) — a path like a file system path:
CN=Alice Smith,OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com

Common LDAP operations:
• Bind – authenticate (log in) to the directory.
• Search – find objects matching a filter.
• Add / Modify / Delete – manage objects (admin only).

Port 389 = plain LDAP  |  Port 636 = LDAPS (TLS encrypted — always prefer this).
# Query AD with Python ldap3 (read-only example) from ldap3 import Server, Connection, ALL, SUBTREE server = Server('ldaps://dc01.corp.example.com', get_info=ALL) conn = Connection(server, user='corp\svc_readonly', password='S3cur3P@ss!', auto_bind=True) # Find all users in the Finance OU conn.search( search_base='OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com', search_filter='(&(objectClass=user)(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))', search_scope=SUBTREE, attributes=['cn', 'mail', 'department'] ) for entry in conn.entries: print(entry.cn, entry.mail) conn.unbind() # The filter above: objectClass=user AND NOT disabled (bit 2 of UAC)
Authentication
Kerberos in Plain English
Kerberos is the default authentication protocol for AD domains. Think of it as a theme-park wristband system:

1. You show your password once to the Key Distribution Center (KDC) on the DC.
2. The KDC gives you a Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) — your all-day wristband.
3. When you access a resource (file share, web app), you show the TGT to get a Service Ticket — a ride ticket for that specific attraction.
4. The resource trusts the service ticket without ever seeing your password again.

Why this matters for beginners: you never type your password again during the work day — Single Sign-On (SSO). Kerberos tickets expire (default 10 hours), so you may be prompted again next day.
Best Practice
Principle of Least Privilege in AD
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a user needs more permissions than their job requires. In AD:

• Give users standard accounts for daily work.
• Admins use a separate admin account (e.g. a-alice) only when elevated tasks are needed.
• Service accounts get only the groups they need.
• Review group memberships quarterly — "account creep" is real.

The Domain Admins group is the most powerful group in the domain. Its membership list should be tiny and audited constantly.
Beginner Cloud Networking – VPC, Subnets & Security Groups
Core Concept
What Is a VPC?
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your own private network inside a cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP). Think of it as renting a section of a data centre and installing your own private network switches — except it's all software.

Key building blocks:
• VPC – the outer boundary; you choose the IP range (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16 = ~65 000 addresses).
• Subnet – a slice of the VPC in one availability zone. Public subnets reach the internet; private subnets do not.
• Internet Gateway (IGW) – the door between your VPC and the public internet.
• NAT Gateway – lets private-subnet resources make outbound internet calls without being reachable from outside.
• Route Table – rules that decide where packets go (like a router's routing table).
• Security Group – a stateful firewall attached to an individual resource (VM, load balancer).

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a cloud resource is private just because it's in a VPC. Check security groups AND network ACLs; both must permit the traffic.
AWS Example
Building a VPC with AWS CLI
AWS CLI lets you build the entire network from the command line. This is the same thing the console does behind the scenes.
# Create a VPC aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text # Output: vpc-0abc1234def567890 # Create a public subnet (AZ us-east-1a) aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a # Create a private subnet aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a # Attach an internet gateway aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id igw-0xyz --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 # Security group: allow SSH from your IP only aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name web-sg --description "Web server SG" --vpc-id vpc-0abc1234def567890 aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0xyz --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.5/32 # your IP only!
Best Practice
The Shared Responsibility Model
Cloud providers operate a Shared Responsibility Model: the provider secures the infrastructure of the cloud; you secure everything in the cloud.

AWS/Azure/GCP handles: Physical data centres, hypervisor security, global network, managed service patches.

You handle: VM OS patches, security group rules, S3 bucket permissions, IAM roles, encryption of your data, application code security.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" only applies to the provider's layer. Misconfigured S3 buckets, open security groups, and leaked IAM keys are 100 % your responsibility. Most cloud breaches are misconfiguration, not a failure by the provider.
Beginner DNS Deep-Dive – How Domain Names Actually Work
Core Concept
The DNS Resolution Walk
When you type www.example.com in a browser, this is what happens before the first byte of the page arrives:

1. Browser checks its local cache — did we look this up recently?
2. OS checks /etc/hosts (or Windows Hosts file) — manual overrides.
3. OS asks the Recursive Resolver (usually your router or ISP, or 8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1).
4. Resolver asks a Root Name Server (.): "Who handles .com?"
5. Root refers to the .com TLD server: "Ask ns1.example.com."
6. Resolver asks ns1.example.com: "What's the IP for www?"
7. Authoritative answer returned: 93.184.216.34.
8. Resolver caches the result for the TTL; returns it to your browser.

Total time: usually 10–100 ms. Cached lookups: <1 ms.
Record Types
DNS Record Types You Must Know
DNS stores different information in different record types:
Record Purpose Example A IPv4 address www A 93.184.216.34 AAAA IPv6 address www AAAA 2606:2800::1 CNAME Alias to another name blog CNAME myapp.netlify.app. MX Mail server (+ priority) @ MX 10 mail.example.com. TXT Arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM) @ TXT "v=spf1 include:..." NS Authoritative name servers @ NS ns1.example.com. PTR Reverse lookup (IP → name) 34.216.184.93.in-addr.arpa PTR www.example.com. SOA Zone metadata (serial, TTL) Start of Authority record SRV Service location _sip._tcp SRV 10 5 5060 sip.example.com. # Query DNS with dig dig www.example.com A # IPv4 dig www.example.com AAAA # IPv6 dig example.com MX # mail servers dig example.com TXT # SPF / DKIM / verification tokens dig -x 93.184.216.34 # reverse lookup (PTR) dig @8.8.8.8 www.example.com # use Google's resolver dig +trace www.example.com # walk the full resolution chain
Security
DNS Security – DNSSEC, DoH, DNS Attacks
DNS was designed in the 1980s with no security. Several attacks exploit this:

DNS Cache Poisoning — attacker injects a false record into a resolver's cache so users get sent to the wrong IP.
Fix: DNSSEC — cryptographic signatures on DNS records.

DNS Hijacking — malware or rogue ISP changes the resolver you use.
Fix: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT) — encrypts queries so no one can tamper in transit.

DNS Tunnelling — attacker encodes data inside DNS queries to exfiltrate data or establish C2 (bypasses firewalls).
Fix: Monitor for unusually long query names, high query volume per host, rare TLDs.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume DNS responses are authentic unless DNSSEC is validated end-to-end.
# Check if a domain has DNSSEC enabled dig example.com DNSKEY +short dig example.com DS +short # Test DNS-over-HTTPS (Cloudflare DoH) curl -sH "accept: application/dns-json" "https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A" | python3 -m json.tool # Detect suspicious long DNS names (potential tunnelling) # In tcpdump: capture DNS on port 53 sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w dns.pcap port 53 # Then grep for names longer than 50 chars tshark -r dns.pcap -T fields -e dns.qry.name | awk 'length > 50' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Operations
Managing DNS Zones
Whether you use Route 53, Cloudflare, or BIND on-prem, the concepts are the same. Best practices:

• Set low TTLs (e.g. 300 s) before planned changes; restore high TTLs (3600+) after.
• Always have at least two NS servers in different locations for redundancy.
• Use split-horizon DNS — internal names resolve to private IPs; external names resolve to public IPs.
• Add SPF, DKIM, DMARC TXT records for every domain that sends email to prevent spoofing.
• You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when a TTL-expired stale record sends users to a dead IP, reduce TTL proactively next time.
Beginner Wireless Security – 802.11 Standards & Wi-Fi Hardening
Core Concept
Wi-Fi Security Evolution: WEP → WPA3
Wi-Fi security has gone through several generations. Knowing the history helps you understand why old protocols are dangerous:

ProtocolYearEncryptionStatus
WEP1997RC4 (broken)Never use
WPA (TKIP)2003RC4 improvedAvoid
WPA2-Personal2004AES-CCMPOK with strong passphrase
WPA2-Enterprise2004AES + 802.1X/RADIUSRecommended for orgs
WPA3-Personal2018AES + SAEBest for home/small biz
WPA3-Enterprise2018AES-256 + SAEBest for enterprise

WPA2-Personal weakness: offline dictionary attacks against the 4-way handshake. A weak passphrase = cracked in hours.
WPA3 fix: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) prevents offline cracking — each authentication is unique.
Enterprise Wi-Fi
WPA2-Enterprise with RADIUS
In corporate environments, each user authenticates with their own AD credentials rather than a shared passphrase. This uses 802.1X and a RADIUS server (FreeRADIUS or Windows NPS).

Benefits:
• No shared secret to leak — each user has unique creds.
• Revoke a single user's access without changing the Wi-Fi password for everyone.
• Full audit trail of who connected when.
• Mutual authentication via certificates prevents evil-twin attacks.
# FreeRADIUS quick test (after setup) radtest alice Password1 localhost 0 testing123 # Output: Access-Accept → credentials valid # Output: Access-Reject → bad credentials ── Key 802.1X flow ────────────────────────────────────────── Client (Supplicant) → AP (Authenticator) → RADIUS Server EAP-Request/Identity <────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── EAP-Response/Identity (alice@corp.com) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────> RADIUS Access-Request (forwarded) ──────────────────────────────> RADIUS Access-Accept / Reject <────────────────────────────── EAP-Success / Failure <────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── [4-way handshake to derive per-session keys]
Attacks
Common Wi-Fi Attacks & Defences
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume the Wi-Fi network you're on is the real one. Rogue APs can be set up in minutes.
Attack Description Defence Evil Twin Fake AP with same SSID captures creds WPA3/EAP-TLS cert auth Deauth flood Force clients to reconnect (DOS) 802.11w Management Frame Protection PMKID attack Capture beacon, crack offline Long random WPA2 passphrase KRACK Key reinstallation in WPA2 handshake Patch all clients and APs WPS PIN bruteforce 8-digit PIN cracked in hours Disable WPS entirely # Check if a Linux NIC supports monitor mode iw list | grep -A5 "Supported interface modes" # Must show "monitor" mode for wireless analysis tools # Detect rogue APs on your network (passive scan) sudo iwlist wlan0 scanning | grep -E "(ESSID|Address|Encryption)" # Compare BSSID (MAC) list against your authorised AP inventory # Check if WPS is enabled (vulnerable) sudo wash -i wlan0 -C # part of reaver suite; scan for WPS-enabled APs
Hardening
Wi-Fi Network Design Best Practices
• Use WPA3 where supported; WPA2-Enterprise for corporate devices.
• Separate SSIDs for different trust levels: Corp, Guest, IoT — each on its own VLAN.
• Guest SSID: internet-only; no access to internal resources.
• Disable SSID broadcast only adds minor friction — determined attackers still find hidden SSIDs. Don't rely on it for security.
• Enable 802.11w (Management Frame Protection) to block deauthentication attacks.
• Use a long, random passphrase (>20 chars) for WPA2-Personal — mix upper/lower/digit/symbol.
• Audit connected clients quarterly; disable MAC addresses that no longer belong to active employees/devices.
• You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when an employee connects a personal rogue AP, your WIDS (Wireless IDS) catches it; have a process to contain it quickly.
Beginner Packet Analysis – Reading the Network's Mind with Wireshark
Core Concept
Why Capture Packets?
Every problem on a network eventually shows up in the packets — slow apps, failed connections, intrusions, misconfigurations. A packet capture (pcap) is ground truth: it shows exactly what was sent and received, byte for byte.

Tools:
• tcpdump — command-line capture; runs anywhere, even on headless servers.
• Wireshark — GUI analysis; the gold standard for deep inspection.
• tshark — Wireshark's CLI sibling; great for scripting and automation.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — capturing traffic on a network you don't own or have authorization for is illegal in most jurisdictions (wiretapping laws). Always get written authorization.
Capture
Capturing Traffic with tcpdump
tcpdump uses Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax to select exactly the traffic you care about — capturing everything creates huge files and noise.
# Capture all traffic on eth0, write to a file (analyse later in Wireshark) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap # Capture only HTTP traffic (port 80) with full packet content sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w http.pcap port 80 # Capture traffic to/from a specific host sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.50 # Capture traffic between two hosts on a specific port sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'host 192.168.1.50 and host 192.168.1.10 and port 443' # Show packets live, with readable ASCII (good for HTTP debugging) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80 # Capture only SYN packets (new connection attempts — good for scan detection) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn' # Rotate captures every 100MB, keep last 10 files (long-running capture) sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /data/cap.pcap -C 100 -W 10
Analysis
Reading a Capture in Wireshark
Wireshark's display filter bar (top of the window) is the most powerful tool — it narrows thousands of packets down to the handful you care about.
─── Useful Wireshark display filters ───────────────────────── ip.addr == 192.168.1.50 # traffic to/from this host tcp.port == 443 # HTTPS traffic http.request.method == "POST" # only POST requests http contains "password" # find plaintext passwords (HTTP only!) tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 # new connections (SYN scan) tcp.analysis.retransmission # packets that had to be resent (perf issue) dns.qry.name contains "evil" # suspicious DNS lookups tls.handshake.extensions_server_name == "example.com" # TLS SNI filter ─── Right-click any packet → Follow → TCP Stream ───────────── # Reconstructs the entire conversation as readable text — # the single most useful feature for understanding "what happened" ─── Statistics menu ─────────────────────────────────────────── # Conversations: who talked to whom, how much data # Protocol Hierarchy: breakdown of traffic by protocol # IO Graph: visualise traffic volume over time (spot spikes)
tshark
Scripting Analysis with tshark
For repeatable analysis or processing huge captures, script it with tshark instead of clicking through the GUI.
# Extract all unique source/destination IP pairs tshark -r capture.pcap -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst | sort -u # Count HTTP requests by destination host tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http.request" -T fields -e http.host | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # Extract all DNS queries (great for spotting C2 domains) tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name # Find the top talkers by byte volume tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip | head -20 # Extract files transferred over HTTP (incident response) tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,/tmp/extracted_files/
Beginner

DNS Deep Dive – How Name Resolution Really Works

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

When a website "won't load," don't assume it's the web server. DNS failures look identical to outages from the user's perspective. Walking the resolution chain step by step — instead of guessing — is what separates a five-minute fix from an hour of chasing the wrong problem.

Concept

The resolution chain, in order

When you type example.com into a browser, your computer doesn't magically know where to send the request. It walks a chain of lookups:

StepWhat happensWhere it's checked
1. Browser cache"Have I looked this up in the last few minutes?"Browser memory
2. OS cache"Does the operating system already know this?"systemd-resolved / dnsmasq / Windows DNS Client
3. Hosts file"Is there a manual override?"/etc/hosts or C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
4. Recursive resolver"Ask my configured DNS server (ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) to find it"/etc/resolv.conf
5. Root → TLD → authoritativeThe resolver walks the DNS hierarchy until it finds the authoritative answerGlobal DNS infrastructure

Most "the website is down" tickets are solved at step 2 or 3 — a stale cache entry or a leftover hosts file edit from testing months ago.

Hands-on

Tracing resolution yourself

# See which resolver your system is configured to use
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Look up a name and show the full trip — timing included
dig example.com

# Trace the entire chain from the root servers down (educational, slower)
dig +trace example.com

# Ask a *specific* DNS server directly, bypassing your default resolver
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com

# Check what record types exist — A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail), TXT, CNAME
dig example.com MX
dig example.com TXT

# Reverse lookup: what name does this IP resolve back to?
dig -x 93.184.216.34

The +trace flag is especially good for learning — it shows the actual hierarchy: your resolver asks a root server "who handles .com?", then asks that TLD server "who handles example.com?", then finally asks the authoritative server for the actual IP.

Common pitfall

"It works on my machine" — DNS cache edition

A classic scenario: a developer changes a DNS record, tells you "it's updated," and your browser still shows the old site. Both of you are right — the record changed at the authoritative server, but your resolver cached the old answer for its full TTL (time-to-live). Common fixes, in order of how invasive they are:

# Flush just your local OS resolver cache (Linux with systemd-resolved)
sudo resolvectl flush-caches

# macOS
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder

# Windows (run as administrator)
ipconfig /flushdns

# Or simply query a different resolver to sanity-check the *real* current value
dig @8.8.8.8 example.com +short

If a record was just changed, remember that TTL still applies globally — other people's resolvers around the world will keep serving the cached answer until their TTL expires too. This is why planned DNS cutovers lower the TTL days in advance.

Beginner

VPNs Explained – Tunnels, Encryption, and What They Don't Do

Concept

A VPN is a private tunnel through a public road

Imagine the internet as a public highway system — anyone running the right equipment at the right point could, in theory, see which trucks are going where. A VPN (Virtual Private Network) builds an encrypted tunnel through that highway: your traffic still travels over the same public infrastructure, but it's wrapped in a layer that hides its contents from anyone watching the road, and makes it appear to originate from the tunnel's far end rather than your actual location.

Concept

Two very different reasons people use VPNs

Use caseWhat it actually doesCommon protocols
Corporate / remote-access VPNLets an employee's laptop join the company's internal network from anywhere, as if it were plugged in at the officeWireGuard, OpenVPN, IPsec/IKEv2, Cisco AnyConnect
Consumer / privacy VPNRoutes your traffic through a third-party provider's server so your ISP and local network can't see *what* you're accessing — though the VPN provider now canWireGuard, OpenVPN (commercial offerings)

These solve different problems for different threat models. A corporate VPN exists so IT can extend a trusted network boundary to remote workers; a consumer VPN exists to shift *who* has visibility into your traffic — from your ISP to the VPN provider — which is a meaningfully different guarantee than "no one can see what I do online."

Hands-on

Setting up a minimal WireGuard tunnel (lab environment)

# Install WireGuard (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo apt install wireguard

# Generate a public/private keypair for this peer
wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey

# Minimal config: /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf
# (replace placeholders with real keys and addresses)
#
# [Interface]
# PrivateKey = <this peer's private key>
# Address = 10.10.0.2/24
#
# [Peer]
# PublicKey = <remote peer's public key>
# Endpoint = vpn.example.com:51820
# AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0
# PersistentKeepalive = 25

# Bring the tunnel up and check its status
sudo wg-quick up wg0
sudo wg show

# Confirm your traffic is actually routing through the tunnel
curl https://ifconfig.me

The AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 line is the one to read carefully — it tells the system to route all traffic through the tunnel ("full tunnel"), versus a narrower range that only sends specific destinations through it ("split tunnel"). Getting this wrong is one of the most common VPN misconfigurations: too broad and you may break local network access; too narrow and traffic you meant to protect goes out in the clear.

Common pitfall

"I'm on a VPN, so I'm anonymous" — assume makes an ass out of you and me

A VPN hides your traffic's path and contents from your local network and ISP — it does not make you anonymous to the websites you visit. You can still be tracked through cookies, browser fingerprinting, account logins, and the VPN provider itself can see (and in some jurisdictions, may be compelled to log and disclose) your activity. Treat "I'm using a VPN" as one layer of a privacy strategy, not a magic cloak — and always read a provider's actual logging policy rather than assuming "no logs" means what it sounds like.

Beginner

Subnetting Without the Headache – CIDR Notation Made Practical

Concept

A subnet is just "how big is this neighborhood?"

An IP address tells you a device's location; a subnet mask tells you how many of its neighbors share the same local "neighborhood" — the group of addresses that can talk to each other directly, without going through a router. CIDR notation (/24, /26, etc.) is just a compact way of writing that mask: the number after the slash tells you how many bits are reserved for identifying the network itself, leaving the rest for individual hosts.

Concept

The CIDR cheat sheet beginners actually reach for

CIDRSubnet maskUsable hostsCommon use
/24255.255.255.0254Typical small office or home network
/25255.255.255.128126Splitting a /24 in half — two departments, one building
/26255.255.255.19262A single floor or smaller team
/27255.255.255.22430A small lab, a rack of servers, a point-to-point link group
/30255.255.255.2522A direct link between two routers — exactly enough for both ends

Notice the pattern: every step from /24 toward /32 cuts the available addresses roughly in half. "Usable hosts" is two less than the raw count — one address is reserved to identify the network itself, and one is reserved as the broadcast address that reaches every device in that subnet at once.

Hands-on

Let the tools do the arithmetic — verify, don't memorize

# pip install — actually it's built into Python's standard library!
import ipaddress

network = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.10.0/26")
print(f"Network address:   {network.network_address}")
print(f"Broadcast address: {network.broadcast_address}")
print(f"Usable hosts:      {network.num_addresses - 2}")
print(f"First usable host: {list(network.hosts())[0]}")
print(f"Last usable host:  {list(network.hosts())[-1]}")

# Quick check: is this address inside that subnet?
ip = ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.10.40")
print(f"{ip} in {network}? {ip in network}")

# Splitting a network into smaller subnets — handy for planning
# departmental allocations from a single block you've been given
for sub in network.subnets(new_prefix=28):
    print(f"  Sub-block: {sub}")

This is the honest secret of subnetting: nobody who works with networks daily does the binary math by hand every time. They've internalized the cheat-sheet patterns for common cases, and they reach for a calculator (or ipaddress, or ipcalc on the command line) to double-check anything unusual. Knowing how it works conceptually — and knowing how to verify it — beats memorizing tables you'll forget under pressure.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

"That device should be able to reach the server, they're both on the 192.168.x.x range" is a classic trap — two addresses can look similar and still be in completely different subnets, unable to communicate without a router between them. Before troubleshooting further up the stack, verify the actual subnet boundaries with a tool like the one above rather than eyeballing the addresses and assuming they're neighbors.

Beginner

Load Balancers Explained – Spreading the Work Around

Concept

A load balancer is a traffic cop for your servers

A load balancer sits in front of a group of servers and decides which one should handle each incoming request — spreading the work around so no single server gets overwhelmed, and so the service keeps running even if one server fails. From the outside, users see a single address; behind that address, the load balancer quietly routes them to whichever healthy server makes the most sense at that moment.

Concept

Common balancing strategies, and when each shines

StrategyHow it decidesGood fit when...
Round robinCycles through servers in order: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3...All servers are roughly equal in capacity and requests are roughly equal in cost
Least connectionsSends the next request to whichever server currently has the fewest active connectionsRequests vary significantly in how long they take to process
IP hashRoutes based on a hash of the client's IP — the same client tends to land on the same serverYou need "session stickiness" without a shared session store
WeightedSome servers get proportionally more traffic than others, based on assigned weightsYour servers have meaningfully different capacities (a newer, beefier box vs. an older one)
Concept

The unsung hero: health checks

A load balancer is only as good as its ability to know which servers are actually healthy. It periodically polls each server — often hitting a dedicated /healthz endpoint — and silently stops sending traffic to any server that fails to respond correctly. This is the mechanism that turns "one server crashed" from a customer-facing outage into a non-event nobody outside the on-call team ever notices.

# A minimal health endpoint, the kind a load balancer polls every few seconds
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/healthz")
def health_check():
    checks = {
        "database": database_is_reachable(),
        "cache": cache_is_reachable(),
        "disk_space_ok": get_free_disk_percent() > 10,
    }
    healthy = all(checks.values())
    status_code = 200 if healthy else 503
    return jsonify(checks), status_code

# A load balancer that sees repeated 503s here will quietly stop
# routing traffic to this instance — without a single human noticing,
# until someone reviews the dashboards and finds the graceful save
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

A health check that only verifies "is the web server process running?" can report "healthy" while the actual database connection behind it is completely down — leaving users staring at error pages from a server the load balancer confidently considers fine. A good health check verifies the things that actually matter to the user's experience, not just the easiest thing to check. "The process is running" and "the service actually works" are two different claims — don't let your monitoring assume they're the same.

Beginner

The TLS Handshake – What Actually Happens Before "https://" Feels Safe

Concept

The padlock icon represents a surprisingly elegant negotiation

Every time you load an HTTPS site, your browser and the server perform a rapid multi-step negotiation called the TLS handshake — establishing trust and agreeing on encryption, all before a single byte of your actual page content is transmitted. It happens in well under a second, which is part of why it's so easy to never think about. Understanding the broad strokes demystifies a huge portion of "how the secure web works."

Concept

The handshake in (roughly) five steps

StepWhat happens
1. Client HelloYour browser says hello and lists the encryption methods ("cipher suites") it supports, plus a random number used later in key generation.
2. Server Hello + CertificateThe server picks a cipher suite both sides support and sends back its digital certificate — proof of identity issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA).
3. Certificate verificationYour browser checks that the certificate is valid, unexpired, matches the domain you're visiting, and was signed by a CA it trusts. This is the step that turns a green padlock into something meaningful rather than decorative.
4. Key exchangeBoth sides use cryptographic math (often Diffie-Hellman) to agree on a shared session key — without ever transmitting that key in a form an eavesdropper could use.
5. Secure session beginsFrom here on, all traffic is encrypted with the session key using fast symmetric encryption — the certificate-based "slow" cryptography has done its job and steps aside.
Concept

Inspecting a real certificate from the command line

You don't need special tools to see this in action — openssl can show you exactly what your browser is silently checking on every visit:

# Connect and dump the certificate chain for a domain:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text

# Useful fields to look for in the output:
#   Issuer:        which Certificate Authority vouched for this site
#   Subject:       the domain(s) the certificate is valid for
#   Validity:      the "Not Before" / "Not After" window -- expired
#                  certificates are a surprisingly common outage cause
#   Signature Algorithm:  the cryptographic method used to sign it
Concept

Why "the padlock is green" isn't the same as "this site is trustworthy"

This is a critical distinction that "assume makes an ass out of you and me" captures perfectly. TLS guarantees two specific things: that your connection to the server is encrypted in transit, and that the certificate matches the domain you typed. It guarantees nothing whatsoever about whether the organization running that domain is honest, competent, or safe to hand your data to. Attackers can — and routinely do — obtain valid certificates for convincingly-misspelled lookalike domains. The padlock confirms "this connection isn't being eavesdropped on right now." It does not confirm "you should trust what's on the other end of it." Those are two different questions, and conflating them is one of the most common (and most exploited) assumptions on the web.

🗺️ BGP — How the Internet Routes Between Networks Routing ▶
Concept
The Protocol That Glues the Internet Together
Protocols like OSPF route inside one organization. But the internet is ~75,000 independent networks (ISPs, clouds, universities) that must agree on how to reach each other. BGP — the Border Gateway Protocol — is how they do it. Each network is an Autonomous System (AS) with a number, and BGP is how ASes advertise which IP ranges they can reach and learn routes to everywhere else. It's the internet's routing table, assembled by agreement rather than central control.
Reference
Key Terms
TermMeaning
Autonomous System (AS)A network under one administrative control, identified by an ASN (e.g. AS15169 = Google).
PrefixAn advertised IP range, e.g. 8.8.8.0/24.
PeeringTwo ASes agree to exchange traffic directly (often settlement-free).
TransitPaying a larger ISP to reach the rest of the internet.
AS_PATHThe list of ASes a route passes through — used to pick paths and prevent loops.
eBGP / iBGPBGP between different ASes / within one AS.
How It Chooses
Path Selection & Why It's Different
BGP is a path-vector protocol: it doesn't pick the route with the least latency or fewest hops the way an interior protocol might — it picks based on policy. Operators tune attributes to prefer cheaper or contractually-preferred paths.
Attribute (in order)Effect
Local PreferenceHighest wins — an AS's own preference for outbound paths.
AS_PATH lengthShorter path preferred (fewer ASes to cross).
MEDA hint to a neighbor about which entry point to prefer.
Fragility
When BGP Goes Wrong
BGP largely runs on trust, which is also its weakness. A route hijack — an AS advertising prefixes it doesn't own — can silently reroute or black-hole traffic (it has taken down large chunks of the internet, sometimes by accident via a route leak, a misconfigured advertisement). Defenses: RPKI (cryptographically validates who may originate a prefix) and prefix filtering between peers. This fragility is why a single fat-fingered BGP change at a big provider can make headlines.
🚦 QoS — Quality of Service & Traffic Shaping Networking ▶
Concept
Not All Packets Are Equal
When a link gets congested, something has to give. Without Quality of Service, the network drops packets indiscriminately — and a big file download can wreck a video call sharing the same pipe. QoS lets you classify traffic and give the time-sensitive kinds (voice, video, gaming) priority over the ones that don't care about a little delay (backups, email, updates). It manages a scarce resource — bandwidth — by policy instead of first-come-first-served.
Reference
The Four Things QoS Manages
MetricWhat It IsHurts…
BandwidthThroughput availableLarge transfers
LatencyDelay end to endVoice, gaming, trading
JitterVariation in latencyReal-time audio/video (choppy calls)
LossPackets droppedEverything; voice can't retransmit
Voice/video care most about jitter and loss; bulk data cares only about eventual bandwidth. QoS trades one for the other on purpose.
How It Works
Classify → Mark → Queue → Shape
StepWhat Happens
ClassificationIdentify traffic by port, app, or existing marking.
MarkingStamp a priority in the packet header — DSCP (6 bits in the IP header) is the standard. EF = Expedited Forwarding for voice.
QueuingHigh-priority marks go into faster queues; routers service them first.
Shaping vs PolicingShaping buffers excess traffic to smooth it; policing just drops it over a limit.
Practical
Where You Meet QoS
QoS only helps on links you control — your router, your WAN, an enterprise LAN — because markings are honored within an administrative domain and often reset at the public internet boundary (the internet is best-effort; your DSCP tags mean nothing to your ISP unless you buy an SLA). Classic uses: prioritizing VoIP on an office network, keeping a video call smooth on a home router, and guaranteeing latency-sensitive traffic across an MPLS or SD-WAN link.
🚀 HTTP/2, HTTP/3 & QUIC — Modern Web Transport Networking ▶
Concept
Making the Web Fast, One Protocol at a Time
HTTP/1.1 (1997) sends one request at a time per connection and in plain text — browsers opened 6+ connections per site just to keep up. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep the same familiar HTTP semantics (methods, headers, status codes) but completely rework how bytes move on the wire to kill latency. Same API, radically faster transport.
Reference
Three Generations
HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3
TransportTCPTCPQUIC (over UDP)
FormatTextBinaryBinary
MultiplexingNo (1 at a time)Yes (many streams)Yes
Header compressionNoneHPACKQPACK
Head-of-line blockPer requestAt TCP layerSolved
Key Ideas
Multiplexing & Head-of-Line Blocking
HTTP/2's big win is multiplexing: many requests share one connection as independent "streams," so a slow response doesn't block the others at the HTTP layer. But they still ride one TCP connection — and if a single TCP packet is lost, TCP stalls all streams until it's retransmitted. That's head-of-line blocking at the transport layer, HTTP/2's remaining weakness.
The Leap
Why HTTP/3 Ditched TCP for QUIC
QUIC featureBenefit
Runs on UDPStreams are independent — one lost packet only stalls its own stream, not all of them.
TLS 1.3 built inEncryption isn't optional; the handshake is baked into the transport.
Faster handshakes0-RTT / 1-RTT connection setup vs TCP+TLS's multiple round trips.
Connection migrationA connection ID (not IP:port) means switching Wi-Fi → cellular doesn't drop the connection.
Because QUIC lives in user space (not the OS kernel like TCP), it evolves faster. The trade-off: some middleboxes/firewalls throttle or block UDP, so clients fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP when needed.
🕰️ NTP & Time Synchronization — Why Clocks Matter Networking ▶
Concept
A Few Seconds of Drift Breaks Surprising Things
Every computer has a cheap quartz clock that drifts — seconds per day. On one laptop that's harmless; across a fleet it's a disaster. The Network Time Protocol keeps machines synchronized to within milliseconds of a reference time by measuring the round-trip delay to time servers and correcting for it. It's invisible infrastructure — until a clock is wrong and logins fail, logs won't correlate, and TLS certificates appear "not yet valid."
Why It Matters
What Breaks When Clocks Disagree
SystemFailure With Bad Time
TLS / certificatesCerts have valid-from/valid-to windows; a skewed clock rejects good certs (or trusts expired ones).
Kerberos / AD authTickets are time-stamped; default tolerance is ~5 minutes — beyond that, logins fail.
MFA / TOTP codesTime-based one-time codes rotate every 30s; a wrong clock rejects valid codes.
Log correlationInvestigating an incident across servers is impossible if their timestamps don't line up.
Databases / distributed systemsOrdering, leases, and conflict resolution can misbehave with clock skew.
Reference
Stratum — The Hierarchy of Trust
StratumSource
0Reference clock — atomic clock, GPS. Not on the network itself.
1Servers directly attached to a stratum-0 source.
2, 3, …Sync from the stratum above; the number grows with distance from the source.
Most machines sync from public pools (pool.ntp.org) or an internal server. Best practice: point your fleet at a couple of internal NTP servers that themselves sync upstream — consistent time, less external dependence.
Commands
Checking Time Sync (Linux)
timedatectl                    # is NTP active & synchronized?
timedatectl show-timesync      # current server & poll interval
chronyc tracking              # chrony: offset, drift, stratum
chronyc sources -v            # which servers, how reachable
ntpq -p                       # classic ntpd: peer list & offsets
Modern Linux uses chrony or systemd-timesyncd; both slew the clock gradually rather than jumping it, so time never runs backward. Always store and compare time in UTC — convert to local only for display.
🚪 Reverse Proxies — nginx, HAProxy & the Front Door Networking ▶
Concept
One Front Door for Many Back-End Services
A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers and receives every client request first, then forwards it to the right back-end. (A forward proxy sits in front of clients; a reverse proxy fronts servers — hence the name.) It's the single front door where you centralize TLS, routing, caching, and protection — so your application servers can stay simple and private.
Reference
What a Reverse Proxy Does For You
JobWhat It Means
TLS terminationHandles HTTPS/certs at the edge; talks plain HTTP to back-ends, so they don't each manage certs.
Load balancingSpreads requests across multiple back-end instances.
RoutingSends /api to one service and / to another by path or hostname.
Caching & compressionServes cached/gzipped responses without hitting the app.
ProtectionRate limiting, request filtering, hiding back-end topology.
Static filesServes assets directly, freeing the app for dynamic work.
Example
A Minimal nginx Reverse Proxy
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name app.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/app.crt;   # TLS ends here
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/app.key;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;  # forward to the app
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;  # keep client IP
    }

    location / {
        root /var/www/site;             # serve static files
    }
}
Reference
The Common Tools
ToolStrength
nginxWeb server + reverse proxy + static + cache. The default workhorse.
HAProxyPurpose-built, high-performance TCP/HTTP load balancer with deep health-check & metrics support.
CaddyAutomatic HTTPS (Let's Encrypt out of the box); simplest config.
Envoy / TraefikCloud-native, dynamic config; common as Kubernetes ingress and service-mesh proxies.
The X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP headers matter: once a proxy is in the path, the back-end sees the proxy's IP unless the proxy passes the real client IP along in these headers.

Sec+ SecX
CIA Triad · AAA · Access Control · PKI · Crypto · Cloud · Zero Trust · Kerberos ▾
🔐 CIA Triad CORE MODEL ▶
Foundational Model
Confidentiality · Integrity · Availability
Every security control maps to one or more CIA pillars. The attacker's mirror is the DAD Triad: Disclosure · Alteration · Destruction/Denial.
🔒
Confidentiality

🔓 Password & Authentication Attack Types ATTACK TAXONOMY ▶
Framework — Source: CEH Cheat Sheet
Online · Offline · Non-Electronic · Sidejacking
Password attacks are categorized by whether an attacker interacts with a live system. CompTIA password policy: Minimum 3 of 4 complexity components — Special, Number, Uppercase, Lowercase.
Attack Type Method Example Tools
Passive Online Sniff wire, intercept cleartext passwords, replay attacks, MITM Wireshark, Ettercap, Responder
Active Online Direct password guessing against live system; credential stuffing Hydra, Medusa, Burp Suite
Offline Steal copy of hash file (e.g., SAM), crack on separate system Hashcat, John the Ripper, Rainbow Crack
Non-Electronic Social engineering, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving —
▸ HASH CRACKING METHODS
Method Description Defense
Brute-Force Try every character combination systematically Long passwords, account lockout
Dictionary Try wordlist of probable passwords Avoid common words; enforce complexity
Rainbow Tables Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables Salt hashes (bcrypt/Argon2)
Credential Stuffing Reuse breached username:password pairs Unique passwords, MFA
Password Spray Try one common password across many accounts Lockout policies, MFA
Pass-the-Hash (PtH) Use stolen NTLM hash without cracking it Credential Guard, least privilege
▸ SIDEJACKING / SESSION HIJACKING
1 — Sniff Traffic
Capture packets between client and server (requires same network or MITM position)
2 — Monitor & Predict
Monitor traffic flow; predict sequence numbers or steal session tokens/cookies
3 — Desynchronise
Knock legitimate client out of session by sending RST or forged packets
4 — Take Over Session
Inject packets with stolen session token/cookie to the target server
🎟️ Kerberos Authentication Flow 4-STEP PROTOCOL ▶
Protocol — Source: CEH + CISSP Cheat Sheets
Kerberos — Ticket-Based Authentication (port 88)
Kerberos uses symmetric + asymmetric encryption. Default in Active Directory environments. Attacks: Kerberoasting (offline crack service ticket), Pass-the-Ticket (reuse TGT/TGS), Golden Ticket (forged TGT using KRBTGT hash).
KDC
Key Distribution Centre — central trust authority (runs AS + TGS)
AS
Authentication Service — validates identity; issues TGT
TGS
Ticket Granting Service — issues service tickets upon valid TGT
TGT
Ticket Granting Ticket — proof of identity; valid for session
1
Client → KDC (AS)
Client sends AS-REQ with username in cleartext. No password sent yet.
2
KDC (AS) → Client
AS responds with TGT encrypted with KRBTGT hash. Client decrypts AS-REP using their password-derived key. If incorrect password → cannot decrypt → fail.
3
Client → KDC (TGS)
Client presents TGT to TGS, requests service ticket for specific service (TGS-REQ).
4
KDC (TGS) → Client → Service
TGS issues service ticket encrypted with service account's hash. Client presents ticket to target service. Access granted without re-entering password.
🏢 Active Directory — Structure, Objects & Attacks SEC+ · CySA+ · PenTest+ ▶
Microsoft Directory Service
AD DS — Authentication, Authorisation & Policy at Enterprise Scale
Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's centralised identity and access management system. Nearly every enterprise Windows environment runs it. AD is the #1 target in corporate intrusions — owning AD means owning the network.
▸ STRUCTURE — LOGICAL HIERARCHY
ObjectDescriptionAnalogy
Forest Top-level security boundary. Contains one or more domains. Shares schema and global catalog. The country
Domain Core admin unit. Has its own policies, database (NTDS.dit), and DNS namespace (corp.local). The state
Organisational Unit (OU) Container inside a domain. Groups objects for delegation and GPO application. The department
Domain Controller (DC) Server running AD DS. Authenticates users, stores NTDS.dit, replicates with other DCs. The HR office
Global Catalog (GC) Partial replica of ALL objects in the forest. Speeds up cross-domain lookups. Port 3268/3269. The central index
NTDS.dit The AD database file on each DC. Contains all objects including password hashes. Primary target. The master HR file
Trust Allows users in one domain/forest to access resources in another. Can be one- or two-way, transitive or non-transitive. Inter-company agreement
▸ AD OBJECTS — THE THREE PRINCIPALS
Object TypePurposeKey Attributes
User Account Represents a person or service. Has SID, SAMAccountName, UPN, password hash. memberOf, lastLogon, pwdLastSet, userAccountControl
Computer Account Every domain-joined machine. Has its own password (changed every 30 days). dNSHostName, operatingSystem, servicePrincipalName
Group Collection of principals. Controls access to resources. Domain Local · Global · Universal (scope)
Service Account (gMSA) Non-interactive account for services. Has SPN registered. Primary Kerberoasting target. servicePrincipalName, msDS-ManagedPassword
privileged groups Domain Admins · Enterprise Admins · Schema Admins · Administrators · Backup Operators · Account Operators Membership = full domain or forest control
▸ GROUP POLICY OBJECTS (GPOs)
GPOs are collections of settings pushed to computers/users in an OU. Applied order: Local → Site → Domain → OU (LSDOU). Later policies override earlier ones. Enforced GPOs cannot be overridden. Block Inheritance stops parent GPOs filtering down.
GPO Use CaseExample Setting
Password PolicyMin length 12, complexity required, 90-day expiry
Account LockoutLock after 5 bad passwords for 30 minutes
Software DeploymentPush MSI packages to all machines in an OU
Script ExecutionRun logon/logoff scripts; restrict PowerShell
Security SettingsDisable guest, rename Administrator, firewall rules
AppLocker / WDACWhitelist which executables are allowed to run

▸ COMMON AD ATTACKS
AttackWhat happensRequiresDefence
Kerberoasting Request TGS for any SPN-registered account. Crack the RC4-encrypted ticket offline. Any domain user Strong passwords on service accounts; use gMSA; AES-only encryption
AS-REP Roasting Request AS-REP for accounts with "Do not require Kerberos pre-auth" set. Crack offline. Network access (no creds) Require pre-auth on all accounts; audit UAC flags
Pass-the-Hash (PtH) Use stolen NTLM hash directly for authentication without cracking it. NTLM hash (from LSASS, SAM, NTDS) Credential Guard; disable NTLM; Protected Users group
Pass-the-Ticket (PtT) Inject stolen Kerberos TGT/TGS into current session. Impersonate user. Valid Kerberos ticket (from LSASS) Protected Users group; session monitoring
DCSync Mimic DC replication to pull all password hashes (including krbtgt) from a DC without touching disk. Domain Admin / Replication rights Monitor for DS-Replication-Get-Changes on non-DC accounts
Golden Ticket Forge a TGT using the krbtgt hash. Valid for 10 years. Persists through password resets. krbtgt hash (from DCSync / NTDS) Reset krbtgt password TWICE; monitor for anomalous TGT lifetimes
Silver Ticket Forge a TGS for a specific service using that service account's hash. No DC contact needed. Service account hash Monitor for service tickets with no corresponding TGT

ControlWhat it does
Tiered Admin ModelTier 0 = DC/AD · Tier 1 = Servers · Tier 2 = Workstations. Admins have separate accounts per tier.

🔒 TLS — Handshake, Cipher Suites & Certificate Chain SEC+ · SECX ▶
Transport Layer Security
How HTTPS Actually Works — Step by Step
TLS (formerly SSL) provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity (MAC), and authentication (certificates) over any transport. Used by HTTPS (443), SMTPS (465), IMAPS (993), and most modern protocols. Current standard: TLS 1.3 (2018).
▸ TLS 1.2 HANDSHAKE (4 ROUND TRIPS)
1
ClientHello
Client → Server. Sends: TLS version, random number (client_random), list of supported cipher suites, compression methods, extensions (SNI, ALPN, supported curves).
2
ServerHello + Certificate
Server → Client. Selects cipher suite and TLS version. Sends server_random. Sends its X.509 certificate chain. Optionally sends ServerKeyExchange (for DHE/ECDHE).
3
Client Key Exchange
Client validates the certificate chain. Generates pre-master secret. If RSA: encrypts with server's public key. If DHE/ECDHE: sends client DH public value. Both sides derive the master secret and session keys independently.
4
Finished (both sides)
Both send a Finished message: HMAC of the entire handshake transcript, encrypted with the new session keys. If both verify correctly — encrypted data transfer begins.
▸ TLS 1.3 IMPROVEMENTS (2 ROUND TRIPS → 1)
FeatureTLS 1.2TLS 1.3
Handshake RTTs2 RTT (full) / 1 RTT (resumption)1 RTT (full) / 0 RTT (resumption — risky)
Key ExchangeRSA or DHE/ECDHEECDHE only — RSA key exchange removed
Forward SecrecyOptional (only with DHE/ECDHE)Mandatory — every session gets unique keys
Cipher SuitesMany including weak ones (RC4, 3DES)5 strong AEAD suites only
EncryptedOnly after FinishedServer certificate encrypted during handshake
Removed—RSA key exchange, static DH, CBC mode ciphers, compression, renegotiation, SHA-1
▸ CERTIFICATE CHAIN VALIDATION
# Certificate chain: End-Entity → Intermediate CA → Root CA # # Root CA (self-signed, in OS/browser trust store) # └─ Intermediate CA (signed by Root) # └─ Server Certificate (signed by Intermediate) # # Validation steps: # 1. Build chain from server cert to trusted root # 2. Verify each signature in chain (cryptographic) # 3. Check each cert is not expired (notBefore / notAfter) # 4. Check each cert is not revoked (CRL or OCSP) # 5. Check server cert CN/SAN matches the hostname (SNI) # 6. Check cert has correct Key Usage / Extended Key Usage # Inspect a certificate from the command line openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout openssl verify -CAfile chain.pem cert.pem # Check cipher suite negotiated openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 | grep Cipher nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com
▸ CIPHER SUITE NOTATION
# TLS 1.2 cipher suite breakdown: TLS _ ECDHE _ RSA _ WITH _ AES_256_GCM _ SHA384 │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─ MAC / PRF algorithm │ │ │ └─ Bulk encryption (AES-256 in GCM mode = AEAD) │ │ └─ Authentication (whose certificate we verify) │ └─ Key Exchange (ECDHE = elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman ephemeral) └─ Protocol # TLS 1.3 suite (simpler — key exchange implicit ECDHE) TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 # 5 suites total in 1.3 TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 # for devices without hardware AES
▸ KEY CONCEPTS
ConceptMeaning
Forward Secrecy (PFS)Each session uses ephemeral keys. Compromising the private key LATER does not decrypt past sessions. Requires DHE or ECDHE.
HSTSHTTP Strict Transport Security. Browser header telling clients to always use HTTPS for N seconds. Defeats SSL stripping.
Certificate PinningApp hardcodes the expected cert/public key. Defeats MITM even with a trusted rogue CA. Used in mobile apps.
OCSP StaplingServer attaches (staples) a pre-fetched OCSP response to handshake. Faster than client fetching OCSP separately.
SNIServer Name Indication. Client sends hostname in ClientHello so server knows which cert to present. Allows virtual hosting.
CT (Cert Transparency)All public certs must be logged in public append-only logs. Lets anyone detect mis-issuance.
▸ COMMON TLS ATTACKS
AttackTargetMechanismFix
BEASTTLS 1.0 CBCIV prediction in CBC mode allows plaintext recoveryTLS 1.1+ or RC4 (deprecated) — use TLS 1.2+
POODLESSLv3 CBCPadding oracle on SSLv3Disable SSLv3 entirely
DROWNSSLv2 shared keySSLv2 oracle decrypts TLS sessions sharing same key pairDisable SSLv2; use separate certs
Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)OpenSSL <1.0.1gBuffer over-read in heartbeat extension leaks server memory (keys, sessions)Patch OpenSSL; revoke exposed certs
CRIME / BREACHTLS compressionCompress-then-encrypt leaks secrets if attacker can injectDisable TLS compression; CSRF tokens
SSL StrippingHTTP redirectMITM downgrades HTTPS to HTTP at the redirectHSTS; HSTS preloading
🧒Security Basics in Plain EnglishSec+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
The CIA Triad (No Spies Involved)
Security protects three things. Confidentiality = only the right people can see it (a sealed letter). Integrity = nobody changed it secretly (a tamper seal). Availability = it's there when you need it (the door is unlocked for you). Almost every security idea protects one of these three.
ANALOGY
Authentication vs. Authorization
Authentication proves who you are (showing your ID at the door). Authorization decides what you're allowed to do once inside (your key only opens certain rooms). You authenticate first, then you're authorized.
ANALOGY
Encryption = a Locked Box
Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Picture putting a note in a locked box: anyone can carry the box, but only the key-holder can open it. That's why 'https' sites are safer.
HABIT
Passwords → Passphrases + MFA
Long beats complicated: 'correct-horse-battery-staple' is stronger and easier than 'P@ss1'. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof (a code on your phone) so a stolen password alone isn't enough.
MINDSET
Least Privilege
Give people (and programs) only the access they truly need — nothing extra. The new intern doesn't get the master key. Less access means less damage if an account is ever stolen.
STREET-SMART
Spotting Phishing
Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into clicking or typing a password. Red flags: urgency ('act now!'), odd sender addresses, surprise links, and requests for credentials. When unsure, don't click — verify through a channel you trust.
You Hear…It Really Means…
VulnerabilityA weakness (an unlocked window)
ThreatSomething that could exploit it (a burglar)
RiskThe chance it actually hurts you (likelihood × impact)
Zero TrustVerify everyone every time — assume nothing is safe by default
HardeningClosing doors you don't use to shrink the target
🧱Everyday Security HygieneSec+ • Start Here▶
DO THESE
The Habits That Stop Most Attacks
You don’t need to be an expert to be safe. A handful of boring habits blocks the vast majority of real-world attacks — the digital equivalent of washing your hands and locking your door.
BACKUPS
The 3-2-1 Rule
Keep 3 copies of anything important, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy kept offsite/offline. Then a lost laptop, a crashed drive, or ransomware becomes an annoyance instead of a disaster — if you’ve tested that the restore actually works.
PASSWORDS
Use a Manager + MFA
Humans can’t remember 100 strong, unique passwords — so don’t. A password manager remembers them for you; you remember one good master passphrase. Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere it’s offered.
HabitWhy It Helps
Install updates promptlyPatches close known holes attackers use
Password managerUnique strong passwords without memorizing
Enable MFAA stolen password alone won’t get in
Think before you clickStops most phishing cold
Lock your screen30 seconds away ≠ open to anyone walking by
Back up (3-2-1)Turns disasters into inconveniences
🔑 Passwords & Hashing — How Logins Are Stored Safely SEC • Start Here ▶
NEVER STORE PLAINTEXT
The Golden Rule of Password Storage
Databases get breached. If passwords are stored as-is, every user's password is exposed instantly. Instead, store a hash — a one-way transformation that cannot be reversed. When a user logs in, hash what they typed and compare hashes.
WHAT IS A HASH
One-Way Fingerprint
A hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-length output. Same input ALWAYS produces same output. Even one character change completely changes the hash (avalanche effect). You cannot go from hash → original (one-way).
import hashlib text = "hunter2" h = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest() # f52fbd32b2b3b86ff88ef6c490628285f482af15ddcb29541f94bcf526a3f6c7 text2 = "hunter3" # one char different h2 = hashlib.sha256(text2.encode()).hexdigest() # 7a20f6f8c04b1a590a39c74b4f6b3c4a8e6a7f1c2d3e4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a2b3 # Completely different — avalanche effect
SALTING
Why Two Users With Same Password Need Different Hashes
Without salts, two users with "password123" produce the same hash — attackers can pre-compute tables (rainbow tables) and look up hashes instantly. A salt is a random value added to the password before hashing. Every user gets a unique salt. Rainbow tables become useless.
RIGHT TOOLS FOR PASSWORDS
Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
SHA-256 is fast — that's GOOD for verifying file integrity, BAD for passwords (attackers can try billions/sec). bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are deliberately slow and memory-hard. They automatically handle salting. Never hand-roll password hashing.
# pip install bcrypt import bcrypt # Hash when user registers password = "my_secure_pass" hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()) # Verify on login entered = "my_secure_pass" if bcrypt.checkpw(entered.encode(), hashed): print("Login OK")
STRONG PASSWORDS
Length Beats Complexity
A 20-character random passphrase is stronger than "P@$$w0rd!" — and much easier to remember. Use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePass). Generate unique passwords for every site. Enable MFA everywhere possible.
📲 Multi-Factor Authentication — Layers of Proof SEC • Foundation ▶
THREE FACTORS
Something You Know, Have, or Are
Knowledge factor — something you know: password, PIN, security questions (weakest).
Possession factor — something you have: phone (SMS code, authenticator app), hardware token (YubiKey), smart card.
Inherence factor — something you are: fingerprint, face, iris, voice.
MFA requires 2 or more different factor types. Two passwords is NOT MFA.
MFA METHODS RANKED
