It's a set of best practices for delivering IT as a service to a business — covering how you handle outages, changes, requests, and continuous improvement. You'll encounter ITIL terminology constantly in enterprise IT, especially on help desks and ops teams. Even if your company doesn't "do ITIL," they probably use its vocabulary.
INCIDENT VS PROBLEM VS CHANGE VS REQUEST
The Four Terms People Mix Up
TypeDefinitionGoalExample
IncidentUnplanned interruption or degradation of a serviceRestore service ASAP (even with a workaround)"Email is down"
ProblemThe underlying root cause of one or more incidentsFind & fix root cause permanently"Why does email keep going down? Bad disk."
ChangeAdding/modifying/removing anything that could affect servicesImplement safely with minimal risk"Upgrade the mail server"
Service RequestA user asking for something standard/pre-approvedFulfill efficiently"I need access to the shared drive"
Key distinction: an incident is "it's broken, fix it now." A problem is "why does it keep breaking?" You restore the incident fast (workaround), then investigate the problem to prevent recurrence.
INCIDENT PRIORITY
Priority = Impact × Urgency
Not every incident is equal. Priority determines what gets worked first. It's calculated from impact (how many people / how critical) and urgency (how fast it needs fixing).
PriorityTypical MeaningExample
P1 — CriticalMajor outage, business stoppedEntire company can't access core system
P2 — HighSignificant impact, no workaroundA department is down
P3 — MediumLimited impact or workaround existsOne team's printer is broken
P4 — LowMinor, single user, cosmetic"My mouse settings reset"
CHANGE MANAGEMENT
Why You Can't Just Push to Production
Most outages are self-inflicted — caused by changes. Change management adds guardrails so changes are reviewed, approved, scheduled, and reversible. The CAB (Change Advisory Board) reviews risky changes.
Change TypeRiskApprovalExample
StandardLow, pre-approvedNone needed (routine)Routine password reset, known patch
NormalVariableCAB review + approvalMajor version upgrade
EmergencyHigh (but necessary)Expedited (ECAB)Patch an actively exploited zero-day
Every change should have a rollback plan ("if it breaks, how do we undo it?") and a maintenance window (a scheduled low-traffic time). "It's just a small change" is the most dangerous phrase in ops.
SLAs, SLOs, SLIs
Measuring Service Quality
TermFull NameWhat It Is
SLIService Level IndicatorThe actual measurement (e.g., 99.95% uptime measured)
SLOService Level ObjectiveYour internal target (e.g., "we aim for 99.9%")
SLAService Level AgreementThe contractual promise with consequences (e.g., "99.9% or refund")
"The number of nines" matters: 99.9% ("three nines") = 8.7 hours downtime/year. 99.99% = 52 minutes/year. 99.999% ("five nines") = 5 minutes/year. Each extra nine costs exponentially more.
📈 Performance & Capacity — Finding and Fixing Bottlenecks OPS • Essential ▶
THE FOUR RESOURCES
Everything Is CPU, Memory, Disk, or Network
When a system is slow, the bottleneck is almost always one of four resources. The skill is identifying which one — guessing wastes time. Start broad (which resource is saturated?), then drill into the offending process.
ResourceSymptomLinux Tool
CPUHigh load, slow computationtop, htop, mpstat, uptime
MemorySwapping, OOM kills, slownessfree -h, vmstat, top
Disk I/OHigh iowait, slow reads/writesiostat, iotop, df, du
NetworkLatency, packet loss, saturationiftop, ss, nload, mtr
READING THE VITALS
Load Average and Resource Commands
# Load average: 1, 5, 15-minute averages uptime # load average: 2.50, 1.80, 1.20 # Rule of thumb: compare to CPU core count. # load 2.5 on a 4-core box = fine. On 1 core = overloaded. nproc # how many cores you have # Memory — is it actually low, or just cached? free -h # "available" is the number that matters, not "free" # Linux uses spare RAM for cache — that's good, not a problem # Disk I/O wait — %wa in top means CPU waiting on disk iostat -x 2 # %util near 100 = disk saturated # Find the hungriest processes top -o %CPU # sort by CPU top -o %MEM # sort by memory ps aux --sort=-%mem | head # top memory consumers
THE USE METHOD
A Systematic Troubleshooting Framework
Brendan Gregg's USE method: for every resource, check three things. It's a checklist that prevents you from missing the obvious.
U-S-EQuestion
UtilizationHow busy is the resource? (% time active)
SaturationIs there a queue/backlog of work waiting?
ErrorsAre there error events? (dropped packets, disk errors)
CAPACITY PLANNING
Don't Wait Until It's On Fire
Capacity planning means predicting future resource needs based on growth trends, so you scale before you run out. Track utilization over time, identify the trend, and add capacity with lead time. The key metrics: current utilization, growth rate, and headroom (how much buffer before you hit limits). A disk filling at 2%/week with 20% free has ~10 weeks — plan now, not at 99%.
🔭 Observability — Knowing What Your Systems Are Doing OPS • Modern ▶
MONITORING VS OBSERVABILITY
Known Unknowns vs Unknown Unknowns
Monitoring answers questions you already know to ask ("is CPU high?"). Observability lets you ask new questions about your system's behavior without shipping new code — crucial for debugging novel failures in complex distributed systems. Monitoring tells you something is wrong; observability helps you figure out why.
THE THREE PILLARS
Metrics, Logs, Traces
PillarWhat It IsAnswersTools
MetricsNumeric time-series (CPU, req/s, error rate)"What is happening?" (trends, alerts)Prometheus, Grafana
LogsTimestamped event records"What happened exactly?" (details)Loki, ELK, Splunk
TracesRequest's full journey across services"Where is the slowness?" (latency per hop)Jaeger, Tempo, OpenTelemetry
THE FOUR GOLDEN SIGNALS
What to Watch for Any Service (Google SRE)
SignalMeaning
LatencyHow long requests take (watch the slow tail: p95, p99)
TrafficHow much demand (requests/sec)
ErrorsRate of failed requests
SaturationHow "full" the system is (the constrained resource)
Alert on symptoms, not causes. Page someone for "users are getting errors" (a symptom they care about), not "CPU is 80%" (which may be totally fine). This keeps alerts meaningful and reduces fatigue.
GITOPS
Git as the Single Source of Truth
GitOps applies software-development practices to operations: the desired state of your infrastructure and apps lives in a Git repo, and an automated agent continuously makes reality match the repo. Want to change production? Open a pull request. This gives you review, audit history, easy rollback (just revert the commit), and no manual kubectl drift.
PrincipleBenefit
Declarative state in GitThe repo IS the documentation of what's deployed
Changes via pull requestReview + approval + audit trail for every change
Automated reconciliationAgent (Argo CD, Flux) keeps cluster matching Git
Rollback = git revertUndo a bad deploy by reverting the commit
🐳 Container Security — Hardening Docker & Images OPS • Security ▶
CONTAINERS AREN'T VMs
Shared Kernel = Shared Risk
Containers share the host's kernel (unlike VMs, which each have their own). That makes them lightweight and fast — but it also means a container escape can potentially compromise the host and every other container. Container security is about reducing what a compromised container can reach and do.
IMAGE SECURITY
Start From a Clean, Minimal Base
PracticeWhy
Use minimal base imagesAlpine/distroless = smaller attack surface, fewer CVEs
Pin image versions (digests)python:3.12 not python:latest — reproducible, no surprise updates
Scan images for vulnerabilitiesTrivy, Grype, Clair find known CVEs in layers
Don't bake in secretsSecrets in image layers persist even if "deleted" later
Use trusted sourcesOfficial images; verify signatures (cosign/Sigstore)
Multi-stage buildsDon't ship build tools/source in the final image
# Scan an image for known vulnerabilities trivy image python:3.12 grype nginx:latest # Multi-stage build — final image has only what it needs # FROM golang:1.22 AS build # ... compile ... # FROM gcr.io/distroless/static # tiny, no shell, no package mgr # COPY --from=build /app /app
RUNTIME HARDENING
Limit What a Container Can Do
ControlHow
Don't run as rootUSER appuser in Dockerfile; --user 1000
Read-only filesystem--read-only — malware can't write
Drop capabilities--cap-drop ALL then add only what's needed
No new privileges--security-opt no-new-privileges
Limit resources--memory --cpus — contain DoS / runaway
Don't mount the Docker socket/var/run/docker.sock inside = root on host
Network segmentationCustom networks; don't expose ports you don't need
THE 4 Cs
Cloud Native Security Layers
Container security is layered — each layer depends on the one outside it. Weakness in an outer layer undermines all the inner ones.
LayerSecure By
Cloud / infrastructureHardened hosts, IAM, network policy
ClusterRBAC, network policies, admission control
ContainerMinimal images, scanning, no root
CodeSecure coding, dependency hygiene, secrets management
🎚️ SRE — Engineering Reliability with Data, Not Heroics OPS • Modern ▶
WHAT IS SRE
"What Happens When a Software Engineer Runs Operations"
Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), pioneered at Google, applies software-engineering thinking to operations. Instead of manually firefighting, SREs use code, automation, and data to make systems reliable at scale. The core insight: reliability is a feature you can measure and budget for — not an absolute. 100% reliability is the wrong target (it's impossibly expensive and users can't even tell).
ERROR BUDGETS
Reliability You Can Spend
If your SLO is 99.9% availability, then 0.1% unreliability is your error budget — about 43 minutes/month you're "allowed" to be down. This brilliantly resolves the eternal dev-vs-ops conflict: as long as you're within budget, ship features fast. Blow the budget? Freeze features and focus on reliability. It turns reliability into a shared, data-driven decision instead of an argument.
SLODowntime/monthDowntime/year
99% (two nines)~7.3 hours~3.65 days
99.9% (three nines)~43 minutes~8.8 hours
99.99% (four nines)~4.3 minutes~52 minutes
99.999% (five nines)~26 seconds~5.3 minutes
TOIL
The Enemy of Engineering
Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales linearly with growth and produces no lasting value — resetting passwords by hand, manually restarting services, copy-pasting between dashboards. SRE culture caps toil (often at ~50% of time) and invests the rest in automation and engineering that eliminates toil. If you're doing something tedious for the third time, that's a signal to automate it.
CHAOS ENGINEERING
Break It on Purpose, on Your Terms
Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures (kill a server, add latency, drop a dependency) into systems — ideally in production, carefully — to discover weaknesses before they cause real outages. Netflix's "Chaos Monkey" randomly kills instances to force engineers to build resilient systems. The philosophy: you don't truly know your system is resilient until you've tested it failing. Start small, in a controlled blast radius, with a hypothesis and a way to abort.
🧯 Incident Command — Running a Major Incident Without Chaos OPS • Critical ▶
WHY STRUCTURE
Big Incidents Fail on Coordination, Not Tech
In a major incident, the technical problem is often not the hardest part — coordination is. Without structure you get chaos: everyone debugging the same thing, no one talking to stakeholders, conflicting changes, decision paralysis. Tech companies borrowed the Incident Command System (ICS) from emergency services (firefighters) to bring order. The key idea: assign clear roles so the responders can focus while someone else coordinates and communicates.
THE ROLES
Who Does What in a Major Incident
RoleResponsibility
Incident Commander (IC)Coordinates the response, makes decisions, owns the incident. Does NOT fix — directs. The single point of accountability.
Operations / RespondersThe hands-on engineers actually investigating and fixing
Communications LeadUpdates stakeholders, status page, customers — frees the IC to lead
ScribeMaintains the timeline of what happened and when (gold for the post-mortem)
Subject Matter ExpertsPulled in as needed for specific systems
In a small incident one person may wear several hats — but even then, declaring who is IC prevents the "everyone assumes someone else has it" failure.
RUNNING IT
The Flow of a Well-Managed Incident
PhaseAction
DeclareCall it an incident, assign an IC, open a dedicated channel/bridge
AssessEstablish severity & impact; who/what is affected
MitigateRestore service first (workarounds OK); root cause can wait
CommunicateRegular updates — internal + external; silence breeds panic
ResolveConfirm service restored & stable
ReviewBlameless post-mortem; turn lessons into action items
GOLDEN RULES
Hard-Won Incident Wisdom
Restore first, diagnose later — users want service back, not your root-cause theory. One person changes things at a time — coordinate through the IC to avoid conflicting fixes that make it worse. Communicate more than feels necessary — stakeholders fill silence with worst-case assumptions. It's OK to escalate / wake people up — a prolonged outage costs far more than someone's sleep. And recall the mindset thread: stay calm, work the process, own what's yours, and don't let panic (or blame) drive decisions. The calm, structured responder is worth ten frantic geniuses.
Beginner PostgreSQL Administration – Database Ops 101
Core Concept
What Is a Database Server?
A database server stores data in structured tables and answers queries from applications. PostgreSQL (Postgres) is the most popular open-source relational database. As an ops person you are responsible for keeping it running, backed up, and fast.

Quick orientation:
• Cluster – one running Postgres instance (port 5432).
• Database – a namespace inside the cluster.
• Schema – a namespace inside a database (default: public).
• Table – rows & columns, like a spreadsheet.
• Role – a user or group (Postgres uses one object for both).
Daily Commands
psql – The Postgres CLI
psql is the interactive terminal for Postgres. Master these and you can do 80 % of admin tasks.
# Connect as the postgres superuser sudo -u postgres psql -- Inside psql (lines starting with -- are SQL comments) -- List all databases \l -- Connect to a specific database \c myapp_db -- List tables in current schema \dt -- Show table structure \d users -- Run a query SELECT id, email FROM users LIMIT 5; -- Show currently running queries SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS duration, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY duration DESC; -- Kill a stuck query (use pid from above) SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345); -- Quit psql \q
Backup & Restore
pg_dump and pg_restore
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — a developer may drop a table by accident. Your job is to have a backup ready so you can restore it.
# Backup a single database to a compressed file pg_dump -U postgres -Fc myapp_db > myapp_db_$(date +%F).dump # Backup all databases (SQL text format) pg_dumpall -U postgres > all_databases_$(date +%F).sql # Restore from a compressed dump pg_restore -U postgres -d myapp_db --clean myapp_db_2026-06-01.dump # Restore from SQL text dump psql -U postgres < all_databases_2026-06-01.sql # Automate nightly backup via cron (runs at 2 AM daily) # Add to crontab with: crontab -e 0 2 * * * pg_dump -U postgres -Fc myapp_db > /backups/myapp_$(date +\%F).dump
Performance
VACUUM, ANALYZE, and Indexes
Postgres uses Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) — deleted rows are not immediately removed, they become "dead tuples." VACUUM reclaims that space. ANALYZE updates statistics so the query planner makes good choices.

Autovacuum handles this automatically in normal operation — never disable it.

Indexes speed up queries on large tables (like a book's index). Add one when a column appears frequently in WHERE clauses, but don't over-index — every index slows down INSERT/UPDATE.
-- Manual vacuum + analyze (safe to run any time) VACUUM ANALYZE users; -- Check table bloat (dead tuple ratio) SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, round(n_dead_tup::numeric / nullif(n_live_tup,0) * 100, 2) AS dead_pct FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY dead_pct DESC NULLS LAST; -- Add an index on the email column CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email ON users(email); -- CONCURRENTLY = no table lock, safe on production -- Explain a query (show execution plan) EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';
Beginner Kubernetes – Container Orchestration Fundamentals
Core Concept
Why Kubernetes Exists
Docker runs one container on one machine. When you need to run hundreds of containers across dozens of machines, you need an orchestrator. Kubernetes (K8s) handles:

• Scheduling — decides which machine runs which container.
• Self-healing — restarts crashed containers automatically.
• Scaling — adds/removes container replicas based on load.
• Rolling updates — deploys new versions with zero downtime.
• Service discovery — containers find each other by name, not IP.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) is managed for you on EKS/GKE/AKS. Your job is to manage your workloads, not the cluster control plane.
Key Objects
The K8s Object Hierarchy
Everything in Kubernetes is a YAML-defined object:

Pod — the smallest unit; one or more containers that share a network namespace. Pods are ephemeral — don't store state in them.

Deployment — manages a set of identical Pod replicas; handles rolling updates and rollbacks.

Service — a stable network endpoint (IP + DNS name) that load-balances across matching Pods.

ConfigMap / Secret — inject configuration or credentials into Pods without baking them into the image.

Namespace — a virtual cluster inside a cluster; used to separate teams or environments.
kubectl
Essential kubectl Commands
kubectl is the CLI to interact with a Kubernetes cluster. Master these first.
# Show cluster nodes kubectl get nodes # Show all pods in a namespace kubectl get pods -n production # Describe a pod (events, resource usage, errors) kubectl describe pod myapp-7d9f8c-xkz9p -n production # View logs (last 100 lines) kubectl logs myapp-7d9f8c-xkz9p -n production --tail=100 # Follow logs in real time (like tail -f) kubectl logs -f deployment/myapp -n production # Exec into a running container (interactive shell) kubectl exec -it myapp-7d9f8c-xkz9p -n production -- /bin/sh # Apply a YAML manifest kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml # Scale a deployment kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=5 -n production # Roll back to the previous version kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp -n production # Check rollout status kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n production
YAML Example
A Minimal Deployment + Service
This is the smallest production-style Kubernetes manifest — a Deployment (runs the app) and a Service (exposes it):
# deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: myapp namespace: production spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: myapp template: metadata: labels: app: myapp spec: containers: - name: myapp image: myregistry/myapp:1.2.3 ports: - containerPort: 8080 resources: requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" } limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" } readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } initialDelaySeconds: 5 --- # service.yaml (ClusterIP = internal only) apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: myapp namespace: production spec: selector: app: myapp # matches pods with label app=myapp ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 8080
Beginner CI/CD Pipelines – From Commit to Production Automatically
Core Concept
What CI/CD Actually Means
Continuous Integration (CI) — every code change is automatically built and tested the moment it's pushed. Catches bugs within minutes instead of weeks.

Continuous Delivery (CD) — every change that passes CI is automatically packaged and ready to deploy (a human clicks "go").

Continuous Deployment — every change that passes CI is automatically deployed to production with no human in the loop.

The pipeline stages (typical order):
1. Checkout code → 2. Install dependencies → 3. Lint/static analysis → 4. Unit tests → 5. Build artifact (binary, container image) → 6. Integration tests → 7. Security scan → 8. Deploy to staging → 9. Smoke tests → 10. Deploy to production.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if your pipeline is red, do not merge more changes on top of it. Fix the pipeline first; a broken main branch blocks everyone.
GitHub Actions
A Real CI/CD Pipeline in YAML
GitHub Actions is one of the most common CI/CD tools — config lives in .github/workflows/*.yml right alongside your code.
# .github/workflows/ci.yml name: CI Pipeline on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" - name: Install dependencies run: pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt - name: Lint run: ruff check . - name: Run tests with coverage run: pytest --cov=src --cov-report=xml --cov-fail-under=80 - name: Security scan run: | pip install bandit bandit -r src/ -ll build-and-push: needs: test # only runs if 'test' job passes runs-on: ubuntu-latest if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Build container image run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} . - name: Scan image run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL myapp:${{ github.sha }} - name: Push to registry run: | echo ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }} | docker login -u user --password-stdin docker push myapp:${{ github.sha }}
Deployment Strategies
How to Ship Without Breaking Things
How you roll out a new version matters as much as the code itself:

• Rolling update — replace instances one at a time; if health checks fail, stop and roll back. Default in Kubernetes.
• Blue-green deployment — run two identical environments ("blue" = current, "green" = new); switch traffic instantly; instant rollback by switching back.
• Canary release — send 5% of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, gradually increase to 100% (or roll back if errors spike).
• Feature flags — deploy code "dark" (disabled), then turn it on for specific users without a new deployment.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a deploy "should be fine" because it worked in staging. Staging never perfectly mirrors production load, data, and integrations.
Failure Recovery
When the Pipeline Ships a Bad Release
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — a teammate's bad commit will reach production eventually. Your safety net matters more than prevention alone.

Build these into every pipeline:
• Automated rollback — if health checks fail post-deploy, automatically revert to the last known-good version.
• Deployment markers — send an event to your monitoring system on every deploy, so spikes can be correlated instantly: "errors started 90 seconds after deploy #4521."
• Fast rollback path — rolling back should take seconds, not the same time as a forward deploy.
• Post-incident review — every bad release gets a blameless writeup: what broke, why CI didn't catch it, what test or gate would have.
Beginner Web Server Hardening – nginx, Apache & TLS Done Right
Core Concept
The Default Config Is Not the Secure Config
Out of the box, web servers prioritise compatibility over security — they'll happily serve old TLS versions, leak version information, and allow risky HTTP methods. Hardening means deliberately tightening these defaults.

The five hardening layers:
1. TLS configuration — which protocol versions and ciphers are allowed.
2. HTTP security headers — instructions to the browser about how to treat your site.
3. Information disclosure — hide server version and technology stack from attackers.
4. Rate limiting — slow down brute-force and scraping attempts.
5. Certificate management — automated renewal so sites never go down from an expired cert (a surprisingly common self-inflicted outage).
nginx Hardening
A Hardened nginx Server Block
This configuration covers the essentials most security scanners and compliance checks look for.
# /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.com server { listen 443 ssl http2; server_name example.com; # ── TLS: only modern protocols and strong ciphers ── ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem; ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; # no SSLv3, TLSv1.0, TLSv1.1 ssl_ciphers HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5:!3DES; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on; ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m; # ── Hide version info (reduces fingerprinting) ── server_tokens off; # ── Security headers ── add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains" always; add_header X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN" always; add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always; add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always; add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'" always; # ── Rate limiting (defined in http{} block, applied here) ── limit_req zone=login_limit burst=5 nodelay; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; } } # Redirect all plain HTTP to HTTPS server { listen 80; server_name example.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } # In the http{} block — define the rate limit zone: # limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login_limit:10m rate=5r/m;
Headers Explained
What Each Security Header Actually Does
HeaderWhat it tells the browser
Strict-Transport-Security"Always use HTTPS for this site, never fall back to HTTP"
X-Frame-Options"Don't let other sites embed me in an iframe" (stops clickjacking)
X-Content-Type-Options"Don't guess file types — trust what I declared" (stops MIME sniffing attacks)
Content-Security-Policy"Only load scripts/styles/images from these approved sources"
Referrer-Policy"Don't leak the full URL to other sites when users click links"

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume adding these headers won't break anything. Content-Security-Policy especially can silently break legitimate site features (third-party widgets, inline scripts). Test in report-only mode first: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only logs violations without blocking anything.
Verification
Testing Your Hardening Actually Worked
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — but you can also verify the choice was made correctly in the first place. Don't trust your config — test it.
# Free online TLS configuration scanner (the industry standard) # https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/ → grades A+ to F # Check from the command line with testssl.sh docker run --rm -ti drwetter/testssl.sh https://example.com # Check which protocols/ciphers your server actually offers nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 example.com # Verify security headers are present curl -sI https://example.com | grep -iE '(strict-transport|x-frame|x-content-type|content-security)' # Check certificate expiration (set up monitoring for this!) echo | openssl s_client -servername example.com -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates # Automated renewal with certbot — verify the timer is active sudo systemctl status certbot.timer sudo certbot renew --dry-run
Beginner

Writing Runbooks That People Actually Follow

Concept

A runbook is a conversation with your future self at 3 AM

A runbook is a step-by-step procedure for handling a specific operational situation — restarting a stuck service, failing over a database, rotating an expired certificate. The test of a good runbook isn't whether the author understands it; it's whether a half-asleep on-call engineer who has never touched this system can follow it correctly under pressure, at 3 AM, without calling anyone for help.

Concept

The anatomy of a runbook that survives contact with reality

SectionPurposeWhat goes wrong without it
Trigger / symptomsHow do you know this runbook applies right now?Engineer wastes 20 minutes confirming they're even looking at the right problem
Blast radius / impactWho and what is affected if this goes wrong further?Nobody escalates because nobody realized how big the problem actually was
PreconditionsWhat access, tools, or state do you need before starting?Engineer gets halfway through and discovers they don't have the right permissions
Numbered steps with exact commandsRemove all guesswork — copy, paste, run"Restart the service" becomes a 45-minute detour into "which service, on which host, with which flag?"
Verification stepHow do you confirm the fix actually worked?Engineer declares victory, closes the ticket, and the issue recurs an hour later
Rollback / escalation pathWhat do you do if this *doesn't* work?Engineer freezes, unsure whether to keep pushing or wake someone up
Hands-on

A short runbook excerpt, written the right way

# RUNBOOK: API gateway returning 503s

# TRIGGER: PagerDuty alert "gateway-503-rate-high" fires when error
# rate > 5% for 5 minutes straight.

# IMPACT: All customer-facing API traffic degraded. Treat as SEV-2.

# STEP 1 — confirm the alert is real, not a monitoring blip
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://api.internal.example.com/healthz
# Expect: 200. If you see 503 here too, this is real — continue.

# STEP 2 — check whether it's one node or all of them
kubectl get pods -n gateway -o wide
# Look for pods stuck in CrashLoopBackOff or 0/1 Ready

# STEP 3 — restart only the unhealthy pods (NOT the whole deployment)
kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -n gateway
# Kubernetes will reschedule it automatically — this is non-destructive

# VERIFY — error rate back under 1% for 5 consecutive minutes
watch -n 10 'curl -s https://api.internal.example.com/metrics | grep error_rate'

# IF STILL FAILING after step 3 — STOP. Escalate to #platform-oncall.
# Do not attempt a full deployment restart without a second engineer present.
Mindset

You can't make someone make the right choice...

...yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards. No matter how clear your runbook is, someone under pressure will eventually skip the verification step, run the command on the wrong host, or improvise instead of escalating. That's not a reason to stop writing good runbooks — it's the reason to also write the recovery procedure for "someone did the wrong thing." The best operational teams plan for both the happy path and the moment a tired human deviates from it.

Beginner

Capacity Planning – Answering "Will We Run Out of Room?" Before You Do

Concept

Capacity planning is forecasting, not firefighting

Capacity planning is the practice of looking at how a resource — disk space, bandwidth, server load, license seats — is being consumed over time, and projecting forward to answer "when will this become a problem, and what should we do about it before it does?" The opposite approach — waiting for an alert that says "disk 98% full" — turns a planning exercise into a 2 AM emergency. Good capacity planning quietly prevents most of the outages that bad capacity planning causes people to brag about firefighting.

Concept

The basic forecasting loop

StepWhat you're doingExample question it answers
1. Measure current usageEstablish a baseline — what does "normal" look like today?"We're using 620 GB of our 1 TB volume"
2. Track the trend over timeIs usage flat, growing steadily, or growing faster than before?"We've added about 15 GB per week for the last two months"
3. Project forwardAt the current rate, when do you cross the danger threshold?"At 15 GB/week, we hit 900 GB (our alert threshold) in about 19 weeks"
4. Plan the interventionWhat needs to happen before that date — and how long does it take to do it?"Provisioning additional storage takes 6 weeks of lead time, so we need to start the request now, not in week 18"
Hands-on

A simple growth projection in Python

# Given a few historical measurements, estimate when you'll hit a threshold
from datetime import date, timedelta

# (date, usage_in_gb) samples taken weekly
history = [
    (date(2026, 5, 4), 590),
    (date(2026, 5, 11), 605),
    (date(2026, 5, 18), 622),
    (date(2026, 5, 25), 636),
]

# Average weekly growth across the sampled period
days_elapsed = (history[-1][0] - history[0][0]).days
total_growth = history[-1][1] - history[0][1]
weekly_growth = total_growth / (days_elapsed / 7)

threshold_gb = 900
current_gb = history[-1][1]
weeks_remaining = (threshold_gb - current_gb) / weekly_growth
projected_date = history[-1][0] + timedelta(weeks=weeks_remaining)

print(f"Growing ~{weekly_growth:.1f} GB/week")
print(f"Projected to hit {threshold_gb} GB around {projected_date}")
print(f"That's roughly {weeks_remaining:.0f} weeks from the last measurement")

This is deliberately simple — straight-line ("linear") projection. Real-world usage often grows in bursts (a new product launch, a seasonal spike), so mature capacity planning layers in seasonality and known upcoming events on top of the trend line. But even this basic version turns a vague worry into a concrete date you can act on.

Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — until the monkey runs out of room

"That's the database team's disk, not mine" works fine right up until their volume fills up and takes down a service your team depends on. Capacity problems rarely stay neatly inside team boundaries — a full log partition can crash an application server, a maxed-out license pool can block an entire department's work. Part of good capacity planning is simply knowing which shared resources you depend on, even ones you don't directly own, so "not my circus" doesn't quietly become "my outage."

Beginner

Writing a Postmortem People Actually Learn From

Concept

A postmortem is a story about a system, not a trial of a person

A postmortem (or "post-incident review") is a written analysis of what happened during an outage or incident, why it happened, and what will change as a result. The single most important design decision in any postmortem process is whether it's blameless — focused on "what conditions made this mistake possible and likely?" rather than "who do we blame for this?" Get that one decision right, and people will tell you the truth about what happened. Get it wrong, and every future postmortem will quietly omit the details that actually mattered.

Concept

The shape of a postmortem that actually gets read

SectionWhat it answersCommon mistake to avoid
SummaryWhat happened, in 3-4 sentences a busy executive could read in 20 secondsBurying the headline under technical preamble nobody reads first
ImpactWho was affected, for how long, and how badly — with real numbersVague language like "some users experienced issues" instead of "approximately 4,200 users over 38 minutes"
TimelineWhat happened, in order, with timestamps — including detection and responseStarting the timeline at "the fix" instead of at the first sign something was wrong
Root cause(s)Why it happened — usually more than one contributing factor, not a single villainStopping at "a bad config was deployed" instead of asking "why was it possible to deploy that config unreviewed?"
Action itemsSpecific, owned, dated changes that reduce the chance of recurrenceVague commitments like "we'll be more careful" — that's not an action item, it's a hope
Hands-on

The "five whys" — finding the real root cause

# A simple technique for digging past the surface-level explanation.
# Keep asking "why" until you reach something you can actually fix.

Problem: The payment service was down for 40 minutes.

Why #1: Why was it down?
   -> The service crashed when it ran out of memory.

Why #2: Why did it run out of memory?
   -> A new code path loaded an entire customer table into memory at once.

Why #3: Why did that code path do that?
   -> The developer tested only against a small sample database in staging.

Why #4: Why didn't testing catch this before production?
   -> Staging databases aren't seeded with production-scale data volumes.

Why #5: Why isn't that part of the standard testing process?
   -> There's no documented requirement for load-realistic staging data.

# Notice where this ended up: not "the developer made a mistake"
# (Why #1-3), but "our process doesn't ensure realistic testing
# conditions" (Why #5) — a SYSTEM problem with a fixable solution,
# not a PERSON problem with only blame to offer.
Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — except blameless culture is everyone's circus

It's easy to think "writing good postmortems is the SRE team's job" — but a blameless culture is built or destroyed by everyone in the room, in the moment someone says "well, obviously they should have known better." One unkind comment in a review meeting can undo months of careful culture-building, and it teaches everyone present — not just the person being criticized — that honesty here has a cost. Protecting that culture, even in a meeting that isn't "yours," is part of keeping the whole system honest enough to actually improve.

🌍 Terraform — Infrastructure as Code in Practice IaC ▶
Concept
Declare Infrastructure, Don't Click It
Terraform lets you define cloud infrastructure — servers, networks, databases, DNS — as text files, then creates or changes it to match. You describe the desired end state in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language); Terraform figures out the steps to get there. Because it's declarative and version-controlled, your whole environment becomes reviewable, repeatable, and rebuildable — no more "click 40 things in the console and pray you remember them next time."
Example
A Minimal Configuration
main.tf
# Which provider (cloud) and version to use
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

# A resource — Terraform will create/manage this
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcd1234"
  instance_type = var.size          # from a variable
  tags          = { Name = "web-server" }
}

variable "size" { default = "t3.micro" }

output "public_ip" {
  value = aws_instance.web.public_ip   # print after apply
}
Reference
The Core Workflow
CommandWhat It Does
terraform initDownload providers & set up the working dir (run first)
terraform fmtAuto-format your .tf files
terraform validateCheck the config for syntax/type errors
terraform planPreview what will change — nothing is applied
terraform applyMake reality match the config (prompts to confirm)
terraform destroyTear down everything this config manages
terraform state listList the resources Terraform is tracking
The golden habit: always read the plan before you apply. It shows adds (+), changes (~), and destroys (-) so nothing surprises you.
Key Ideas
State, Plan & Idempotence
ConceptWhy It Matters
State fileTerraform records what it created in terraform.tfstate. It's the source of truth for "what exists" — store it remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud) so a team shares one, and lock it to prevent concurrent applies.
Desired vs actualplan diffs your config against state and the real world, then computes the minimal change set.
IdempotenceRunning apply twice with no config change does nothing the second time — the end state is what's declared, not a pile of commands.
ModulesReusable bundles of resources with inputs/outputs — package a "VPC" or "web app" once, use it everywhere.
Never edit state by handUse terraform state subcommands; hand-editing the JSON corrupts tracking.
📬 Message Queues & Event-Driven Architecture Architecture ▶
Concept
Decouple With a Buffer in the Middle
When service A calls service B directly, A waits for B and breaks if B is down. A message queue puts a durable buffer between them: A drops a message and moves on; B picks it up when ready. This decouples producers from consumers — they can scale, fail, and deploy independently. It's the backbone of event-driven systems, where components react to things that happened rather than calling each other in lockstep.
Reference
Queue vs Pub/Sub & Key Terms
▸ TWO MESSAGING SHAPES
PatternDeliveryExample
Queue (point-to-point)Each message goes to one consumer in a pool — spreads workTask/job processing (RabbitMQ, SQS)
Pub/Sub (topic)Each message goes to every subscriber — fan-outEvent broadcasting (Kafka, SNS, Redis)
▸ VOCABULARY
TermMeaning
ProducerPublishes messages
ConsumerReads and processes them
BrokerThe queue/log system in the middle (Kafka, RabbitMQ)
AckConsumer confirms "done" so the broker can drop the message
Dead-letter queueWhere messages go after repeated processing failures
BackpressureThe queue absorbs bursts so a slow consumer isn't overwhelmed
Delivery
Guarantees & Idempotence
Distributed messaging can't cheaply promise "exactly once," so you pick a guarantee and design around it:
GuaranteeMeaning
At-most-onceFast, but a message can be lost. Fine for disposable telemetry.
At-least-onceNever lost, but may be redelivered. The common default.
Exactly-onceIdeal but expensive/limited — usually emulated via dedup.
Because at-least-once means duplicates happen, make consumers idempotent — processing the same message twice has the same effect as once (e.g. key writes on a unique message ID). This is the single most important habit in event-driven systems.
Trade-offs
What You Gain and Pay
Detail
Gain: resilienceA consumer can crash or deploy; messages wait in the queue.
Gain: elastic scaleAdd consumers to drain a backlog faster; smooth out traffic spikes.
Gain: decouplingProducers don't know or care who consumes — add new consumers freely.
Cost: complexityAnother system to run/monitor; harder to trace a request end-to-end.
Cost: eventual consistencyWork happens asynchronously — the result isn't ready the instant you publish.
⚡ Caching Strategies — From App to CDN Performance ▶
Concept
Store the Answer, Skip the Work
A cache keeps a copy of expensive-to-compute or slow-to-fetch data somewhere fast, so repeated requests don't redo the work. Done right, it's the single biggest performance lever you have. The catch is the famous one: "There are only two hard things in computer science — cache invalidation and naming things." A stale cache serves wrong data; the art is knowing when to trust the copy and when to refresh it.
Reference
Where Caches Live (the Layers)
LayerExampleCaches
BrowserHTTP cacheStatic assets on the user's device
CDN / edgeCloudflare, CloudFrontContent served near the user, globally
App / in-memoryRedis, MemcachedQuery results, sessions, computed values
DatabaseQuery & buffer cacheHot pages & plans in RAM
The closer to the user a cache sits, the faster and cheaper the hit — but the harder it is to invalidate. Each layer is a trade of speed vs freshness.
Patterns
Read & Write Strategies
PatternHow It Works
Cache-aside (lazy)App checks cache; on a miss, reads the DB and populates the cache. Most common.
Read-throughThe cache itself loads from the DB on a miss — app only talks to the cache.
Write-throughWrites go to cache and DB together — always fresh, slightly slower writes.
Write-backWrite to cache now, flush to DB later — fast, but risks loss on crash.
▸ CACHE-ASIDE IN CODE
function getUser(id) {
  let u = cache.get(`user:${id}`);
  if (u) return u;                 // hit
  u = db.query("SELECT ...", id);  // miss → load
  cache.set(`user:${id}`, u, { ttl: 300 }); // store 5 min
  return u;
}
Invalidation
Keeping Copies Honest
TechniqueWhat It Does
TTL (expiry)Data auto-expires after N seconds. Simple; tolerates brief staleness.
Explicit purgeDelete the key when the source changes. Precise; needs write-path hooks.
Versioned keysBake a version/hash into the key (user:42:v3); old keys just age out.
Cache-Control headersFor HTTP/CDN: max-age, no-store, ETag for revalidation.
Watch for the thundering herd / stampede: when a hot key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and hammer the DB. Mitigate with a short lock, request coalescing, or staggered TTLs.
🐒 Chaos Engineering — Breaking Things on Purpose Reliability ▶
Concept
Find the Weakness Before It Finds You
Chaos engineering is the discipline of deliberately injecting failure into a system — killing servers, adding network latency, exhausting disk — to discover how it actually behaves under stress, rather than how you hope it does. The insight: distributed systems fail in ways no one predicted, so you'd rather trigger those failures in a controlled experiment (business hours, watching closely) than at 3 a.m. during a real outage. Netflix pioneered it with Chaos Monkey, which randomly kills production instances to force teams to build resilience in.
Method
Running an Experiment
StepWhat You Do
1. Steady stateDefine a measurable "healthy" metric (e.g. checkout success rate > 99%).
2. Hypothesis"If we kill one payment node, checkout success stays above 99%."
3. Blast radiusStart tiny — one instance, small % of traffic — to limit harm.
4. Inject & observeIntroduce the failure; watch the metric and your alerts.
5. Learn & fixIf the hypothesis breaks, you found a real weakness — fix it, then re-run.
Always have an abort switch to stop the experiment instantly, and never run one you're confident will cause a major outage — the goal is learning, not self-inflicted downtime.
Reference
Common Failures to Inject
FailureTests Whether…
Kill an instanceLoad balancing & auto-healing actually replace it
Add network latencyTimeouts & retries are tuned; slow ≠ down
Drop a dependencyCircuit breakers & fallbacks kick in (graceful degradation)
Fill the disk / CPUResource limits & alerts fire before a crash
Zone/region outageFailover to another region works end-to-end
Tooling: Chaos Monkey / Simian Army, Gremlin, LitmusChaos and Chaos Mesh (Kubernetes).
Prerequisites
Don't Start Here
Chaos engineering pays off only once you already have solid monitoring and alerting (or you won't see what breaks) and the basics of resilience — retries, timeouts, health checks, redundancy. Injecting failure into a system you can't observe just causes an outage with no lesson. It's an advanced reliability practice that builds on observability and SRE fundamentals, not a starting point.
☁️ Serverless & FaaS — Code Without Managing Servers Cloud ▶
Concept
There Are Still Servers — You Just Don't Touch Them
Serverless means you deploy code and the cloud runs it on demand — provisioning, scaling, patching, and capacity are the provider's problem. The flagship form is Functions as a Service (FaaS): you upload a single function that runs in response to an event (an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message) and you're billed only for the milliseconds it executes. Idle costs nothing. It's the far end of the "managed" spectrum beyond containers.
Example
A Function That Runs on an Event
AN HTTP-TRIGGERED FUNCTION (NODE)
// The cloud invokes this on each request; no server to run
export async function handler(event) {
  const name = event.queryStringParameters?.name ?? "world";
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({ message: `Hello, ${name}` }),
  };
}
Deploy it, wire a trigger (API Gateway, a bucket event, a cron schedule), and it scales from zero to thousands of concurrent invocations automatically — each request gets its own isolated run.
Reference
Providers & the Compute Spectrum
▸ THE BIG FaaS PLATFORMS
ProviderService
AWSLambda
AzureFunctions
Google CloudCloud Functions / Cloud Run
EdgeCloudflare Workers, Netlify/Vercel Functions
▸ HOW MUCH DO YOU MANAGE?
ModelYou Manage
On-premEverything — hardware to app
IaaS (VMs)OS + runtime + app
ContainersThe image + app
Serverless / FaaSJust the code
Trade-offs
Where Serverless Shines — and Bites
Detail
Scale to zeroNo traffic = no cost. Great for spiky or unpredictable load.
No opsNo servers to patch or capacity-plan; ship features faster.
Cold startsAn idle function takes extra time to spin up on the first request — latency-sensitive paths feel it.
Stateless & time-limitedFunctions keep no memory between runs and have a max duration — long jobs and in-memory state don't fit.
Vendor lock-inTriggers and runtimes are provider-specific; portability takes effort.
Harder local debuggingThe event-driven, managed environment is tricky to reproduce on your laptop.
🪣 Object Storage — S3 & the Cloud Storage Model Cloud ▶
Concept
A Different Way to Store Data
Traditional storage is files (a tree of folders) or blocks (raw disk a filesystem sits on). Object storage is a third model: every piece of data is an object — the bytes plus metadata plus a unique key — living in a flat bucket, retrieved over HTTP. There are no real folders (the "path" in a key is just a naming convention), and you can't edit part of an object — you replace the whole thing. Amazon S3 defined the model; Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage, and MinIO all speak a similar API.
Comparison
Object vs File vs Block
ObjectFileBlock
UnitObject + keyFile in foldersRaw blocks
AccessHTTP APINFS/SMBAttached disk
Edit in placeNo — replace wholeYesYes
Scales toEffectively unlimitedLimitedLimited
Best forMedia, backups, data lakes, static sitesShared docsDatabases, VMs
Reference
Key Features You'll Use
FeatureWhat It Does
Storage classesTrade price for access speed: hot (Standard) → cool → cold archive (Glacier). Cheaper to store, pricier/slower to retrieve.
Lifecycle rulesAuto-move objects to colder tiers or delete them after N days.
VersioningKeep old copies so an overwrite/delete is recoverable.
Presigned URLsA time-limited link that grants temporary access to one object without exposing credentials.
Static website hostingServe a bucket of HTML/JS directly — often fronted by a CDN.
DurabilityProviders replicate objects across facilities — S3 advertises 99.999999999% ("11 nines") durability.
Commands
Working With a Bucket (AWS CLI)
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket                 # make bucket
aws s3 cp report.pdf s3://my-bucket/       # upload an object
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/                  # list objects
aws s3 sync ./site s3://my-bucket/         # upload a whole folder
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/report.pdf   # temp shareable URL
Security note: the classic cloud breach is a bucket left public. Keep buckets private by default, use IAM policies for access, and reach for presigned URLs when you need to share a single object.
🎚️ Deployment Strategies — Blue-Green, Canary & Rolling Reliability ▶
Concept
Shipping New Code Without Taking the Site Down
The naive deploy — stop the app, swap the code, start it — means downtime and a scary all-or-nothing cutover. Modern strategies release new versions gradually and reversibly, so you can catch a bad release before it reaches everyone and roll back in seconds instead of scrambling. The common thread: never bet all your traffic on an unproven version at once.
Reference
The Main Strategies
StrategyHow It Works
RollingReplace instances a few at a time until all run the new version. No extra capacity needed; rollback is slow (roll the other way).
Blue-GreenRun two full environments. Blue serves live; deploy to idle Green, test it, then flip all traffic. Instant rollback = flip back. Costs 2× capacity during the switch.
CanarySend a small % of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then ramp up. Limits blast radius; needs good monitoring.
Feature flagsShip code dark, then toggle it on for cohorts at runtime — decouples deploy from release.
Trade-offs
Choosing One
If you want…Use
Instant rollback, simple cutoverBlue-Green
To catch bad releases with real trafficCanary
Zero extra infrastructure costRolling
To release to specific users / A-B testFeature flags
They combine: canary-deploy behind a feature flag on rolling infrastructure. Kubernetes and load balancers make traffic-splitting easy, which is why these went mainstream.
Prerequisites
What Makes Safe Deploys Possible
RequirementWhy
Backward-compatible changesOld and new versions run at once — the DB schema and APIs must serve both. Use expand-then-contract migrations.
Health checksThe orchestrator must know a new instance is actually ready before sending it traffic.
Good metrics/alertsCanary is blind without error-rate and latency dashboards to compare versions.
Automated rollbackA deploy that can't auto-revert on failing metrics isn't really safe.
🔺 CAP Theorem & Consistency Models Architecture ▶
Concept
Pick Two — the Fundamental Trade-off
The CAP theorem says a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), and Partition tolerance (it keeps working when the network splits). Since networks will partition, partition tolerance isn't optional in practice — so the real choice, during a partition, is consistency vs availability.
Reference
The Three Letters
LetterGuarantee
ConsistencyAll nodes return the same, most-recent data. A read never sees stale values.
AvailabilityEvery request gets a (non-error) response, even if some nodes are down.
Partition toleranceThe system keeps operating even when nodes can't talk to each other.
Note: CAP's "Consistency" is stricter than ACID's — it means linearizability (one up-to-date copy), not "constraints hold." Different word, different guarantee.
In Practice
CP vs AP — What You Choose During a Split
CP (consistency)AP (availability)
During a partitionRefuse/blocks writes to stay correctKeep serving, reconcile later
Read might beAlways currentStale for a moment
Good forBanking, inventory, bookingsFeeds, carts, social, DNS
Examplesetcd, ZooKeeper, HBaseCassandra, DynamoDB, Riak
Most real systems aren't purely one or the other — they tune per-operation (a shopping cart is AP; the final checkout is CP).
Beyond CAP
Consistency Is a Spectrum
ModelPromise
Strong / linearizableReads always see the latest write — as if one copy existed.
EventualGiven no new writes, all replicas eventually converge. Cheap & available.
Read-your-writesYou always see your own updates (even if others lag).
CausalRelated events are seen in order; unrelated ones may not be.
A related lens, PACELC, extends CAP: even when there's no partition (Else), you still trade Latency vs Consistency — stronger guarantees cost round-trips. There's no free lunch in distributed data.
🕸️ Service Mesh — Istio, Linkerd & the Sidecar Pattern Cloud Native ▶
Concept
Move Networking Concerns Out of Your Code
When one app becomes 50 microservices, every service needs retries, timeouts, TLS, load balancing, and metrics for its calls to the others. Building that into each service — in every language — is repetitive and inconsistent. A service mesh extracts all of it into the infrastructure: a proxy runs alongside each service and handles service-to-service traffic, so your application code just makes a plain request and the mesh does the hard parts.
Architecture
Sidecars & the Two Planes
PieceRole
Sidecar proxyA proxy (often Envoy) deployed next to every service instance. All traffic in/out flows through it — the app is unaware.
Data planeThe collection of all sidecars actually moving the traffic.
Control planeThe brain (e.g. Istio's istiod) that configures every sidecar with routing rules, certs, and policy.
You change behavior by updating the control plane; it pushes config to the sidecars. Newer meshes offer a "sidecar-less" (per-node) mode to cut the per-pod overhead.
Reference
What a Mesh Gives You
CapabilityDetail
mTLS everywhereAutomatic mutual-TLS encryption + identity between services — zero app changes.
Traffic controlCanary/blue-green by shifting % of traffic; retries, timeouts, circuit breaking.
ObservabilityUniform metrics, logs, and traces for every call, for free.
PolicyWho may call whom (authorization), rate limits, fault injection for testing.
Trade-offs
Do You Actually Need One?
Detail
Worth it whenMany services, multiple languages, strict security/compliance, and you need uniform mTLS + observability.
Overkill whenA handful of services — the operational complexity and latency/resource overhead outweigh the benefit.
OptionsIstio (powerful, complex), Linkerd (lightweight, simpler), Cilium (eBPF-based), Consul.
A mesh solves the same problems an API gateway does between internal services — the gateway is the front door for outside traffic; the mesh is the internal road network.
🧵 Distributed Tracing & OpenTelemetry Observability ▶
Concept
Following One Request Across Many Services
In a microservice system, a single user click might touch a gateway, an auth service, three back-ends, and a database. When it's slow, which hop is to blame? Logs from each service in isolation can't tell you. Distributed tracing stitches the whole journey together: it tags the request with an ID that travels with it, so you can see the end-to-end path and exactly where the time went.
Reference
Traces, Spans & Context
TermMeaning
TraceThe whole journey of one request, identified by a trace_id.
SpanOne unit of work within the trace (an HTTP call, a DB query) — with a start, duration, and metadata.
Parent/childSpans nest — a service call's span contains the spans of what it triggered.
Context propagationThe trace_id + span info passed between services (via headers like W3C traceparent) so the trace stays connected.
Rendered as a waterfall, a trace shows each span as a bar — one long bar instantly reveals the bottleneck.
Reference
The Three Pillars & Where Tracing Fits
PillarAnswers
Metrics"Is something wrong?" — aggregate numbers, cheap, great for alerts.
Logs"What happened here?" — detailed events from one component.
Traces"Where is it slow / failing?" — the request's path across services.
You use all three together: a metric alerts you, a trace localizes the slow hop, and logs on that span explain why.
Standard
OpenTelemetry — One SDK to Instrument Them All
OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for generating traces, metrics, and logs. You instrument your code once with the OTel SDK (much of it automatic for popular frameworks), and it exports to whatever backend you choose — Jaeger, Tempo, Zipkin, or a commercial tool — with no code change to switch. That freedom from lock-in is why it won.
Practical noteDetail
SamplingTracing everything is expensive at scale — sample a fraction (head or tail sampling) while keeping error traces.
CollectorThe OTel Collector receives, batches, and routes telemetry so apps don't talk to backends directly.
🔃 GitOps — Git as the Source of Truth for Operations DevOps ▶
Concept
If It's Not in Git, It Doesn't Exist
GitOps applies the software workflow you already know — pull requests, review, merge, history — to infrastructure and deployments. The desired state of your whole system lives in a Git repo as declarative config; an automated agent continuously makes the real cluster match it. You never kubectl apply by hand — you change a file, open a PR, and merging is the deploy.
How It Works
Push vs Pull Deployment
Traditional CI pushes changes into the cluster (the pipeline has cluster credentials and runs apply). GitOps flips it: an agent inside the cluster pulls the desired state from Git and reconciles continuously.
StepWhat Happens
1. DeclareDesired state (Kubernetes manifests, Helm, Terraform) is committed to Git.
2. ObserveAn in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) watches the repo.
3. DiffIt compares Git (desired) against the live cluster (actual).
4. ReconcileIt applies changes to close the gap — automatically and continuously.
Reference
Why Teams Adopt It
BenefitDetail
Git is the audit logEvery change is a reviewed, attributed, revertible commit. Rollback = git revert.
No config driftThe agent fixes manual/out-of-band changes automatically — the cluster can't silently diverge.
Better securityCI no longer needs cluster credentials; the pull agent lives inside and reaches out.
ReproducibleRebuild an entire environment from the repo — great for DR and new clusters.
Practical
Tools & Gotchas
PointDetail
ToolsArgo CD and Flux are the two dominant Kubernetes GitOps agents.
SecretsYou can't commit plaintext secrets — use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external secrets operator.
Repo layoutCommon pattern: separate app-code repos from a config repo; a merge to config triggers the deploy.
Fits declarative bestGitOps assumes a system that reconciles to a declared state (Kubernetes shines); imperative steps fit less cleanly.
💰 FinOps — Cloud Cost Management Cloud ▶
Concept
The Cloud Bill Is a Team Sport
In the data-center era, capacity was a big upfront purchase the finance team controlled. In the cloud, any engineer can spin up expensive resources in seconds — and the bill is pay-as-you-go and variable. FinOps is the practice of bringing financial accountability to that model: giving engineers cost visibility, so the people who create spend can make informed trade-offs between speed, quality, and cost. It's a culture, not just a dashboard.
Framework
Inform → Optimize → Operate
PhaseWhat You Do
InformMake cost visible & attributable — tag resources, allocate spend to teams/products, show dashboards.
OptimizeCut waste — rightsize, delete idle resources, buy commitments, pick cheaper options.
OperateMake it continuous — budgets, alerts, and cost as a normal engineering metric.
Reference
Where the Savings Are
LeverWhat It Means
RightsizingMatch instance size to real usage — most VMs are wildly overprovisioned.
Kill idle / zombiesUnattached disks, idle load balancers, forgotten dev environments burn money 24/7.
CommitmentsReserved Instances / Savings Plans trade a 1–3 yr commitment for ~30–70% off steady workloads.
Spot instancesSpare capacity at up to ~90% off — for fault-tolerant, interruptible jobs.
AutoscalingScale to demand (and to zero) instead of provisioning for peak always-on.
Storage tieringMove cold data to cheaper classes; set lifecycle rules.
Egress awarenessData transfer out is a sneaky cost — cross-region/cross-cloud traffic adds up.
Practice
Habits That Keep Costs Sane
HabitWhy
Tag everythingWithout tags for team/env/product, you can't attribute spend or find waste.
Budgets & anomaly alertsCatch a runaway job or a misconfigured autoscaler before the invoice does.
Unit economicsTrack cost per customer / per request, not just the total — growth should scale efficiently.
Right time to optimizeDon't micro-optimize a tiny bill; focus effort where spend is largest.
🤖 SOAR — Security Orchestration, Automation & Response SecOps ▶
Concept
Automating the SOC's Busywork
A security team drowns in alerts — thousands a day, most of them the same repetitive triage: look up an IP's reputation, check if a user clicked the phishing link, isolate a host. SOAR platforms automate those workflows with playbooks: codified, if-this-then-that response procedures that run in seconds instead of an analyst doing 20 manual steps. The goal is to let humans focus on the hard decisions and let machines handle the rote work.
Reference
The Three Letters
CapabilityWhat It Does
OrchestrationConnect all your security tools (SIEM, EDR, firewall, threat intel, ticketing) so they act together via APIs.
AutomationRun response steps without a human — enrich an alert, block an IP, disable an account.
ResponseManage the incident end to end — case tracking, timelines, and collaboration.
Example
A Phishing Playbook
# Trigger: a user reports a suspicious email
1. Extract URLs, attachments, sender from the email
2. Enrich → check URL/hash against threat intel (VirusTotal, etc.)
3. IF malicious:
     - Search mail server for other copies → quarantine them
     - Check who else clicked (proxy/EDR logs)
     - Reset creds / isolate any host that visited the link
4. Open a case, attach all evidence, notify the analyst
5. ELSE: close as false positive with a note
Steps 1–2 and 5 run fully automatically; the risky containment in step 3 can require a human approval gate — a common "automate enrichment, gate the destructive action" pattern.
Reference
SOAR vs SIEM & What to Watch
Detail
SIEM findsCollects & correlates logs to detect and alert.
SOAR actsTakes those alerts and responds via playbooks. They're complementary — SIEM feeds SOAR.
PayoffLower MTTR (mean time to respond), consistent handling, less analyst burnout.
Watch outAutomating a bad decision at machine speed scales the mistake. Start with enrichment, gate containment, and test playbooks carefully.
📈 Load & Performance Testing Reliability ▶
Concept
Find the Breaking Point Before Your Users Do
A system that's fast for one user can collapse for ten thousand. Performance testing simulates realistic (and unrealistic) traffic to answer questions you can't answer by clicking around: How many users can we handle? Where's the bottleneck — CPU, database, a single service? What happens at 2× expected peak? You'd much rather learn this in a test than during a product launch or a viral moment.
Reference
Types of Test
TestQuestion It Answers
LoadHow does it behave at expected peak traffic?
StressWhere does it break, and how? (Push past capacity.)
SpikeCan it survive a sudden traffic surge (a launch, a link going viral)?
Soak / enduranceDoes it degrade over hours/days? (Catches memory leaks, resource exhaustion.)
ScalabilityDoes adding servers actually increase throughput linearly?
Metrics
Measure Percentiles, Not Averages
The classic mistake is reporting average latency. Averages hide pain: if 99% of requests are 50 ms but 1% take 5 seconds, the average looks fine while your worst-affected users suffer. Report percentiles.
MetricMeaning
ThroughputRequests/sec the system handles (RPS).
Latency p50 / p95 / p99The value below which 50/95/99% of requests fall. p99 = your unluckiest 1%.
Error rate% of failed requests — watch it climb as load rises.
SaturationHow full the resources are (CPU, memory, connections) — the leading indicator of trouble.
Practice
Doing It Well
GuidelineWhy
Test like productionRealistic data volumes and traffic mix — a test on an empty DB lies.
Ramp up graduallyIncrease load in steps to see where metrics bend, not just where they snap.
Watch the whole stackCorrelate the test with server metrics/traces to find which component is the bottleneck.
Mind the environmentA scaled-down staging env gives relative, not absolute, numbers. Note the difference.
Toolsk6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust generate the traffic; pair with your observability stack.
♾️ What DevOps Actually Is — Culture Over Tools DevOps ▶
Concept
Breaking the Wall Between Dev and Ops
DevOps isn't a job title or a toolchain — it's a culture that removes the traditional wall between developers (who want to ship change) and operations (who want stability). The mantra is "you build it, you run it": the team that writes the code also operates it, so quality and reliability become everyone's job, not a handoff. Tools (CI/CD, IaC, containers) enable it, but adopting them without the culture just automates the old dysfunction faster.
▸ CALMS — THE FIVE PILLARS
PillarMeans
CultureShared ownership, blameless learning, collaboration over silos
AutomationAutomate the repetitive path (build, test, deploy, infra)
LeanSmall batches, remove waste, optimize flow end-to-end
MeasurementInstrument everything; decide with data (see DORA)
SharingOpen knowledge, feedback, and tooling across teams
🔁 The Three Ways — Flow, Feedback, Learning DevOps ▶
Concept
The Principles Behind DevOps (The DevOps Handbook)
The Three Ways are the underlying principles all DevOps practices derive from — a useful lens for judging why a practice helps.
WayPrinciplePractices
1. FlowSpeed work left→right (dev→prod)Small batches, CI/CD, limit WIP, remove bottlenecks
2. FeedbackFast signal right→leftMonitoring, automated tests, alerting, stop-the-line on failure
3. LearningContinual experimentationBlameless postmortems, chaos drills, psychological safety
Flow gets change out fast; feedback catches problems fast; learning makes the system better over time. Skip feedback and you ship bugs faster; skip learning and you repeat incidents.
📊 DORA Metrics — Measuring Delivery Performance DevOps ▶
Reference
The Four Numbers That Predict Elite Teams
The DORA (DevOps Research & Assessment) research found four metrics that correlate with high-performing organizations. Crucially, speed and stability rise together — elite teams deploy more often and break less. If you measure one thing about delivery, measure these.
MetricQuestionElite
Deploy frequencyHow often do you ship?On-demand / many per day
Lead time for changeCommit → production?< 1 day
Change failure rate% of deploys causing a problem0–15%
MTTRTime to restore after an incident< 1 hour
First two = throughput; last two = stability. (A fifth, reliability, was later added.) Use them as a trend, not a stick — gaming "deploy frequency" by shipping trivial changes helps no one.
🗺️ Value Stream Mapping — Find the Bottleneck DevOps ▶
Concept
Where Does the Time Actually Go?
A value stream map traces every step from idea to production, recording for each: process time (actual work) vs wait time (queued, waiting for approval/review/ environment). The revelation is almost always that waiting dwarfs working — a code change might take 2 hours to write and 2 weeks to ship, stuck in queues. You improve flow by attacking the biggest wait, not by making developers type faster.
%C/A (percent complete & accurate) at each step reveals rework loops — if QA sends 40% back, that handoff is your real problem. Map it, find the fattest wait/rework, fix that, remap. It's the Lean tool DevOps borrowed to make "optimize flow" concrete.
🛝 Platform Engineering & the Internal Developer Platform DevOps ▶
Concept
Paving a Golden Path So Every Team Doesn't Reinvent It
"You build it, you run it" can overload product teams with infra complexity — Kubernetes, pipelines, secrets, observability, all per team. Platform engineering answers this by building an Internal Developer Platform (IDP): a self-service layer that packages the infra into golden paths, so a developer can provision a service, database, and pipeline with a form or a CLI command — without becoming a cloud expert.
PrincipleDetail
Self-serviceDevelopers get what they need without filing tickets
Golden pathsPaved, opinionated defaults that are easy to follow and secure by default
Product mindsetThe platform team treats developers as customers (adoption, not mandate)
Not a rename of opsIt's a product, not a gatekeeper — paved roads, not roadblocks
Tools in the space: Backstage (developer portal), Crossplane/Terraform (provisioning), Port/Humanitec (IDP orchestration).
🏭 CI/CD Pipeline Design — Stages, Gates & Artifacts DevOps ▶
Concept
The Assembly Line From Commit to Production
A pipeline runs a series of stages on every change, each a quality gate that must pass before the next. Build once, produce an immutable artifact, and promote that same artifact through environments — never rebuild per stage, or you're testing something different than you ship.
StageGate
BuildCompiles; produces the artifact (jar, image)
TestUnit + integration pass; coverage threshold
ScanSAST/SCA/secrets clean (fail on high sev)
Deploy → stagingSmoke/e2e tests green
Deploy → prodManual approval or automated canary
CI = integrate + test every change automatically. CD = that artifact is always deployable (Continuous Delivery) or actually auto-deployed (Continuous Deployment). Keep pipelines fast — a 40-minute pipeline kills the feedback loop.
🎬 GitHub Actions — Workflows, Jobs & Secrets DevOps ▶
How-To
CI/CD Built Into Your Repo
GitHub Actions runs YAML workflows in .github/workflows/ triggered by events (push, PR, schedule). A workflow has jobs (run in parallel by default) made of steps (shell commands or reusable actions). 
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix: { node: [18, 20] }   # test on multiple versions
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '${{ matrix.node }}' }
      - run: npm ci && npm test
      - run: deploy.sh
        env: { TOKEN: '${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}' }
ConceptDetail
MatrixRun the job across a combination of versions/OSes
Secrets${{ secrets.X }} — never hard-code creds
Reusable/compositeFactor shared steps into called workflows/actions
OIDCAssume a cloud role with no stored keys (ties to IAM)
🔧 Jenkins · GitLab CI · CircleCI — The Landscape DevOps ▶
Reference
Which CI Tool, and Why
ToolCharacter
GitHub ActionsNative to GitHub, huge marketplace — the default for GitHub repos
GitLab CIDeeply integrated with GitLab; one .gitlab-ci.yml; strong self-hosted story
JenkinsThe veteran — infinitely pluggable, self-hosted, but you maintain it (Jenkinsfile/Groovy)
CircleCI / Travis / DroneHosted CI, config-as-YAML, fast setup
Argo / TektonKubernetes-native pipelines (GitOps-friendly)
They all share the model — YAML/DSL pipeline, runners/agents, stages, artifacts, secrets. Learn the concepts once; the syntax is a lookup. Pick by where your code lives and whether you want hosted vs self-managed.
🌿 Branching Strategies — Trunk vs GitHub Flow vs GitFlow DevOps ▶
Concept
How Your Team Moves Code to Main
StrategyHowFits
Trunk-basedEveryone commits to main behind feature flags; tiny short-lived branchesHigh-velocity CD; elite DORA teams
GitHub FlowBranch → PR → review → merge → deploy mainMost web teams; simple & effective
GitFlowLong-lived develop/release/hotfix branchesVersioned/released software; heavier
The trend is toward trunk-based: long-lived branches cause painful merges and delay integration (the opposite of "continuous integration"). Short-lived branches + feature flags let you merge constantly and release independently of deploy.
🚦 Progressive Delivery — Flags + Canary in the Pipeline DevOps ▶
Concept
Release ≠ Deploy
Progressive delivery separates deploy (code is on the servers) from release (users see it), and ramps exposure gradually so a bad change hits few people. It stitches together patterns you already know into the pipeline.
TechniqueRole
Feature flagsShip code dark; toggle on for cohorts at runtime
CanaryRoute 1% → 10% → 100% while watching metrics
Blue-greenInstant switch + instant rollback
Automated rollbackBad canary metrics → pipeline reverts automatically
Tools: LaunchDarkly/Unleash/Flagsmith (flags), Argo Rollouts/Flagger (automated canary on Kubernetes). This is how elite teams deploy dozens of times a day with a low change-failure rate — the two DORA goals reconciled.
🐳 Docker Deep — Multi-Stage Builds & Image Slimming DevOps ▶
How-To
Small, Fast, Secure Images
A naive Dockerfile produces bloated, slow, insecure images. Two techniques fix most of it: multi-stage builds (build in a fat image, copy only the artifact into a tiny final image) and layer caching (order instructions so dependencies cache across builds). 
# Stage 1: build
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.* ./
RUN go mod download        # cached unless go.* changes
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app

# Stage 2: tiny runtime — just the binary
FROM gcr.io/distroless/base
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
TechniqueWin
Multi-stageMB-sized final image, no build tools shipped
Distroless / AlpineMinimal base = smaller attack surface
Layer orderCopy deps before source → fast rebuilds
Non-root USERDon't run containers as root
.dockerignoreKeep secrets/junk out of the build context
☸️ Kubernetes Objects — The Ones You Actually Use DevOps ▶
Reference
The Building Blocks of a Deployment
Kubernetes has dozens of object types, but day-to-day you use a handful. They compose: a Deployment manages Pods; a Service gives them a stable address; an Ingress routes external traffic in.
ObjectRole
PodThe smallest unit — one or more containers sharing network/storage
DeploymentManages a replicated, self-healing set of Pods + rolling updates
ServiceStable virtual IP/DNS load-balancing to a set of Pods
IngressHTTP(S) routing from outside into Services
ConfigMap / SecretConfig & credentials injected into Pods
StatefulSetPods with stable identity/storage (databases)
NamespaceVirtual cluster for isolation/multi-tenancy
Everything is declarative YAML reconciled to desired state — you describe what you want; the controllers make it so (kubectl apply -f).
⎈ Helm & Kustomize — Packaging Manifests DevOps ▶
Reference
Stop Copy-Pasting YAML Per Environment
Raw manifests don't scale across dev/staging/prod. Two tools solve it differently: Helm templates manifests with variables into reusable "charts" (the K8s package manager); Kustomize layers overlays that patch a common base — no templating language.
HelmKustomize
ApproachTemplating + values.yamlBase + overlay patches
PackagingCharts, repos, releases, rollbackNo packaging
ComplexityPowerful but templating can get gnarlySimple, YAML-native (built into kubectl)
Best forDistributing apps (Postgres, nginx)Your own app across environments
🔒 Kubernetes Security — RBAC, Network Policies & Pod Security DevOps ▶
Reference
A Cluster Is Insecure by Default
Out of the box, K8s is permissive — pods can talk to everything, run as root, and service accounts may be over-privileged. Hardening is a checklist every production cluster needs.
ControlDoes
RBACLeast-privilege for users & service accounts (who can do what)
Network PoliciesDefault-deny pod-to-pod traffic; allow only what's needed
Pod Security StandardsBlock root, privileged, host mounts (restricted profile)
Admission controlOPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno enforce policy at deploy time
Image scanningTrivy/Grype in CI; only signed images (see supply chain)
SecretsEncrypt at rest (etcd); external secrets operators
This is where the Red Team's "Kubernetes attacks" meet defense — RBAC abuse and container escape are exactly what these controls stop.
⚙️ Configuration Management — Ansible & the Alternatives Config Mgmt ▶
Reference
Make Servers Match a Desired State
Config management enforces how a server is set up — packages, files, services, users — declaratively and repeatably. Ansible dominates because it's agentless (just SSH + Python) and its YAML playbooks are readable. 
# A tiny playbook: install & start nginx, idempotently
- hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt: { name: nginx, state: present }
    - name: Ensure it is running
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }
ToolModel
AnsibleAgentless, push, YAML — easiest to adopt
Puppet / ChefAgent-based, pull, mature at large scale
SaltAgent or agentless; very fast event bus
Idempotency is the whole point: run it 100 times, the box ends in the same state. Config management handles mutable servers; it complements Terraform (which provisions the infra) — ties to the IaC card.
🔐 Secrets Management — Vault & Kubernetes Secrets Secrets ▶
Concept
Stop Putting Passwords in Git
Hardcoded credentials are one of the most common breach causes. A secrets manager stores them centrally, encrypted, with access control and audit — and the best systems issue short-lived, dynamic creds so a leak expires on its own.
ApproachDetail
HashiCorp VaultCentral secrets + dynamic DB/cloud creds + encryption-as-a-service
Cloud-nativeAWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault
External Secrets OperatorSync a manager's secrets into K8s Secrets
Sealed Secrets / SOPSEncrypt secrets so they're safe to commit to Git (GitOps)
Note: plain Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default — enable encryption providers and prefer a real manager. Dynamic short-TTL creds beat static ones every time.
🔗 Software Supply Chain Security — SBOM, SLSA & Sigstore Supply Chain ▶
Concept
Know & Trust What You Ship
After SolarWinds and Log4Shell, securing the build pipeline itself is a first-class concern. The goal: know every component in your artifact, and prove the artifact came from your pipeline unmodified.
