The OS is the manager between you and the hardware — it hands out memory, runs programs, and talks to the disk and network. Windows, macOS, and Linux are all operating systems; Linux runs most of the servers on the Internet.
ANALOGY
The Terminal Isn't Scary
The terminal (or shell) is just a text way to give commands instead of clicking. Typing 'copy this file there' can be faster and more exact than dragging icons. The blinking prompt is simply asking 'what next?'
MENTAL MODEL
Everything Is a File
In Linux, your documents, your devices, even some settings are all treated as files in one big tree that starts at / (the root). Learn to move around that tree and you've learned half of Linux.
GOTCHA
Case & Spaces Matter
'Report.txt' and 'report.txt' are different files, and a space can confuse a command. Beginners trip on this constantly — when something 'isn't found,' check capitalization and spelling first.
CommandSays…Like…
pwdWhere am I?Checking your current room
lsWhat's here?Looking around the room
cd folderGo insideWalking through a door
cp / mvCopy / moveDuplicating or relocating
cat fileShow contentsReading the page out loud
man cmdShow the manualReading the instructions
🧭Permissions & Packages for NewcomersLinux+ • Start Here▶
WHO CAN DO WHAT
Read, Write, Execute
Every file says what three groups may do with it: the owner, the group, and everyone else. The three powers are read (look), write (change), and execute (run it as a program). ‘rwx’ is just those three letters.
ADMIN MODE
sudo = “do this as admin”
Normal users can’t break the whole system by accident — a safety feature. Putting sudo in front of a command says “I really mean it, run this with admin power.” Use it deliberately; with great power comes great rm -rf.
sudo apt update      # run as administrator
chmod +x script.sh   # make a file runnable
APP STORE FOR THE TERMINAL
Package Managers
You don’t download installers in Linux — a package manager fetches, installs, and updates software from trusted repositories, handling all the pieces it depends on. apt (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf (Fedora), and pacman (Arch) are the common ones.
You Want To…Command (Ubuntu/Debian)
Refresh the catalogsudo apt update
Install a programsudo apt install name
Update everythingsudo apt upgrade
Remove a programsudo apt remove name
Search for oneapt search keyword
📜 Shell Scripting — Automate Repetitive Work LINUX • Practical ▶
WHAT IS A SHELL SCRIPT
A File Full of Commands
A shell script is a plain text file with a list of commands that the shell runs in order. Anything you can type at the prompt, you can put in a script. Scripts automate backups, deployments, user creation, log parsing — anything tedious and repeated.
YOUR FIRST SCRIPT
Hello World in Bash
#!/bin/bash # The shebang line tells the OS which interpreter to use echo "Hello, World!" echo "Today is $(date)" # $() runs a command and inserts output
Make it executable: chmod +x hello.sh
Run it: ./hello.sh
VARIABLES & INPUT
Storing and Reading Values
#!/bin/bash # Variables (no spaces around =) name="Alice" count=5 echo "Name: $name, Count: $count" # Read user input read -p "Enter your name: " username echo "Hello, $username!" # Command-line arguments echo "Script: $0" # script name echo "Arg 1: $1" # first argument echo "All args: $@" # all arguments echo "Count: $#" # number of arguments
CONDITIONALS & LOOPS
If/Else and For in Bash
#!/bin/bash # If statement if [ -f "/etc/passwd" ]; then echo "File exists" elif [ -d "/etc/passwd" ]; then echo "It's a directory" else echo "Not found" fi # For loop over a list for fruit in apple banana cherry; do echo "I like $fruit" done # For loop over files for file in /var/log/*.log; do echo "Processing: $file" done # While loop i=1 while [ $i -le 5 ]; do echo "Count: $i" ((i++)) done
TEST OPERATORS
Common [ ] Conditions
TestMeaning
[ -f file ]File exists and is a regular file
[ -d dir ]Directory exists
[ -z "$var" ]String is empty
[ -n "$var" ]String is not empty
[ "$a" = "$b" ]Strings are equal
[ $x -eq $y ]Numbers are equal
[ $x -gt $y ]x is greater than y
[ $x -lt $y ]x is less than y
[ ! condition ]NOT (negate)
FUNCTIONS
Reusable Blocks in Bash
#!/bin/bash # Define a function greet() { local name="$1" # local vars don't leak echo "Hello, $name!" } # Function that returns a value via exit code is_root() { [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] } greet "Alice" greet "Bob" if is_root; then echo "Running as root" fi
⏰ Cron Jobs — Scheduling Tasks in Linux LINUX • Ops ▶
WHAT IS CRON
Linux's Built-In Task Scheduler
Cron is a daemon (background service) that runs commands on a schedule. It reads configuration files called crontabs that list when and what to run. Use cases: backups, log rotation, report generation, health checks, certificate renewal.
CRONTAB SYNTAX
Five Fields + Command
# Cron format: # ┌─── minute (0-59) # │ ┌─── hour (0-23) # │ │ ┌─── day of month (1-31) # │ │ │ ┌─── month (1-12) # │ │ │ │ ┌─── day of week (0-7, 0=Sun) # │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * command_to_run # Run backup every day at 2am 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh # Run every 15 minutes */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/check.sh # Run every Monday at 9am 0 9 * * 1 /usr/local/bin/weekly-report.sh # Run 1st of every month at midnight 0 0 1 * * /usr/local/bin/monthly-cleanup.sh
MANAGING CRONTABS
crontab Commands
# Edit YOUR crontab (opens in default editor) crontab -e # List your cron jobs crontab -l # Remove all your cron jobs (dangerous!) crontab -r # Edit another user's crontab (root only) crontab -u username -e # System-wide cron directory (any executable file runs) ls /etc/cron.daily/ ls /etc/cron.weekly/ ls /etc/cron.monthly/
COMMON GOTCHAS
Why Cron Jobs Silently Fail
• Cron uses a minimal environment — PATH is different from your login shell. Use absolute paths everywhere (/usr/bin/python3 not just python3).
• Redirect output or you'll never see errors: command >> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1
• File permissions — the script must be executable: chmod +x script.sh
• Use crontab.guru (online) to build and verify expressions before deploying.
⚙️ Processes & Signals — Running Programs in Linux LINUX • Foundation ▶
WHAT IS A PROCESS
A Running Program with an ID
When you run a program, the kernel creates a process — an isolated execution environment with its own memory, file handles, and PID (Process ID). The first process is init or systemd (PID 1). Every process has a parent.
VIEWING PROCESSES
ps, top, htop
# Snapshot of all running processes ps aux # Process tree (parent-child relationships) pstree # Find a process by name pgrep nginx ps aux | grep nginx # Live process monitor (like Task Manager) top htop # nicer version, install with: apt install htop # See what a process has open lsof -p PID
SIGNALS
Talking to Processes
Signals are messages sent to processes. The kernel or another process sends them; the receiving process handles (or ignores) them.
SignalNumberDefault ActionCommon Use
SIGTERM15TerminatePolite kill — let process clean up
SIGKILL9Kill immediatelyForce kill — cannot be caught or ignored
SIGHUP1Hang upReload config (nginx, sshd use this)
SIGINT2InterruptWhat Ctrl+C sends
SIGSTOP19PauseWhat Ctrl+Z sends
SIGCONT18ContinueResume a paused process
# Polite stop (give process time to clean up) kill -15 PID kill PID # same — SIGTERM is default # Force kill (last resort) kill -9 PID # Kill all processes named "python3" pkill python3 # Reload nginx config without downtime kill -HUP $(pgrep nginx)
BACKGROUND & FOREGROUND
Job Control
# Run in background from the start python3 server.py & # Ctrl+Z pauses a foreground process # bg resumes it in background bg %1 # fg brings background job to foreground fg %1 # List background jobs jobs # Keep running after logout (nohup) nohup python3 server.py > server.log 2>&1 &
⚙️ systemd — Managing Linux Services LINUX • Ops ▶
WHAT IS SYSTEMD
PID 1 — The Init System
systemd is the first process started by the kernel (PID 1) and the parent of all other processes. It manages:
• Starting/stopping services (daemons)
• Parallel boot for faster startup
• Service dependencies and ordering
• Logging (journald)
• Socket activation, timers (replacement for cron), mounts
systemctl COMMANDS
Start, Stop, Enable, Status
# Service status systemctl status nginx systemctl status ssh # Start / stop / restart sudo systemctl start nginx sudo systemctl stop nginx sudo systemctl restart nginx # Reload config without full restart sudo systemctl reload nginx # Enable at boot / disable sudo systemctl enable nginx sudo systemctl disable nginx # Enable AND start immediately sudo systemctl enable --now nginx # List all running services systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running # List failed services systemctl --failed
JOURNALCTL
Reading Service Logs
# All logs (most recent at bottom) journalctl # Logs for a specific service journalctl -u nginx journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" # Follow in real time (like tail -f) journalctl -u nginx -f # Only errors and above journalctl -p err # Since last boot journalctl -b # From a time range journalctl --since "2024-01-15 09:00" --until "2024-01-15 10:00"
WRITE A UNIT FILE
Run Your Script as a Service
# Create /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service [Unit] Description=My Python Application After=network.target [Service] Type=simple User=www-data WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/myapp/server.py Restart=always RestartSec=5 StandardOutput=journal StandardError=journal [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target
# Reload systemd, start, enable sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
💾 Disk Management — Partitions, Filesystems & LVM LINUX • Foundation ▶
CHECK DISK USAGE
df and du — Your First Diagnostic
# Disk space by filesystem df -h # Where is space being used in a directory? du -sh /var/log/* # sizes in human readable du -sh /* 2>/dev/null # top-level dirs # Find the 10 largest files find / -type f -printf '%s %p ' 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head -10 # What files are open (and may not show freed space) lsof +L1 | grep deleted
PARTITIONS
Dividing Physical Disks
A partition divides a physical disk into logical sections. Common layout:
/boot — kernel and boot files (~500MB)
/ — root filesystem (everything else)
/home — user data (separate so OS reinstall preserves data)
swap — overflow memory (RAM extension on disk; slow)
Tools: fdisk (MBR), gdisk (GPT), parted (both)
FILESYSTEMS
How Data Is Organized on Disk
FilesystemOSStrengths
ext4LinuxDefault Linux; journaled; stable; 16TB max file
xfsLinuxHigh-performance; great for large files; RHEL default
btrfsLinuxCopy-on-write; snapshots; checksums; still maturing
NTFSWindowsWindows default; full permissions; mountable on Linux
FAT32/exFATUniversalUSB drives; read/write anywhere; no permissions
APFSmacOSApple default; encrypted; snapshot support
ZFSBSD/LinuxEnterprise; built-in RAID; checksums; snapshots
🐳 Docker & Containers — Package Once, Run Anywhere LINUX • Modern Ops ▶
WHAT IS A CONTAINER
Isolated Process, Not a Full VM
A container packages your app + its dependencies + runtime into one portable unit. It shares the host OS kernel (unlike a VM which has its own). Result: starts in milliseconds, uses far less memory than a VM, runs identically everywhere. "Works on my machine" is solved — because you ship the machine.
CONTAINER vs VM
Isolation Trade-offs
ContainerVM
StartupMillisecondsMinutes
Memory overheadMBsGBs
IsolationProcess-level (shares kernel)Full OS isolation
SecurityLower (kernel shared)Higher (separate kernel)
PortabilityVery highHigh (but larger images)
BASIC DOCKER COMMANDS
Pull, Run, List, Stop, Remove
# Pull an image from Docker Hub docker pull ubuntu:22.04 docker pull nginx:latest # Run a container docker run nginx # foreground docker run -d nginx # detached (background) docker run -it ubuntu bash # interactive terminal # Port mapping (host:container) docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx # localhost:8080 → container:80 # List running containers docker ps docker ps -a # including stopped # Logs docker logs container_id docker logs -f container_id # follow # Stop, start, remove docker stop container_id docker start container_id docker rm container_id # Get a shell in a running container docker exec -it container_id bash
DOCKERFILE
Recipe to Build Your Image
# Dockerfile — simple Python app FROM python:3.12-slim # base image WORKDIR /app # working directory inside container COPY requirements.txt . # copy deps first (cache layers) RUN pip install -r requirements.txt COPY . . # then copy app code ENV PORT=8080 # environment variable EXPOSE 8080 # document port (doesn't publish) CMD ["python3", "app.py"] # default command
# Build the image docker build -t myapp:latest . # Run it docker run -d -p 8080:8080 myapp:latest
DOCKER COMPOSE
Multi-Container Applications
# docker-compose.yml version: "3.9" services: web: build: . ports: - "8080:8080" environment: - DB_HOST=db depends_on: - db db: image: postgres:16 environment: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: devpassword POSTGRES_DB: myapp volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data volumes: pgdata:
# Start all services docker compose up -d # Stop all services docker compose down # View logs for all services docker compose logs -f
✂️ AWK & sed — The Text Processing Powerhouses LINUX • Power Tools ▶
SED
Stream Editor — Find and Replace on Steroids
# Basic substitution (first occurrence per line) sed 's/old/new/' file.txt # Global (all occurrences) sed 's/old/new/g' file.txt # In-place edit (BACKUP FIRST!) sed -i 's/localhost/192.168.1.5/g' config.txt sed -i.bak 's/localhost/192.168.1.5/g' config.txt # with .bak backup # Delete lines matching pattern sed '/^#/d' config.txt # remove comment lines sed '/^$/d' file.txt # remove empty lines # Print specific line numbers sed -n '10,20p' file.txt # lines 10-20 # Insert text before/after line sed '5i\New line above' file.txt # insert before line 5 sed '5a\New line below' file.txt # append after line 5
AWK
Field-Based Text Processing
AWK processes text line-by-line, splitting each line into fields ($1, $2, ..., $NF = last field). Powerful for structured text like logs and CSV files.
# Print specific columns from a log awk '{print $1, $4}' access.log # IP and timestamp # Sum the 5th column awk '{sum += $5} END {print "Total:", sum}' data.txt # Filter: print lines where 3rd field > 1000 awk '$3 > 1000 {print $0}' data.txt # Print with custom delimiter awk -F':' '{print $1, $6}' /etc/passwd # username, home dir # Count unique values in column 1 awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (k in count) print count[k], k}' log.txt | sort -rn | head -10 # Process CSV: print name,email from CSV with header awk -F',' 'NR > 1 {print $2, $3}' users.csv
CUT, SORT, UNIQ
The Classic Pipeline Trio
# cut: extract columns by delimiter cut -d':' -f1,3 /etc/passwd # username and UID cut -d',' -f1,2 data.csv # first two CSV columns # sort: alphabetically or numerically sort names.txt # A-Z sort -r names.txt # Z-A sort -n numbers.txt # numeric sort sort -t':' -k3 -n /etc/passwd # sort by 3rd field numerically sort -u names.txt # sort and remove duplicates # uniq: collapse adjacent duplicate lines sort log.txt | uniq # must sort first! sort log.txt | uniq -c # count occurrences sort log.txt | uniq -d # only show duplicates # Classic combo: most common IPs in access log awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
👥 User & Group Management — Who Can Do What in Linux LINUX • Admin ▶
USERS & GROUPS
The Linux Identity Model
Every file and process has an owner (user) and a group. Permissions are set for: owner, group, and everyone else. UID 0 is root — the superuser with no restrictions. UIDs below 1000 are typically system accounts; 1000+ are human users.
USER MANAGEMENT COMMANDS
Create, Modify, Delete
# Create user sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice # -m creates home, -s sets shell sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin svc # system account, no login # Set/change password sudo passwd alice # Modify user sudo usermod -aG sudo alice # add to sudo group sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh alice # change shell sudo usermod -L alice # lock account sudo usermod -U alice # unlock account # Delete user sudo userdel alice # keep home dir sudo userdel -r alice # also remove home dir # View user info id alice # UID, GID, groups groups alice # group memberships finger alice # detailed info (if installed) who # who is currently logged in last alice # login history
SUDO
Controlled Privilege Escalation
sudo lets authorized users run commands as root (or another user) without knowing root's password. The /etc/sudoers file controls who can use sudo and what they can run. Always edit with visudo — it validates syntax before saving (a broken sudoers file locks you out).
# Common sudoers entries (in /etc/sudoers) alice ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL # full sudo bob ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart nginx # one command only %ops ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL # entire group ops # Check what you can run sudo -l # Run as different user sudo -u www-data whoami
📦 Package Management — Installing and Managing Software LINUX • Essential ▶
THE BIG PICTURE
How Linux Software Installation Works
Unlike Windows (download .exe, double-click) or Mac (drag to Applications), Linux uses package managers — tools that download software from trusted repositories, handle dependencies automatically, and keep everything updated consistently. Different Linux distributions use different package managers.
Distro FamilyExamplesPackage ManagerFile Format
DebianUbuntu, Mint, Kali, Raspberry Pi OSapt.deb
Red HatRHEL, CentOS, Fedora, Rocky, AlmaLinuxdnf (old: yum).rpm
ArchArch Linux, Manjaro, EndeavourOSpacman.pkg.tar.zst
openSUSEopenSUSE Leap/Tumbleweedzypper.rpm
UniversalAny distrosnap, flatpak, AppImageVarious
APT COMMANDS
Debian/Ubuntu Package Manager
apt (Advanced Package Tool) manages software on Debian-based systems. Always run apt update first to refresh the list of available packages before installing.
# Update package index (does NOT upgrade software) sudo apt update # Upgrade all installed packages sudo apt upgrade -y # Install a package sudo apt install nginx sudo apt install -y git curl wget tree # -y skips confirmation # Remove a package (keep config files) sudo apt remove nginx # Remove package AND its config files sudo apt purge nginx # Remove unused dependencies sudo apt autoremove # Search for a package apt search nmap apt-cache search "web server" # Show package info apt show nginx # List installed packages apt list --installed dpkg -l | grep nginx # check if specific package installed # Full system update (one-liner) sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y && sudo apt autoremove -y
DNF / YUM COMMANDS
Red Hat Family Package Manager
# dnf is the modern replacement for yum (same concepts) sudo dnf update # update package index AND upgrade sudo dnf install httpd # install (httpd = nginx equivalent) sudo dnf remove httpd # uninstall sudo dnf search nginx sudo dnf info nginx sudo dnf list installed # Enable EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux) sudo dnf install epel-release # unlocks many extra packages
SNAP & FLATPAK
Universal Package Formats
Snap and Flatpak are universal package formats that bundle all dependencies — they run the same on any Linux distro. Useful for software not in your distro's repos, or for getting the latest version of an app.
# SNAP (Canonical/Ubuntu's universal packages) sudo snap install code --classic # VS Code snap list # list installed snaps snap find "media player" sudo snap refresh code # update specific snap sudo snap remove code # FLATPAK (community alternative, works on all distros) flatpak install flathub com.spotify.Client flatpak run com.spotify.Client flatpak list flatpak update # APPIMAGE (no install needed — just download and run) chmod +x SomeApp.AppImage # make executable ./SomeApp.AppImage # run directly, no installation
COMPILING FROM SOURCE
When Packages Don't Exist
Sometimes software isn't in any package manager. The classic way is to compile from source code. This requires build tools and is slower, but gives you the exact version you need.
# Install build essentials first sudo apt install build-essential # Ubuntu/Debian sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" # Red Hat # Classic build pattern (configure / make / make install) wget https://example.com/app-1.0.tar.gz tar -xzf app-1.0.tar.gz cd app-1.0 ./configure # checks dependencies, generates Makefile ./configure --prefix=/usr/local # custom install location make # compile (uses all CPU cores with -j4) make -j$(nproc) # parallel compile — much faster sudo make install # copy to system # Clean up make clean # remove compiled objects
✏️ Terminal Text Editors — Editing Files Without a GUI LINUX • Essential ▶
NANO
The Beginner-Friendly Editor
Nano is simple and shows keyboard shortcuts at the bottom of the screen. No modes, no memorizing commands — just type. Perfect when you need to quickly edit a config file.
# Open a file nano /etc/hosts nano filename.txt # Essential shortcuts (^ = Ctrl, M = Alt) Ctrl+O # Save (Write Out) Ctrl+X # Exit (prompts to save if modified) Ctrl+W # Search (Where Is) Ctrl+\ # Find and replace Ctrl+K # Cut line Ctrl+U # Paste (Un-cut) Ctrl+G # Help Alt+U # Undo
VIM SURVIVAL GUIDE
Enough Vim to Get Out Alive
Vim is powerful but modal — different keys do different things depending on which mode you're in. Knowing the basics is essential because many servers only have vi/vim available, and some programs (like git commit without EDITOR set) drop you into vim unexpectedly.
# The famous "how to exit vim" — memorize these first :q # quit (only if no changes) :q! # FORCE quit, discard changes :wq # save and quit :x # save and quit (same as :wq) ZZ # save and quit (in normal mode) # Modes i # → INSERT mode (type text) Esc # → NORMAL mode (navigate/commands) v # → VISUAL mode (select text) : # → COMMAND mode (run :wq, :set, etc.) # Navigation (normal mode) hjkl # left/down/up/right (arrow keys also work) gg # go to first line G # go to last line :50 # go to line 50 # Essential edits (normal mode) dd # delete current line yy # yank (copy) current line p # paste after cursor u # undo /pattern # search forward n # next search result
🔑 Linux Permissions — Who Can Do What, In Depth LINUX • Essential ▶
THE PERMISSION MODEL
Reading rwxr-xr-- at a Glance
Every Linux file has an owner, a group, and a set of permissions for three categories: user (owner), group, and others. Permissions are read (r), write (w), and execute (x). When you run ls -l, the first 10 characters tell the whole story.
# ls -l output explained -rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devs 2048 Jan 15 script.sh ^└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘ └─┬─┘ └┬─┘ │ │ │ │ │ └── group name │ │ │ │ └──────── owner name │ │ │ └── others: r-- (read only) │ │ └───── group: r-x (read + execute) │ └──────── owner: rwx (read + write + execute) └────────── type: - file, d dir, l symlink # Numeric (octal) — each digit is a sum: r=4 w=2 x=1 rwx = 4+2+1 = 7 r-x = 4+0+1 = 5 r-- = 4+0+0 = 4 # So rwxr-xr-- = 754
CHMOD & CHOWN
Changing Permissions and Ownership
# Numeric (octal) mode — set absolute permissions chmod 755 script.sh # rwxr-xr-x (common for scripts) chmod 644 file.txt # rw-r--r-- (common for files) chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa # rw------- (private keys MUST be this) chmod 700 ~/.ssh # rwx------ (private dir) # Symbolic mode — modify relative to current chmod u+x script.sh # add execute for owner chmod g-w file.txt # remove write for group chmod o= secret.txt # remove ALL for others chmod a+r public.txt # add read for all (a = all) chmod -R 755 /var/www # recursive # Change ownership (usually needs sudo) chown alice file.txt # change owner chown alice:devs file.txt # change owner AND group chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www # recursive chgrp devs file.txt # change group only
SPECIAL PERMISSION BITS
SUID, SGID, and the Sticky Bit
Beyond rwx, there are three special bits that change execution and inheritance behavior. These matter for both administration and security (SUID binaries are a classic privilege-escalation target).
BitOctalEffectExample
SUID4000Run file as the FILE's owner, not the runnerpasswd runs as root so users can change their own password
SGID2000On file: run as group. On dir: new files inherit the dir's groupShared project directories
Sticky1000On dir: only the file owner can delete their files/tmp — anyone can write, but can't delete others' files
# Set special bits chmod u+s binary # SUID chmod g+s shared_dir # SGID chmod +t /shared # sticky bit # SECURITY: hunt for SUID binaries (privilege escalation recon) find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
UMASK & ACLs
Default Permissions and Fine-Grained Control
# umask — sets DEFAULT permissions for new files umask # show current (often 022) # New files: 666 - umask. New dirs: 777 - umask # umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755 # ACLs — go beyond owner/group/other for specific users getfacl file.txt # view ACLs setfacl -m u:bob:rw file.txt # give bob read+write setfacl -m g:contractors:r file.txt # give a group read setfacl -x u:bob file.txt # remove bob's ACL # A "+" after permissions in ls -l means ACLs are present
MANDATORY ACCESS CONTROL
SELinux and AppArmor
Standard permissions are Discretionary Access Control (DAC) — owners decide. SELinux (Red Hat) and AppArmor (Ubuntu/SUSE) add Mandatory Access Control (MAC): a system-wide policy enforces what processes can do, regardless of file ownership. Even root is constrained. This contains compromised services — a hacked web server can only touch what its policy allows.
# SELinux (Red Hat family) getenforce # Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled sestatus # detailed status ls -Z file.txt # show SELinux context setenforce 0 # temporarily permissive (testing) # Tip: don't disable SELinux to "fix" an issue — fix the policy # AppArmor (Ubuntu/Debian/SUSE) sudo aa-status # list profiles and their mode sudo aa-complain /path/to/program # log violations, don't block sudo aa-enforce /path/to/program # enforce the profile
🔑 SSH — Secure Remote Access Done Right LINUX • Essential ▶
SSH BASICS
The Universal Remote Access Protocol
SSH (Secure Shell) is how you remotely access and manage Linux/Unix servers over an encrypted connection. It's foundational — every sysadmin, DevOps engineer, and security professional lives in SSH. It replaced the old, insecure Telnet (which sent passwords in plaintext).
# Connect to a server ssh alice@server.example.com ssh -p 2222 alice@server.com # custom port # Run a single command remotely ssh alice@server "df -h" # Copy files over SSH scp file.txt alice@server:/tmp/ # local → remote scp alice@server:/var/log/app.log . # remote → local rsync -avz ./data/ alice@server:/backup/ # efficient sync
KEY-BASED AUTH
Stop Using Passwords — Use Keys
SSH key pairs are far more secure than passwords: a private key (kept secret on your machine) and a public key (placed on servers). Authentication happens via cryptography, not a guessable password. This is THE standard for professional server access.
# Generate a modern key pair (ed25519 preferred) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop" # Creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) and id_ed25519.pub (public) # Copy your PUBLIC key to a server (enables key login) ssh-copy-id alice@server.example.com # Now you can log in without a password ssh alice@server.example.com # Permissions MUST be strict or SSH refuses the key chmod 700 ~/.ssh chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # private key chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # public key # Use ssh-agent so you don't retype the passphrase eval $(ssh-agent) ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
SSH CONFIG
Save Yourself Typing with ~/.ssh/config
# ~/.ssh/config — define shortcuts and defaults Host web HostName web1.example.com User alice Port 2222 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 Host bastion HostName jump.example.com User admin # Reach internal host through the bastion automatically Host internal-db HostName 10.0.5.20 User dbadmin ProxyJump bastion # Now just: ssh web (instead of the full command)
HARDENING SSHD
Locking Down the SSH Server
SSH is the #1 target of automated internet attacks — bots constantly try to brute-force it. Hardening /etc/ssh/sshd_config dramatically reduces risk.
SettingValueWhy
PermitRootLoginnoForce use of named accounts + sudo (accountability + harder to brute-force)
PasswordAuthenticationnoKeys only — defeats password brute-forcing entirely
PubkeyAuthenticationyesEnable key-based auth
Port2222 (non-standard)Reduces noise from automated bots (not real security, just quieter)
AllowUsersalice bobWhitelist who can SSH in
MaxAuthTries3Limit guesses per connection
# Apply changes safely sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config sudo sshd -t # test config syntax FIRST sudo systemctl restart sshd # Add fail2ban to auto-ban brute-forcers sudo apt install fail2ban # Bans IPs after repeated failed logins
🥾 Boot Process & Logs — Understanding How Linux Starts and Speaks LINUX • Essential ▶
THE BOOT SEQUENCE
From Power Button to Login Prompt
Knowing the boot sequence helps you troubleshoot a system that won't start — you can pinpoint which stage failed. Modern Linux boots in roughly these steps:
StageWhat HappensIf It Fails
1. Firmware (BIOS/UEFI)Hardware self-test (POST), finds boot deviceNo display, beeps — hardware/firmware issue
2. Bootloader (GRUB)Loads kernel, shows boot menu"No bootable device", GRUB rescue prompt
3. KernelInitializes hardware, mounts initramfsKernel panic
4. init (systemd)PID 1; starts all services in dependency orderHangs on a service, emergency mode
5. Targets/servicesReaches multi-user or graphical targetService failures (check journalctl)
6. Logingetty/display manager presents loginCan't log in — auth/PAM/disk-full
WHERE THE LOGS LIVE
Important Log Locations
PathContains
/var/log/syslog or /var/log/messagesGeneral system messages
/var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secureAuthentication, sudo, SSH logins
/var/log/kern.logKernel messages
/var/log/dmesgBoot-time hardware messages
/var/log/nginx/, /var/log/apache2/Web server access/error logs
journalctl (systemd journal)Unified binary log for everything systemd manages
JOURNALCTL
Querying the systemd Journal
journalctl # all logs (q to quit) journalctl -e # jump to end (newest) journalctl -f # follow live (like tail -f) journalctl -u nginx # logs for one service journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" journalctl --since "2024-01-15 09:00" --until "10:00" journalctl -p err # only errors and worse journalctl -b # since this boot journalctl -b -1 # the PREVIOUS boot (for crash analysis) journalctl -k # kernel messages (= dmesg) journalctl --disk-usage # how much space logs use journalctl --vacuum-time=7d # delete logs older than 7 days
A TROUBLESHOOTING FLOW
"The Server Is Acting Weird" — Where to Start
# 1. Is it up? Can you reach it? ping host; ssh host # 2. What's the overall health? uptime # load average free -h # memory df -h # disk full? (a VERY common cause of weirdness) # 3. Any failed services? systemctl --failed # 4. What's in the recent logs? journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | tail -50 journalctl -u suspect-service -e # 5. What's eating resources? top # or htop # 6. Recent changes? (the usual culprit) journalctl --since "30 min ago" | grep -i -E "error|fail|warn"
💾 Storage Management — Disks, Partitions, LVM & RAID LINUX • Essential ▶
THE STACK
From Physical Disk to Mounted Directory
Linux storage is layered: a physical disk is divided into partitions, each formatted with a filesystem, then mounted onto a directory in the unified tree. Understanding the layers is key to managing storage and troubleshooting "disk full" emergencies.
# See block devices and their layout lsblk # tree of disks/partitions/mounts lsblk -f # include filesystem + UUID fdisk -l # detailed partition tables # Disk usage df -h # free space per filesystem df -i # inode usage (can fill before space!) du -sh /var/* # what's eating space in /var du -h --max-depth=1 / | sort -h # biggest dirs
PARTITION → FORMAT → MOUNT
Adding a New Disk
# 1. Partition the new disk (e.g., /dev/sdb) sudo fdisk /dev/sdb # interactive: n, w (or use parted) # 2. Create a filesystem sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1 # or xfs, btrfs # 3. Mount it sudo mkdir /mnt/data sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data # 4. Make it permanent — add to /etc/fstab (use UUID!) blkid /dev/sdb1 # get the UUID # /etc/fstab line: # UUID=xxxx-xxxx /mnt/data ext4 defaults 0 2 sudo mount -a # test fstab WITHOUT rebooting
Always use UUIDs in fstab, not /dev/sdb1 — device names can change between boots, and a bad fstab can prevent the system from booting. Test with mount -a before rebooting.
LVM
Logical Volume Manager — Flexible Storage
LVM adds a layer of abstraction so you can resize volumes, span disks, and snapshot — without repartitioning. The hierarchy: Physical Volumes (PV) → grouped into a Volume Group (VG) → carved into Logical Volumes (LV) that you format and mount. The killer feature: grow a volume on the fly when you add a disk.
# PV → VG → LV sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc # mark disks as PVs sudo vgcreate data_vg /dev/sdb /dev/sdc # pool them into a VG sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n data_lv data_vg # carve a 50G LV sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/data_vg/data_lv sudo mount /dev/data_vg/data_lv /mnt/data # The magic: extend it later (no downtime) sudo lvextend -L +20G /dev/data_vg/data_lv sudo resize2fs /dev/data_vg/data_lv # grow the filesystem too
RAID LEVELS
Redundancy and Performance Tradeoffs
RAID combines multiple disks for redundancy, performance, or both. RAID is not a backup — it protects against disk failure, not against deletion, corruption, or ransomware.
LevelMin DisksRedundancyNotes
RAID 0 (stripe)2NoneFast, but ANY disk loss = all data lost
RAID 1 (mirror)21 diskFull copy; simple, safe, 50% capacity
RAID 5 (parity)31 diskGood balance; slow rebuilds on big disks
RAID 6 (dual parity)42 disksSurvives 2 failures; safer for large arrays
RAID 10 (1+0)4Per mirrorFast AND redundant; popular for databases
🧩 The ip Command — Modern Linux Networking LINUX • Essential ▶
OUT WITH ifconfig
ip Replaced the Old net-tools
The classic commands (ifconfig, route, netstat, arp) are deprecated and often not even installed on modern Linux. The ip command (from iproute2) replaces them all with a consistent syntax: ip OBJECT COMMAND. Learn it — it's what you'll find everywhere now.
Old CommandNew ip Equivalent
ifconfigip addr
ifconfig eth0 up/downip link set eth0 up/down
route -nip route
arp -aip neigh
netstat -tulpnss -tulpn
ADDRESSES & LINKS
Viewing and Configuring Interfaces
# Show IP addresses ip addr # all interfaces (or: ip a) ip addr show eth0 # one interface ip -br addr # brief, clean output ip -4 addr # IPv4 only # Show link (layer 2) state ip link # interfaces up/down, MAC # Bring an interface up/down sudo ip link set eth0 up sudo ip link set eth0 down # Assign an IP (temporary — lost on reboot) sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0 sudo ip addr del 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0
ROUTING & NEIGHBORS
Inspecting the Routing Table
# Show the routing table ip route # (or: ip r) ip route get 8.8.8.8 # which route/iface for this dest? # Default gateway line looks like: # default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 # Add/delete routes (temporary) sudo ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.1 sudo ip route del 10.0.0.0/24 # ARP table (IP ↔ MAC mappings on the local link) ip neigh # Socket statistics (replaces netstat) ss -tulpn # listening TCP/UDP + process ss -tn state established # active connections
PERSISTENT CONFIG
Making Changes Survive Reboot
ip changes are temporary. To make networking persistent, edit the distro's config system — which varies. Know which your system uses.
SystemUsed ByConfig
NetplanModern UbuntuYAML in /etc/netplan/ → netplan apply
NetworkManagerDesktop, RHEL/Fedoranmcli / nmtui
systemd-networkdServers, containers/etc/systemd/network/*.network
ifupdownOlder Debian/etc/network/interfaces
🐚 Robust Bash — Scripts That Don't Silently Destroy Things LINUX • Advanced ▶
THE UNSAFE DEFAULT
Bash Keeps Going After Errors
By default, a bash script continues after a command fails — which can be catastrophic (imagine cd /backup; rm -rf * where the cd silently failed). The first thing every serious bash script should do is enable strict mode. This one line prevents a huge class of disasters.
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # -e : exit immediately if any command fails # -u : error on use of undefined variables (catches typos!) # -o pipefail : a pipeline fails if ANY part fails (not just the last) IFS=$'\n\t' # safer word-splitting (avoid spaces breaking loops)
QUOTING & VARIABLES
The #1 Source of Bash Bugs
# ALWAYS quote variable expansions — unquoted breaks on spaces file="my report.txt" rm $file # ✗ tries to rm "my" AND "report.txt"! rm "$file" # ✓ correct # Default values and required checks name="${1:-world}" # use $1, or "world" if unset : "${API_KEY:?API_KEY must be set}" # abort if unset # Command substitution — prefer $() over backticks count=$(grep -c ERROR app.log) today=$(date +%F) # Arithmetic if (( count > 10 )); then echo "too many"; fi
ARRAYS & LOOPS
Handling Lists Safely
# Arrays servers=("web1" "web2" "db1") echo "${servers[0]}" # web1 echo "${#servers[@]}" # length: 3 # Loop over array — quote "${arr[@]}" ! for s in "${servers[@]}"; do echo "Checking $s" done # Loop over files SAFELY (handles spaces/newlines) while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do echo "Found: $f" done < <(find . -name "*.log" -print0)
CLEANUP & FUNCTIONS
Traps and Reusable Code
# trap — run cleanup on exit (even on error/Ctrl-C) tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmpdir"; } trap cleanup EXIT # guaranteed cleanup, no leftover temp files # Functions with local variables log() { local level="$1"; shift echo "[$(date +%T)] $level: $*" >&2 } log INFO "Starting backup" log ERROR "Disk full"
Lint your scripts with shellcheck — it catches quoting bugs, unsafe patterns, and common mistakes automatically. Run it on every script; it will make you a dramatically better bash author.
🧬 Under the Hood — Namespaces & cgroups LINUX • Advanced ▶
THE SECRET
Containers Are Just Linux Processes
A container isn't a lightweight VM — it's a normal Linux process that's been isolated using two kernel features: namespaces (what a process can SEE) and cgroups (what a process can USE). Docker just orchestrates these kernel primitives nicely. Understanding this demystifies containers — and explains both their efficiency and their security model (shared kernel = the isolation boundary).
NAMESPACES
Isolating What a Process Sees
Namespaces give a process its own private view of a system resource — so a container thinks it has its own hostname, network, process tree, etc., while really sharing one kernel.
NamespaceIsolates
PIDProcess IDs — container sees its own PID 1, not the host's processes
NETNetwork interfaces, IPs, routing, ports
MNTMount points / filesystem view
UTSHostname and domain name
IPCInter-process communication (shared memory)
USERUser/group IDs — can be root inside, unprivileged outside
# See namespaces a process belongs to ls -l /proc/$$/ns # $$ = current shell's PID # Run a process in a new namespace (the raw primitive) sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash # Inside: ps aux shows almost nothing — isolated PID namespace
CGROUPS
Limiting What a Process Can Use
Control groups (cgroups) limit and account for resource usage — CPU, memory, disk I/O, network. This is how docker run --memory 512m works, and how the kernel prevents one container from starving the others. Hit a memory cgroup limit and the OOM killer terminates the process.
# Docker resource limits are cgroups under the hood docker run --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp # systemd uses cgroups too — limit a service systemctl set-property nginx.service MemoryMax=1G CPUQuota=50% # Inspect cgroup hierarchy systemd-cgls # tree of cgroups systemd-cgtop # top-like view of cgroup resource use
THE SECURITY ANGLE
Why "Shared Kernel" Matters
Because all containers share the host kernel, a kernel vulnerability or a misconfiguration can allow a container escape — breaking isolation to reach the host. This is why container hardening matters (no root, drop capabilities, read-only, seccomp profiles that restrict syscalls) and why high-security workloads sometimes use stronger isolation: gVisor (sandboxed kernel), Kata Containers (lightweight VMs per container), or just plain VMs. Defense in depth applies even to containers.
🔬 Performance Debugging — When You Need to Go Deeper LINUX • Advanced ▶
BEYOND top
Tools for "Why Is This Process Doing That?"
When the basic tools (top, free, df) tell you which process is misbehaving but not why, Linux has powerful introspection tools. These let you see exactly what a running process is doing — which system calls it makes, which files it touches, where it's stuck.
STRACE & LTRACE
Watch a Process Talk to the Kernel
strace traces system calls (a process's requests to the kernel — open files, read, write, network). It's invaluable for "why is this hanging?" or "what file is it failing to find?" ltrace does the same for library calls.
# Trace system calls of a command strace ls /tmp # Attach to a RUNNING process (find why it's stuck) sudo strace -p 12345 # Only file-related calls — "what file can't it find?" strace -e trace=open,openat,stat myprogram # Count syscalls + time spent (find the bottleneck) strace -c myprogram # Classic use: a program fails silently → strace reveals # ENOENT (missing file) or EACCES (permission denied)
LSOF & FUSER
Who Has That File/Port Open?
# What files does a process have open? lsof -p 12345 # Which process is using a port? (the classic "port in use") sudo lsof -i :8080 sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080 # Why can't I unmount this disk? What's using it? lsof +D /mnt/data fuser -m /mnt/data # Find deleted-but-still-open files eating disk space lsof | grep deleted # common cause of "df full but du not"
DEEPER TOOLS
When You Need the Heavy Artillery
ToolUse
vmstat 1System-wide CPU/memory/IO/swap, refreshed each second
iostat -x 1Per-disk I/O — find the saturated disk (%util)
perf topReal-time CPU profiling — which functions burn CPU
pidstat 1Per-process resource use over time
eBPF tools (bcc/bpftrace)Deep, low-overhead kernel observability (modern frontier)
Flame graphsVisualize where CPU time goes across the call stack
Methodology beats tools: recall the USE method — for each resource check Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Start broad (which resource?), then reach for these tools to drill into the specific process. Don't randomly run tools hoping for an answer.
Beginner NFS & Samba – Sharing Files Across the Network
Core Concept
NFS vs Samba – When to Use Which
Two protocols dominate network file sharing on Linux:

NFS (Network File System)
• Linux-to-Linux sharing (Unix permissions, UIDs).
• Fast and simple; no user login required (host-based trust).
• Best for: server-to-server shares, Kubernetes persistent volumes, developer workstations on the same trusted LAN.

Samba (SMB/CIFS)
• Linux server sharing files to Windows clients (and macOS).
• Supports AD authentication — Windows users log in with their domain credentials.
• Best for: office file servers, home directories for Windows users.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if Windows clients are complaining about a share, check with the Windows team before touching Samba config; their GPOs may be overriding settings.
NFS Server
Setting Up an NFS Export
The NFS server exposes directories via /etc/exports. Each line names the directory and which clients may mount it.
# Install NFS server (Debian/Ubuntu) sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server # Create a shared directory sudo mkdir -p /srv/share sudo chown nobody:nogroup /srv/share sudo chmod 755 /srv/share # Edit /etc/exports # Format: /path client(options) # rw = read-write | sync = safe writes | no_subtree_check = faster /srv/share 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check) # Apply changes and restart sudo exportfs -ra sudo systemctl restart nfs-kernel-server ─────────── NFS CLIENT SIDE ─────────── # Install NFS client tools sudo apt install nfs-common # Mount the share temporarily sudo mount 192.168.1.10:/srv/share /mnt/nfs # Make it persistent (add to /etc/fstab) 192.168.1.10:/srv/share /mnt/nfs nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0
Samba Server
Setting Up a Samba Share
Samba's configuration lives in /etc/samba/smb.conf. The [global] section sets domain-wide options; each [share-name] section defines one share.
# Install Samba sudo apt install samba # /etc/samba/smb.conf snippet [global] workgroup = CORP server string = File Server security = user ; or 'ads' for AD integration map to guest = Bad User ; unauthenticated = read-only guest [documents] path = /srv/samba/documents browseable = yes read only = no valid users = @finance ; only 'finance' Linux group create mask = 0664 directory mask = 0775 # Create a Samba user (must already be a Linux user) sudo smbpasswd -a alice # Check config for errors testparm # Restart Samba sudo systemctl restart smbd nmbd # Mount from Linux client (CIFS) sudo mount -t cifs //fileserver/documents /mnt/docs -o username=alice,password=secret,uid=$(id -u)
Troubleshooting
Common NFS & Samba Gotchas
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — don't assume the firewall allows NFS/SMB traffic. Always verify:

NFS troubleshooting:
• sudo showmount -e 192.168.1.10 — list exports from a server.
• NFS needs ports 111 (rpcbind) and 2049 (nfsd) open in the firewall.
• UID mismatch = files owned by wrong user; use idmapd or explicit UID mapping.

Samba troubleshooting:
• smbclient -L //server -U alice — list shares.
• sudo smbstatus — show connected clients and locked files.
• Check /var/log/samba/log.smbd for auth failures.
• SMB needs TCP 445 (and 139 for older clients).
Intermediate Advanced Bash Scripting – Patterns for Reliable Scripts
Robustness
The Safe-Script Header
Every production bash script should start with these four settings. They turn silent failures into loud, debuggable errors.
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # set -e : exit immediately on any command error # set -u : treat unset variables as errors (catches typos) # set -o pipefail : pipeline fails if any command in it fails # (without this: cmd1 | cmd2 — cmd1 failure is hidden) # Add a trap to print the line number that failed trap 'echo "ERROR: line $LINENO exit code $?"' ERR # Constant: mark read-only variables readonly LOG_DIR="/var/log/myapp" readonly MAX_RETRIES=3 # ─── Example: fail loudly ──────────────────────────────────── # Without set -u: echo $UNSET_VAR → empty string (silent bug) # With set -u: echo $UNSET_VAR → "unbound variable" error → exit
Functions
Reusable Functions & Logging
Good scripts have a log function, a die function, and small single-purpose helper functions.
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # Logging with timestamps and levels log() { echo "[$(date +%T)] INFO $*" ; } warn() { echo "[$(date +%T)] WARN $*" >&2; } die() { echo "[$(date +%T)] ERROR $*" >&2; exit 1; } # Check dependencies at script start require() { for cmd in "$@"; do command -v "$cmd" >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "Required: $cmd" done } require curl jq aws # Retry a command up to N times with backoff retry() { local max="$1"; shift local delay=2 local attempt=1 while ! "$@"; do (( attempt++ )) [[ attempt -gt max ]] && die "Command failed after $max attempts: $*" warn "Attempt $attempt/$max failed. Retrying in ${delay}s..." sleep "$delay" (( delay *= 2 )) done } retry 3 curl -sf https://api.example.com/health log "Health check passed"
Input Handling
Argument Parsing & Validation
Scripts that accept arguments need clear usage messages and input validation. Use getopts for short flags or manual case for long options.
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail die() { echo "ERROR: $*" >&2; exit 1; } usage() { cat <<EOF Usage: $0 -e ENV -r REGION [-d] -e Environment (dev|staging|prod) -r AWS region (e.g. us-east-1) -d Dry-run mode (no changes) EOF exit 1 } ENV=""; REGION=""; DRYRUN=false while getopts ":e:r:dh" opt; do case "$opt" in e) ENV="$OPTARG" ;; r) REGION="$OPTARG" ;; d) DRYRUN=true ;; h|*) usage ;; esac done [[ -z "$ENV" ]] && die "Environment (-e) is required" [[ -z "$REGION" ]] && die "Region (-r) is required" [[ "$ENV" =~ ^(dev|staging|prod)$ ]] || die "Invalid env: $ENV" echo "Deploying to $ENV / $REGION (dryrun=$DRYRUN)" if [[ "$DRYRUN" == false ]]; then echo "... would deploy here ..." fi
Process Control
Background Jobs, Signals & Cleanup
Production scripts often run long background jobs and need to clean up temp files even if they are interrupted.
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail TMPDIR_WORK=$(mktemp -d) # Cleanup on exit, interrupt, or error cleanup() { rm -rf "$TMPDIR_WORK"; echo "Cleaned up $TMPDIR_WORK"; } trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM # Run two jobs in parallel, wait for both process_chunk() { local chunk="$1" echo "Processing $chunk ..." sleep 2 # simulate work echo "Done $chunk" } for chunk in A B C; do process_chunk "$chunk" & # & runs in background done wait # wait for all background jobs to finish echo "All chunks processed" # Check exit code of a background job my_job & job_pid=$! wait "$job_pid" job_exit=$? [[ $job_exit -eq 0 ]] || die "my_job failed (exit $job_exit)"
Beginner LVM & Storage – Flexible Disk Management on Linux
Core Concept
Why LVM? The Problem with Fixed Partitions
Traditional partitions are fixed-size — if /var fills up, resizing it usually means backing up data, repartitioning, and restoring. LVM (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer between physical disks and filesystems.

The LVM stack (bottom to top):
1. Physical Volume (PV) — a disk or partition (e.g. /dev/sdb1).
2. Volume Group (VG) — a pool combining one or more PVs.
3. Logical Volume (LV) — a "virtual partition" carved from the VG; this is what you format and mount.

Benefits: resize volumes live, add disks to a VG without downtime, take instant snapshots, and move data between physical disks transparently.
Building Blocks
Creating an LVM Setup From Scratch
This walks through turning a raw disk into a mounted, growable filesystem.
# 1. Create a physical volume on a new disk sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb # 2. Create a volume group from one or more PVs sudo vgcreate data_vg /dev/sdb # 3. Create a logical volume (50 GB) inside the VG sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n app_data data_vg # 4. Format it with a filesystem sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/data_vg/app_data # 5. Mount it sudo mkdir -p /data sudo mount /dev/data_vg/app_data /data # 6. Make it persistent — add to /etc/fstab echo '/dev/data_vg/app_data /data ext4 defaults 0 2' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab # Inspect the stack at any layer sudo pvdisplay # physical volumes sudo vgdisplay # volume groups sudo lvdisplay # logical volumes lsblk # visual block-device tree
Resizing
Growing a Volume Without Downtime
This is LVM's superpower — extending storage on a live system, no reboot required. Always shrink with extreme care (and a backup) — growing is safe, shrinking can destroy data.
# Scenario: /data is filling up. Add a new disk and grow it live. # 1. Add the new disk to the volume group sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc sudo vgextend data_vg /dev/sdc # 2. Grow the logical volume by 20 GB sudo lvextend -L +20G /dev/data_vg/app_data # 3. Resize the filesystem to use the new space (ext4 — does this LIVE) sudo resize2fs /dev/data_vg/app_data # For XFS filesystems, use xfs_growfs instead (also live): sudo xfs_growfs /data # Verify the new size df -h /data ─── SHRINKING (dangerous — backup first!) ─────────────────── # ext4 must be unmounted to shrink; XFS cannot be shrunk at all sudo umount /data sudo e2fsck -f /dev/data_vg/app_data sudo resize2fs /dev/data_vg/app_data 30G sudo lvreduce -L 30G /dev/data_vg/app_data
Snapshots
LVM Snapshots – Instant Point-in-Time Backups
A snapshot freezes the state of a volume at an instant, so you can back it up consistently while the original keeps changing — essential for backing up live databases.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when someone runs a bad migration against production, an LVM snapshot from five minutes earlier can save the day.
# Create a snapshot before a risky change (10GB reserved for changes) sudo lvcreate -L 10G -s -n app_data_snap /dev/data_vg/app_data # Mount the snapshot read-only to inspect/back it up sudo mkdir /mnt/snapshot sudo mount -o ro /dev/data_vg/app_data_snap /mnt/snapshot # ... run backup tools against /mnt/snapshot ... sudo umount /mnt/snapshot # Roll back to the snapshot if the change went wrong sudo umount /data sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/data_vg/app_data_snap # Volume reverts to the snapshot's state on next activation # Remove a snapshot once you no longer need it (frees space) sudo lvremove /dev/data_vg/app_data_snap # Note: snapshots are NOT a substitute for off-site backups — # they live on the same physical disks as the original data!
Beginner Mail Servers – Postfix, Dovecot & Email Plumbing
Core Concept
How Email Actually Travels
Email involves more moving parts than people realise. Three protocols and two server roles cover almost everything:

• MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) — moves mail between servers using SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, port 25/587). Examples: Postfix, Exim, Sendmail.
• MDA / IMAP-POP server — stores mail and lets users retrieve it. Examples: Dovecot.
• IMAP (port 143/993) — keeps mail on the server, syncs across devices (the modern standard).
• POP3 (port 110/995) — downloads mail to one device, often deletes it from the server (legacy).

The journey of an email:
Your client → your MTA (SMTP) → recipient's MX server (SMTP) → recipient's mailbox store → recipient's client (IMAP/POP3).
Postfix Setup
Basic Postfix Configuration
Postfix is the most widely deployed open-source MTA. Its main config file is /etc/postfix/main.cf.
# Install Postfix (choose "Internet Site" during setup) sudo apt install postfix mailutils # Key settings in /etc/postfix/main.cf myhostname = mail.example.com mydomain = example.com myorigin = $mydomain inet_interfaces = all mydestination = $myhostname, localhost.$mydomain, $mydomain # Restrict who can relay mail through your server (CRITICAL — # an open relay gets you blacklisted within hours) smtpd_relay_restrictions = permit_mynetworks, permit_sasl_authenticated, reject_unauth_destination # Enforce TLS for incoming and outgoing mail smtpd_tls_cert_file = /etc/letsencrypt/live/mail.example.com/fullchain.pem smtpd_tls_key_file = /etc/letsencrypt/live/mail.example.com/privkey.pem smtpd_tls_security_level = may smtp_tls_security_level = may # Apply config and restart sudo postfix check sudo systemctl restart postfix # Test sending mail from the CLI echo "Test body" | mail -s "Test subject" alice@example.com # Watch the mail log in real time sudo tail -f /var/log/mail.log
Security
Don't Become an Open Relay
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume your default mail server config is safe to expose. The single most common rookie mistake is leaving a server as an open relay — anyone on the internet can use it to send mail through you.

Within hours, spammers find it, your server's IP lands on every major blacklist (Spamhaus, SORBS), and legitimate mail from your domain stops being delivered anywhere.

Checklist before going live:
• Test from an external network — try relaying through your server from outside; it must be rejected.
• Require SASL authentication for any relay.
• Set up SPF, DKIM, DMARC (covered in the Social Engineering topic) — receivers use these to validate your mail.
• Check your IP against blacklists regularly: https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx
# Test for open relay from an external host (use mail-tester.com # or manually with telnet — should be REJECTED for unauth relay) telnet mail.example.com 25 EHLO test.com MAIL FROM:<attacker@evil.com> RCPT TO:<victim@someoneelse.com> # Expected: "554 5.7.1 Relay access denied" — if you get "250 OK" # at this stage, YOU ARE AN OPEN RELAY. Fix immediately. # Check your sending IP reputation dig +short mail.example.com # Then check at: mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx
Troubleshooting
Diagnosing Common Mail Delivery Issues
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when "my email isn't sending" tickets come in, work through this systematically:

1. Check the mail queue: postqueue -p — stuck messages reveal delivery problems.
2. Read /var/log/mail.log for the message ID — it shows every hop and any errors.
3. Verify DNS — does your MX record point to the right server? dig example.com MX
4. Test authentication — can the user actually log in via IMAP/SMTP with their credentials?
5. Check spam folder and recipient's blacklist status — sometimes "not delivered" really means "filtered as spam."
6. Use mail-tester.com — sends a test email and grades your entire setup (SPF/DKIM/DMARC/blacklist/content).
Beginner High Availability – Keeping Services Up When Servers Fail
Core Concept
What "High Availability" Actually Means
High Availability (HA) means a service keeps running even when individual components fail. The goal isn't "never fails" (impossible) — it's "fails without anyone noticing."

Availability is usually expressed in "nines":
Availability Downtime per year Downtime per month Common label 99% 3.65 days 7.3 hours "Two nines" 99.9% 8.77 hours 43.8 minutes "Three nines" 99.99% 52.6 minutes 4.4 minutes "Four nines" 99.999% 5.26 minutes 26 seconds "Five nines" # The jump from 99.9% to 99.99% looks small on paper # but represents 10x more engineering effort and cost. # Most businesses don't NEED five nines — that's a question # for the business, not a default engineering goal.
Building Blocks
The Three Pillars of HA Architecture
• Redundancy — more than one of everything that can fail (servers, disks, network paths, power supplies, even data centres). "One is none, two is one."

• Load balancing — distributes traffic across multiple servers; if one fails, traffic routes around it automatically.

• Failover — automatic detection of failure and automatic switch to a standby. The faster and more silent the failover, the higher the availability.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — true HA requires cooperation across teams: network (redundant paths), ops (clustering software), and the application itself (must handle being restarted/relocated gracefully). No single team can build HA alone.
keepalived
Floating IPs with keepalived (VRRP)
keepalived implements VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) — two or more servers share a "virtual" IP address. If the active server dies, a standby instantly takes over the IP — clients never notice.
# Install on both servers sudo apt install keepalived # /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf — PRIMARY server vrrp_instance VI_1 { state MASTER interface eth0 virtual_router_id 51 priority 150 # higher number = preferred primary advert_int 1 authentication { auth_type PASS auth_pass mysecret } virtual_ipaddress { 192.168.1.100/24 # the floating/shared IP } } # /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf — BACKUP server # Same config, but: state BACKUP and priority 100 # Start and watch the failover live sudo systemctl enable --now keepalived sudo journalctl -u keepalived -f # Test it: stop keepalived on the primary, watch the IP migrate sudo systemctl stop keepalived ip addr show eth0 # run this on the backup — it now owns .100
Pacemaker/Corosync
Cluster Resource Management
For more complex services (databases, file servers), you need a full cluster resource manager: Corosync handles cluster membership/messaging; Pacemaker decides what runs where and handles failover logic.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — never assume a cluster is healthy just because the service responds. Check cluster status directly; a "split-brain" scenario (both nodes think they're primary) can silently corrupt data.
# View overall cluster status sudo pcs status # Output shows: which node is active, resource locations, any failures Cluster name: web_cluster Stack: corosync Current DC: node1 (version ...) - partition with quorum 2 nodes configured 2 resource instances configured Online: [ node1 node2 ] Full list of resources: Floating_IP (ocf::heartbeat:IPaddr2): Started node1 WebServer (systemd:nginx): Started node1 # Manually move a resource to test failover sudo pcs resource move WebServer node2 # Check for "quorum" — without it, clusters refuse to act # (this is the safety mechanism that PREVENTS split-brain) sudo corosync-quorumtool
Intermediate Container Internals – What Docker Is Actually Built From
Core Concept
Containers Are Not Magic — They're Linux Features
Here's the secret that demystifies Docker: "containers" aren't a real thing in the Linux kernel. Docker (and Podman, containerd, etc.) is really just a friendly interface around two much older Linux kernel features:

• Namespaces — make a process think it's alone on the system (its own PIDs, network, filesystem, hostname).
• cgroups (control groups) — limit and measure how much CPU, memory, and I/O a process (or group of processes) can use.

Put these two together — a process that can't see anything outside its bubble (namespaces) and can't consume more than its allotted resources (cgroups) — and you have a "container."

Understanding this helps you debug containers like Linux processes (because that's exactly what they are) and explains why container escapes are possible — they exploit gaps in this kernel-level isolation.
Namespaces
The Six Linux Namespace Types
Each namespace type isolates a different slice of what a process can see:
Namespace What it isolates What this means for a container PID Process IDs Container's PID 1 looks like the only process on the system NET Network interfaces, routes, ports Container has its own IP, can't see the host's network traffic MNT Filesystem mount points Container sees its own root filesystem, not the host's UTS Hostname and domain name Container can have its own hostname (e.g. "web-7d9f8c") IPC Inter-process communication Container can't access host's (shared memory, semaphores) shared memory segments USER User and group IDs "root" inside the container can map to an unprivileged host user # See the namespaces of a running process ls -la /proc/$(pgrep -f myapp | head -1)/ns/ # Output looks like: # lrwxrwxrwx ... net -> 'net:[4026532245]' # lrwxrwxrwx ... pid -> 'pid:[4026532248]' # lrwxrwxrwx ... uts -> 'uts:[4026532246]' # Compare to the host's own namespaces (PID 1) ls -la /proc/1/ns/ # Different numbers = different namespace = isolated # Run your own minimal "container" with unshare (no Docker needed!) sudo unshare --pid --net --mount --uts --fork bash hostname my-fake-container # changes hostname ONLY inside this shell ps aux # shows almost nothing — your own PID namespace
cgroups
cgroups – Resource Limits in Action
cgroups are how Docker enforces --memory=512m and --cpus=1. They live in a virtual filesystem you can explore directly.
# Find a container's cgroup (modern systems use cgroup v2) docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' myapp_container # Explore its resource limits directly in the filesystem cd /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<container-id>.scope/ cat memory.max # memory limit in bytes (or "max" = unlimited) cat memory.current # current memory usage RIGHT NOW cat cpu.max # CPU quota and period cat io.stat # disk I/O statistics # Watch a container's resource consumption live docker stats myapp_container # Create your own cgroup limit manually (educational — Docker # does this automatically, but seeing it raw removes the mystery) sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/my_limited_group echo "100000 100000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/my_limited_group/cpu.max echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/my_limited_group/cgroup.procs # Now THIS SHELL is limited to 100% of one CPU core
Why It Matters
Using This Knowledge to Debug Real Problems
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — when a container mysteriously gets killed or throttled, knowing the internals turns "it's broken, restart it" into "I found exactly why, here's the fix":

• "My container keeps getting OOM-killed" → Check memory.current vs memory.max — the cgroup is enforcing a limit you set too low.
• "My container is randomly slow" → Check cpu.max — CPU throttling from cgroup limits looks exactly like random slowness from the inside.
• "Processes inside my container can see host processes" → The container may be running with --pid=host — a misconfiguration that breaks PID namespace isolation (and is a security risk).
• "I need to debug a container that has no shell" → Use nsenter to attach to its namespaces directly from the host: nsenter -t <PID> -n -p -m sh
Beginner

systemd Essentials – Services, Units, and Why Things Start at Boot

Concept

systemd is the "stage manager" of a modern Linux system

When a Linux machine boots, dozens of things need to happen in roughly the right order — mount filesystems, bring up networking, start the SSH daemon, launch your web server. systemd is the init system (process ID 1) responsible for orchestrating all of that, and for keeping track of every running service afterward. Almost every major distribution (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL/CentOS/Fedora, Arch) uses it today, which makes it one of the highest-leverage things a beginner can learn — the same handful of commands work nearly everywhere.

Concept

Units: the building blocks systemd manages

Unit typeManagesExample
.serviceA long-running background process (a daemon)nginx.service, sshd.service
.timerA scheduled job — systemd's modern alternative to cronlogrotate.timer
.socketA network or IPC socket that can start a service on demand when something connectsdocker.socket
.mountA filesystem mount pointhome.mount
.targetA grouping of other units — a "milestone" the system reaches during bootmulti-user.target, graphical.target
Hands-on

The commands you'll reach for constantly

# Check whether a service is running right now
systemctl status nginx

# Start / stop / restart a service immediately (this run only)
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
# 'reload' re-reads config without dropping active connections — gentler than restart
sudo systemctl reload nginx

# Make a service start automatically at every future boot
# (note: this does NOT start it right now — the two are independent!)
sudo systemctl enable nginx

# Do both at once — enable AND start immediately
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx

# See WHY something failed — the most useful troubleshooting command here
journalctl -u nginx -n 50 --no-pager

# Follow a service's logs live, the way you'd 'tail -f' a log file
journalctl -u nginx -f
Common pitfall

"I started it, why didn't it survive the reboot?" (and the reverse)

enable and start are two completely independent switches that beginners frequently conflate:

CommandRunning right now?Will it start on next boot?
systemctl start fooYesNo — forgotten on reboot unless also enabled
systemctl enable fooNo — stays stopped until startedYes — but won't help you *today*
systemctl enable --now fooYesYes

"I enabled it but it's still not running" and "it was working until the server rebooted" are two of the most common systemd tickets — and both trace back to this exact distinction. Assume makes an ass out of you and me: always run systemctl status to confirm both the current state and whether it's enabled, rather than assuming one implies the other.

Beginner

File Permissions Demystified – rwx, Octal Notation, and chmod

Concept

Reading the permission string, left to right

Run ls -l and you'll see a string like -rwxr-xr-- at the start of each line. It looks cryptic until you break it into four pieces:

PositionMeansIn -rwxr-xr--
1st characterFile type: - regular file, d directory, l symlink- (a regular file)
Characters 2-4Owner's permissions: read, write, executerwx — owner can do all three
Characters 5-7Group's permissionsr-x — group can read and execute, not write
Characters 8-10Everyone else's permissionsr-- — others can only read

For a directory, the meaning of each letter shifts slightly: r lets you list its contents, w lets you create/delete files inside it, and x lets you actually enter it (via cd) or access files inside by full path. A directory with r-- but no x is a common source of confusing "permission denied" errors — you can see what's there but can't actually get in.

Concept

Octal notation: the same thing, in a faster shorthand

Each rwx triplet can be represented as a single digit by adding up values: read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. So rwx = 4+2+1 = 7, r-x = 4+0+1 = 5, and r-- = 4+0+0 = 4. That makes -rwxr-xr-- equivalent to the much more typeable 754 — which is exactly the form you'll see in chmod commands and deployment scripts everywhere.

Octal digitPermissions grantedCommon use
7rwx — read, write, executeScripts and programs you own and run
6rw- — read and write, no executeRegular documents and config files
5r-x — read and execute, no writeShared programs others should run but not modify
4r-- — read onlyReference files nobody but the owner should change
Hands-on

Setting permissions deliberately

# View permissions in detail
ls -l deploy.sh

# Make a script executable for the owner only — common for personal scripts
chmod 700 deploy.sh
# Result: rwx------  (owner: full control, everyone else: nothing)

# Make a shared script runnable by the whole team, editable only by the owner
chmod 755 deploy.sh
# Result: rwxr-xr-x  (owner: full, group/others: read+execute)

# Symbolic form — same end result, sometimes clearer to read in scripts
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx deploy.sh

# Add execute permission without disturbing existing read/write bits
chmod +x deploy.sh

# Recursively fix an entire directory tree (use carefully!)
chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /opt/myapp
Mindset

"chmod 777 it" is the duct tape of permissions — and just as ugly under the surface

chmod 777 grants read, write, and execute to literally everyone — the owner, the group, and every other user on the system. It "fixes" almost any permission error instantly, which is exactly why it spreads through forums and Stack Overflow answers as a quick solution. Assume makes an ass out of you and me: assuming "wide open" is harmless because "it's just my home lab" is how a small convenience habit becomes a real vulnerability the day that file matters. Take the extra thirty seconds to figure out the narrowest permission that actually solves the problem — your future self (and anyone auditing the system later) will thank you.

Beginner

Process Management – Finding and Taming Runaway Processes

Concept

Every running thing is a process — and every process tells a story

A process is a running instance of a program — and at any moment, a Linux system might have hundreds of them, most quietly doing their job. The skill of process management is being able to quickly answer "what's running, what's it doing, is it behaving normally, and how do I deal with it if it isn't?" — questions that come up constantly in troubleshooting, whether the symptom is "the server feels slow" or "this thing won't quit."

Hands-on

Seeing what's running, and how it's behaving

# The classic snapshot view — every process, full detail
ps aux

# Live, auto-refreshing view sorted by resource usage —
# your first stop when something "feels slow"
top
# or, with friendlier output and mouse support:
htop

# Find processes by name — handy when you know what you're
# looking for but not its process ID (PID)
pgrep -fl nginx

# See the full ancestry — what launched what, and in what order
# (extremely useful for understanding "where did this come from?")
ps -ef --forest

# Check what files and network connections a specific process has open —
# great for "why won't this file unmount?" or "what is this PID
# actually talking to?"
lsof -p 4821
Concept

Stopping a process: three signals, three very different outcomes

SignalCommandWhat it actually means
SIGTERM (15)kill 4821"Please shut yourself down gracefully" — gives the process a chance to save state, close connections, and clean up
SIGKILL (9)kill -9 4821"Stop immediately, no negotiation" — the kernel terminates it on the spot; the process gets no chance to clean up anything
SIGHUP (1)kill -1 4821"Reload your configuration" — many daemons treat this as "re-read your config file without fully restarting"

The escalation order matters: try SIGTERM first, wait a few seconds, and reach for SIGKILL only if the process genuinely won't respond. Reaching straight for kill -9 out of habit is how database processes end up with corrupted files and temp directories end up full of orphaned lock files — the very cleanup steps SIGTERM would have given the process a chance to perform.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — verify the PID before you kill it

Process IDs get reused constantly as old processes exit and new ones start — the PID you noted five minutes ago in a different terminal might belong to a completely different program by the time you act on it. Before running kill on a number you wrote down earlier, re-run ps or pgrep to confirm that PID still belongs to what you think it does. The few seconds that takes is far cheaper than explaining why you killed the wrong service.

Beginner

"The Disk Is Full" – Diagnosing Storage Problems Like a Calm Professional

Concept

The classic 2 AM page: "No space left on device"

Few alerts feel as urgent as a server running out of disk space — services start failing to write logs, databases stop accepting writes, and everything gets weird in ways that don't immediately look storage-related. The good news: diagnosing where the space went is usually a five-minute job once you know the right three commands and the order to run them in.

Concept

Step 1 — confirm it, and find which filesystem is the problem

df ("disk free") shows you space at the filesystem level — this is where you confirm the emergency is real and identify exactly which mount point is the culprit:

# -h = human-readable sizes (GB/MB instead of raw byte counts)
df -h

# Typical output -- the "Use%" column is what you're scanning for:
# Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
# /dev/sda1        50G   48G  0.5G  99% /
# /dev/sdb1       200G   80G  110G  43% /var/log
#
# Here, the root filesystem ("/") is the emergency -- 99% full.
# /var/log on its own disk is fine. Now we know WHERE to dig.
Concept

Step 2 — find which directory is actually eating the space

Once you know which filesystem is full, du ("disk usage") helps you walk down the directory tree to find the actual offender — usually a runaway log file, an old backup nobody cleaned up, or a temp directory that grew out of control:

# Summarize top-level directory sizes, sorted largest first:
du -h --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -10

# Drill into the biggest offender, one level deeper:
du -h --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -10

# Often the trail leads somewhere very specific, e.g.:
#   23G   /var/log/myapp/debug.log
#   -- a log rotation policy was never configured for this app
Concept

Step 3 — understand the "phantom space" trap before you panic further

Here's a scenario that confuses almost every beginner at least once: you delete a huge file, run df again, and the space still isn't free. This isn't a bug — it's how Unix-like systems handle deletion. If a running process still has the file open, the space isn't released until that process closes it (or restarts). lsof ("list open files") reveals exactly this:

# Find processes holding open file handles to deleted files
# (the "(deleted)" marker is the giveaway):
lsof +L1 2>/dev/null | grep deleted

# Output might show something like:
# myapp     2841  root   12w   REG   8,1  19327352  (deleted) /var/log/myapp/debug.log
#
# The fix isn't deleting it again -- it's already gone from the
# directory listing. Restart (or signal) the process holding it open,
# and the space returns immediately.

This is also a perfect moment to remember "assume makes an ass out of you and me" — assuming a deleted file's space was reclaimed (when it wasn't) has led more than one engineer to delete more files in a panic, sometimes ones that were actually needed. Confirm with lsof before escalating to more drastic measures.

🧱 Linux Firewalls — iptables, nftables & ufw Hardening ▶
Concept
The Kernel Decides What Packets Live or Die
Every Linux host has a packet filter built into the kernel (Netfilter). You program it with rules that ACCEPT, DROP, or REJECT packets based on source, destination, port, and protocol. Three tools front it: iptables (classic), its successor nftables, and ufw (a friendly wrapper). The default posture you want: deny inbound, allow outbound, permit only the ports you actually serve.
Reference
Chains & Policy — The Mental Model
ChainHandles
INPUTPackets destined for this host (protect your services here)
OUTPUTPackets originating from this host
FORWARDPackets routed through this host (routers, NAT, containers)
Rules in a chain are checked top to bottom; the first match wins. If nothing matches, the chain's default policy applies. Set the INPUT policy to DROP and explicitly allow what you need.
Commands
ufw — The Easy Path
SENSIBLE DEFAULTS IN FOUR LINES
sudo ufw default deny incoming     # block all inbound by default
sudo ufw default allow outgoing    # let the host reach out
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp             # SSH — do this BEFORE enabling!
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp            # HTTPS
sudo ufw enable                    # turn it on
sudo ufw status numbered           # review the ruleset
Commands
iptables & nftables — The Raw Tools
iptables — CLASSIC
# Allow established replies + SSH, then drop the rest
sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP        # set default policy last
sudo iptables -L -n -v            # list with packet counts
nftables — MODERN REPLACEMENT
sudo nft add table inet filter
sudo nft add chain inet filter input { type filter hook input priority 0\; policy drop\; }
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept
sudo nft list ruleset            # show everything
Gotchas
Don't Lock Yourself Out
RuleWhy
Allow SSH before default-denySet the DROP policy or run ufw enable without an SSH allow rule and your remote session dies — with no way back in.
Allow ESTABLISHED,RELATEDWithout it, replies to your own outbound connections get dropped and everything appears broken.
Rules are not persistent by defaultiptables/nft rules vanish on reboot — save them (netfilter-persistent, nft list ruleset > /etc/nftables.conf) or use ufw, which persists.
Test with a safety netSchedule an at job to flush rules in 5 min while you test, so a mistake auto-recovers.
🛂 SELinux & AppArmor — Mandatory Access Control Hardening ▶
Concept
A Second Lock Even Root Can't Pick
Normal Linux permissions are discretionary (DAC): the file's owner decides who gets access, and root can do anything. Mandatory Access Control (MAC) adds a second layer the kernel enforces from a central policy — even against root. So if a web server is compromised, MAC can still stop it from reading /etc/shadow or opening a network port it was never meant to. It confines each program to exactly what it legitimately needs.
Comparison
SELinux vs AppArmor
SELinuxAppArmor
Confines bySecurity labels on every file/processFile paths in a profile
Default onRHEL, Fedora, CentOSUbuntu, Debian, SUSE
PowerVery fine-grainedSimpler, path-based
Learning curveSteepGentle
Both solve the same problem — least privilege enforced by the kernel — just with different models. You typically use whichever ships with your distro rather than swapping.
Commands
SELinux — Modes & Troubleshooting
getenforce                  # Enforcing | Permissive | Disabled
sudo setenforce 0            # temporarily → Permissive (logs, doesn't block)
ls -Z /var/www/html         # -Z shows the security context (label)
ps -eZ | grep httpd         # process labels

# The #1 gotcha: wrong file label. Restore the default context:
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html

# See WHY something was denied (AVC denials):
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent
