🎨 CSS — Cascading Style Sheets WEB STYLING ▶
Reference
CSS3 — Selectors · Box Model · Flexbox · Grid · Variables · Animations
CSS controls visual presentation. The cascade order: inline > id > class > element. Specificity: inline(1000) > id(100) > class(10) > element(1).
SELECTORS & SPECIFICITY
/* Universal, type, class, id */ * { box-sizing: border-box; } h1 { color: red; } .card { padding: 1rem; } #hero { background: blue; } /* Combinators */ div p { } /* descendant */ div > p { } /* direct child */ h1 + p { } /* adjacent sibling */ h1 ~ p { } /* general sibling */ /* Pseudo-classes */ a:hover { color: cyan; } li:nth-child(2n) { } /* even rows */ li:nth-child(3n+1) { } /* 1,4,7... */ :is(h1,h2,h3) { } /* matches any */ :not(.disabled) { } :focus-visible { outline: 2px solid cyan; } /* Pseudo-elements */ p::before { content: "→ "; } p::after { content: ""; display: block; } ::selection { background: #00d4ff; }
CUSTOM PROPERTIES & CALC
:root { --color-primary: #00d4ff; --spacing-md: 1rem; --font-mono: "Fira Code", monospace; } .card { color: var(--color-primary); padding: calc(var(--spacing-md) * 2); width: clamp(200px, 50%, 800px); font-size: min(4vw, 2rem); }
FLEXBOX
.flex-container { display: flex; flex-direction: row; /* row|column|row-reverse */ justify-content: space-between; /* main axis */ align-items: center; /* cross axis */ flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; } .flex-item { flex: 1 1 200px; /* grow shrink basis */ align-self: flex-start; order: 2; }
CSS GRID
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer"; gap: 16px; } .header { grid-area: header; } .item { grid-column: 1 / -1; grid-row: span 2; }
ANIMATIONS & TRANSITIONS
.btn { transition: all 0.3s ease-in-out; transform: translateX(0) scale(1); } .btn:hover { transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.05); } @keyframes fadeIn { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(20px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); } } .animate { animation: fadeIn 0.6s ease forwards; animation-delay: 0.2s; } /* Media queries */ @media (max-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { body { background: #000; } } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none; } }
⚡ JavaScript — ES6 through ES2025 SCRIPTING LANGUAGE ▶
Reference
JavaScript — Variables · Functions · Arrays · Async · DOM · Modern APIs
Dynamically typed, prototype-based. Runs in browser and Node.js. Key paradigm shift: ES6 (2015) introduced let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules, Promises.
VARIABLES & TYPES
// Declarations — always prefer const, use let when reassigning const PI = 3.14; let count = 0; // var — function-scoped, hoisted — avoid in modern code // Primitives typeof "hello" // "string" typeof 42 // "number" typeof true // "boolean" typeof undefined // "undefined" typeof null // "object" ← famous JS quirk typeof Symbol() // "symbol" typeof 42n // "bigint" // Destructuring const [a, b, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const { name, age = 25 } = person; const { x: lat, y: lng } = coords; // rename const { a: { b } } = nested; // deep
FUNCTIONS
// Arrow functions (no own this/arguments) const add = (a, b) => a + b; const greet = name => `Hello ${name}`; const noop = () => {}; // Default, rest, spread function log(msg = "default", ...args) {} Math.max(...[1,2,3]); // spread // Higher-order functions [1,2,3].map(x => x * 2) // [2,4,6] [1,2,3].filter(x => x > 1) // [2,3] [1,2,3].reduce((acc,x) => acc+x, 0) // 6 [3,1,2].sort((a,b) => a - b) // [1,2,3] arr.flatMap(x => [x, x*2]) // ES2019
OBJECTS & CLASSES
// Object methods (ES6+) const obj = { x, y, greet() { return this.x; } }; Object.assign({}, defaults, overrides); const clone = { ...original, extra: 1 }; Object.keys(obj) / Object.values(obj) / Object.entries(obj) Object.fromEntries([["a",1],["b",2]]) // ES2019 Object.freeze(obj) // immutable // Classes (syntactic sugar over prototypes) class Animal { #sound = "..."; // private field (ES2022) constructor(public name) {} // TypeScript-style get label() { return this.name; } set label(v) { this.name = v; } speak() { return this.#sound; } static create(n) { return new Animal(n); } } class Dog extends Animal { speak() { return `${super.speak()} Woof!`; } }
ASYNC & PROMISES
// Promise chain → async/await (preferred) async function fetchUser(id) { try { const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.statusText); return await res.json(); } catch (err) { console.error(err); } } // Parallel execution const [u, p] = await Promise.all([fetchUser(), fetchPosts()]); const first = await Promise.race([p1, p2]); const results = await Promise.allSettled([p1, p2]); const any = await Promise.any([p1, p2]); // first resolved // Optional chaining & nullish coalescing (ES2020) const zip = user?.address?.zip ?? "unknown"; user?.save?.(); // call only if method exists
DOM & EVENTS
// Query document.querySelector(".card") document.querySelectorAll("li") // NodeList document.getElementById("main") // Manipulate el.textContent = "safe text"; el.innerHTML = "<b>unsafe</b>"; el.classList.toggle("active"); el.setAttribute("data-id", 42); el.style.color = "cyan"; // Create / insert const div = document.createElement("div"); parent.append(div); // at end parent.prepend(div); // at start el.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", html); el.remove(); // Events btn.addEventListener("click", e => { e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); }, { once: true, passive: true }); // Storage / History / Location localStorage.setItem("k", JSON.stringify(val)); JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("k")); history.pushState({}, "", "/new-path");
📋 JSON — JavaScript Object Notation DATA FORMAT ▶
Reference
JSON — Syntax · Data Types · Parse · Stringify · Schema
Language-agnostic text format for data interchange. Keys must be double-quoted strings. No comments, no trailing commas, no undefined/functions. MIME type: application/json.
SYNTAX & DATA TYPES
{ "string": "hello world", "number": 42, "float": 3.14, "boolean": true, "null": null, "array": [1, "two", false, null], "object": { "nested": true }, "array_of_objects": [ { "id": 1, "name": "Alice" }, { "id": 2, "name": "Bob" } ] } // NOT valid JSON: // { key: "no quotes on key" } ← must quote keys // { "a": 1, } ← no trailing comma // { "fn": function(){} } ← no functions // { "date": new Date() } ← no JS expressions
JAVASCRIPT PARSE / STRINGIFY
// Parse JSON string → JS value const obj = JSON.parse('{"name":"Alice","age":30}'); // → { name: "Alice", age: 30 } // Stringify JS value → JSON string const json = JSON.stringify({ name: "Alice", age: 30 }); // → '{"name":"Alice","age":30}' // Pretty-print with indentation JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2); // Replacer function — filter/transform values JSON.stringify(obj, (key, val) => { if (key === "password") return undefined; // omit return val; }); // Reviver function — parse Date strings etc. JSON.parse(str, (key, val) => typeof val === "string" && val.match(/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/) ? new Date(val) : val ); // Deep clone (simple objects only) const clone = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(original)); // Note: loses undefined, functions, Dates, Map, Set, etc. // Prefer structuredClone() for modern environments
COMMAND-LINE — JQ
cat data.json | jq '.' # pretty-print jq '.name' data.json # extract field jq '.users[] | .email' data.json # iterate array jq '.users | length' data.json # count items jq 'select(.age > 18)' data.json # filter jq '{name, email}' data.json # project fields jq '.[] | @base64' data.json # encode values # Python quick-parse from terminal python3 -m json.tool data.json # validate + pretty-print curl api.example.com | python3 -m json.tool
🐍 Python — Scripting & Automation GENERAL PURPOSE ▶
Reference
Python 3 — Syntax · Data Structures · OOP · I/O · Stdlib · Comprehensions
Interpreted, dynamically typed, garbage-collected. PEP 8 style guide. Significant whitespace (indentation defines blocks). CPython 3.10+ for match/case, 3.12 for f-string improvements.
CORE SYNTAX
# Variables — duck-typed, no declaration needed name = "Alice" age = 30 pi = 3.14 active = True # bool (capital T/F) empty = None # null equivalent # F-strings (3.6+) — preferred string formatting print(f"Hello {name}, age {age}") print(f"PI = {pi:.2f}") # format spec print(f"Debug: {age = }") # 3.8+ self-doc # Multiple assignment / unpacking a, b, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4] a, b = b, a # swap x = y = z = 0 # chain assign
DATA STRUCTURES
# List — ordered, mutable, O(1) append lst = [1, 2, 3] lst.append(4); lst.extend([5,6]) lst.insert(0, 99); lst.pop() lst[1:3] # slice [2,3] lst[::-1] # reversed # Dict — ordered (3.7+), key→value d = {"a": 1, "b": 2} d.get("c", 0) # safe get with default d.setdefault("c", []).append(1) d.update({"c": 3}); merged = {**d, **e} for k, v in d.items(): print(k, v) # Set, Tuple, Named Tuple s = {1,2,3} | {3,4} # union {1,2,3,4} t = (1, 2) # immutable from collections import namedtuple Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x","y"])
CONTROL FLOW & COMPREHENSIONS
# Conditionals if x > 0: ... elif x == 0: ... else: ... # Structural pattern matching (3.10+) match command: case "quit": quit() case {"action": act}: run(act) case [x, y]: move(x, y) case _: print("unknown") # Loops for i, v in enumerate(lst): ... for a, b in zip(l1, l2): ... while x > 0: x -= 1 [x for x in lst if x > 0] # list comp {k: v*2 for k,v in d.items()} # dict comp (x**2 for x in range(10)) # generator
FUNCTIONS, DECORATORS & OOP
def greet(name: str, *, loud: bool = False) -> str: """Greet a person. loud=True → UPPERCASE.""" msg = f"Hello {name}" return msg.upper() if loud else msg # *args / **kwargs def variadic(*args, **kwargs): ... # Decorators from functools import wraps, lru_cache def timer(fn): @wraps(fn) def wrapper(*a, **kw): start = time.time() res = fn(*a, **kw) print(f"{fn.__name__}: {time.time()-start:.3f}s") return res return wrapper @lru_cache(maxsize=128) # memoize def fib(n): return n if n < 2 else fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) # Dataclass (3.7+) — concise class with auto-methods from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass(frozen=True) class User: name: str age: int = 0 tags: list = field(default_factory=list)
FILE I/O & COMMON STDLIB
# File I/O — always use context manager with open("file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: content = f.read() # whole file lines = f.readlines() # list of lines with open("out.txt", "w") as f: f.write("hello ") # Path manipulation (pathlib — preferred over os.path) from pathlib import Path p = Path("/etc/hosts") p.parent / "other" # /etc/other p.stem; p.suffix; p.name # hosts "" hosts list(Path(".").glob("**/*.py")) # recursive find p.read_text(); p.write_text("data") # Common imports import os, sys, re, json, csv, time, datetime from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque from itertools import chain, product, combinations import subprocess subprocess.run(["ls","-la"], capture_output=True, text=True)
ERROR HANDLING & CONTEXT MANAGERS
try: result = int("bad") except (ValueError, TypeError) as e: print(f"Error: {e}") except Exception: # catch-all raise # re-raise else: print("success") # runs if no exception finally: print("always runs") # Custom context manager from contextlib import contextmanager @contextmanager def managed(): print("enter"); yield; print("exit") with managed(): print("inside")
🔷 PowerShell — Windows Automation SHELL SCRIPTING ▶
Reference
PowerShell 5/7 — Cmdlets · Variables · Pipeline · Scripting · Remoting
Object-based shell and scripting language. Verbs: Get/Set/New/Remove/Invoke. Get-Command *firewall* discovers cmdlets. Execution policy controls script runs.
VARIABLES & TYPES
# Variables prefix with $ $name = "Alice" $count = 42 $active = $true $nothing = $null # Strong typing [int]$x = 10 [string]$s = "hi" [datetime]$d = "2025-01-01" [array]$arr = 1,2,3 [hashtable]$h = @{ a=1; b=2 } # Here-string $text = @" Multiline string here "@ # Environment variables $env:PATH; $env:USERPROFILE; $env:COMPUTERNAME
PIPELINE & COMMON CMDLETS
# Pipeline passes objects (not text) Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 10 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.log | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } | ForEach-Object { Remove-Item $_.FullName } # Essential cmdlets Get-Command *service* # find cmdlets Get-Help Get-Process -Full # full help Get-Member # show object properties Get-Service | Format-Table -AutoSize Get-Content file.log | Select-String "ERROR" Set-Content / Add-Content / Out-File / Tee-Object Copy-Item; Move-Item; Remove-Item -Recurse -Force
SCRIPTING CONSTRUCTS
# If / switch if ($x -gt 10) { "big" } elseif ($x -gt 5) { "med" } else { "small" } switch ($role) { "admin" { ... } "user" { ... } default { ... } } # Loops foreach ($item in $collection) { $item.Name } for ($i=0; $i -lt 10; $i++) { $i } 1..5 | ForEach-Object { $_ * 2 } while ($x -gt 0) { $x-- } # Functions function Get-Square { param([int]$n) return $n * $n } Get-Square 5 # Try/catch try { Get-Item "missing" -ErrorAction Stop } catch [System.IO.FileNotFoundException] { "not found" } finally { "always" }
SECURITY & REMOTING
# Execution policy Get-ExecutionPolicy Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser # Restricted | AllSigned | RemoteSigned | Unrestricted | Bypass # Bypass for single script (pentest / admin) powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File script.ps1 # Base64 encoded payload execution powershell -EncodedCommand <base64string> # Remoting (WinRM) Enable-PSRemoting -Force Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SERVER01 -Credential $cred Invoke-Command -ComputerName SERVER01 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service } New-PSSession; Disconnect-PSSession # Credential object $cred = Get-Credential $cred = New-Object PSCredential("user", (ConvertTo-SecureString "pass" -AsPlainText -Force))
🔶 Bash — Bourne Again Shell SHELL SCRIPTING ▶
Reference
Bash 5 — Variables · Conditionals · Loops · Functions · Parameter Expansion
Default shell on most Linux distros. Scripts start with #!/usr/bin/env bash. Use set -euo pipefail for safe scripting. POSIX-compatible subset runs everywhere.
SCRIPT HEADER & VARIABLES
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # exit on error, unset var, pipe fail IFS=$' ' # safer field splitting # Variables — no spaces around = NAME="Alice" COUNT=42 readonly PI=3.14 # Special variables $0 # script name $1..$9, ${10} # positional args $# # number of args $@ # all args (separate) $* # all args (one string) $? # last exit code (0 = success) $$ # current PID $! # last background PID $_ # last argument of previous command
PARAMETER EXPANSION
${var:-default} # use default if unset/empty ${var:=default} # set AND use default if unset ${var:?error msg} # exit with error if unset ${#var} # length of string ${var^} # uppercase first char ${var^^} # uppercase all ${var,,} # lowercase all ${var/old/new} # replace first match ${var//old/new} # replace all matches ${var#prefix} # strip shortest prefix ${var##prefix} # strip longest prefix ${var%suffix} # strip shortest suffix ${var:2:5} # substring: offset:length
CONDITIONALS & TESTS
# [[ ]] preferred over [ ] — no word splitting if [[ $x -gt 10 ]]; then ...; elif ...; else ...; fi # File tests [[ -f $file ]] # exists and is regular file [[ -d $dir ]] # exists and is directory [[ -e $path ]] # exists (any type) [[ -r/-w/-x ]] # readable/writable/executable [[ -z $str ]] # string is empty [[ -n $str ]] # string is non-empty # Numeric comparisons -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge # String comparisons == != < > $str =~ ^[0-9]+$ # regex match # Logical && || ! [[ $a -gt 0 && $b -lt 10 ]]
LOOPS & FUNCTIONS
# For loops for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done for f in *.txt; do process "$f"; done for ((i=0; i<10; i++)); do ...; done for key in "${!assoc[@]}"; do echo ${assoc[$key]}; done # While / until / read lines while read -r line; do echo $line; done < file.txt while true; do ping host && break; sleep 5; done # Functions greet() { local name="${1:?name required}" echo "Hello, $name" return 0 # 0 = success } result=$(greet Alice) # capture stdout # Arrays & associative arrays arr=("a" "b" "c") echo ${arr[0]} ${#arr[@]} ${arr[@]} declare -A map=([key]="val") echo ${map[key]}
🐚 ZSH — Z Shell INTERACTIVE SHELL ▶
Reference
ZSH — Config · Aliases · Completion · Globbing · Oh My Zsh
Default shell on macOS (10.15+). Extends Bash with better tab-completion, globbing, plugins, themes. Config file: ~/.zshrc. Framework: Oh My Zsh.
~/.ZSHRC ESSENTIALS
# History HISTSIZE=10000 SAVEHIST=10000 HISTFILE=~/.zsh_history setopt HIST_IGNORE_DUPS HIST_IGNORE_SPACE SHARE_HISTORY # Navigation setopt AUTO_CD # type dir name to cd into it setopt AUTO_PUSHD # cd pushes to directory stack setopt PUSHD_IGNORE_DUPS # Completion autoload -Uz compinit && compinit zstyle ':completion:*' menu select zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-zA-Z}={A-Za-z}' # case-insensitive # Key bindings bindkey -v # vi mode (or -e for emacs) bindkey '^R' history-incremental-search-backward
ALIASES & FUNCTIONS
# Aliases alias ll='ls -lAFh --color=auto' alias la='ls -A' alias ..='cd ..' alias ...='cd ../..' alias g='git' alias gs='git status -sb' alias grep='grep --color=auto' alias ports='ss -tulanp' # Suffix aliases — run file by extension alias -s {yml,yaml}=$EDITOR alias -s py=python3 # Global aliases — used anywhere on command line alias -g L='| less' alias -g G='| grep' alias -g NUL='> /dev/null 2>&1' # ZSH functions (superior to aliases for complex logic) mkcd() { mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1"; } up() { cd $(printf "%0.s../" $(seq 1 $1)); } # up 3 = cd ../../..
ADVANCED GLOBBING
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB NULL_GLOB # Extended glob patterns ls **/*.py # recursive glob (setopt GLOB_STAR) ls ^*.log # negate: everything except .log ls *.{txt,md} # brace expansion ls (foo|bar)* # alternation ls **/*(.) # only files (. qualifier) ls **/*(/) # only directories ls **/*(Om) # sorted by modification time ls *(Lm+1) # files larger than 1MB ls *(mh-1) # modified in last hour
OH MY ZSH & PLUGINS
# Install sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)" # ~/.zshrc config ZSH_THEME="robbyrussell" # popular themes: agnoster, powerlevel10k plugins=(git docker kubectl python zsh-autosuggestions zsh-syntax-highlighting) # Useful OMZ git aliases (from git plugin) gst # git status gco # git checkout gcmsg # git commit -m gp # git push gl # git pull glog # git log --oneline --graph
🐹 Go — Systems & Cloud Language COMPILED LANGUAGE ▶
Reference
Go 1.22+ — Types · Functions · Structs · Goroutines · Channels · HTTP
Statically typed, compiled, garbage-collected. Strong concurrency model (goroutines + channels). Toolchain: go build/run/test/mod/vet/fmt. No classes — composition via interfaces and embedding.
PROGRAM STRUCTURE & TYPES
package main import ( "fmt" "os" "net/http" ) func main() { // Short variable declaration (type inferred) name := "Alice" age := 30 pi := 3.14 // Explicit declaration var count int = 0 var (x, y float64) // Constants const MaxSize = 1024 const ( StatusOK = 200 StatusErr = 500 ) fmt.Printf("Hello %s, age %d ", name, age) fmt.Println(count, x, y, pi) }
FUNCTIONS & ERROR HANDLING
// Multiple return values — idiomatic Go func divide(a, b float64) (float64, error) { if b == 0 { return 0, fmt.Errorf("division by zero") } return a / b, nil } // Error handling pattern — always check errors result, err := divide(10, 2) if err != nil { fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v ", err) os.Exit(1) } // Named return values + defer func readFile(path string) (data []byte, err error) { f, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { return } defer f.Close() // runs when function returns return io.ReadAll(f) } // Variadic + first-class functions func sum(nums ...int) int { total := 0 for _, n := range nums { total += n } return total } apply(func(x int) int { return x*2 }, 5)
STRUCTS, INTERFACES & METHODS
// Struct definition type User struct { Name string `json:"name"` Age int `json:"age"` email string // unexported (lowercase) } // Methods (receiver on value or pointer) func (u User) String() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%s (%d)", u.Name, u.Age) } func (u *User) Birthday() { u.Age++ } // pointer = mutate // Interface — satisfied implicitly type Stringer interface { String() string } func print(s Stringer) { fmt.Println(s.String()) } // Embedding (composition over inheritance) type Admin struct { User Level int } a.Name // promoted from User
GOROUTINES & CHANNELS
// Goroutine — lightweight thread (go keyword) go func() { fmt.Println("async") }() // Unbuffered channel — sync sender and receiver ch := make(chan int) go func() { ch <- 42 }() v := <-ch // Buffered channel bch := make(chan string, 10) // Select — multiplex channels select { case msg := <-ch1: fmt.Println(msg) case ch2 <- 99: fmt.Println("sent") case <-ctx.Done(): return default: fmt.Println("no-op") } // WaitGroup — wait for goroutines var wg sync.WaitGroup for i := range 10 { // range int (1.22+) wg.Add(1) go func() { defer wg.Done() process(i) }() } wg.Wait()
SLICES, MAPS & HTTP
// Slices (dynamic arrays) s := []int{1, 2, 3} s = append(s, 4, 5) s2 := make([]int, 0, 10) // len=0, cap=10 copy(dst, src) // Maps m := map[string]int{"a": 1} m["b"] = 2 if v, ok := m["c"]; ok { fmt.Println(v) } delete(m, "a") // HTTP server http.HandleFunc("/health", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK) json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]any{"status": "ok"}) }) http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
💙 PowerShell — Scripting Reference WINDOWS / CROSS-PLATFORM ▶
Reference — PowerShell 7+
Cmdlets · Variables · Flow Control · Pipelines · Common Patterns
PowerShell uses Verb-Noun cmdlet naming. Everything is an object. Pipeline passes objects (not text) between commands. Cross-platform: Windows, macOS, Linux (PS7+).
▸ VARIABLES & DATA TYPES
# Variables always start with $ $name = "Alice" $count = 42 $pi = 3.14 $flag = $true # $true / $false / $null # Typed declaration [int]$n = 10 [string]$s = "hello" [bool]$b = $false [array]$arr = 1,2,3 # Arrays $fruits = @("apple", "banana", "cherry") $fruits[0] # → apple $fruits.Count # → 3 $fruits += "date" # append # Hash tables (dictionaries) $user = @{ Name = "Bob"; Age = 30; Admin = $false } $user.Name # → Bob $user["Age"] # → 30 $user.Role = "Dev" # add key
▸ STRING OPERATIONS
# Interpolation (double quotes only) $msg = "Hello, $name!" $msg = "Count is $($arr.Count) items" # expression inside $() # Here-string (multiline) $text = @" Line one Line two — value is $name "@ # Common string methods "hello world".ToUpper() # HELLO WORLD " trim me ".Trim() # "trim me" "a,b,c".Split(",") # @("a","b","c") "hello".Replace("l","r") # herro "hello world" -match "w\w+" # $true; $Matches[0] = "world" "hello" -like "hel*" # $true (wildcard) -join ("a","b","c") # "abc" ("a","b","c") -join "-" # "a-b-c"
▸ FLOW CONTROL
# If / elseif / else if ($x -gt 10) { Write-Host "big" } elseif ($x -eq 10) { Write-Host "ten" } else { Write-Host "small" } # Comparison operators (not symbols) # -eq -ne -gt -ge -lt -le (numbers) # -like -notlike -match -notmatch (strings/regex) # -and -or -not (logical) # -contains -in (arrays) # Foreach loop foreach ($item in $fruits) { Write-Host $item } # For / While for ($i=0; $i -lt 5; $i++) { Write-Host $i } while ($x -gt 0) { $x-- } # Switch switch ($day) { "Mon" { "Start of week" } "Fri" { "End of week" } default { "Midweek" } }
▸ FUNCTIONS & PIPELINE
# Function definition function Get-Greeting { param( [string]$Name = "World", [switch]$Loud ) $msg = "Hello, $Name!" if ($Loud) { $msg.ToUpper() } else { $msg } } Get-Greeting -Name "Alice" -Loud # Pipeline — pass objects between cmdlets Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 10 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Get-ChildItem "C:\logs" -Filter "*.log" | ForEach-Object { Write-Host $_.Name } Get-Content log.txt | Select-String "ERROR" | Measure-Object -Line
▸ FILE SYSTEM & SECURITY COMMON CMDLETS
Cmdlet Action Alias
Get-ChildItem List directory contents ls, dir, gci
Set-Location Change directory cd, sl
Get-Content Read file cat, type, gc
Set-Content Write/overwrite file sc
Add-Content Append to file ac

Remove-Item Delete file/directory rm, del
Get-Process List running processes ps, gps
Stop-Process Kill a process kill, spps
Get-Service List Windows services gsv
Get-EventLog Read Windows event logs —
Invoke-WebRequest HTTP requests curl, wget, iwr
ConvertTo-Json Object → JSON string —
ConvertFrom-Json JSON string → object —
🟢 Bash Scripting — Debian / Ubuntu Reference SHELL SCRIPTING ▶
Reference — Bash 5+
Variables · Conditionals · Loops · Functions · Common Patterns
Bash scripts start with a shebang: #!/usr/bin/env bash. Make executable with chmod +x script.sh. Prefer [[ ]] over [ ] for tests.
▸ VARIABLES & QUOTING
# Assign — no spaces around = name="Alice" count=42 files=("a.txt" "b.txt" "c.txt") # indexed array # Read variables echo "Hello $name" # interpolation in double quotes echo 'Literal $name' # single quotes = no interpolation echo "Count: ${count}" # braces for clarity/adjacency # Default values echo "${var:-default}" # use default if var unset/empty echo "${var:=default}" # assign default if unset # Special variables $0 # script name $1 $2 # positional args $@ # all args as separate words $# # number of args $? # exit code of last command $$ # PID of current script $! # PID of last background job
▸ CONDITIONALS
# if / elif / else if [[ $x -gt 10 ]]; then echo "big" elif [[ $x -eq 10 ]]; then echo "ten" else echo "small" fi # Integer tests: -eq -ne -gt -ge -lt -le # String tests: == != < > -z (empty) -n (not empty) # File tests: -f (file) -d (dir) -e (exists) -r -w -x if [[ -f "$file" && -r "$file" ]]; then echo "readable file" fi # One-liner shortcuts [[ -d "/tmp/work" ]] || mkdir -p "/tmp/work" # create if missing command -v git &>/dev/null && echo "git found" # check command exists
▸ LOOPS
# for — iterate array for fruit in apple banana cherry; do echo "$fruit" done # for — C-style for ((i=0; i<5; i++)); do echo $i done # for — glob / find for f in /var/log/*.log; do echo "Processing: $f" done # while while read -r line; do echo "Line: $line" done < file.txt # until until [[ $count -ge 5 ]]; do (( count++ )) done
▸ FUNCTIONS
greet() { local name="$1" # local = scoped to function [[ -z "$name" ]] && { echo "Usage: greet <name>" >&2; return 1; } echo "Hello, $name!" } greet "Alice" # Hello, Alice! greet # prints usage, returns 1 # Return values via echo + command substitution get_date() { date +"%Y-%m-%d"; } today=$(get_date) echo "Today: $today"
▸ SCRIPT BEST PRACTICES
#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # -e exit on error, -u error on unset var, -o pipefail IFS=$'\n\t' # safer word splitting # Trap for cleanup cleanup() { rm -f /tmp/work.$$; } trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM # Logging helper log() { echo "[INFO] $*"; } warn() { echo "[WARN] $*" >&2; } die() { echo "[ERROR] $*" >&2; exit 1; } # Require dependencies for cmd in curl jq git; do command -v "$cmd" &>/dev/null || die "$cmd is required" done
🏷️ HTML — Structure & Semantic Elements WEB MARKUP ▶
Reference — HTML5
Document Structure · Semantic Tags · Forms · Meta · Accessibility
HTML defines structure, not style. Use semantic elements (<main>, <nav>, <article>) for accessibility and SEO. Always include lang, charset, and viewport.
▸ DOCUMENT BOILERPLATE
<!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> <meta name="description" content="Page description for SEO"> <title>Page Title</title> <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> </head> <body> <header><nav>...</nav></header> <main> <article>...</article> <aside>...</aside> </main> <footer>...</footer> <script src="script.js" defer></script> </body></html>
▸ SEMANTIC ELEMENTS
Element Purpose
<header> Site/section header, logo, top nav
<nav> Primary navigation links
<main> Primary content — one per page
<article> Self-contained content (blog post, card)
<section> Thematic grouping with a heading
<aside> Supplementary content, sidebar
<footer> Bottom of page/section, links, copyright
<figure> / <figcaption> Image + caption pair
<details> / <summary> Native accordion / disclosure widget
<dialog> Native modal dialog
<time datetime="…"> Machine-readable date/time
<mark> Highlighted/relevant text
<abbr title="…"> Abbreviation with expansion
▸ FORMS & INPUTS
<form action="/submit" method="post" novalidate> <label for="email">Email</label> <input type="email" id="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com" required autocomplete="email"> <select name="role"> <option value="" disabled selected>Choose…</option> <option value="admin">Admin</option> </select> <textarea name="notes" rows="4" maxlength="500"></textarea> <input type="checkbox" id="agree" required> <label for="agree">I agree</label> <button type="submit">Submit</button> </form> <!-- Input types: text email password number tel url date range color file search checkbox radio hidden submit -->
🎨 CSS — Selectors, Layout & Variables WEB STYLING ▶
Reference — CSS3 / Modern CSS
Selectors · Box Model · Flexbox · Grid · Custom Properties
Cascade order: !important > inline > ID > class/pseudo > element. Specificity: (0,1,0,0) = ID, (0,0,1,0) = class, (0,0,0,1) = element. Use custom properties for theming.
▸ SELECTORS & SPECIFICITY
p { } /* element (0,0,0,1) */ .card { } /* class (0,0,1,0) */ #hero { } /* id (0,1,0,0) */ a:hover { } /* pseudo-class (0,0,1,1) */ p::first-line { } /* pseudo-element (0,0,0,2) */ [type="text"] { } /* attribute (0,0,1,0) */ .nav > a { } /* child combinator */ .nav a { } /* descendant */ h2 + p { } /* adjacent sibling */ h2 ~ p { } /* general sibling */ :is(h1,h2,h3) { } /* :is() forgiving list */ :where(h1,h2) { } /* :where() — zero specificity */ :not(.hidden) { } /* negation */ :has(img) { } /* parent selector (modern) */
▸ CUSTOM PROPERTIES & CALC
:root { --color-primary: #00d4ff; --spacing-md: 1rem; --radius: 6px; } .card { color: var(--color-primary); padding: var(--spacing-md); width: calc(100% - 2rem); /* arithmetic */ font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem); /* fluid type */ }
▸ FLEXBOX
.container { display: flex; flex-direction: row; /* row | column */ flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: space-between; /* main axis */ align-items: center; /* cross axis */ gap: 1rem; } .item { flex: 1 1 200px; /* grow shrink basis */ align-self: flex-start; order: 2; }
▸ CSS GRID
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); grid-template-rows: auto; gap: 1.5rem; } .featured { grid-column: 1 / -1; /* span all columns */ grid-row: 1 / 3; }
⚡ JavaScript — ES2022+ Reference ES2022 · ES2023 · ES2025 ▶
Reference — Modern JavaScript
Variables · Functions · Async · DOM · Modern Features
Use const by default, let when reassignment is needed, never var. Modules use import/export. Always await inside async functions or use .catch().
▸ VARIABLES & DESTRUCTURING
const name = "Alice" let count = 0 // Array destructuring const [first, second, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4] // Object destructuring const { name: n, age = 25 } = user // rename + default // Optional chaining (?.) — ES2020 const city = user?.address?.city // no throw if undefined const n = arr?.[0] // optional index // Nullish coalescing (??) — ES2020 const label = value ?? "default" // only falls back on null/undefined // Logical assignment — ES2021 a ||= "fallback" // assign if falsy a &&= transform(a) // assign if truthy a ??= "default" // assign if null/undefined
▸ FUNCTIONS & ARROWS
// Arrow — implicit return when no braces const double = x => x * 2 const add = (a, b) => a + b // Default params + rest function greet(name = "World", ...extras) { return `Hello, ${name}! Extras: ${extras.join(", ")}` } // Spread const merged = { ...defaults, ...overrides } const copy = [...arr, newItem] // Async / await — ES2017+ async function fetchUser(id) { try { const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`) if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status) return await res.json() } catch (e) { console.error("Fetch failed:", e) } }
▸ ARRAY & OBJECT METHODS
// Array — non-mutating arr.map(x => x * 2) // transform each → new array arr.filter(x => x > 0) // keep matching → new array arr.reduce((acc, v) => acc + v, 0) // fold to single value arr.find(x => x.id === id) // first match or undefined arr.findIndex(x => x > 5) // first matching index arr.every(x => x > 0) // all pass? arr.some(x => x > 0) // any pass? arr.flat(2) // flatten 2 levels — ES2019 arr.flatMap(x => [x, x*2]) // map then flatten — ES2019 arr.at(-1) // last element — ES2022 // Object Object.keys(obj) // string[] of own keys Object.entries(obj) // [key,value][] pairs Object.fromEntries(entries) // reverse of entries — ES2019 Object.assign({}, src) // shallow clone/merge structuredClone(obj) // deep clone — ES2022
▸ ES2023 – ES2025 HIGHLIGHTS
// ES2023 — Array methods by copy (non-mutating) arr.toSorted() // like sort() but returns new array arr.toReversed() // like reverse() but returns new array arr.with(2, "x") // replace index 2, returns new array arr.findLast(fn) // find from end arr.findLastIndex(fn) // findIndex from end // ES2024 Promise.withResolvers() // {promise, resolve, reject} object Object.groupBy(arr, fn) // group array into object by key Map.groupBy(arr, fn) // group into Map // ES2025 (Stage 4) import source from "./data.json" with { type: "json" } // import assertions const it = iter[Symbol.iterator]() // explicit iterator protocol RegExp.escape(str) // escape special regex chars (Stage 4)
📦 JSON & jq — Data Format & CLI Processor DATA FORMAT ▶
Reference — JSON RFC 8259 & jq 1.7
JSON Syntax · Data Types · jq Filters & Transforms
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the universal API data format. jq is the standard CLI tool for parsing and transforming JSON. Install: sudo apt install jq · brew install jq.
▸ JSON SYNTAX & TYPES
{ "string": "hello world", "number": 42, "float": 3.14, "bool": true, "null": null, "array": [1, "two", false, null], "object": { "nested": true, "count": 3 } } // Rules: keys must be double-quoted strings, // trailing commas are NOT allowed, // comments are NOT part of JSON spec.
▸ JQ FILTERS
# Identity — pretty-print jq '.' data.json # Field access jq '.name' # top-level field jq '.user.email' # nested field jq '.items[0]' # first array element jq '.items[-1]' # last element jq '.items[1:3]' # slice index 1–2 jq '.items[]' # iterate all elements jq '.items[].name' # field from each element # Pipe and transform jq '.users[] | .email' # extract field from each jq '.[] | select(.active == true)' # filter — keep matching jq 'map(.score * 2)' # transform every element jq 'map(select(.age > 18))' # filter array jq '[.[] | select(.role=="admin")]' # collect into new array # Construct new shapes jq '{name: .name, email: .email}' # object construction jq '[.users[] | {id, name}]' # array of objects # Aggregation jq 'length' # count keys or elements jq '[.[] | .price] | add' # sum all prices jq '[.[] | .score] | max' # max value jq 'group_by(.category)' # group array by field jq 'sort_by(.name)' # sort by field jq 'unique_by(.id)' # deduplicate by field # String operations jq '.name | ascii_upcase' # uppercase jq '.items | join(", ")' # join array to string jq '"prefix_\(.name)"' # string interpolation # Useful flags jq -r '.name' # -r raw output (no quotes) jq -c '.' # -c compact (one line) jq -n '{a:1}' # -n null input (construct without file) jq --arg key val '.name == $key' # pass shell var as jq var
🗃️ SQL — Query Reference DATABASE LANGUAGE ▶
Reference — ANSI SQL / MySQL / PostgreSQL
DDL · DML · DQL · Joins · Aggregates · Window Functions
SQL has four main categories: DDL (schema) · DML (data) · DQL (query) · DCL (permissions). Execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
▸ DDL — SCHEMA DEFINITION
CREATE TABLE users ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE, name TEXT NOT NULL, role TEXT DEFAULT 'user', created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age INT; ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN age; CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email); DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp_data; TRUNCATE TABLE logs; -- delete all rows, keep structure
▸ DML — DATA MANIPULATION
-- INSERT INSERT INTO users (email, name, role) VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Alice', 'admin'); -- INSERT multiple rows INSERT INTO tags (name) VALUES ('sql'), ('data'), ('query'); -- UPDATE UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'; -- DELETE DELETE FROM users WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'; -- UPSERT (PostgreSQL) INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('bob@x.com', 'Bob') ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;
▸ DQL — QUERYING
-- Basic SELECT SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE role = 'admin' AND created_at > '2024-01-01' ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 25 OFFSET 0; -- Pattern matching SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'A%'; -- starts with A SELECT * FROM users WHERE email ~* '@gmail'; -- regex (PostgreSQL) -- Aggregate functions SELECT role, COUNT(*) AS total, AVG(age) AS avg_age, MAX(age) AS oldest FROM users GROUP BY role HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY total DESC;
▸ JOINS
-- INNER JOIN — only matching rows SELECT u.name, o.total FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id; -- LEFT JOIN — all users, nulls if no order SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.name; -- Subquery SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE total > 100); -- CTE (Common Table Expression) WITH big_orders AS ( SELECT user_id, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING SUM(total) > 500 ) SELECT u.name, b.spent FROM users u JOIN big_orders b ON b.user_id = u.id;
▸ WINDOW FUNCTIONS (PostgreSQL)
-- ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK SELECT name, score, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS row_num, LAG(score, 1) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS prev_score, SUM(score) OVER (PARTITION BY team) AS team_total FROM leaderboard;
🔗 URL Encoding — Percent Encoding Reference ENCODING REFERENCE ▶
Reference — W3Schools · MDN · Google · Sigma
URL / Percent Encoding — Rules, Characters & Interactive Decoder
URLs can only contain a safe subset of ASCII characters. Any character outside that set must be percent-encoded: replaced with %XX where XX is the two-digit uppercase hex value of the UTF-8 byte. Also called percent-encoding (RFC 3986).
▸ ENCODING RULES
Safe Characters
Never encoded: A–Z a–z 0–9 - _ . ~
Also safe in specific URL parts: ! * ' ( )
Reserved Characters
Have special URL meaning — encode when used as data:
: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =
Always Encode
Spaces, Unicode, control chars, and anything outside ASCII printable range must always be percent-encoded. Space → %20 (or + in query strings only)
Query String Rule
In application/x-www-form-urlencoded (HTML forms), space becomes +. In all other contexts use %20.
▸ COMMON PERCENT-ENCODED CHARACTERS
Character Name %Encoded Context / Notes
Space Space %20 (or +) %20 in paths; + valid in query strings only
! Exclamation %21 Sub-delimiter — encode in path data
" Double Quote %22 Always encode — not valid in URLs
# Hash / Pound %23 Fragment delimiter — encode when literal # needed
$ Dollar Sign %24 Reserved sub-delimiter
% Percent %25 Must encode % itself to avoid ambiguity
& Ampersand %26 Query param separator — encode in values
' Single Quote %27 Encode in param values to prevent injection
( Open Paren %28 Sub-delimiter
) Close Paren %29 Sub-delimiter
* Asterisk %2A Sub-delimiter
+ Plus %2B Encode in query values; + means space in forms
, Comma %2C Sub-delimiter; often safe but encode in values
/ Forward Slash %2F Path delimiter — encode when literal slash in data
: Colon %3A Scheme separator — encode in userinfo/path
; Semicolon %3B Path parameter separator
< Less Than %3C Always encode — invalid in URLs
= Equals %3D Key=value separator — encode in values
> Greater Than %3E Always encode — invalid in URLs
? Question Mark %3F Query string start — encode in path data
@ At Sign %40 User-info delimiter — encode in path/query
[ Open Bracket %5B IPv6 address delimiter only; encode elsewhere
\ Backslash %5C Always encode
] Close Bracket %5D IPv6 address delimiter only; encode elsewhere
^ Caret %5E Always encode
` Backtick %60 Always encode
{ Open Brace %7B Always encode
| Pipe %7C Always encode
} Close Brace %7D Always encode
~ Tilde %7E Unreserved — safe, no encoding needed
▸ URL STRUCTURE — WHICH PARTS GET ENCODED
# Full URL anatomy https://user:pass@example.com:8080/path/to/page?key=val&x=1#anchor │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ scheme │ │ host port path query fragment │ │ user password ← encode : and @ when used as data here # Path segment — encode everything except unreserved + sub-delimiters https://example.com/search/hello%20world # space in path → %20 https://example.com/file/report%232024.pdf # literal # → %23 # Query string — key=value pairs, separate with & https://example.com/search?q=C%2B%2B&lang=en # C++ → C%2B%2B https://example.com/api?name=John+Doe # space in form → + https://example.com/api?name=John%20Doe # space in URL → %20 # Fragment (hash) — not sent to server https://example.com/page#section-2 # fragment rarely needs encoding
▸ ENCODING IN CODE
## JavaScript encodeURIComponent("hello world & more") # → "hello%20world%20%26%20more" (encodes everything except unreserved) encodeURI("https://example.com/path with spaces") # → "https://example.com/path%20with%20spaces" (preserves URL structure chars) decodeURIComponent("%48%65%6C%6C%6F") # → "Hello" ## Python 3 from urllib.parse import quote, quote_plus, unquote quote("hello world/path") # → 'hello%20world/path' (/ safe by default) quote("hello world/path", safe='') # → 'hello%20world%2Fpath' (encode / too) quote_plus("hello world") # → 'hello+world' (form encoding) unquote('hello%20world') # → 'hello world' ## Bash / curl curl --data-urlencode "param=hello world & more" https://example.com python3 -c "import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote('hello world'))"
▸ GOOGLE MAPS / SPECIAL CONTEXTS
# Google Maps Embed API — address params must be encoded https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/geocode/json?address=1600+Amphitheatre+Parkway,+Mountain+View,+CA # Sigma Computing — special chars in URL parameters # Pipe | → %7C (used as multi-value separator) # Comma , → %2C (used in array parameters) # Colon : → %3A (used in filter syntax) https://app.sigmacomputing.com/embed?:filter=status%3Aactive%7Cpending # Double-encoding pitfall — only encode ONCE # Wrong: %2520 (encoded the % of %25, giving %%20) # Right: %20 (encode space once)

📐 Programming Fundamentals — Concepts & Vocabulary UNIVERSAL ▶
Foundation
Core Concepts Every Language Shares
Before syntax, every language shares the same underlying ideas. These concepts appear in every section of this reference — understanding them once means understanding every language faster.
▸ VARIABLES — NAMED STORAGE
A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value. The name is the label; the value is the content; the type defines what kind of content is allowed (number, text, true/false…).
# Python — dynamically typed (type is inferred at runtime) age = 30 # int — whole number price = 9.99 # float — decimal number name = "Alice" # str — text / string active = True # bool — True or False only data = None # NoneType — the absence of a value // JavaScript — same idea, explicit declaration keywords const MAX = 100 // const — cannot be reassigned let score= 0 // let — block-scoped, can reassign var old = "avoid" // var — function-scoped, legacy
▸ DATA TYPES — THE BUILDING BLOCKS
TypeWhat it storesExamplesNotes
IntegerWhole numbers0, 42, -7No decimal point; exact arithmetic
Float / DoubleDecimal numbers3.14, -0.5Approximate; IEEE 754 standard
StringText (sequence of chars)"hello", 'world'Immutable in most languages
BooleanTrue or Falsetrue, false, True, FalseFoundation of all conditions
Null / None / NilAbsence of valuenull, None, nil, undefined≠ zero, ≠ empty string
Array / ListOrdered collection[1, 2, 3], ["a","b"]Indexed from 0 in most languages
Object / Dict / MapKey → value pairs{"name":"Alice"}Fundamental to OOP and JSON
▸ OPERATORS
CategorySymbolsWhat they doExample
Arithmetic+ - * / % **Math operations10 % 3 → 1 (remainder)
Comparison== != < > <= >=Compare two values → boolean5 > 3 → true
Logical&& || ! (and or not)Combine boolean expressionstrue && false → false
Assignment= += -= *= /=Store a value in a variablex += 5 ≡ x = x + 5
== vs ===JS: == coerces types (1 == "1" → true). === checks type AND value (1 === "1" → false). Use === always.
▸ SCOPE — WHERE A VARIABLE EXISTS
// Scope controls VISIBILITY. A variable only exists within its scope. globalVar = "I exist everywhere" // global scope function example() { let localVar = "I only exist inside this function" console.log(globalVar) // ✓ can see global console.log(localVar) // ✓ can see local if (true) { let blockVar = "I only exist inside this if-block" } // console.log(blockVar) ← ✗ ReferenceError: blockVar is not defined } // console.log(localVar) ← ✗ ReferenceError: localVar is not defined # Scope rules: inner blocks can see outer; outer CANNOT see inner. # Closures: a function that "remembers" variables from its outer scope # even after the outer function has returned.
▸ CONTROL FLOW — DIRECTING EXECUTION
# Every language has three fundamental flow structures: # 1. SEQUENCE — code runs top to bottom (default) x = 5 y = x * 2 print(y) # → 10 # 2. SELECTION — branch based on a condition if score >= 90: print("A") elif score >= 70: print("B") else: print("C") # 3. ITERATION — repeat until a condition is met for i in range(5): print(i) # known count while queue is not None: process() # unknown count # break — exit loop immediately # continue — skip to next iteration # return — exit a function and optionally send a value back
🧱 Object-Oriented Programming — Classes, Objects & the 4 Pillars OOP ▶
Paradigm
OOP — Modelling the World as Objects
OOP organises code around objects — bundles of related data (fields / properties) and behaviour (methods / functions). A class is the blueprint; an object (instance) is a copy built from that blueprint. Used in Python, Java, C#, C++, JavaScript, Go, Ruby, and most modern languages.
▸ CLASS vs OBJECT — THE KEY DISTINCTION
# CLASS = blueprint. Defined once. Lives in your source file. # OBJECT = instance. Created at runtime. Can have thousands. # Blueprint (Class) class Dog: # __init__ is the CONSTRUCTOR — runs when object is created def __init__(self, name, breed): self.name = name # PROPERTY (instance data) self.breed = breed def speak(self): # METHOD (behaviour) return f"{self.name} says Woof!" # Objects (Instances) dog1 = Dog("Rex", "Husky") # new Dog object in memory dog2 = Dog("Bella","Poodle") # different object, same class print(dog1.speak()) # → Rex says Woof! print(dog2.name) # → Bella (dot notation accesses properties) # dog1 and dog2 share the CLASS but have INDEPENDENT DATA. # Changing dog1.name does NOT affect dog2.name.
▸ THE FOUR PILLARS OF OOP
1. Encapsulation
Bundle data + methods together. Hide internal state — only expose a controlled interface (public vs private). Why: protects data from accidental corruption. The object is a black box; you call methods, not raw variables.
2. Inheritance
A child class inherits properties & methods from a parent class. Child can extend or override them. Why: reuse code without copy-pasting. Cat extends Animal → Cat automatically has all Animal behaviour.
3. Polymorphism
"Many forms." The same method name behaves differently depending on the object it's called on. animal.speak() returns "Woof" for Dog, "Meow" for Cat. Why: write one piece of code that works with any subtype.
4. Abstraction
Hide complex implementation; expose only what the user needs. You call car.start() without knowing about fuel injectors. Why: reduces cognitive load and prevents misuse of internals.
▸ INHERITANCE & METHOD OVERRIDE IN PRACTICE
class Animal: # PARENT / base class def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def speak(self): return "..." # default — generic class Dog(Animal): # CHILD class — inherits Animal def speak(self): return "Woof!" # OVERRIDE parent method class Cat(Animal): def speak(self): return "Meow!" # POLYMORPHISM in action — same loop works on any Animal subtype animals = [Dog("Rex"), Cat("Luna"), Dog("Max")] for a in animals: print(f"{a.name}: {a.speak()}") # → Rex: Woof! | Luna: Meow! | Max: Woof!
▸ ENCAPSULATION — PUBLIC vs PRIVATE
class BankAccount: def __init__(self, balance): self.__balance = balance # __ prefix = PRIVATE (Python convention) def deposit(self, amount): # PUBLIC method — safe interface if amount > 0: self.__balance += amount def get_balance(self): return self.__balance # controlled read-only access acct = BankAccount(1000) # acct.__balance = -99999 ← blocked by convention / name mangling acct.deposit(500) # ✓ safe controlled change print(acct.get_balance()) # → 1500

📦 Data Structures — How Data is Organised in Memory CS FUNDAMENTALS ▶
Computer Science
Choosing the Right Container for Your Data
A data structure is a way of organising data in memory so it can be accessed and modified efficiently. Choosing the right one directly impacts speed and memory use. Every language provides these — sometimes built-in, sometimes as library types.
▸ THE CORE EIGHT
StructureWhat it isAccessInsert/DeleteUse When
Array / List Ordered, indexed, contiguous memoryO(1) by indexO(n) middle, O(1) end Order matters; frequent reads by position
Linked List Nodes each pointing to the nextO(n)O(1) head/tail Frequent insert/delete; no random access needed
Stack LIFO — Last In, First OutO(1) top onlyO(1) push/pop Undo systems, call stacks, DFS traversal
Queue FIFO — First In, First OutO(1) front onlyO(1) enqueue/dequeue Task scheduling, BFS traversal, print spoolers
Hash Map / Dict Key → Value pairs via hash functionO(1) avgO(1) avg Fast lookup by key; caches, frequency counts
Set Unordered unique valuesO(1) containsO(1) add/remove Deduplication, membership testing, intersections
Tree Hierarchical parent→child nodesO(log n) BSTO(log n) BST File systems, DOM, databases, sorted data
Graph Nodes + edges (directed or undirected)VariesVaries Networks, social graphs, routing, dependencies
▸ STACK vs QUEUE — VISUALISED
# STACK — think of a stack of plates # You can only add/remove from the TOP (LIFO) stack = [] stack.append("A") # push → stack: [A] stack.append("B") # push → stack: [A, B] stack.append("C") # push → stack: [A, B, C] stack.pop() # pop → returns C (last in, first out) # QUEUE — think of a supermarket checkout line # You add to the BACK and remove from the FRONT (FIFO) from collections import deque q = deque() q.append("A") # enqueue → [A] q.append("B") # enqueue → [A, B] q.popleft() # dequeue → returns A (first in, first out)
▸ HASH MAP — WHY O(1) LOOKUP IS MAGIC
# Problem: find if "alice" exists in 1,000,000 names # List search: check every item → O(n) — slow # Hash map: compute hash("alice") → jump to bucket → O(1) — instant # How it works internally: # 1. hash("alice") → 2847 (deterministic integer) # 2. 2847 % bucket_count → bucket index # 3. Look in that bucket only → ~1 comparison phone_book = {"alice": "555-1234", "bob": "555-5678"} print(phone_book["alice"]) # O(1) — instant regardless of size print("alice" in phone_book) # O(1) membership test # Collision: two keys hash to same bucket → handled by chaining or probing # Worst case O(n) if all keys collide — rare with a good hash function
📈 Big O Notation — Measuring Algorithm Efficiency ALGORITHMS ▶
Complexity Analysis
How Fast Does This Slow Down as Data Grows?
Big O describes how runtime (or memory) scales as input size n grows toward infinity. It ignores constants and lower-order terms — only the dominant growth pattern matters. Used in every technical interview and embedded in every data structure choice.
▸ COMPLEXITY CLASSES — FASTEST TO SLOWEST
NotationNamen=10n=1 000n=1 000 000Example
O(1)Constant 111 Hash map lookup, array index
O(log n)Logarithmic 31020 Binary search, balanced BST
O(n)Linear 101 0001 000 000 Linear search, single loop
O(n log n)Linearithmic 3310 00020 000 000 Merge sort, heap sort
O(n²)Quadratic 1001 000 00010¹² Nested loops, bubble sort
O(2ⁿ)Exponential 1 02410³⁰⁰impossible Recursive Fibonacci (naive), subsets
O(n!)Factorial 3 628 800impossible Travelling salesman (brute force)
▸ HOW TO IDENTIFY BIG O IN CODE
# O(1) — single operation regardless of input size def first_item(arr): return arr[0] # O(n) — one loop over all n items def find_max(arr): m = arr[0] for x in arr: # ← this loop runs n times if x > m: m = x return m # O(n²) — nested loops (each loops n times) def bubble_sort(arr): for i in range(len(arr)): # outer: n for j in range(len(arr)-1): # inner: n → n × n = n² if arr[j] > arr[j+1]: arr[j], arr[j+1] = arr[j+1], arr[j] # O(log n) — halves the problem each step (binary search) def binary_search(arr, target): lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1 while lo <= hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if arr[mid] == target: return mid elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1 # discard left half else: hi = mid - 1 # discard right half

GoF Patterns · MVC
23 Patterns in 3 Categories — The Most Useful 8
Design patterns are named, repeatable solutions to problems that come up constantly in software. Coined by the "Gang of Four" (GoF) in 1994. They're not code to copy — they're vocabulary for communicating architectural decisions.
▸ THREE CATEGORIES
Creational
How objects are created. Decouple creation from usage. Factory, Singleton, Builder, Prototype.
Structural
How objects are composed into larger structures. Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade, Composite.
Behavioural
How objects communicate and share responsibility. Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator.
▸ THE MOST IMPORTANT PATTERNS EXPLAINED
PatternCategoryProblem it solvesReal example
SingletonCreational Ensure only ONE instance of a class exists globally Database connection pool, config object, logger
FactoryCreational Create objects without specifying the exact class GUI toolkit (Button → WindowsButton or MacButton based on OS)
AdapterStructural Make incompatible interfaces work together Converting a legacy XML API to JSON for a modern service
DecoratorStructural Add behaviour to an object without changing its class Python @decorator, middleware chains in web frameworks
ObserverBehavioural Notify many objects when one object changes state Event listeners in JS, pub/sub systems, React state
StrategyBehavioural Swap algorithms at runtime without changing the client Sorting: choose QuickSort vs MergeSort based on data size
MVCArchitectural Separate data (Model), UI (View), and logic (Controller) Django, Rails, Angular, most web frameworks
RepositoryArchitectural Abstract database access behind a clean interface UserRepository.find_by_id() hides the SQL from business logic
▸ OBSERVER PATTERN — THE MOST COMMON IN WEB DEV
# Publisher (subject) holds a list of subscribers # When state changes, it notifies ALL subscribers automatically class EventEmitter: def __init__(self): self._listeners = {} def on(self, event, fn): # SUBSCRIBE self._listeners.setdefault(event, []).append(fn) def emit(self, event, data): # PUBLISH — notify all for fn in self._listeners.get(event, []): fn(data) emitter = EventEmitter() emitter.on("login", lambda u: print(f"Welcome {u}")) emitter.on("login", lambda u: log_event(f"{u} logged in")) emitter.emit("login", "Alice") # both listeners fire automatically # Same pattern as: btn.addEventListener("click", fn) in JavaScript
🌐 REST & HTTP APIs — How the Web Communicates API DESIGN ▶
Web Development · Backend
HTTP Methods · Status Codes · REST Principles
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract: "call this URL with these inputs and I'll return this output." REST (Representational State Transfer) is the dominant architectural style for web APIs. It uses HTTP as its transport.
▸ HTTP METHODS (VERBS)

POSTCreate new resourceYesNoPOST /users → create a user

PATCHPartial updateYesNoPATCH /users/42 → update one field
DELETERemove resourceNoYesDELETE /users/42 → remove user 42
HEADGET without bodyNoYesCheck if resource exists
OPTIONSWhat methods are allowed?NoYesCORS preflight check
▸ HTTP STATUS CODES

2xxSuccess200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content
3xxRedirect301 Moved Permanently · 302 Found · 304 Not Modified

▸ REST RESOURCE DESIGN CONVENTIONS
# Resources are NOUNS (not verbs). Actions come from HTTP methods. # ✓ Good REST URLs ✗ Bad (RPC-style) URLs GET /users # vs GET /getUsers GET /users/42 # vs GET /getUserById?id=42 POST /users # vs POST /createUser PUT /users/42 # vs POST /updateUser/42 DELETE /users/42 # vs POST /deleteUser?id=42 GET /users/42/orders # nested: orders belonging to user 42 GET /users?role=admin # query params for filtering GET /users?page=2&limit=25 # pagination # A complete REST call in Python import requests resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/users/42", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer <token>"}) if resp.status_code == 200: user = resp.json() # parse JSON body into dict
🔀 Git — Version Control Reference DEVOPS · DAILY USE ▶
Distributed VCS
Git — Track, Branch, Merge, and Collaborate
Git is the universal version control system. It tracks every change to every file in a project, lets multiple people work simultaneously via branches, and merges everything back together. A repository (repo) is the folder Git watches. A commit is a saved snapshot.
▸ THE THREE AREAS OF GIT
Working Directory
Your actual files on disk. Changes here are untracked until you stage them.
Staging Area (Index)
git add moves changes here. A holding zone — you choose exactly what goes into the next commit.
Repository (.git)
git commit permanently saves the staged snapshot here. The full history lives in this hidden folder.
▸ DAILY WORKFLOW COMMANDS
# ── Setup ────────────────────────────────────────────────── git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" git init # create new local repo git clone <url> # copy remote repo locally # ── Core workflow ────────────────────────────────────────── git status # what's changed? what's staged? git add file.txt # stage one file git add . # stage ALL changed files git commit -m "feat: add login" # save snapshot with message git push origin main # upload commits to remote git pull # fetch + merge remote changes # ── Branching ────────────────────────────────────────────── git branch # list branches git switch -c feature/login # create + switch to new branch git switch main # go back to main git merge feature/login # merge branch into current git branch -d feature/login # delete merged branch # ── History & inspection ─────────────────────────────────── git log --oneline --graph # visual commit history git diff # unstaged changes git diff --staged # staged vs last commit git show <hash> # what changed in that commit # ── Undo ─────────────────────────────────────────────────── git restore file.txt # discard unstaged changes (safe) git restore --staged file.txt # unstage a file (safe) git revert <hash> # undo commit, keep history (safe) git reset --hard <hash> # ⚠ destroy history to this point git stash # temporarily shelve WIP changes git stash pop # restore shelved changes
▸ BRANCHING STRATEGIES
StrategyConceptBest for
Git Flow main + develop + feature/* + release/* + hotfix/* Versioned releases; larger teams
GitHub Flow main + short-lived feature branches + PRs Continuous deployment; most teams today
Trunk-Based Everyone commits directly to main; tiny short branches High-velocity CI/CD; requires strong test coverage
Conventional Commits Structured messages: feat: / fix: / docs: / chore: / refactor: Auto-changelogs, semantic versioning, clarity
👋Programming from Zero — Start HereBeginner • Foundations▶
BIG IDEA
What Is Code?
Code is a set of precise instructions you give a computer — like a recipe. The computer follows it exactly and literally, top to bottom, with zero common sense. Most 'bugs' are just the computer doing exactly what you said instead of what you meant.
PLAIN
Program vs. Script
A program is any software built from code. A script is a smaller program, usually run line-by-line to automate a task (rename 1,000 files, back up a folder). The line is blurry — don't worry about it as a beginner.
HOW IT RUNS
Compiled vs. Interpreted
Computers only understand 1s and 0s (machine code). Compiled languages (C, Go) translate your whole file to machine code once, then run fast. Interpreted languages (Python, JavaScript, Bash) translate line-by-line as they run — easier to start with, a little slower.
DON'T PANIC
You Don't Memorize It
Nobody remembers every command. Real developers look things up constantly, read documentation, and copy-adapt examples. The skill isn't memory — it's breaking a problem into small steps and knowing what to search for.
Word You'll HearWhat It Means
SyntaxThe grammar/spelling rules of a language
Source codeThe human-readable text you write
RuntimeWhile the program is actually running
Compiler / InterpreterTranslates your code so the CPU can run it
IDE / EditorThe app you write code in (VS Code, etc.)
LibraryPre-written code you borrow instead of reinventing
📦Variables & Data Types — Storing InformationBeginner • Core▶
ANALOGY
Variables Are Labeled Boxes
A variable is a named box that holds a value you want to reuse. You put something in ('age = 30') and later open the box by name. Change the contents anytime — that's why it's 'variable.'
# Bash
name="Sam"
echo "Hi $name"

// JavaScript
let name = "Sam";
console.log(`Hi ${name}`);
THE BASICS
Common Data Types
Data comes in flavors and the computer treats each differently. The number 5 and the text “5” look the same to you but not to the computer — one does math, the other is just characters.
TypeHoldsExample
StringText"hello", "192.168.0.1"
IntegerWhole numbers42, -7, 0
FloatDecimal numbers3.14, 0.5
BooleanTrue or falsetrue, false
Null / NoneNothing / empty on purposenull, None
Array / ListAn ordered collection["a", "b", "c"]
GOTCHA
"5" + 5 Isn't Always 10
Mixing types causes classic beginner surprises. In JavaScript "5" + 5 is "55" (it glues text), while 5 + 5 is 10 (math). When numbers act weird, check whether they're secretly text.
🔀Control Flow — Decisions & RepetitionBeginner • Core▶
DECISIONS
if / else
An if statement lets code choose a path based on a condition — exactly like 'IF it's raining, take an umbrella, ELSE wear sunglasses.' The condition is a yes/no (boolean) question.
# Bash
if [ $age -ge 18 ]; then
  echo "Adult"
else
  echo "Minor"
fi
REPETITION
Loops
A loop repeats steps so you don't copy-paste. A 'for' loop repeats a set number of times (or once per item); a 'while' loop repeats as long as something stays true. This is where computers crush humans — tireless repetition.
// JavaScript: do something 3 times
for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log("Attempt " + i);
}
BUILDING BLOCKS
Boolean Logic
Conditions combine with AND, OR, NOT. 'Let in IF member AND over-18.' Comparisons (== equal, != not-equal, > greater, < less) produce the true/false that decisions and loops run on.
WATCH OUT
Infinite Loops
If a while-loop's condition never becomes false, it runs forever and freezes the program. Always make sure something inside the loop moves it toward the exit. Ctrl + C stops a runaway script in the terminal.
🧩Functions — Reusable Building BlocksBeginner • Core▶
ANALOGY
A Function Is a Mini-Recipe
A function is a named block of steps you can run again and again. Define it once, 'call' it whenever. Like a coffee machine: you press the button (call it), it does the steps inside, you get coffee (the result).
INPUTS & OUTPUTS
Parameters & Return
Parameters are the inputs you hand in (the beans and water); the return value is what comes back out (the coffee). Good functions do one clear job and hand back a result you can use.
// JavaScript
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
add(2, 3);  // returns 5
WHY BOTHER
Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)
If you copy-paste the same five lines in ten places and later need a fix, you fix it ten times. Put it in a function and you fix it once. Less copy-paste = fewer bugs.
🗂️Data Structures — Lists & Key/ValueBeginner • Core▶
ORDERED
Arrays / Lists
An array is a numbered shelf of items in order. You grab items by position — and most languages start counting at 0, so the first item is index 0 (a famous beginner trip-up).
// JavaScript
let fruits = ["apple", "pear"];
fruits[0];  // "apple"
LABELED
Objects / Dictionaries
When order doesn't matter but labels do, use key→value pairs: look things up by name instead of number — like a contact card with labeled fields. This is exactly what JSON is built from.
// JavaScript object
let user = {
  name: "Sam",
  age:  30
};
user.name;  // "Sam"
PICK ONE
Which Do I Use?
Need a sequence you'll loop through? Use a list. Need to look things up by a name/ID? Use an object/dictionary. You'll nest them constantly — lists of objects are everywhere in real data.
🐞Errors & Debugging — When Things BreakBeginner • Survival▶
REFRAME
Bugs Are Normal
Every programmer writes bugs every day — the term comes from a real moth found in a 1947 computer. Errors aren't failure; they're the computer telling you precisely where it got confused. Read the message; don't fear it.
SKILL
Read the Error Message
Error messages usually name the file, the line number, and the problem. Start at the top, read the actual words, and look up anything unfamiliar. 90% of beginner debugging is simply slowing down to read what it says.
TECHNIQUE
Print & Rubber-Duck
Two timeless tricks: (1) print values along the way to see what the code actually has, not what you assume. (2) Explain the code out loud, line by line, to a rubber duck — you'll often hear your own mistake.
METHOD
Change One Thing at a Time
Debug like a scientist: form one guess, change one thing, test, repeat. Changing five things at once means you won't know which fixed (or broke) it. Small steps, frequent saves.
🛠️The Workflow & Good HabitsBeginner • Practice▶
THE LOOP
Edit → Run → Test → Fix
Programming is a tight loop: make a small change, run it, see what happens, fix, repeat. Tiny iterations beat writing 200 lines and praying. If it works, save; then change the next small thing.
PLAN FIRST
Pseudocode & Decomposition
Before coding, write the steps in plain English (pseudocode), then translate each line. Break a scary task into boring small ones: 'read file → split lines → count words → print total.' Small problems are solvable problems.
BE KIND
Name Things Clearly + Comment Why
Code is read far more than it's written — usually by future-you. Use names like totalPrice, not x. Comments should explain WHY, not restate the obvious. Clear beats clever.
# Good: a name that explains itself
# and a comment that adds the reason
retry_limit=3  # API drops ~1 in 5 calls
HABIT
Save Early, Save Often
Save your file constantly (Ctrl + S) and, once you learn Git, commit small working steps. Losing two hours of work to a crash is a rite of passage you can skip.
🌿Version Control with Git — Save PointsBeginner • Tooling▶
ANALOGY
Git = Save Points for Code
Git records snapshots of your project over time, like save points in a video game. Made a mess? Load an earlier save. It also lets a team work on the same project without overwriting each other.
THE WORDS
Repo, Commit, Push, Pull
A repository (repo) is your project folder under Git's watch. A commit is one saved snapshot with a note. Push uploads your commits (to GitHub); pull downloads others'. GitHub is the cloud home where repos live and are shared.
FIRST FLOW
The Everyday Cycle
The loop you'll use 95% of the time: change files, stage them, commit with a message, push. Short, frequent commits with clear messages are a gift to your future self.
git add .
git commit -m "Add login form"
git push
WHY IT MATTERS
Fearless Experimentation
Because every good state is saved, you can try a wild idea on a 'branch' knowing you can always get back. Version control turns 'I'm scared to touch it' into 'let's try and see.'
🔌APIs & Data Formats — How Programs TalkBeginner • Tooling▶
ANALOGY
An API Is a Waiter
An API (Application Programming Interface) lets one program ask another for something. You (the app) don't go into the kitchen; you give the waiter (the API) an order from the menu, and it brings back the dish (the data).
REQUEST → RESPONSE
How a Call Works
Your app sends a request to a web address (endpoint); the server sends back a response, usually as JSON. A status code rides along: 200 = OK, 404 = not found, 500 = server broke. You'll learn to read those fast.
THE FORMAT
JSON in One Card
JSON is how programs swap data as text — just the objects and lists you already met: keys, values, {curly braces}, [square brackets]. It's readable by humans and every language, which is why it's everywhere.
// A JSON response
{
  "user": "sam",
  "admin": true,
  "roles": ["read", "write"]
}
🧮Operators & ExpressionsBeginner • Core▶
DO MATH
Arithmetic Operators
Operators are the verbs of code. The math ones work like a calculator, with one extra: % (modulo) gives the remainder — handy for “is this number even?” (n % 2 == 0).
// JavaScript
7 + 2   // 9   add
7 - 2   // 5   subtract
7 * 2   // 14  multiply
7 / 2   // 3.5 divide
7 % 2   // 1   remainder
COMPARE
Comparison & Logic
Comparisons ask a true/false question; logical operators combine them. Watch the classic trap: = assigns a value, but == (or ===) compares two. One equals sign in an if statement is a top-three beginner bug.
OperatorMeansExample → result
== / ===Equal to5 == 5 → true
!=Not equal5 != 4 → true
> <Greater / less than5 > 4 → true
>= <=Greater/less or equal5 >= 5 → true
&&AND (both true)true && false → false
||OR (either true)true || false → true
!NOT (flips it)!true → false
ORDER
Precedence — Use Parentheses
Just like math, * happens before +. When in doubt, add parentheses to make the order obvious — they cost nothing and save confusion: (price * qty) + tax reads clearly.
🔤Working with Text — StringsBeginner • Core▶
BASICS
Strings Are Just Text
A string is any run of characters in quotes: a name, an address, a whole paragraph. You can measure it, change its case, search it, and stitch pieces together (concatenation).
// JavaScript
let s = "Hello";
s.length              // 5
s.toUpperCase()       // "HELLO"
s + " world"        // "Hello world"
MODERN
Templates Beat Gluing
Instead of mashing strings and variables with +, most languages let you drop variables right inside a string. It’s easier to read and harder to break.
// JavaScript template literal (back-ticks)
let name = "Sam";
`Hi ${name}, you have ${3 + 2} alerts`
# Bash
echo "Hi $name"
GOTCHA
Quotes & Escaping
If your text contains a quote, you either switch quote styles or “escape” it with a backslash (\"). A stray quote is the reason a script suddenly refuses to run — count your quotes when text breaks.
📥Input & Output — Talking to the UserBeginner • Core▶
OUTPUT
Printing Results
The first thing every coder does is print something — the classic “Hello, world!”. Printing is also how you peek at what your code is doing while you build it.
# Bash
echo "Hello, world!"
// JavaScript
console.log("Hello, world!");
INPUT
Arguments & Reading In
Scripts often take input two ways: arguments typed after the command, or by asking the user mid-run. Arguments make scripts reusable on different files or values.
# Bash: first argument after the script name
echo "Backing up $1"
# run as:  ./backup.sh  /home/sam
THREE STREAMS
stdin, stdout, stderr
Programs have an in-tray (stdin), a normal out-tray (stdout), and a separate error out-tray (stderr). Keeping errors separate lets you log problems without polluting real results — and lets you pipe output into the next tool.
SIGNAL
Exit Codes
When a program finishes it returns a number: 0 means success, anything else means a problem. Scripts use this to decide what to do next — “if the backup succeeded, then delete the temp file.”
🔭Scope — Where Variables LiveBeginner • Core▶
IDEA
Local vs. Global
Scope is where a variable can be seen. A variable made inside a function is usually local — it exists only in that room and vanishes when the function ends. A global is visible everywhere, like a notice on the front door.
WHY CARE
Globals Cause Spooky Bugs
If everything is global, any line anywhere can change it, and tracking down “who set this to 0?” becomes misery. Keep variables as local as possible; pass what a function needs in, and return what it produces out.
// JavaScript
function tip(bill) {
  let rate = 0.2;  // local: lives only here
  return bill * rate;
}
🧰Which Language Should I Learn First?Beginner • Guidance▶
RELAX
The Concepts Transfer
Don’t agonize over the “best” first language — variables, loops, functions, and data structures exist in all of them. Learn one well and the next one is mostly new vocabulary, not new ideas.
HONEST PICK
A Simple Recommendation
For most beginners: start with Python — it reads almost like English and is used everywhere from security scripting to AI. Add JavaScript when you want things to happen in a web browser.
GoalGood First LanguageWhy
General / automation / AIPythonReadable, huge library ecosystem
Websites & browser appsJavaScriptThe only language browsers run
Glue tasks on Linux/serversBashBuilt into every Unix shell
Asking questions of dataSQLThe language of databases
Windows administrationPowerShellDeep control of Windows + objects
🌐How the Web Works (for Coders)Beginner • Web▶
THE TRIO
HTML, CSS, JavaScript
Every web page is three layers working together: HTML is the structure (the skeleton), CSS is the style (the skin and clothes), and JavaScript is the behavior (the muscles that react when you click).
<!-- a tiny page -->
<h1>Hello</h1>          <!-- HTML: structure -->
<style> h1 { color: teal } </style>  <!-- CSS -->
<script> alert('hi') </script>   <!-- JS -->
THE TRIP
What Happens When You Click a Link
Your browser (the client) asks a server for a page. DNS turns the name into an address, the request travels over the Internet, the server replies with HTML/CSS/JS, and the browser paints it on screen — usually in under a second.
TWO SIDES
Frontend vs. Backend
Frontend is what runs in the browser — what you see and click. Backend is what runs on the server — databases, logins, business logic. “Full-stack” just means someone comfortable on both sides.
LayerJobBeginner Analogy
HTMLContent & structureThe walls and rooms
CSSLook & layoutPaint and furniture
JavaScriptInteractivityLight switches that do things
Backend / APIData & rulesThe staff in the back office
🔐Secure Coding Basics (Beginner)Beginner • SecX▶
RULE #1
Never Trust Input
Anything a user (or another system) sends could be a mistake or an attack. Always check it: right type, sane length, expected format. “Validate, don’t assume” is the whole game — and ties straight back to ASS-U-ME.
CLASSIC ATTACK
SQL Injection, Simply
If you build a database query by gluing in raw user text, a clever user can write text that changes your query. The fix: use parameters / prepared statements so input is treated as data, never as commands.
# BAD — user text becomes part of the command
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'"

# GOOD — the ? is a safe placeholder for data
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
SECRETS
Don’t Hardcode Passwords
Never paste passwords, API keys, or tokens directly into code that gets shared or pushed to GitHub. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. Leaked keys in public repos are scooped up by bots within minutes.
HABITS
The Cheap Wins
Keep dependencies updated (old libraries have known holes), give code the least access it needs, log errors but never log passwords, and let proven libraries handle crypto — never invent your own encryption.
Beginner MistakeSafer Habit
Trusting user inputValidate & sanitize everything
Building queries by gluing stringsParameterized / prepared statements
Passwords in the source codeEnvironment variables / secrets vault
Showing raw errors to usersFriendly message + log the detail
Rolling your own cryptoUse vetted, standard libraries
🧠How Computers Think — Bits & BinaryBeginner • Foundations▶
THE ATOM
Bits & Bytes
Deep down, a computer only knows two states: on/off, 1/0. One of those is a bit. Eight bits make a byte, which is enough to store one character like the letter ‘A’. Everything — text, photos, music — is ultimately just bytes.
WHY HEX
Binary, Decimal & Hex
Binary (base-2) is how the machine counts; it gets long fast, so coders often write numbers in hex (base-16, 0–9 then A–F) as a compact shorthand. That’s why colors look like #FF8800 — three hex bytes for red, green, blue.
TEXT IS NUMBERS
ASCII & Unicode
Computers store letters as numbers using a lookup table. ASCII covered English; Unicode extended it to every language and emoji on Earth. So 😀 and ‘A’ are both just agreed-upon numbers under the hood.
UnitSizeRough Real-World Amount
Bit1 or 0A single yes/no
Byte8 bitsOne character
Kilobyte (KB)~1,000 bytesA short email
Megabyte (MB)~1,000 KBA minute of music
Gigabyte (GB)~1,000 MBA long movie
Terabyte (TB)~1,000 GBA big hard drive
📁Files, Paths & the Command LineBeginner • Foundations▶
ADDRESS
Absolute vs. Relative Paths
A path is a file’s address. Absolute starts from the root and is the full address (/home/sam/notes.txt) — true from anywhere. Relative starts from where you currently are (notes.txt or ../notes.txt) — like “two doors down from here.”
SHORTHAND
The Symbols You’ll See
A few path symbols show up constantly: . is here, .. is up one folder, ~ is your home folder, and / separates folders (\ on Windows). Learn these four and the command line stops feeling like a maze.
SUPERPOWER
Pipes & Redirects
The Unix philosophy: small tools that do one thing, joined together. A pipe (|) feeds one command’s output into the next; a redirect (>) sends output into a file. This is how huge tasks get built from tiny pieces.
# count how many lines contain "error"
cat app.log | grep error | wc -l
# save the matches to a file
grep error app.log > errors.txt
TIP
Tab Completion & History
Two habits that make the terminal feel fast: press Tab to auto-finish file names (fewer typos), and press the Up arrow to recall commands you already ran. Lazy is efficient here.
🧩Thinking in AlgorithmsBeginner • Problem-Solving▶
PLAIN
An Algorithm Is Just a Plan
An algorithm is a clear, finite list of steps to get a result — a recipe, directions to a friend’s house, the steps to make tea. Coding is mostly writing the plan precisely enough that a literal machine can follow it.
WORKED EXAMPLE
Find the Biggest Number
Watch how a vague goal becomes steps: assume the first item is the biggest, look at each remaining item, and whenever you see a bigger one, remember it instead. At the end, you’re holding the biggest. That’s an algorithm.
# pseudocode
biggest = first item
for each item in list:
    if item > biggest:
        biggest = item
return biggest
WHY IT MATTERS
Some Plans Are Faster
Finding a name in a shuffled pile means checking every card; in a sorted phone book you can flip to the middle and halve the search each time. Same goal, wildly different speed — that idea (Big-O) is why algorithm choice matters as data grows.
🏛️Programming Paradigms (Gently)Beginner • Concepts▶
DON'T PANIC
Different Styles, Same Goal
A paradigm is just a style of organizing code. You’ll hear scary words — they describe how people keep big programs tidy. As a beginner you’ll mostly write procedural code (step by step) and that’s perfectly fine.
OBJECTS
What ‘Object-Oriented’ Means
OOP bundles data with the actions on it into ‘objects’ — nouns that can do verbs. A Car object holds its speed and color (data) and can drive() or brake() (actions). It mirrors how we already think about things in the world.
ParadigmThe IdeaOne Line
