const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(
  fetch("image-filter.wasm")
);
const result = instance.exports.applyBlur(ptr, len);
JS and WASM share memory via a typed ArrayBuffer. Modern toolchains (Emscripten for C/C++, wasm-pack for Rust) generate the glue so you mostly call WASM like a normal library.
Reference
Where It Shines — and WASI Beyond the Browser
Use caseExample
Compute-heavy appsFigma, Photoshop web, video/audio editing, 3D/CAD, games
Port existing codeBring a mature C/C++ library to the web unchanged (ffmpeg, SQLite)
Server / edgeVia WASI, WASM runs outside the browser — fast-starting, sandboxed serverless & plugins
Not for everything: WASM can't directly touch the DOM (it calls back into JS for that), and simple UI logic is still easier in plain JavaScript. Reach for it when performance is the bottleneck.
📱 Progressive Web Apps (PWA) — Web Apps That Feel Native Web ▶
Concept
One Codebase, App-Like Experience
A Progressive Web App is a website that uses modern browser capabilities to behave like an installed app — it can be added to the home screen, work offline, load instantly, and send push notifications — all from a single web codebase, no app store required. "Progressive" means it works as a normal site everywhere and enhances where the browser supports more. It's the middle ground between a website and a native app.
Reference
The Three Core Ingredients
PieceWhat It Provides
Service WorkerA script that runs in the background between the page and network — enables offline, caching, and push. The heart of a PWA.
Web App ManifestA JSON file describing the app (name, icons, colors, display mode) so it can be installed to the home screen.
HTTPSRequired — service workers only run over secure connections (they're powerful, so they must be trusted).
Key Idea
The Service Worker — Offline & Caching
A service worker sits between your app and the network as a programmable proxy. It can intercept every request and decide: serve from cache, fetch from network, or both. That's what makes a PWA load instantly and keep working with no connection. 
// Cache-first: serve from cache, fall back to network
self.addEventListener("fetch", (e) => {
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request)
      .then((hit) => hit ?? fetch(e.request))
  );
});
Common strategies: cache-first (assets), network-first (fresh data), and stale-while-revalidate (fast + eventually fresh).
Trade-offs
PWA vs Native
PWANative app
CodebaseOne (web)Per platform
InstallFrom a URL, no storeApp store
Device APIsGrowing, but limitedFull access
UpdatesInstant (it's a website)Store review + user update
iOS supportPartial (some APIs gated)Full
Great for content, commerce, and productivity apps where reach and instant updates matter; native still wins for deep hardware access and demanding games.
♿ Web Accessibility (a11y) — Building for Everyone Web ▶
Concept
The Web Should Work for Every User
Accessibility (abbreviated a11y — "a", 11 letters, "y") means building sites people can use regardless of ability: someone navigating by keyboard, hearing a screen reader, zooming to 400%, or avoiding motion. It's not a niche — it overlaps with good UX for everyone (captions help in loud rooms; keyboard support helps power users), it's often a legal requirement (ADA, EU EN 301 549), and the standard to aim for is WCAG at level AA.
Framework
POUR — The Four Principles
PrincipleMeans
PerceivableUsers can sense the content — alt text on images, captions on video, sufficient color contrast.
OperableEverything works by keyboard, not just mouse; enough time; no seizure-inducing flashing.
UnderstandableClear language, predictable navigation, helpful error messages.
RobustWorks across browsers and assistive tech — valid, semantic HTML.
Practical
The Highest-Impact Habits
DoWhy
Use semantic HTMLA real <button> is focusable, clickable, and announced correctly for free. A <div onclick> is none of those.
Alt text on imagesDescribe meaningful images; use empty alt="" for decorative ones so screen readers skip them.
Label every inputA <label> tied to its field tells users what to type.
Keyboard + visible focusTab through the whole page; never remove the focus outline without replacing it.
Color contrast ≥ 4.5:1Body text must stand out from its background (WCAG AA).
Respect reduced motionHonor prefers-reduced-motion for users who get motion sickness.
Reference
ARIA — Use Sparingly
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds roles and states (role, aria-label, aria-expanded) so screen readers understand custom widgets. But the first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if native HTML can do it — a real <nav>/<button>/<input> beats a div patched with attributes. Bad ARIA is worse than none.
TestingHow
Automatedaxe, Lighthouse, WAVE — catch ~30–40% of issues fast.
ManualUnplug the mouse and navigate; turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA). No tool replaces this.
🦀 Rust — Safe Systems Programming Language ▶
Reference
Memory Safety Without a Garbage Collector
Rust's ownership and borrow checker guarantee memory safety at compile time — no GC, no use-after-free, no data races. That's why it's winning in systems, WASM, CLI tools, and increasingly the Linux kernel. 
fn main() {
    let mut nums = vec![1, 2, 3];
    nums.push(4);
    let sum: i32 = nums.iter().sum();   // 10
    println!("sum = {sum}");
}
ConceptDetail
Ownership / borrowEach value has one owner; borrows are checked at compile time
Option / ResultNo null; errors are values you must handle
CargoBuild tool + package manager (crates.io)
TraitsShared behavior (like interfaces) with zero-cost generics
Trade-off: a steep learning curve ("fighting the borrow checker") buys you C-like speed with safety guarantees. If it compiles, a whole class of bugs is simply gone.
☕ Java — The Enterprise Workhorse Language ▶
Reference
Write Once, Run Anywhere on the JVM
Java compiles to bytecode that runs on the JVM, making it portable and battle-tested for large backends. Statically typed, object-oriented, with a massive ecosystem (Spring) and a mature GC. 
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var nums = List.of(1, 2, 3);
        int sum = nums.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("sum = " + sum);
    }
}
ConceptDetail
JVM / bytecodePortable runtime; also hosts Kotlin, Scala, Clojure
Spring BootThe dominant framework for services
Maven / GradleBuild & dependency management
Modern JavaRecords, sealed types, virtual threads (Project Loom)
Kotlin is the modern, less-verbose JVM language (and Android's default) — worth reaching for on new JVM projects.
🎯 C# & .NET — Microsoft's Cross-Platform Stack Language ▶
Reference
Java's Sibling, Now Open & Everywhere
C# runs on .NET, which is now open-source and cross-platform. Strong tooling (Visual Studio), first-class async, and used for web (ASP.NET), desktop, games (Unity), and cloud. 
var nums = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
var sum = nums.Sum();            // LINQ
Console.WriteLine($"sum = {sum}");
ConceptDetail
.NET (Core)Cross-platform runtime & SDK (dotnet CLI)
LINQQuery collections/DBs with a fluent, SQL-like syntax
async/awaitC# pioneered the pattern most languages now copy
ASP.NET Core / BlazorWeb APIs & SPA-in-C# via WASM
Familiar if you know Java; NuGet is the package manager. Unity makes C# a major game-development language too.
💎 Ruby — Optimized for Developer Happiness Language ▶
Reference
Elegant, Dynamic, and All About Rails
Ruby is a dynamic, purely object-oriented language prized for readable, expressive code. Its killer app is Ruby on Rails, the convention-over-configuration framework that shaped modern web development. 
nums = [1, 2, 3]
sum = nums.reduce(0, :+)   # or nums.sum
puts "sum = #{sum}"
ConceptDetail
Everything is an objectEven numbers; blocks & iterators everywhere
RailsMVC, "convention over configuration", rapid CRUD apps
Gems / BundlerPackages & dependency locking
MetaprogrammingPowerful DSLs (Rails leans on this heavily)
Great for startups and prototyping — you go from idea to CRUD app fast. Trade-off: dynamic typing and slower raw speed than compiled languages.
🐘 PHP — The Language That Runs the Web Language ▶
Reference
Still Powering the Majority of Websites
PHP is a server-side language built for the web — it powers WordPress, and thus a huge share of all sites. Modern PHP (8.x) is genuinely good: typed, fast, with a strong framework in Laravel. 
<?php
$nums = [1, 2, 3];
$sum = array_sum($nums);
echo "sum = $sum";
ConceptDetail
Request-per-scriptClassic model: each request runs a script fresh
ComposerThe modern package manager (Packagist)
Laravel / SymfonyFull-featured modern frameworks
PHP 8+JIT, typed properties, enums, attributes, fibers
Don't judge it by 2005 — modern PHP is a competent, fast web language. Its ubiquity in shared hosting and WordPress keeps demand high.
🔩 C — Close to the Metal Language ▶
Reference
The Language Everything Else Is Built On
C is small, fast, and gives you direct control over memory via pointers. Operating systems, embedded firmware, databases, and language runtimes are written in it. Learning C teaches how computers actually work. 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {1, 2, 3}, sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) sum += nums[i];
    printf("sum = %d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}
ConceptDetail
PointersVariables that hold memory addresses — power & footguns
Manual memorymalloc/free — you own leaks & use-after-free
CompilationPreprocess → compile → link (gcc/clang, make)
Undefined behaviorOff-the-rails when you break the rules (buffer overflows)
C's manual memory is exactly what Rust set out to make safe. Its lack of guardrails is why memory-safety bugs dominate CVEs — the security case for newer languages.
⚙️ Assembly & How Programs Actually Run Fundamentals ▶
Concept
Registers, the Stack & the CPU's Real Job
Under every language is machine code the CPU executes. Assembly is the human-readable form. You rarely write it, but understanding it demystifies performance, debugging, and — crucially — how exploits like buffer overflows work (ties to the reverse-engineering material).
ConceptDetail
RegistersTiny ultra-fast CPU storage (rax, rsp, rip…)
The stackGrows down; holds locals, args & return addresses
Calling conventionRules for passing args & returns (System V, stdcall)
Instructionsmov, push, call, ret, jmp
Why it matters: overwriting a saved return address on the stack is the classic buffer-overflow exploit — and why we have stack canaries, ASLR, and NX. Reading disassembly is core to malware analysis and CTF pwn/rev challenges.
🏷️ Semantic Versioning & Dependency Management Fundamentals ▶
Reference
What ^1.2.3 Actually Means
SemVer gives version numbers meaning so tools can update safely. MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for fixes.
RangeAllows
^1.2.3≥1.2.3, <2.0.0 (compatible: minor+patch)
~1.2.3≥1.2.3, <1.3.0 (patch only)
1.2.3Exactly that version (pinned)
Lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, Cargo.lock) pin the exact resolved tree so builds are reproducible — commit them. Ranges say "what's allowed"; the lockfile says "what you actually got." A 0.x version signals anything may break at any time.

💙 PowerShell — Windows (and Cross-Platform) Scripting SHORTCUTS • Scripting ▶
POWERSHELL VS CMD
Why PowerShell Replaced Command Prompt
CMD (Command Prompt) is ancient — 1980s DOS heritage. PowerShell is a modern scripting environment built on .NET. Everything is an object (not just text), making it far more powerful. PowerShell Core (PS 7+) runs on Linux and Mac too — making it cross-platform. Windows admins and security teams must know it.
FeatureCMDPowerShell
Output typePlain text.NET objects (piped, filtered, sorted)
ScriptingBatch files (.bat) — limitedFull scripting language (.ps1) with loops, functions, classes
PipingText pipesObject pipes — access properties directly
Windows integrationLimitedFull access to WMI, .NET, COM, Registry
Cross-platformWindows onlyPowerShell 7+ runs on Linux/Mac
Security loggingMinimalTranscription, ScriptBlock logging
CORE CONCEPTS
Cmdlets, Objects, and the Pipeline
PowerShell commands are called cmdlets (pronounced "command-lets"). They follow a Verb-Noun naming pattern (Get-Process, Set-Item, New-Item). Output is objects with properties — you can access, filter, and pipe them.
# Get-Help is your best friend Get-Help Get-Process Get-Help Get-Process -Examples Get-Help *service* # find cmdlets about services # Basic navigation (aliases match Linux commands) ls # alias for Get-ChildItem cd C:\Users\Alice # alias for Set-Location pwd # Print Working Directory cat file.txt # alias for Get-Content cp source dest # alias for Copy-Item rm file.txt # alias for Remove-Item mkdir NewFolder # alias for New-Item -ItemType Directory # Object pipeline — output is objects, not text Get-Process # list all processes Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.CPU -gt 50} # filter by CPU Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 Get-Process | Select-Object Name, CPU, WorkingSet
COMMON TASKS
PowerShell Cheat Sheet
# Services Get-Service # list all services Get-Service -Name "wuauserv" # Windows Update service Start-Service -Name "wuauserv" Stop-Service -Name "wuauserv" Restart-Service -Name "wuauserv" Set-Service -Name "wuauserv" -StartupType Disabled # Files and text Get-Content C:\log.txt # read file Get-Content C:\log.txt | Select-String "error" # grep equivalent "Hello World" | Out-File C:\output.txt Add-Content C:\log.txt "new line" # append # Network Test-NetConnection google.com # ping + port check Test-NetConnection google.com -Port 443 # test specific port Get-NetIPAddress # your IP addresses Resolve-DnsName google.com # DNS lookup Get-NetTCPConnection # netstat equivalent # System info Get-ComputerInfo # detailed system info Get-EventLog -LogName Security -Newest 20 # security log Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_LogicalDisk # disk info # Users Get-LocalUser # list local accounts New-LocalUser -Name "alice" -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString "P@ss!" -AsPlainText -Force) Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "alice"
SCRIPTING
Writing PowerShell Scripts
# Variables start with $ $name = "Alice" $count = 42 $pi = 3.14159 # String interpolation Write-Host "Hello, $name!" # Hello, Alice! Write-Host "Pi is approximately $pi" # Arrays $fruits = @("apple", "banana", "cherry") $fruits[0] # apple $fruits.Count # 3 $fruits += "date" # add element # Hash tables (dicts) $user = @{ Name = "Alice"; Age = 30; Role = "Admin" } $user["Name"] # Alice $user.Role # Admin # If / ForEach / While if ($count -gt 10) { Write-Host "Big" } elseif ($count -gt 5) { Write-Host "Medium" } else { Write-Host "Small" } foreach ($fruit in $fruits) { Write-Host "I like $fruit" } 1..10 | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "Item $_" } # 1 to 10 # Functions function Get-Greeting { param([string]$Name = "World") return "Hello, $Name!" } Get-Greeting -Name "Alice"
EXECUTION POLICY
Why Your Script Won't Run
PowerShell's execution policy restricts which scripts can run. This is a security feature — not a permission system. On a new Windows machine, scripts are often blocked by default.
# Check current policy Get-ExecutionPolicy # Policy levels (most to least restrictive) Restricted # No scripts (default on Win clients) AllSigned # Only code-signed scripts RemoteSigned # Local scripts OK; downloaded must be signed Unrestricted # All scripts run (prompt for remote) Bypass # Nothing blocked (used in automation) # Set for current user (doesn't require admin) Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser # Run a script bypassing policy (one-time) powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File myscript.ps1
🌳 Git Power User — Beyond add, commit, push SHORTCUTS • Version Control ▶
STASHING
Set Work Aside Temporarily
You're mid-change and suddenly need to switch branches for an urgent fix — but your work isn't ready to commit. git stash shelves your changes so you have a clean working directory, then restores them later.
git stash # shelve current changes git stash -u # include untracked files git stash list # see all stashes git stash pop # restore most recent & remove from list git stash apply # restore but KEEP in stash list git stash drop # delete a stash git stash save "wip: login" # named stash
REBASE
Rewrite History for a Clean Timeline
Rebasing moves your commits to start from a different base — useful for keeping a linear, clean history instead of merge bubbles. Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared branch (it rewrites history others depend on).
# Update your feature branch with latest main (linear) git checkout feature git rebase main # replay your commits on top of main # Interactive rebase — clean up your last N commits git rebase -i HEAD~3 # edit/squash/reorder last 3 commits # In the editor: pick / squash / reword / drop / edit # If conflicts arise during rebase # fix files, then: git add <files> git rebase --continue git rebase --abort # bail out, restore original state
UNDOING THINGS
The Commands That Save You
GoalCommand
Unstage a file (keep changes)git restore --staged file
Discard local changes to a filegit restore file
Amend the last commitgit commit --amend
Undo last commit, keep changes stagedgit reset --soft HEAD~1
Undo last commit, keep changes unstagedgit reset HEAD~1
Nuke last commit and changes (danger)git reset --hard HEAD~1
Safely undo a pushed commitgit revert <hash> (makes a new inverse commit)
Recover "lost" commitsgit reflog (your safety net — shows ALL HEAD moves)
GIT BISECT
Binary Search to Find the Bug-Introducing Commit
A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits but you don't know where. git bisect does a binary search — you test the midpoint, tell git "good" or "bad", and it homes in on the exact commit that broke things in ~log₂(n) steps.
git bisect start git bisect bad # current commit is broken git bisect good v1.0 # this old tag worked # Git checks out a commit halfway between. Test it, then: git bisect good # this one works # — or — git bisect bad # this one is broken # Repeat. Git narrows down to the exact culprit commit. git bisect reset # done — return to where you started # Automate it with a test script! git bisect run ./test.sh # git runs the script at each step
INSPECTING
Useful Investigation Commands
git log --oneline --graph --all # visual branch history git blame file.py # who changed each line and when git show <hash> # view a specific commit's changes git diff main..feature # compare two branches git log --grep="bug" # search commit messages git log -p file.py # full history of one file git log --author="alice" # commits by author
🪟 tmux — Never Lose a Session Again SHORTCUTS • Productivity ▶
WHY TMUX
The Persistent, Splittable Terminal
tmux (terminal multiplexer) solves two huge problems: (1) Persistence — your session keeps running on the server even if your SSH connection drops or you close your laptop. Reconnect and everything's exactly where you left it. (2) Layout — split one terminal into multiple panes and windows. For anyone who works on remote servers, tmux is life-changing. A long-running job no longer dies when your Wi-Fi hiccups.
THE PREFIX KEY
Everything Starts with Ctrl+b
tmux commands begin with a prefix — by default Ctrl+b — then a key. Notation: C-b means Ctrl+b, release, then press the next key. (Many people remap the prefix to Ctrl+a for ergonomics.)
# Session management (from the shell) tmux # start a new session tmux new -s work # named session "work" tmux ls # list sessions tmux attach -t work # reattach to "work" tmux kill-session -t work # THE killer feature: detach and reattach # C-b d → detach (session keeps running on the server) # Later: tmux attach → everything's still there
PANES & WINDOWS
Splitting and Navigating
Keys (after C-b)Action
%Split pane vertically (left/right)
"Split pane horizontally (top/bottom)
arrow keysMove between panes
oCycle to next pane
zZoom pane to fullscreen (toggle)
xClose current pane
cCreate a new window (like a tab)
n / pNext / previous window
0-9Jump to window by number
,Rename current window
[Enter scroll/copy mode (q to exit)
CONFIG
A Sensible ~/.tmux.conf Starter
# ~/.tmux.conf # Remap prefix to Ctrl+a (easier reach) unbind C-b set -g prefix C-a # Start windows/panes at 1, not 0 set -g base-index 1 # Enable mouse (scroll, click panes, resize) set -g mouse on # More scrollback history set -g history-limit 10000 # Easier splits that remember current path bind | split-window -h -c "#{pane_current_path}" bind - split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}" # Reload config without restarting: C-a r bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "Reloaded!"
⚡ Text Processing Mastery — Combining the Classic Tools SHORTCUTS • Power User ▶
THE UNIX PHILOSOPHY
Small Tools That Do One Thing, Piped Together
The power of the command line comes from composing small, focused tools with pipes (|). Each tool does one thing well; the pipe feeds one's output into the next. Mastering a handful of these — and how to chain them — lets you answer questions about logs and data in seconds that would take ages in a GUI.
GREP — FIND LINES
Search Text Like a Pro
grep "ERROR" app.log # lines containing ERROR grep -i "error" app.log # case-insensitive grep -r "TODO" ./src # recursive through dir grep -v "DEBUG" app.log # INVERT — lines WITHOUT DEBUG grep -c "404" access.log # count matching lines grep -n "fail" app.log # show line numbers grep -A3 -B3 "panic" app.log # 3 lines After + Before context grep -E "warn|error|fatal" app.log # regex (extended) OR grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" log # extract just IPs
FIND — LOCATE FILES
Search the Filesystem by Any Attribute
find . -name "*.log" # by name pattern find / -type f -size +100M # files over 100MB find . -mtime -1 # modified in last 24h find /var/log -mtime +30 -delete # delete logs older than 30 days find . -type f -name "*.sh" -perm -u+x # executable scripts # find + exec / xargs — act on results find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; # delete each match find . -name "*.py" | xargs grep "import os" # grep in matches
THE CLASSIC PIPELINE
cut · sort · uniq · awk — Together
# "Top 10 IPs hitting my web server" — a legendary one-liner cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10 # cut field 1 (IP) → sort → count dups → sort by count desc → top 10 # Count HTTP status codes awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # Sum a column (e.g., total bytes transferred) awk '{sum += $10} END {print sum}' access.log # Unique users who logged in today grep "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)" auth.log | grep "session opened" \ | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -u # Find the 5 largest files under /var, human-readable find /var -type f -printf '%s %p\n' | sort -rn | head -5 \ | awk '{printf "%.1f MB %s\n", $1/1048576, $2}'
MODERN ALTERNATIVES
Faster, Friendlier Replacements
ClassicModernWhy
grepripgrep (rg)Much faster, respects .gitignore, nicer output
findfdSimpler syntax, fast, sane defaults
catbatSyntax highlighting, line numbers
lseza / lsdColors, icons, git status
tophtop / btopInteractive, visual
Learn the classics first — they're on every server, everywhere, forever. The modern tools are great for your own machine but won't be on that random production box at 3am.
⌨️ Intermediate Vim — Editing as a Language SHORTCUTS • Power User ▶
THE BIG IDEA
Vim Is a Language: Verb + Motion
Vim's power isn't memorizing hundreds of commands — it's that commands compose like a language. You combine a verb (operator: what to do) with a motion (where). Learn a handful of each and you can express thousands of edits. d (delete) + w (word) = dw "delete word." Once it clicks, editing becomes thought-speed.
# GRAMMAR: [count] operator motion dw # delete word d3w # delete 3 words c$ # change to end of line y} # yank (copy) to next blank line >i{ # indent inside { } block =G # auto-indent to end of file
OPERATORS (VERBS)
What to Do
OperatorAction
dDelete (cut)
cChange (delete + enter insert mode)
yYank (copy)
> / <Indent / dedent
=Auto-format/indent
gu / gULowercase / uppercase
MOTIONS & TEXT OBJECTS
Where to Act
MotionMoves / Selects
w / b / eWord forward / back / end
0 / $Start / end of line
gg / GTop / bottom of file
f{char} / t{char}Jump to / before next char
%Matching bracket
iw / awText object: inner / a word
i" / i( / i{Inside quotes / parens / braces
it / ipInside tag / paragraph
Text objects are the superpower: ci" = "change inside quotes" (deletes text between quotes, drops you in insert mode) — works no matter where your cursor is in the string. di( = delete inside parens. dit = delete inside HTML tag. These feel magical once learned.
HIGH-VALUE COMMANDS
Things That Save Real Time
. # REPEAT last change (incredibly powerful) ciw # change inner word, then . to repeat on others * # search for word under cursor ggVG # select entire file (gg, Visual, G) :%s/old/new/g # replace all "old" with "new" in file :%s/old/new/gc # ...with confirmation each time u / Ctrl-r # undo / redo A # jump to end of line + insert o / O # open new line below / above >G # indent from cursor to end of file Ctrl-v # VISUAL BLOCK — edit columns (great for tables)
The . command repeats your last change — pair it with a motion-based edit and you can fix dozens of spots with single keystrokes. Mastering "edit once, repeat with ." is the hallmark of a fluent Vim user.

If you spend your day in a browser — and almost everyone in IT does — a handful of muscle-memory shortcuts can save you dozens of clicks an hour. These work across Chrome, Edge, and Firefox unless noted otherwise (swap Ctrl for Cmd on macOS).

Hands-on

DevTools shortcuts every helpdesk and dev should know

ShortcutWhat it does

Ctrl+Shift+C"Inspect element" mode — click anything on the page to see its underlying HTML/CSS

When a user reports "the website is broken," opening the Console tab before doing anything else often shows you the actual JavaScript error in seconds — turning a vague complaint into an actionable bug report you can hand to a developer.

Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me

"It works fine for me" is rarely the end of the story — it might be a cached version of the page, a browser extension interfering, or a cookie holding onto stale session data. Before assuming the user is "doing something wrong," try Ctrl+Shift+N for a clean incognito window: if the problem disappears there, you've just proven it's local to their browser profile, not the website — and saved everyone a lot of back-and-forth.

Beginner

Tmux Survival Kit – Never Lose a Terminal Session Again

Concept

The problem tmux solves: "the SSH connection dropped, and I lost everything"

Tmux (terminal multiplexer) lets you create terminal sessions that keep running even after you disconnect — whether your laptop sleeps, your VPN drops, or you just want to walk away and resume later from a different machine. Without it, a long-running command in an SSH session dies the instant the connection does. With it, you simply reconnect and find everything exactly where you left it, still running.

Concept

The mental model: sessions, windows, and panes

ConceptThink of it as...Why it matters
SessionAn entire workspace — everything you're doing on this server right nowYou can detach from it and it keeps running; reattach later from anywhere
WindowA tab within that sessionSwitch between separate tasks (editing, monitoring logs, running tests) without separate connections
PaneA split within a window — multiple terminals visible side by sideWatch logs in one pane while running commands in another, all on one screen
Reference

The shortcuts that get you 90% of the way there

Every tmux command starts with a "prefix" key — by default Ctrl+b — released, then followed by another key. Below, "prefix" means "press Ctrl+b, let go, then press the next key."

ShortcutWhat it does
tmux new -s workStart a new named session called "work" (naming sessions makes them MUCH easier to find later)
prefix dDetach from the current session — it keeps running in the background
tmux attach -t workReattach to that session from anywhere — even a different computer
tmux lsList all running sessions — "what do I have going on right now?"
prefix cCreate a new window (tab) in the current session
prefix n / prefix pMove to the next / previous window
prefix %Split the current pane vertically (side by side)
prefix "Split the current pane horizontally (stacked)
prefix arrow-keyMove between panes in that direction
Hands-on

A realistic first session, start to finish

# 1. SSH into a remote server, then start a named session
ssh admin@server.example.com
tmux new -s deploy

# 2. Kick off something long-running — a deployment, a big sync, a build
./run_deployment.sh

# 3. Your laptop goes to sleep / VPN hiccups / you close the lid.
#    The deployment KEEPS RUNNING on the server — tmux doesn't care
#    that your connection dropped.

# 4. Reconnect later (even from a different machine entirely)
ssh admin@server.example.com
tmux attach -t deploy
# ...and there it is, exactly where you left it, still running

# 5. When you're completely done with it
exit   # closes the window/session from inside
# or from outside: tmux kill-session -t deploy
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — name your sessions

"I'll remember which session is which" is a confident assumption at 2 PM and a source of genuine confusion at 2 AM when tmux ls shows four unnamed sessions and you can't recall which one has the thing you actually need. The thirty seconds it costs to type tmux new -s deploy-prod-db-migration instead of tmux new pays for itself the very first time you have more than one session running — which, if you use tmux at all regularly, will be sooner than you think.

🧰 VS Code — Setup, Settings & Profiles VS Code ▶
How-To
Make It Yours — and Keep It Everywhere
VS Code is configured through settings.json (per-user and per-workspace). Settings Sync pushes your settings, keybindings, and extensions to every machine via your GitHub/Microsoft account. Profiles let you keep clean, separate setups per stack (a lean Python profile vs a heavy web profile) so extensions don't pile up.
▸ SETTINGS WORTH SETTING (settings.json)
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,       // auto-format every save
  "editor.rulers": [80, 120],       // visual line-length guides
  "files.autoSave": "onFocusChange",
  "editor.minimap.enabled": false,
  "workbench.editor.enablePreview": false,  // stop tabs replacing each other
  "editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled": true
}
Tip: commit a .vscode/settings.json to a repo to share team defaults, and a .editorconfig for cross-editor consistency.

🛰️ VS Code — Remote Dev & Dev Containers VS Code ▶
How-To
Edit Locally, Run Anywhere
VS Code's Remote Development splits the editor (your machine) from the workspace (elsewhere): a server component runs on the target and the UI stays local, so it feels native even though the code, terminal, and extensions execute remotely.
ModeRuns your code…
Remote-SSHOn a remote server over SSH
WSLInside the Linux subsystem on Windows
Dev ContainersInside a Docker container defined by devcontainer.json
CodespacesIn a cloud-hosted dev container (GitHub)
Dev Containers are the big win: a devcontainer.json in the repo pins the exact toolchain, extensions, and settings, so every teammate (and CI) gets an identical, disposable environment — "works on my machine" disappears.

🗃️ Dotfiles & Environment Management Dev Env ▶
How-To
Your Setup, Version-Controlled & Portable
Your shell config, editor settings, git config, and aliases (the "dotfiles" — .bashrc, .gitconfig, …) are your personal productivity layer. Put them in a Git repo so a new machine is one command away from feeling like home, and you never lose that alias you set up two years ago.
ToolApproach
chezmoiPowerful: templating, secrets, per-machine differences
GNU stowSimple symlink farm — great for basic setups
bare git repoTrack $HOME directly with an alias
Never commit secrets — keep API keys/tokens out of dotfiles (use a secrets tool or machine-local files in .gitignore). A public dotfiles repo is a classic accidental-leak source.
🐚 Shell & Terminal Setup Dev Env ▶
Reference
A Terminal That Works With You
A little terminal investment pays off every day. Pick a shell, add a fast prompt, and layer in modern CLI tools that are strictly better than the classics.
PieceOptions
Shellzsh (+ oh-my-zsh) or fish (great defaults)
Promptstarship — fast, shows git/context, one config
Multiplexertmux — persistent sessions & splits (see the tmux topic)

🔢 Runtime & Version Managers Dev Env ▶
How-To
The Right Language Version, Per Project
Project A needs Node 18, Project B needs Node 22; one needs Python 3.11, another 3.13. Version managers let you install many versions and switch automatically per directory — no more "works on my machine" from a version mismatch.
ToolManages
mise / asdfOne tool for many languages (Node, Python, Go, …)
nvm / fnmNode versions
pyenv + uv/venvPython versions + isolated envs
direnvAuto-load per-directory env vars & tool versions
Commit a version file (.tool-versions, .nvmrc) so the whole team — and CI — uses the same runtime. mise is the rising all-in-one; direnv makes it automatic on cd.
🤖 AI Pair Programming — Using It Well Dev Env ▶
Reference
A Force Multiplier — If You Stay in Charge
AI assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and others) generate code, explain unfamiliar code, write tests, and draft boilerplate fast. Used well they're a big accelerant; used blindly they introduce subtle bugs and security holes. You stay the engineer — the AI drafts, you own.
DoWatch out for
Great for boilerplate, tests, glue codePlausible-but-wrong code (hallucinated APIs)
Explaining a codebase / errorInsecure defaults (no input validation)
Refactoring with a clear specOutdated patterns from training data
Review every line before you commitLeaking secrets/proprietary code to a service
Treat AI output like a junior's PR: read it, test it, understand it before it ships. The engineers who benefit most are the ones who could have written it themselves and can spot when it's wrong.

BASH READLINE SHORTCUTS
Move Without the Arrow Keys
ShortcutAction
Ctrl+AMove cursor to beginning of line
Ctrl+EMove cursor to end of line
Ctrl+F / Ctrl+BMove forward/back one character
Alt+F / Alt+BMove forward/back one WORD
Ctrl+WDelete word before cursor
Alt+DDelete word after cursor

Ctrl+UDelete from cursor to beginning of line

HISTORY TRICKS
Never Retype Long Commands
# See your command history history | tail -20 # Run command #42 from history !42 # Run last command starting with "nmap" !nmap # Substitute in last command (fix typos fast) # If you typed: cat /etc/paaswd ^paaswd^passwd # re-runs with correction # Search history with fzf (install separately) Ctrl+R # built-in incremental search
TMUX BASICS
Multiple Terminals in One Window
tmux is a terminal multiplexer — splits your terminal into multiple panes, creates persistent sessions that survive network disconnects, and lets you detach/reattach from long-running tasks.
# Start new session tmux new -s mysession # Detach (leaves session running) Ctrl+B then D # Reattach later tmux attach -t mysession # Key bindings (all start with Ctrl+B, the prefix) # Split horizontally Ctrl+B then % # Split vertically Ctrl+B then " # Move between panes Ctrl+B then arrow key # New window (tab) Ctrl+B then C # Switch windows Ctrl+B then N / P # Kill current pane Ctrl+B then X
ALIASES
Shortcut Your Most-Used Commands
# Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc # Shorter ls with detail alias ll='ls -lah --color=auto' # Never accidentally remove files alias rm='rm -i' # Quick git shortcuts alias gs='git status' alias gd='git diff' alias gl='git log --oneline --graph -20' # SSH with key timeout alias ssha='eval $(ssh-agent) && ssh-add' # Python shortcut alias py='python3' # Apply changes source ~/.bashrc
PIPES & REDIRECTION
Compose Powerful One-Liners
# | pipes output of one command into next ps aux | grep python | grep -v grep # > overwrites file, >> appends echo "hello" > output.txt echo "world" >> output.txt # 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 merges with stdout command > out.log 2>&1 # /dev/null discards output command > /dev/null 2>&1 # tee: write to file AND stdout simultaneously ls -la | tee listing.txt # xargs: turn output into arguments find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm -f

🐙 GitHub & Git — Command Reference DEV · VERSION CONTROL ▶
Concept
Git vs GitHub
Git is a distributed version-control system that runs locally — it tracks changes, branches, and history entirely on your machine. GitHub is a cloud hosting service for Git repositories that adds pull requests, Actions CI/CD, Issues, and collaboration features. You push local Git commits to a remote GitHub repository.
Reference
Core Workflow — Init · Clone · Stage · Commit · Push
▸ SETUP & REPO CREATION
CommandWhat It Does
git initCreate a new Git repo in the current directory
git clone <url>Download a remote repo and all its history
git remote add origin <url>Link local repo to a remote (usually GitHub)
git remote -vList all configured remotes and their URLs
git config --global user.name "Name"Set your display name for commits globally
git config --global user.email "e@x.com"Set your email for commits globally
▸ STAGE & COMMIT
CommandWhat It Does
git statusShow staged, unstaged, and untracked files
git add <file>Stage a specific file for the next commit
git add .Stage all changed files in current directory
git commit -m "message"Save staged snapshot with a descriptive message
git commit --amendEdit the last commit message or add staged changes to it
git diffShow unstaged changes line by line
git diff --stagedShow staged changes that will go into the next commit
▸ PUSH & PULL
CommandWhat It Does
git push -u origin mainPush main branch & set upstream tracking for future pushes
git pushPush current branch to its tracked remote branch
git pullFetch remote changes and merge into current branch
git fetch originDownload remote changes without merging them
git push origin --delete <branch>Delete a branch on the remote
▸ BRANCHING & MERGING
CommandWhat It Does
git branchList all local branches (* = current)
git branch <name>Create a new branch at current commit
git switch <name>Switch to an existing branch (modern syntax)
git switch -c <name>Create and switch to a new branch in one step
git merge <branch>Merge named branch into current branch
git rebase mainReplay current branch commits on top of main (cleaner history)
git branch -d <name>Delete a local branch (safe — fails if unmerged)
▸ INSPECTION & HISTORY
CommandWhat It Does
git log --onelineCompact one-line-per-commit history
git log --oneline --graphASCII branch graph alongside commit log
git show <commit>Display diff and metadata for a specific commit
git blame <file>Show who last changed each line of a file
git tag v1.0.0Create a lightweight tag at current commit
▸ UNDO & RECOVERY
CommandWhat It Does
git restore <file>Discard unstaged changes to a file (permanent)
git restore --staged <file>Unstage a file (keeps changes on disk)
git revert <commit>Create a new commit that undoes a past commit (safe for shared repos)
git reset --soft HEAD~1Undo last commit but keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1Undo last commit AND discard changes entirely (destructive)
git stashShelve current changes to a temporary stack
git stash popApply most-recent stash and remove it from the stack

🔑 API Keys & Gateways — Netlify · GitHub · REST DEV · WEB · DEPLOY ▶
Concept
What Is an API Key?
An API key is a unique string a server issues to identify and authorize a client. When you make a request to an external service (weather data, payment processor, AI model), you include the key so the server knows who you are and what you're allowed to do. Keys are like passwords for machines — they should never be hard-coded in source code or committed to Git.
Reference
API Key Types & Token Formats
▸ KEY & TOKEN TYPES
TypeHow It WorksExample Use
API Key (static)A long random string sent with every requestOpenWeather, Stripe publishable key
Secret KeyServer-side only — never exposed to browsersStripe secret key, Twilio auth token
Bearer Token (OAuth 2.0)Short-lived token exchanged after auth flowGoogle APIs, GitHub OAuth Apps
Personal Access Token (PAT)Long-lived user token with scoped permissionsGitHub PAT, GitLab personal token
JWT (JSON Web Token)Self-contained signed payload: header.payload.sigAuth0, Firebase, custom auth backends
Service Account KeyJSON credential file for machine-to-machine authGoogle Cloud service accounts
Webhook SecretHMAC signature to verify incoming webhook payloadsGitHub webhooks, Stripe webhooks
▸ HOW API KEYS ARE SENT
MethodExampleNotes
HTTP Header (preferred)Authorization: Bearer <token>Most secure — not in logs or browser history
Custom HeaderX-API-Key: <key>Common with REST APIs (e.g. AWS, Twilio)
Query Parameter?api_key=<key>Convenient but appears in server logs — avoid for secrets
Request Body{ "api_key": "..." }Used by some legacy APIs; only safe over HTTPS
Basic AuthAuthorization: Basic base64(user:pass)Username = key, password = secret (e.g. Twilio)
▸ API GATEWAY PATTERNS
Gateway TypeProtocolKey Trait
REST APIHTTP/HTTPSStateless; uses GET/POST/PUT/DELETE + JSON responses
GraphQLHTTP/HTTPSSingle endpoint; client specifies exactly what data it needs
WebSocketws:// / wss://Persistent two-way connection; used for real-time data
WebhookHTTP/HTTPSServer pushes data to YOUR URL when an event occurs
gRPCHTTP/2Binary protocol; used for high-performance microservices
Netlify FunctionsHTTPSServerless endpoints at /.netlify/functions/<name>
Platform
Netlify — Environment Variables & Deploy Keys
Netlify injects environment variables at build time and into serverless functions. Never hard-code secrets in netlify.toml — store them in the Netlify dashboard under Site settings → Environment variables.
▸ KEY NETLIFY VARIABLES
VariableWhat It Holds
NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKENPersonal access token for the Netlify CLI and API
NETLIFY_SITE_IDUnique ID of the target site (used by netlify deploy)
NODE_VERSIONNode.js version to use during build (e.g. 18)
CONTEXTBuild context: production, deploy-preview, branch-deploy
DEPLOY_URLURL of this specific deploy (injected automatically by Netlify)
URLPrimary site URL (e.g. https://mysite.netlify.app)
BRANCHGit branch that triggered this build
COMMIT_REFFull SHA of the Git commit that triggered the build
▸ NETLIFY CLI COMMANDS
CommandWhat It Does
netlify loginAuthenticate CLI with your Netlify account via browser
netlify initLink current directory to a Netlify site (or create one)
netlify devRun local dev server that emulates Netlify Functions & redirects
netlify buildRun the build command locally (same as the Netlify CI build)
netlify deployDeploy site to a draft URL for preview
netlify deploy --prodDeploy site to the production URL
netlify env:listList all environment variables for the linked site
netlify env:set KEY valAdd or update an environment variable in the Netlify dashboard
netlify env:get KEYPrint the value of a single environment variable
netlify functions:listList all serverless functions deployed on the site
▸ netlify.toml — KEY CONFIG FIELDS
FieldPurposeExample
[build] commandBuild command Netlify runs"npm run build"
[build] publishFolder containing built output to deploy"dist"
[build] functionsFolder containing serverless function files"netlify/functions"
[build.environment]Non-secret env vars baked into the buildNODE_VERSION = "18"
[[redirects]]URL redirect / rewrite rulesfrom = "/*" to = "/index.html"
[[headers]]HTTP response headers to add to matched pathsCSP, CORS, caching headers
Platform
GitHub — Personal Access Tokens & Actions Secrets
GitHub uses Personal Access Tokens (PATs) to let scripts, CI pipelines, and tools authenticate as you without needing your password. GitHub Actions has a built-in GITHUB_TOKEN automatically available in every workflow — no setup needed.
▸ TOKEN TYPES
TokenScopeUse Case
Classic PATCoarse — whole account, broad permission bucketsQuick scripts, legacy integrations
Fine-grained PATSpecific repos + specific permissions (read/write)Preferred for new integrations — least privilege
GITHUB_TOKENAuto-scoped to current repo during the workflow runGitHub Actions — push, comment on PRs, publish packages
Deploy KeySSH key tied to a single repo (read or read/write)Server-side deploys, CI systems without a user account
OAuth App TokenUser grants specific scopes via OAuth flowThird-party apps that need to act on behalf of users
GitHub App TokenInstallation token issued per-repo, short-livedAutomated bots, CI/CD integrations (preferred for orgs)
▸ GITHUB ACTIONS SECRETS
How ToSteps
Add a secretRepo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret
Use in workflow${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }} in any step's env: or command
Org-level secretOrg → Settings → Secrets → can be shared across multiple repos
Built-in token${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} — always available, no setup needed
▸ COMMON PAT PERMISSION SCOPES
ScopeGrants Access To
repoFull read/write access to private and public repos
public_repoRead/write access to public repos only
workflowCreate and update GitHub Actions workflow files
read:userRead your public profile data
user:emailRead your verified email addresses
packagesUpload/download GitHub Packages
delete_repoDelete repositories (avoid granting unless needed)
Best Practices
Keeping API Keys Secure
RuleWhy It Matters
Never commit keys to GitOnce pushed (even deleted later), keys are in git history forever and can be scraped
Use .env files locally.env holds secrets for local dev — always add it to .gitignore
Use platform secret storesNetlify env vars, GitHub Actions secrets, AWS Secrets Manager — not plain config files
Least privilegeGrant only the minimum permissions the key actually needs — limits blast radius if leaked
Rotate regularlyExpire and replace tokens on a schedule; immediately rotate any key that may have been exposed
Separate keys per environmentDev, staging, and production should each have their own keys so a test leak doesn't hit prod
Use secret scanningGitHub scans pushes for known token formats and alerts you (or blocks the push) automatically
Use HTTPS onlySending a key over plain HTTP exposes it to anyone watching the network
🧘 Lifestyle & Philosophy
LIFE
Stoicism · Buddhism · Taoism · Existentialism · Minimalism · Wicca · Paganism · Druidism ▾
🏛️ Stoicism — The Art of Rational Endurance PHILOSOPHY ▶
Ancient Greek · Roman
Core Doctrines & Daily Practice
Founded ~300 BC by Zeno of Citium. Stoics held that virtue alone is sufficient for happiness and that emotions rooted in false judgements must be overcome through reason.
▸ THE FOUR CARDINAL VIRTUES
Wisdom (Sophia)
Knowing what is good, bad, and indifferent. The foundation of all other virtues.
Justice (Dikaiosyne)
Acting rightly toward others. Social duty; fairness in all dealings.
Courage (Andreia)
Facing hardship, pain, and death without flinching. Moral as well as physical.
Temperance (Sophrosyne)
Self-discipline and moderation. Mastery over appetites and impulses.
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Principle Meaning Practice
Dichotomy of Control Some things are "up to us" (prohairesis) — judgements, impulses, desires. Everything else is external and indifferent. Ask "Is this in my control?" before reacting to any event.
Memento Mori "Remember you will die." Mortality awareness as a tool for gratitude and urgency. Morning reflection: treat each day as a gift, not a given.
Amor Fati "Love of fate." Accept and embrace everything that happens — not mere tolerance, but affirmation. Reframe obstacles as opportunities; say "it was meant to be" and mean it.
Negative Visualization (Premeditatio Malorum) Deliberately imagine loss — of health, relationships, possessions — to appreciate what you have. Evening: briefly imagine losing what you value most, then feel gratitude for its presence.
Sympatheia All things are interconnected in one rational whole (the Logos). We are citizens of the universe. When frustrated by others: "They act from ignorance, not malice. I would do the same without better judgement."
▸ KEY FIGURES & TEXTS
Figure Era Key Work Contribution
Marcus Aurelius 121–180 AD Meditations Roman Emperor. Private journal of self-discipline; applied Stoicism in governance.
Epictetus 50–135 AD Enchiridion, Discourses Former slave. Focused on inner freedom regardless of external circumstance.
Seneca 4 BC–65 AD Letters to Lucilius, On the Shortness of Life Statesman and playwright. Practical moral essays on time, wealth, and death.
Zeno of Citium 334–262 BC — Founder of the Stoic school in Athens' painted porch (Stoa Poikile).
▸ DAILY STOIC PRACTICE
AM
Morning Journal
What obstacles might I face today? How will I respond virtuously? Rehearse the day — adversities and all.
MID
Pause & Label
When emotion arises, name it: "I notice anger." The gap between stimulus and response is where virtue lives.
PM
Evening Review
What did I do well? What could I have done better? No self-flagellation — just honest assessment. (Seneca's method)
♟️ Machiavellianism — Power, Realism & Strategy POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY ▶
Niccolò Machiavelli · 1469–1527
The Prince & the Discourses — Realpolitik Framework
Machiavelli separated political science from ethics. His work describes how power actually operates, not how it ideally should. Often misread as endorsing cruelty; actually a clinical observer of political reality.
▸ CORE CONCEPTS
Concept Meaning
Virtù Not "virtue" but prowess — strength, skill, cunning, willpower. The ruler's capacity to shape events through force of character and action.
Fortuna Fortune/chance — the unpredictable half of all outcomes. Virtù can master ~50% of fate; the rest is Fortuna. She favors the bold.
The Lion & the Fox A ruler must be both: the lion to frighten wolves (force), the fox to recognize traps (cunning). Neither alone is sufficient.
Economy of Violence Cruelties must be committed all at once; benefits distributed gradually. Sudden harshness is quickly forgotten; lingering harm festers.
Appearance vs. Reality It is unnecessary to actually possess virtues — it is sufficient to appear to have them. People judge by what they see, not what is.
Love vs. Fear It is safer to be feared than loved if you cannot be both. But avoid being hated — hatred is fatal; fear can be managed.
▸ THE 48 LAWS — ROBERT GREENE'S SYNTHESIS
Never Outshine the Master
Always make those above you feel superior. Conceal your talent when needed.
Conceal Your Intentions
Keep people off-balance. Reveal purpose only when it cannot be stopped.
Guard Your Reputation
Reputation is the cornerstone of power. A single crack and you are vulnerable.
Play on People's Need to Believe
People crave meaning. Offer a cause, a vision — they will follow willingly.
▸ DARK TRIAD CONTEXT (Psychology)
Trait Core Distinction
Machiavellianism Cynical worldview, strategic manipulation, delayed gratification Calculating and patient; manipulates for long-term gain
Narcissism Grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration Emotional; manipulates for ego supply and status
Psychopathy Low empathy, impulsivity, callousness Reactive; least strategic of the three
🧠 Psychology — Mind, Behavior & Biases COGNITIVE SCIENCE ▶
Applied Psychology
Cognitive Biases · Defense Mechanisms · Frameworks
Psychology studies the mind and behavior. Understanding your cognitive architecture is the first step to overcoming it. "Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom." — Aristotle
▸ KEY COGNITIVE BIASES
Bias Description Example
Confirmation Bias Seek info that confirms existing beliefs; ignore contradicting evidence Only reading news aligned with your politics
Dunning-Kruger Effect Incompetent people overestimate ability; experts underestimate theirs Beginner investor convinced they've outsmarted the market
Sunk Cost Fallacy Continue bad decisions because of past investment (time/money/effort) Finishing a terrible book because you've read half of it
Availability Heuristic Judge probability by how easily examples come to mind Fear flying after seeing news of a crash; ignoring car risk
Fundamental Attribution Error Over-attribute others' behavior to character; under-attribute to situation "They cut me off — they're a bad person" (vs. they're late for hospital)
Anchoring Over-rely on first piece of information encountered $100 item marked down to $70 feels like a deal regardless of value
Negativity Bias Negative events register more strongly than equally positive ones One criticism outweighs ten compliments
Halo Effect One positive trait causes assumption of other positive traits Attractive people assumed to be more competent
▸ EGO DEFENSE MECHANISMS (Freud / Anna Freud)
Mechanism Description
Repression Unconsciously pushing threatening thoughts out of awareness
Rationalization Creating logical explanations to justify unacceptable behavior
Projection Attributing your own unacceptable feelings to others
Denial Refusing to acknowledge a painful reality
Displacement Redirecting emotion from original source to safer target
Sublimation Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activity (e.g., aggression → sport)
▸ KEY FRAMEWORKS
Maslow's Hierarchy
Physiological → Safety → Love/Belonging → Esteem → Self-Actualization. Lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones motivate.
Locus of Control
Internal: outcomes result from your actions. External: outcomes are luck/fate. Internal LoC correlates strongly with resilience and achievement.
Growth vs Fixed Mindset
Carol Dweck. Fixed: ability is innate and static. Growth: ability is developed through effort. Growth mindset predicts higher achievement and resilience.
Flow State (Csikszentmihalyi)
Optimal experience at the intersection of high challenge + high skill. Time distorts. Deep absorption. Intrinsic reward. Cultivated through deliberate practice.
📜 Philosophy — Schools of Thought WESTERN TRADITION ▶
Epistemology · Metaphysics · Ethics · Logic
Major Schools & Key Thinkers
▸ MAJOR SCHOOLS
School Era Core Claim Key Figures
Rationalism 17th–18th c. Knowledge derived primarily from reason, not senses. Innate ideas exist. Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz
Empiricism 17th–18th c. All knowledge derives from sensory experience. The mind starts as a blank slate (tabula rasa). Locke, Hume, Berkeley
Pragmatism 19th–20th c. Truth is what works in practice. Ideas are tools; their value is in their consequences. Peirce, James, Dewey
Existentialism 20th c. Existence precedes essence. Individuals create their own meaning in an indifferent universe. Sartre, Camus, Heidegger, de Beauvoir
Utilitarianism 18th–19th c. The morally right action maximizes overall happiness (utility) for the greatest number. Bentham, Mill
Kantian Ethics (Deontology) 18th c. Act only according to maxims you could will to be universal laws. Duty above consequences. Immanuel Kant
Virtue Ethics Ancient Greek Focus on developing good character (virtues) rather than rules or outcomes. Aristotle, MacIntyre
Nihilism 19th–20th c. Life has no intrinsic meaning, purpose, or value. Traditional morality is groundless. Nietzsche (critic), Cioran
▸ ESSENTIAL CONCEPTS
Concept Definition
Cogito ergo sum "I think, therefore I am." Descartes' foundational certainty — even a deceiver cannot doubt the existence of the doubter.
Categorical Imperative Kant: act only on maxims that could become universal laws. Treat humanity never merely as means but always as ends.
Absurdism Camus: life is inherently meaningless yet humans persistently seek meaning — this conflict is the Absurd. Response: revolt (not suicide, not faith).
Veil of Ignorance Rawls: design a just society without knowing your position in it. Ensures impartiality — you'd design fairness since you might be disadvantaged.
Übermensch Nietzsche's "Overman" — one who creates their own values after the "death of God." Not a racial concept; a call to self-overcoming.
Solipsism Only one's own mind is certain to exist. All else may be illusion. A logical extreme rarely endorsed but philosophically significant.
☸️ Buddhism — The Path to Liberation SPIRITUAL PHILOSOPHY ▶
Siddhartha Gautama · ~563–483 BC
Four Noble Truths · Eightfold Path · Core Concepts
Buddhism is both a religion and a philosophy. Its goal is the cessation of dukkha (suffering) through understanding the nature of mind and reality. Not theistic in the Western sense — the Buddha is a teacher, not a god.
▸ THE FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS (Catvāri Āryasatyāni)
1
Dukkha (Suffering)
Life inherently contains suffering, dissatisfaction, and imperfection. Birth, aging, sickness, death, getting what we don't want, not getting what we want — all are dukkha.
2
Samudāya (Origin)
The origin of suffering is craving (tanha) — for pleasure, for existence, for non-existence. Attachment and aversion are the roots.
3
Nirodha (Cessation)
Suffering can cease. Nirvana is the complete extinguishing of craving — a state of peace, freedom, and liberation.
4
Magga (The Path)
The Noble Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering. Practical and systematic — not metaphysical belief but lived practice.
▸ THE NOBLE EIGHTFOLD PATH
Path Category Meaning
Right View Wisdom Understanding the Four Noble Truths; seeing reality as it is, not as we wish it to be.
Right Intention Wisdom Commitment to non-attachment, non-ill-will, and non-harmfulness.
Right Speech Ethics Abstaining from lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
Right Action Ethics Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Right Livelihood Ethics Earning a living that does not cause harm to others or oneself.
Right Effort Meditation Cultivating wholesome states and abandoning unwholesome ones continuously.
Right Mindfulness Meditation Present-moment awareness of body, feelings, mind-states, and phenomena.
Right Concentration Meditation Developing deep meditative absorption (jhanas) as foundation for insight.
▸ CORE CONCEPTS (THE THREE MARKS OF EXISTENCE)
Anicca — Impermanence
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Clinging to what is transient is the source of suffering. Release attachment.
Dukkha — Unsatisfactoriness
Even pleasant experiences carry an undercurrent of dissatisfaction because they end. Nothing conditioned can permanently satisfy.
Anatta — Non-Self
The "self" is not a fixed, permanent entity but a changing process of aggregates (skandhas). Liberating when truly understood.
☯️ Taoism — The Way of Nature CHINESE PHILOSOPHY ▶
Lao Tzu · ~6th–4th c. BC
Tao Te Ching — The Classic of the Way and Its Power
The Tao (道) — the Way — is the fundamental, unnamed principle underlying all of reality. It cannot be named or fully grasped, only lived. "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao."
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Principle Meaning Application
Wu Wei (無為) "Non-action" or effortless action. Acting in harmony with the natural flow rather than forcing outcomes. Avoid unnecessary struggle. Like water: yield, go around, persist gently.
Pu (樸) — Simplicity The uncarved block. Original nature before social conditioning. Simplicity as strength. Strip away pretense. Return to what is essential and natural.
Te (德) — Virtue/Power Inner virtue or power that arises naturally when aligned with the Tao. Not morality imposed from outside but integrity from within. Be genuinely good, not performatively good.
Yin-Yang (陰陽) All opposites are interdependent and contain each other's seed. Darkness within light, light within darkness. Change is constant. Stop seeing circumstances as purely good or bad. Both are transforming.
Ziran (自然) Self-so, naturalness. Things should be allowed to follow their own nature. Stop trying to control what is inherently wild and self-organizing.
▸ WATER AS TAOIST METAPHOR
Water is the supreme Taoist metaphor. It is:
· Soft yet wears down the hardest rock (persistence)
· Low — it always seeks the lowest point (humility)
· Yielding — flows around obstacles rather than fighting them
· Essential — all life depends on it, yet it does not demand recognition
"Nothing in the world is as soft and yielding as water, yet nothing is better at dissolving the hard and inflexible."
🌑 Existentialism & Absurdism 20TH C. PHILOSOPHY ▶
Sartre · Camus · Kierkegaard · Heidegger
"Existence precedes essence" — Building meaning in a meaningless universe
Existentialism holds that there is no pre-given human nature or purpose. We exist first, then create ourselves through choices. This is both terrifying (radical freedom) and liberating.
▸ KEY CONCEPTS
Concept Thinker Meaning
Radical Freedom Sartre We are "condemned to be free" — there is no escape from choice. Even refusing to choose is a choice. Total responsibility for self.
Bad Faith (Mauvaise Foi) Sartre Pretending you have no choice; adopting a fixed identity to escape freedom. E.g., "I can't help it, that's just who I am."
The Absurd Camus The conflict between humans' need for meaning and the universe's silent indifference. Three responses: physical suicide (wrong), philosophical suicide (religion — bad faith), or revolt (the only authentic response).
Authenticity Heidegger Owning your existence — facing death (Being-toward-death) rather than fleeing into das Man (the "they-self" of conformity).
Leap of Faith Kierkegaard Rational thought cannot resolve the deepest questions. Authentic existence requires a passionate, subjective commitment despite uncertainty.
Thrownness (Geworfenheit) Heidegger We are "thrown" into existence — we did not choose our time, place, language, culture. But we are responsible for what we do with this situation.
▸ THE MYTH OF SISYPHUS — CAMUS
Sisyphus is condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity — it always rolls back down. Camus argues this is the human condition.

The resolution: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."
Not because the task is meaningful in any cosmic sense, but because the struggle itself fills his heart. Revolt against absurdity — continuing to live, create, love — is the only authentic response.
⬜ Minimalism & Intentional Living LIFESTYLE ▶
Modern Practice
Intentionality · Essentialism · Deep Work
▸ CORE PRINCIPLES
Essentialism (Greg McKeown)
The disciplined pursuit of less. Not about doing more things — about doing the right things. "If it's not a clear yes, it's a no."
Deep Work (Cal Newport)
Cognitively demanding tasks performed in a state of distraction-free concentration. The skill of the 21st century. Rare + valuable = leverage.
KonMari Method
Keep only what "sparks joy." Tidy by category, not location. The goal: create an environment that supports who you want to become.
Parkinson's Law
Work expands to fill the time allotted. Impose artificial constraints. Deadlines create focus. Less time + clear priority = better output.
▸ HIGH-PERFORMANCE LIFESTYLE FRAMEWORKS
Framework Key Idea Source
80/20 Principle (Pareto) 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. Identify and double down on the vital few. Ruthlessly eliminate the trivial many. Vilfredo Pareto / Tim Ferriss
Atomic Habits Systems over goals. 1% better every day = 37x better in a year. Identity-based habits: "I am a writer" vs "I want to write." James Clear
Ikigai Japanese: reason for being. The intersection of what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. Japanese philosophy
Memento Vivere "Remember to live." The counterpoint to Memento Mori — not just contemplating death, but using that awareness to fully inhabit life. Stoic tradition
Wabi-Sabi Japanese aesthetic: find beauty in imperfection, transience, and incompleteness. A cracked bowl repaired with gold (Kintsugi) is more beautiful for its history. Japanese philosophy
🌙 Wicca — Sabbats, Elements & Tools PRACTICE GUIDE ▶

Wicca is a modern Pagan religion codified by Gerald Gardner (1954) and further shaped by Doreen Valiente. It centres on reverence for nature, polarity of Goddess and God, seasonal cycles, and magical practice.

Wiccan Rede: "An it harm none, do what ye will."  ·  Rule of Three: Energy sent returns threefold.

☀️ Paganism — Traditions & Core Concepts OVERVIEW ▶
Overview
Contemporary Paganism — Nature-Based Spirituality
Paganism is a broad category of earth-centred, polytheistic, or animistic spiritual traditions. Common themes: reverence for nature, cyclical time, pre-Christian deities or archetypes, and personal spiritual sovereignty. No single holy text or central authority governs all paths.

🌳 Druidism — Grades, Awen & Sacred Concepts PRACTICE GUIDE ▶
Tradition
Druidry — Celtic Spiritual Path
Druidry draws on Celtic heritage, nature mysticism, and Bardic oral tradition. Modern revival began in the 18th century. Major orders: OBOD (Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids, est. 1964) and ADF (Ár nDraíocht Féin, est. 1983). Awen (Welsh: /ˈaʊ.ɛn/) — divine inspiration flowing through all things; symbolised by three rays of light ☀.
▸ THREE GRADES
🎵
Bard
First grade. Keeper of memory, story, and song. Develops creative voice, poetry, and the craft of sacred expression. Studies Celtic mythology & lore.
🌿
Ovate
Second grade. Seer, healer, and naturalist. Works with divination (Ogham, scrying), herbalism, communion with ancestors and the spirit world.
🌳
Druid
Third grade. Philosopher, ritualist, and mediator. Deep study of cosmology, ceremony, law & ethics. Bridge between the human and divine.

Realm Element Associations
Land Earth Physical world, ancestors, stability, the body

🏛️StoicismPhilosophy • Virtue Ethics▶

The Dichotomy of Control
Focus only on what is up to you — your judgments and actions — and accept the rest. Live by the four virtues: wisdom, justice, courage, temperance.

♟️MachiavellianismPhilosophy • Political Realism▶
SOURCE
The Prince (1532)
Niccolò Machiavelli analyzed power as it is, not as it should be. A ruler must master virtù (skill/decisiveness) to manage fortuna (chance).
IDEAS
Realpolitik
Outcomes can justify hard means; it is safer to be feared than loved if you cannot be both. Pragmatic statecraft over idealism.

Two Meanings
Distinguish the political philosophy from the psychology term 'Machiavellianism' — a dark-triad trait describing manipulative, self-serving behavior.
