✍️ Technical Writing — The Underrated Career Superpower LIFESTYLE • Communication ▶
WHY IT MATTERS
The Engineer Who Writes Well Gets Promoted
In IT, your impact is multiplied by how well you communicate it. The brilliant fix nobody understands has limited value; the clearly-documented one helps the whole team forever. Writing well — runbooks, post-mortems, design docs, tickets, emails — is one of the highest-ROI skills you can build, and it's rare enough that it makes you stand out immediately. As you grow senior, writing matters MORE, not less.
PRINCIPLES
How to Write So People Actually Understand
PrincipleWhat It Means
Know your audienceWrite for THEM — exec summary vs. engineer deep-dive are different
BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)Put the conclusion/ask first. Don't bury it (military + journalism wisdom)
One idea per paragraphWalls of text don't get read
Show, don't tellConcrete examples and commands beat abstract description
Cut ruthlesslyDelete every word that doesn't earn its place
Active voice"The script deletes logs" not "Logs are deleted by the script"
DOCUMENT TYPES
The Docs Every IT Pro Writes
DocumentPurpose & Tip
RunbookStep-by-step ops procedure. Write it so a tired person at 3am can follow it.
Post-mortemWhat broke and why. Blameless. Timeline + root cause + action items.
Design doc / RFCPropose a change before building. Forces clear thinking; gets buy-in.
READMEHow to set up and use a project. The first thing anyone reads.
Ticket / bug reportSteps to reproduce, expected vs. actual, environment. Specifics save hours.
🌟 Building in Public — Your Reputation Compounds LIFESTYLE • Career ▶
THE IDEA
Let Your Work Be Findable
You don't need to be an influencer. But a small, genuine public footprint — a GitHub with your projects, a blog documenting what you learn, a few helpful answers online — compounds over a career. It creates serendipity: recruiters find you, peers vouch for you, and writing things down deepens your own learning. The person who shares what they learn becomes the person others associate with that knowledge.
LOW-EFFORT, HIGH-RETURN
Where to Start (No Burnout Required)
ActionWhy It Pays Off
Keep a GitHub with real projectsProof of skill that beats resume bullet points
Write up things you figured out"How I fixed X" posts help others + cement your learning
A clean, current LinkedInWhere recruiters and peers actually look
Answer questions (forums, Discord, Stack Overflow)Builds reputation; teaching reveals your own gaps
Document your home labTangible portfolio + interview talking points
The mindset: share to help and to learn, not to chase clout. Consistency beats intensity — one short post a month for a year is a body of work. Your future self (and your future employers) will thank you.
📟 Surviving On-Call — When the Pager Owns Your Night LIFESTYLE • Sustainability ▶
THE REALITY
On-Call Is Part of Most IT/Ops Jobs
Being "on-call" means you're responsible for responding to incidents outside business hours. It's a normal part of ops, SRE, and many IT roles — and it can be stressful, especially early on. The good news: most of the stress comes from being unprepared, and that's fixable. A well-run on-call rotation is sustainable; a badly-run one burns people out fast.
BE PREPARED
Reduce the 3am Panic
Before Your ShiftWhy
Test your access & toolsDon't discover your VPN is broken during an incident
Read recent incidents/changesKnow what's fragile right now
Know the runbooksA clear runbook turns panic into a checklist
Know the escalation pathWho to call when you're stuck — it's OK to escalate
Set up your environmentCharged phone, laptop ready, alerts working
DURING AN INCIDENT
Stay Calm, Work the Process
When the page fires, panic is the enemy. A structured approach keeps you effective under pressure (this is the OODA loop and incident command in action).
StepAction
1. AcknowledgeAck the page so others know it's being handled
2. AssessWhat's the actual impact? How bad, how many users?
3. Stabilize firstRestore service (even a workaround) before root-causing
4. CommunicatePost status updates — silence makes everyone anxious
5. Escalate if stuckDon't be a hero — pull in help early, not at hour 3
6. Post-mortem laterBlameless review once it's resolved (not at 3am)
PROTECT YOURSELF
Sustainable On-Call Habits
On-call should not destroy your life. If it consistently does, that's an organizational problem worth raising (politely, with data). Healthy practices: take comp time after rough nights, push to fix the root causes of repeat pages (toil reduction), ensure rotations are large enough that nobody is always on, and use the "follow-the-sun" model across time zones where possible. Recall "not my circus, not my monkeys": respond to what's genuinely yours, escalate what isn't, and don't absorb the consequences of problems you flagged but couldn't control. An alert that pages you every night for something you can't fix is a process failure to escalate — not a personal burden to silently carry.
⚖️ Professional Ethics — The Responsibility That Comes With Access LIFESTYLE • Integrity ▶
WHY ETHICS MATTERS HERE
You Hold Keys to the Kingdom
IT professionals — especially in security and admin roles — have extraordinary access: to private data, to systems that affect people's lives, to the ability to surveil or disrupt. With that access comes responsibility. Your reputation for integrity is the single most valuable asset in your career; it takes years to build and seconds to destroy. Employers hire trust as much as skill.
CORE PRINCIPLES
Common Threads Across IT Codes of Ethics
Organizations like (ISC)², ISACA, and ACM publish codes of ethics. The recurring principles:
PrincipleIn Practice
Protect the public & common goodPublic safety and trust come before employer or self-interest
Act with integrity & honestyDon't misrepresent your skills, findings, or qualifications
Respect privacy & confidentialityDon't snoop in data you can access but have no business reason to view
Provide diligent, competent serviceStay within your competence; keep learning; don't fake it on critical systems
Avoid conflicts of interestDisclose anything that could bias your judgment
Authorized access only"I can" never means "I may" — access requires authorization AND a reason
THE "JUST BECAUSE YOU CAN" TRAP
Access Is Not Permission
The most common ethical failure in IT isn't dramatic sabotage — it's curiosity. An admin who reads a colleague's emails "out of curiosity," peeks at executive salaries in a database, or looks up an ex's records. You may have the technical access, but using it without a legitimate business reason is a serious ethical (and often legal) violation. The rule: access data only when you have both authorization and a genuine work reason. Assume every access is logged — because it usually is.
WHEN YOU'RE PRESSURED
Doing the Right Thing Under Pressure
Sometimes a manager or client pressures you to do something wrong: ignore a vulnerability, falsify a report, cut a security corner to ship faster, delete logs, grant inappropriate access. This is where the mindsets earlier in this guide come together. "Assume makes an ass of u and me" — get the request in writing; don't assume you understood the intent or that it's authorized. "You can't make someone make the right choice, but you can pick up the pieces" — state your professional objection clearly and in writing, offer the safer alternative, and escalate if needed; if they still choose poorly, you've created a record and done your duty. And "not my circus, not my monkeys" protects you from owning the emotional weight of a bad decision that wasn't yours to make.
When Pressured To...Professional Response
Ignore a serious vulnerabilityDocument the risk in writing; recommend the fix; escalate per policy
Grant access that violates least privilegeAsk for written authorization from the data owner
Delete or alter logs/evidenceRefuse — this may be illegal (obstruction, spoliation); escalate
Cut a security corner to hit a deadlineSurface the tradeoff to decision-makers in writing; let them own the risk decision
Know your organization's whistleblower and escalation channels before you need them. A clear, calm, documented objection protects both your integrity and your career — and is exactly what separates a trusted professional from a liability.
🚀 Breaking Into IT — From Zero to Hired LIFESTYLE • Career ▶
THE GOOD NEWS
IT Is One of the Most Accessible Skilled Careers
You don't need a computer science degree or to be a "genius." IT rewards curiosity, persistence, and the willingness to learn by doing. People break in from every background — military, retail, trades, teaching. What employers actually want is proof you can learn, troubleshoot, and show up reliably. The path below has worked for countless career-changers.
A REALISTIC ROADMAP
The Proven On-Ramp
StepWhat to Do
1. Pick a direction (loosely)Help desk/support is the classic entry point — it touches everything and teaches fundamentals
2. Learn fundamentalsNetworking, OS (Win + Linux), basic security — free resources abound
3. Get one foundational certA+ or Network+ or Security+ — passes HR filters, proves baseline
4. Build a home labHands-on proof > theory. Document it publicly.
5. Polish resume + LinkedInHighlight transferable skills + your lab/projects
6. Apply widely, networkMost jobs come through people — referrals beat job boards
7. Get the first role, then growThe first job is the hardest. After that, experience compounds.
TRANSFERABLE SKILLS
You Already Have Valuable Experience
Career-changers undersell themselves. Skills from other fields are genuinely valuable in IT — name them explicitly on your resume.
From...Translates To...
MilitaryDiscipline, working under pressure, security clearance, following + giving procedures
Customer service / retailHelp desk gold: patience, communication, de-escalation
Trades (electrician, etc.)Systematic troubleshooting, reading diagrams, safety mindset
TeachingExplaining complex things simply, documentation, patience
Any jobReliability, teamwork, ownership — never underrated
THE FIRST 90 DAYS
How to Start Strong in a New Role
DoWhy
Listen and learn before changing thingsUnderstand why things are the way they are first
Ask questions — write down answersNobody expects you to know everything; they expect you to learn
Find the docs / runbooks / wikiRamp up faster; spot what's missing (and fix it)
Build relationshipsKnowing who to ask is half the job
Deliver one small win earlyBuilds trust and confidence both ways
Admit what you don't knowFaking it on real systems causes outages. Honesty builds trust.
The meta-lesson: getting in is the hard part. Once you have a foothold and keep learning, IT offers a long ladder — and the compounding skills, network, and reputation you build carry you up it for decades.
🌱 Growing Into Senior — Beyond Technical Skill LIFESTYLE • Career ▶
THE SHIFT
Senior Isn't "Knows More Commands"
The jump from junior to senior isn't about memorizing more technology — it's about scope and judgment. Juniors are given problems and solve them. Seniors find the right problems, navigate ambiguity, anticipate consequences, and make others around them better. The technical bar matters, but what truly distinguishes seniors is how they think, communicate, and multiply the team's output.
JuniorSenior
Solves the task givenQuestions whether it's the right task
Needs clear instructionsThrives in ambiguity, defines the approach
Focuses on "does it work?"Considers maintainability, risk, tradeoffs, the team
Local view (my task)Systems view (how it fits the whole)
Asks "how do I do X?"Asks "should we do X, and what breaks if we do?"
FORCE MULTIPLIERS
Habits That Build Seniority
HabitWhy It Compounds
Write things downDocs/designs scale your knowledge beyond your hours
Make others betterMentoring, good code reviews — your impact multiplies
Think in tradeoffs"It depends" + explaining why = senior judgment
Communicate up and acrossTranslate tech ↔ business; influence without authority
Own outcomes, not just tasksSee it through to working in production
Reduce, don't add, complexityThe best seniors make systems simpler
IC OR MANAGER?
Two Valid Ladders
Growth doesn't require becoming a manager. Most organizations have two parallel tracks: the Individual Contributor (IC) track (Senior → Staff → Principal engineer) and the Management track (Lead → Manager → Director). Staff+ ICs have just as much seniority and impact as managers — through deep technical leadership rather than people management. Choose based on what energizes you: solving hard technical problems, or growing people and teams. Neither is "higher."
THE LONG GAME
Mindsets That Sustain a Decades-Long Career
The wisdom threaded through this whole guide applies most at senior levels. "Verify, don't assume" — senior mistakes are bigger, so your discipline matters more. "Not my circus, not my monkeys" — seniors are pulled in every direction; protecting your focus and boundaries is survival. "You can't make someone make the right choice, but you can pick up the pieces" — you'll advise leaders who overrule you; document, let go, and be the calm one who helps recover. Add to these: stay curious (the field never stops changing), be generous with knowledge (reputation compounds), and protect your health and relationships — a burned-out expert helps no one. The marathon, not the sprint, is what builds a great career.
🧗 The Craftsperson's Mindset — Tying It All Together LIFESTYLE • Synthesis ▶
FROM BEGINNER TO PROFESSIONAL
It's a Way of Working, Not a Finish Line
Everything in this guide — networking, code, security, Linux, the war stories and the wisdom — adds up to something bigger than a pile of facts. It's a way of approaching work: with curiosity, rigor, humility, and care. You will never "finish" learning IT; the field reinvents itself every few years. The professionals who thrive aren't the ones who know everything — they're the ones who've built a durable way of thinking that lets them learn whatever comes next. That mindset is the real skill.
THE TECHNICAL HABITS
What Separates Pros From Beginners
HabitIn Practice
Understand, don't memorizeKnow WHY, and you can derive the how anywhere
Read the error messageIt's usually telling you the answer — actually read it
Reproduce before fixingYou can't fix what you can't reliably trigger
Change one thing at a timeOtherwise you never know what worked
Automate the third repetitionToil compounds; so does the automation that kills it
Leave it better than you found itFix the doc, add the test, clean the config
THE THREE MINDSETS, REVISITED
The Wisdom That Holds It All Together
Three sayings recur throughout this guide because they apply to nearly every situation a technical professional faces — across every domain, from your first help-desk ticket to running a major incident decades later:
SayingWhat It ProtectsWhere It Shows Up
"Assume makes an ass of u and me"Your technical rigorVerify the backup, test the change, check the logs, confirm the firewall rule — never assume
"Not my circus, not my monkeys"Your energy & boundariesOwn what's yours fully; support (don't absorb) what isn't; escalate rather than silently carry others' dysfunction
"You can't make someone make the right choice — but you can pick up the pieces"Your sanity & reputationAdvise clearly in writing, accept the decision isn't yours, then be the calm one who helps recover — no "I told you so"
THE LONG VIEW
Build a Career You Can Sustain
Technical skill gets you in the door; judgment, communication, and integrity build the career. Stay curious — the learning never stops, and that's a feature, not a bug. Be generous with knowledge; teaching others cements your own understanding and your reputation compounds. Protect your health, relationships, and focus — a burned-out expert helps no one, and "not my monkeys" exists precisely so you don't carry weight that isn't yours. Verify relentlessly, communicate clearly, document your reasoning, stay calm when others panic, and keep learning. Do that, and you'll not only survive in IT — you'll become the steady professional others rely on, for decades. That's the whole game.
Beginner Windows Administration Fundamentals
Core Concept
The Windows Admin Toolkit
Enterprise Windows administration revolves around a handful of tools. Learn these early — they show up in every IT job that involves Windows:

GUI Tools (MMC Snap-ins):
• dsa.msc — Active Directory Users & Computers (ADUC).
• gpmc.msc — Group Policy Management Console.
• compmgmt.msc — Computer Management (local users, disks, services).
• eventvwr.msc — Event Viewer (logs for everything).
• services.msc — Start/stop/configure Windows services.

Command-line:
• cmd.exe — the classic command prompt (legacy but everywhere).
• powershell.exe / pwsh.exe — the modern admin shell.
• wmic / winrm — remote management from CLI.
User Management
Managing Users in Active Directory
Common day-one helpdesk tasks in Active Directory Users & Computers (ADUC):
-- Open ADUC: Win+R → dsa.msc -- Or via PowerShell (if RSAT tools installed): # Create a new AD user New-ADUser ` -Name "Bob Jones" ` -SamAccountName "bjones" ` -UserPrincipalName "bjones@corp.example.com" ` -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "TempP@ss1" -AsPlainText -Force) ` -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true ` -Enabled $true ` -Path "OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" # Unlock a locked-out account Unlock-ADAccount -Identity bjones # Reset a password Set-ADAccountPassword bjones ` -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "NewP@ss99" -AsPlainText -Force) ` -Reset # Disable an account (departing employee) Disable-ADAccount -Identity bjones # Find all disabled accounts in an OU Search-ADAccount -SearchBase "OU=Finance,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" ` -AccountDisabled | Select Name, SamAccountName
Group Policy
Group Policy Objects (GPOs) Explained
A GPO is a collection of settings pushed from the domain controller to computers and users automatically. Examples of what GPOs control:

• Password complexity requirements.
• Screen lock after N minutes of inactivity.
• Mapped drives (e.g. H: = home folder on file server).
• Software deployment (install apps on logon).
• Firewall rules, browser settings, USB restrictions.

GPOs apply in order: Local → Site → Domain → OU (LSDOU). Later policies win unless "Enforced" is set. Use gpresult /r on a PC to see which GPOs actually applied.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — GPOs don't stop a determined user completely, but they raise the barrier and give you an audit trail when something goes wrong.
Remote Access
Remote Desktop & PowerShell Remoting
Two primary ways to manage remote Windows machines:
# ── Remote Desktop (RDP) ── # From Linux: install freerdp2 xfreerdp /v:workstation01.corp.example.com /u:alice /d:CORP # From Windows: mstsc.exe mstsc /v:workstation01.corp.example.com # ── PowerShell Remoting (WinRM) ── # Enable on the target machine (run as admin once): Enable-PSRemoting -Force # Connect to a remote session Enter-PSSession -ComputerName workstation01 -Credential CORPlice # Run a command on multiple machines at once Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01, srv02, srv03 ` -ScriptBlock { Get-Service -Name Spooler | Select Name, Status } # Copy a file to a remote machine $s = New-PSSession -ComputerName srv01 -Credential CORPlice Copy-Item -Path C:\patch.msi -Destination C:\Temp\ -ToSession $s Remove-PSSession $s
Beginner Soft Skills – The Difference Between a Good and Great IT Pro
Core Concept
Why Soft Skills Matter More Than You Think
Technical skill gets you hired. Soft skills get you promoted, trusted, and recommended. Most IT failures aren't technical — they're communication failures: unclear tickets, blame-shifting, talking over people's heads, or simply not listening.

The best engineers aren't always the smartest — they're the ones people want to work with. That reputation compounds over a career far more than any certification.
Communication
Translating Tech for Non-Technical People
A huge part of IT work is explaining technical issues to people who don't share your vocabulary — managers, customers, other departments. Three techniques:

1. Lead with impact, not mechanism. Instead of "the database connection pool exhausted its max_connections limit," say "the system is slow because too many people are using it at once — we're adding capacity now."
2. Use analogies. "Think of a firewall like a bouncer at a club door — it checks IDs (rules) before letting anyone in."
3. Answer the question they're really asking: usually "is this bad?", "how long until it's fixed?", and "do I need to do anything?"

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — don't assume the person you're explaining to already knows the basics. Asking "would it help if I explained how DNS works first?" is a sign of respect, not condescension — when offered with the right tone.
Teamwork
Working Well on a Team Under Pressure
Incidents and deadlines bring out the worst in some people — finger-pointing, panic, talking over each other. Stand out by doing the opposite:

• State facts, not blame. "The deploy at 2 PM correlates with the spike" lands very differently from "Bob's deploy broke everything."
• Ask clarifying questions before jumping to solutions. "What changed right before this started?"
• Volunteer for the unglamorous work — writing the postmortem, updating the runbook, taking notes during the incident call. People remember who showed up.
• Give credit publicly, give feedback privately.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" applies to drama, not to people. Stay out of office politics — but always be willing to help a colleague who's struggling with a technical problem.
Self-Management
Owning Your Mistakes — and Your Growth
Everyone breaks production eventually. What defines your career is what happens next.

When you make a mistake:
1. Say so immediately — hiding it always makes it worse.
2. Focus on fixing it before discussing how it happened.
3. After it's resolved, write down what you learned.
4. Build a safeguard so it can't happen the same way again.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — this applies to yourself too. You will misjudge things. The professionals who last decades aren't the ones who never err — they're the ones who recover gracefully, learn fast, and don't repeat the same mistake twice.

Career compounding tip: keep a personal log of problems you've solved. In a year, it becomes your interview stories, your mentoring material, and proof of how far you've come.
Beginner Home Lab – Practicing IT Skills Without Breaking Production
Core Concept
Why a Home Lab Accelerates Your Career
You cannot learn to fix a server outage by reading about one. A home lab — your own small collection of virtual or physical systems — gives you a safe place to break things, fix them, and build muscle memory before it matters in production.

Hiring managers consistently say the same thing: candidates who can talk through a real project they built and broke and fixed stand out from candidates who can only recite definitions. Your home lab becomes your interview stories, your portfolio, and your testing ground for certifications — all at once.

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — your home lab is the one circus that is yours. Break it as much as you want; that's the entire point.
Getting Started
Three Ways to Build a Lab (Pick Your Budget)
You don't need a server rack to start — most skills can be learned on hardware you already own.
TIER 1 — $0 (use what you have) - VirtualBox or VMware Workstation Player (free) on your laptop - Run 2-3 VMs: a Linux server, a Windows Server eval, a "router" VM - Practice: Linux administration, networking basics, AD fundamentals TIER 2 — $0-50 (cloud free tiers) - AWS Free Tier / Azure free account / Google Cloud free tier - Practice: cloud networking, IAM, real production-like environments - CAUTION: set billing alerts! "Free tier" usage limits are easy to exceed TIER 3 — $100-500 (dedicated hardware) - Used enterprise mini PC (Dell OptiPlex, Lenovo ThinkCentre — ~$80-150) - Or a Raspberry Pi cluster (~$150 for 3-4 nodes) - Run Proxmox or ESXi as a hypervisor; host many VMs/containers 24/7 - Practice: Kubernetes clusters, self-hosted services, network segmentation # Recommended starter lab build (Tier 1, totally free): # VM1: Ubuntu Server — practice Linux admin, web servers, Docker # VM2: Windows Server Evaluation — practice AD, GPO, PowerShell # VM3: pfSense or OPNsense — practice firewall rules, VPN, routing # VM4: Kali Linux — practice security tools (on YOUR OWN lab only)
Project Ideas
Lab Projects That Actually Build Skills
Don't just install things — build small projects that mirror real work. Here are projects mapped to the domains in this guide:

• Networking: Set up a router/firewall VM, create VLANs, configure DHCP/DNS, capture and analyse your own traffic with Wireshark.
• Security/SOC: Deploy Wazuh or Security Onion; generate "attacks" against your own lab; practice finding them in the SIEM.
• Linux/Ops: Stand up a web app behind nginx, add a database, set up automated backups, then practice restoring from them.
• Scripting: Write a script that monitors your lab's services and alerts you (Slack/email/Discord webhook) when something goes down.
• AI: Train a small model on a public dataset; deploy it as an API in your lab; monitor its performance over time.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — assume your first attempt at any of these will fail in some way. That failure IS the lesson. Document what broke and how you fixed it.
Turning Practice Into Career
Documenting Your Lab Work for Job Hunting
You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — and you can also build proof of your competence so the right choice (hiring you) is easy for someone else to make.

Turn lab work into career capital:
• Keep a build log — a simple markdown file or blog documenting what you built, what broke, and how you fixed it. This becomes your interview stories almost verbatim.
• Push configs and scripts to GitHub — a public repo of "my home lab automation" shows real, verifiable work.
• Write short posts about problems you solved — you'll be surprised how often "I had this exact issue" comments turn into networking connections.
• Use lab achievements to anchor certification study — pass the exam AND have hands-on proof you can do the thing the cert says you can do.

Five years from now, "I taught myself this in a home lab and now I run it in production" is one of the most compelling sentences you can say in an interview.
Beginner Certification Roadmap – Charting a Path Through the Alphabet Soup
Core Concept
What Certifications Actually Do For You
Certifications are not magic keys that open doors by themselves — but they do three concrete things:

1. Get your resume past automated filters — many companies' applicant tracking systems literally search for certification keywords.
2. Give you a structured syllabus — studying for a cert forces you to learn breadth you might otherwise skip.
3. Signal commitment — passing a hard exam shows you can set a goal and follow through, which matters as much as the content itself.

"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — don't assume a certification alone gets you the job. Pair it with hands-on proof (home lab projects, GitHub repos, write-ups) — that combination is what actually gets you hired.
Foundational
Tier 1 — Entry-Level Certifications (Start Here)
These build the broad foundation this entire guide is structured around. Most people new to IT should start with one of these:
Certification Domain Why start here CompTIA A+ IT fundamentals Hardware, OS, troubleshooting basics — the classic "first cert" for helpdesk CompTIA Network+ Networking TCP/IP, subnetting, devices, protocols — pairs perfectly with this guide's net domain CompTIA Security+ Security Widely required for government/defense contractor jobs (DoD 8570 baseline) Google IT Support IT fundamentals Free on Coursera; project-based, Professional Cert beginner-friendly, includes a portfolio AWS Cloud Practitioner Cloud Non-technical intro to AWS — good for anyone, technical or not, entering cloud # Recommended starting combo for a brand-new IT career: # A+ → Network+ → Security+ → (then branch toward your specialty)
Specialization
Tier 2 — Picking a Specialty Track
Once the fundamentals are solid, branch toward the area that excites you most — this guide's domain structure maps directly onto these tracks:
If you enjoyed... → Consider this track → Certifications to target net domain → Networking → Cisco CCNA, Juniper JNCIA sec/threat domains → Security Analyst/SOC → CompTIA CySA+, Blue Team Level 1 pentest domain → Offensive Security → eJPT, PNPT, OSCP (advanced) linux domain → Systems Admin → RHCSA, LFCS (Linux Foundation) ops domain → Cloud/DevOps → AWS SAA, Azure Administrator, Certified Kubernetes Admin (CKA) ai domain → Data/ML Engineering → AWS ML Specialty, TensorFlow Cert grc domain → Governance/Compliance → CISA, CRISC, ISO 27001 Lead Auditor (usually needs experience first — these are mid-career certs)
Study Strategy
How to Actually Pass (Not Just Study)
"Not my circus, not my monkey" — don't get pulled into certification debates online ("is X cert worth it?" threads are endless and rarely conclusive). Pick one aligned with your goals and commit.

A study approach that actually works:
1. Get the official exam objectives — they tell you exactly what will be tested, often down to the percentage weight of each topic.
2. Build something related to each major topic — reading about subnetting is forgettable; calculating subnets for your home lab sticks.
3. Use practice exams from reputable sources — they reveal gaps and build the stamina for a 90-180 minute test under pressure.
4. Schedule the exam date early — a deadline on the calendar turns "someday" into "by March 15th."

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — if you fail an exam, that's data, not a verdict on your ability. Review what you missed, study that specific gap, and schedule a retake. Plenty of senior engineers have a "failed it the first time" story in their past.
Beginner

Building a Home Lab Without Breaking the Bank

Why this matters

You learn IT by breaking things you're allowed to break

Reading about Linux, networking, or virtualization only gets you so far — at some point you need a place to actually try things, watch them fail, and figure out why. A home lab is exactly that: an environment that's entirely yours, where "I broke it" is a learning opportunity instead of an incident report. The good news is that a genuinely useful lab doesn't require expensive server hardware — many people start with nothing more than the laptop they already own.

Concept

Three tiers of home lab, roughly by budget

TierWhat it looks likeWhat you can practice
$0 — Virtual onlyVirtualBox or VMware Workstation Player on your existing laptop, running Linux/Windows VMsOS administration, networking basics, scripting, vulnerable-VM practice (CTF-style boxes)
~$100–300 — Single-board / mini PCA Raspberry Pi, a used mini PC (e.g. an old Dell Optiplex), or a NAS deviceAlways-on services (Pi-hole, file sharing, monitoring dashboards), real hardware troubleshooting
$300+ — Small cluster / used enterprise gearSeveral mini PCs or a used rack-mount server running a hypervisor (Proxmox, ESXi)Virtualization at scale, container orchestration (Kubernetes), simulating multi-server environments

Most people get more learning value from spending six months deeply exploring a $0 virtual lab than from buying $1,000 of gear and never finding time to use it. Start at the bottom of this table — you can always grow upward once you've outgrown what virtualization alone can teach you.

Hands-on

Your first lab session, start to finish

# 1. Install a free hypervisor (VirtualBox shown; VMware Player works too)
#    Download from the official site — never a third-party mirror.

# 2. Download a beginner-friendly Linux ISO
#    Ubuntu Server, Debian, or a purpose-built vulnerable distro
#    like those found on VulnHub or in TryHackMe/HackTheBox labs

# 3. Create a VM with isolated "host-only" or "internal" networking
#    so it can't reach (or be reached from) your real home network —
#    this matters MOST when you're deliberately running vulnerable software

# 4. Once it's running, practice the fundamentals:
ssh labuser@192.168.56.20
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo systemctl status ssh
ip a
df -h

# 5. Take a snapshot BEFORE you experiment — this is the home lab's
#    superpower. Break something? Restore the snapshot and you're
#    back to a clean state in seconds, no consequences.
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — isolate before you experiment

Before you spin up a deliberately vulnerable VM to practice exploitation, double — then triple — check that its network adapter is set to host-only or internal mode, not bridged. A bridged vulnerable machine is directly reachable from (and can potentially reach out to) your entire home network and, depending on your router, the wider internet. "I assumed it was isolated" is one of the most common — and most avoidable — home lab mistakes.

Beginner

Surviving (and Thriving In) Your First On-Call Rotation

Why this matters

Everyone remembers their first page

Being on-call means carrying responsibility for responding to issues outside normal working hours — and for most people new to it, the first 2 AM page triggers a flood of adrenaline that makes clear thinking surprisingly hard. That reaction is completely normal. The goal of preparing for on-call isn't to eliminate that feeling — it's to have enough structure in place that you can function well *despite* it.

Concept

The five-minute checklist for "I just got paged"

StepWhat to doWhy it helps
1. Acknowledge firstHit "acknowledge" in your paging tool before doing anything elseStops the alert from escalating to someone else, and signals "I've got this"
2. Read before you actActually read the alert text and any linked runbook — don't start typing commands from memoryHalf of "wrong fix" stories start with skipping this step while half-asleep
3. Assess blast radiusIs this affecting one customer or all of them? One service or several?Determines whether you handle it solo or escalate immediately
4. Follow the runbookIf one exists for this alert, follow it — don't improvise a "better" approach at 3 AM3 AM you is not as clever as you feel; trust daytime you's preparation
5. When in doubt, escalateWaking up a second person is a minor inconvenience; a worsened outage is notNo one who matters will ever fault you for escalating a real problem
Hands-on

Preparing your "on-call kit" before your rotation starts

# Things to set up and verify BEFORE your first on-call shift begins —
# not during your first incident

# 1. Confirm your paging app actually wakes you up
#    (test it during the day — set it to override silent/DND mode)

# 2. Bookmark the runbooks for the services you're covering
#    — know where they live before you need them under pressure

# 3. Make sure your laptop, VPN, and credentials all actually work
#    from outside the office network — discovering an expired VPN
#    cert during a live incident is a uniquely bad way to start a shift

# 4. Know EXACTLY who to escalate to and how — name, contact method,
#    and what counts as a good reason to wake them up

# 5. Keep a notes file or doc open during your shift — jot down what
#    you tried and what happened. Future-you writing the postmortem
#    will be enormously grateful to past-you for these notes
Mindset

You can't make someone make the right choice...

...yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards. At some point during your on-call career, you (or a teammate) will make the wrong call under pressure — escalate when it wasn't needed, or not escalate when it was. That's not a personal failing; it's an inherent risk of making time-pressured decisions with incomplete information. What separates healthy on-call cultures from miserable ones is what happens next: a blameless retrospective that asks "how do we make the right choice easier to find next time?" rather than "whose fault was this?" The first builds better systems and braver engineers. The second just teaches people to hide their mistakes — which is far more dangerous in the long run.

Beginner

Imposter Syndrome in IT – You're Not the Only One Faking It (a Little)

Why this matters

The feeling that everyone else "gets it" and you're just guessing

Imposter syndrome is the persistent feeling that you don't actually deserve your role or success — that you've somehow fooled everyone, and it's only a matter of time before they "find out." It's remarkably common in IT specifically, because the field changes constantly: there will always be a tool, a framework, or an acronym you've never heard of, no matter how senior you become. That's not a sign you don't belong. It's the actual, permanent shape of working in technology — and recognizing that is half the battle.

Concept

Reframing three thoughts that fuel it

The thoughtA more accurate reframe
"Everyone else seems to know what they're doing"You're seeing their confident output, not their search history, their Stack Overflow tabs, or their private doubts. Confidence is often a performance, not a measure of actual certainty.
"I had to look that up — a 'real' expert wouldn't need to"Looking things up efficiently is the actual skill. The most senior engineers you'll meet Google things constantly — they've just gotten faster at finding good answers and verifying them.
"I only got this opportunity by luck / good timing"Being prepared when an opportunity appeared is the skill. Luck without preparation produces nothing; preparation without any luck rarely gets noticed. Both matter — and you supplied the half that was actually yours to supply.
Hands-on

A concrete habit that actually helps: the "evidence log"

# A simple personal practice: keep a running note — a text file,
# a notes app, anything — where you record concrete moments that
# contradict the "I don't actually know what I'm doing" narrative.
# Re-read it specifically on the days that narrative gets loud.

2026-04-02 - Diagnosed the VPN issue that had stumped two other
             people for three days. Turned out to be a routing
             rule from an old config nobody remembered existed.

2026-04-19 - A junior teammate asked ME to explain subnetting.
             I actually understood it well enough to teach it —
             six months ago I was the one asking that question.

2026-05-30 - Wrote a script that automated a task that used to
             eat up two hours of someone's Friday every week.
             They actually said thank you, unprompted.

# None of these are "I am a genius." They're all just small,
# factual, undeniable evidence that you are, in fact, learning,
# contributing, and growing — which is the entire actual job.
Mindset

You can't make someone make the right choice...

...yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — including your own. You can't will away every doubt, and you can't make your brain stop occasionally whispering "you don't belong here." What you can do is decide, in advance, how you'll respond to that whisper when it shows up: by checking it against actual evidence, by talking to someone who's been there, and by remembering that the discomfort of learning something new is not the same thing as evidence that you can't. Almost everyone you admire in this field felt exactly what you're feeling right now, at some point — they just kept showing up anyway. That's the whole secret, and it's available to you too.

Beginner

Negotiating Your First IT Offer Without Feeling Like You're Being Greedy

Concept

The discomfort is normal — and it's not a sign you're doing something wrong

For a lot of people moving into IT — especially career-changers and those coming from environments where you didn't negotiate your compensation — the idea of pushing back on a job offer feels presumptuous, even rude. It isn't. Negotiation is a completely normal, expected part of professional hiring. Companies build room into their offers anticipating it. Not asking doesn't make you "easy to work with" — it usually just means leaving money and terms on the table that were available the whole time.

Concept

What's actually negotiable (it's often more than just salary)

ItemNotes
Base salaryThe most obvious lever, and often the most flexible at larger companies with defined pay bands.
Sign-on bonusSometimes easier for a company to grant than raising base salary, since it's a one-time cost rather than an ongoing commitment.
Start dateWorth negotiating if you need time to relocate, finish a certification, or just decompress between jobs.
Remote / hybrid flexibilityIncreasingly common to discuss explicitly rather than assume — get it in writing if it matters to you.
TitleCan matter more than people expect for future job searches — "Associate" vs. "Engineer" can change how recruiters filter you years later.
PTO / professional development budgetTraining budgets and certification reimbursement are often easier for companies to grant than cash, and can be worth thousands over a year.
Concept

A simple, low-stress script for the conversation

You don't need to be a slick negotiator. A calm, direct, appreciative tone works better than an aggressive one — and it's far more sustainable for your own nerves:

# A reasonable, low-drama way to open the conversation:

"Thank you so much for the offer -- I'm genuinely excited about this role
and the team. Before I confirm, I wanted to ask whether there's any
flexibility on the base salary. Based on my research into similar roles
in this market, I was hoping for something closer to $X."

# If they can't move on salary, pivoting is completely normal:

"I understand if there's not room to move on the base right now -- would
there be flexibility on a sign-on bonus, or on the start date? I'd also
love to understand what the path to [next title] typically looks like
on this team."

# And if you decide to accept as-is, that's a perfectly valid outcome too --
# the goal isn't "always get more," it's "never wonder whether you should have asked."
Concept

What to do when the answer is "no" — because it sometimes will be

This is where "you can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards" becomes genuinely useful. You can present your case clearly, professionally, and with good research behind it — but you cannot force a hiring manager or a budget committee to say yes. Some companies genuinely have no room to move; others simply won't, regardless of how reasonable the ask is. Either way, the decision about how to respond stays entirely yours: accept as-is, counter once more, or walk away. None of those are failures — they're just different valid endings to a conversation you were right to have started.

📐 How Staff Codes Work — Letter + Number + Sub SYSTEM OVERVIEW ▶
Structure
Decoding Any Staff Designator
Military staff designators follow a consistent three-part formula. Letter = which organization/level this staff belongs to. First number = the functional area (what they do). Second number (optional) = the branch or sub-section within that function.

S=Battalion, N=Navy…

3=Ops, 4=Logistics…

(optional, used in larger HQs)
J63 decoded: J = Joint command · 6 = Communications & IT directorate · 3 = Operations branch within that directorate.
= The section that runs day-to-day network and communications operations for a joint command.
S4 decoded: S = Staff (battalion/brigade level) · 4 = Logistics & Supply.
= The logistics officer at a battalion — responsible for supply, maintenance, and equipment for that unit.
🔤 Prefix Letters — J · G · S · N · A · C · M · F ALL PREFIXES ▶
Reference — All Major Prefixes
Organization Level & Service Branch Designators
The prefix letter indicates which command level and which military service the staff section belongs to. The same number (e.g., 3 = Operations) means the same function regardless of letter prefix.
Prefix Stands For Used By / Level Example Commands Numbers Used
J Joint Unified & combatant commands with two or more service branches CENTCOM, INDOPACOM, SOCOM, DIA, CJCS, USFK, NATO HQ J1–J9
G General Staff Army divisions, corps, and above (General Officer-led commands) 82nd Airborne HQ, 1st Cav HQ, Army corps HQs G1–G9
S Staff Army & Marine Corps at battalion and brigade level (below division) 1-8 Infantry Bn, 2d Marines Regt, Brigade Combat Teams S1–S6 (S7–S9 uncommon)
N Navy Navy headquarters, fleet commands, and naval installations CNO staff, NAVAIR, NAVSEA, Fleet Forces Command N1–N9
A Air Force HAF (Headquarters Air Force) and major command (MAJCOM) staff HAF, ACC, AMC, AFSOC, PACAF, USAFE A1–A10
AF Air Force (alt form) Used in some Air Force numbered air force HQs and wing-level staff for formal documents 1st Air Force, 12th Air Force Same as A-series
M Marine Corps Marine Expeditionary Force (MEF) and Marine division level I MEF, II MEF, III MEF, MARFORPAC M1–M9 (MEF uses G at div, S at bn)
C Combined Multinational/coalition commands where two or more nations operate together Combined Forces Command Korea, NATO Allied Command Ops C1–C9
F Fleet / Force Navy fleet-level commands; also used for some Air Force force-level designations 3rd Fleet, 7th Fleet, U.S. Fleet Forces Command F1–F9
CG Coast Guard U.S. Coast Guard headquarters and district commands COMDT staff, Coast Guard districts CG-1 through CG-9
ⓘ Combined vs Joint: Joint (J) = multiple US military services working together. Combined (C) = multiple nations working together. A command can be both — e.g., Combined Joint Task Force = multinational + multi-service.
🔢 Functional Numbers 1 through 9 — What Each Number Means ALL NUMBERS ▶
Reference — Universal Functional Areas
Numbers are consistent across ALL prefix letters
Regardless of whether the prefix is J, G, S, N, or A — the number always means the same functional area. A J3 and an S3 both handle Operations — just at different command levels.
1
Manpower & Personnel
Human resources, strength reporting, assignments, promotions, awards, disciplinary actions, casualty reporting, morale and welfare. The "HR department" of a military headquarters. J1 · G1 · S1 · N1 · A1
2
Intelligence
All-source intelligence: HUMINT, SIGINT, GEOINT, OSINT, MASINT. Threat assessments, enemy order of battle, ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance), targeting. J2 · G2 · S2 · N2 · A2
3
Operations
Current and ongoing operations — the main effort of any HQ. Battle rhythm, OPORD execution, fires coordination, battle tracking, exercises, and training management. The largest and busiest staff section. J3 · G3 · S3 · N3 · A3
4
Logistics & Supply
Sustainment: supply (Class I–IX), maintenance, transportation, field services, mortuary affairs, contracting. Ensures the force has what it needs to fight and survive. J4 · G4 · S4 · N4 · A4
5
Plans & Strategy
Future operations planning — from 96 hours out through long-range strategy. Operational plans (OPLANs), concept development, war gaming, campaign design, interagency coordination. Distinct from J3 (current ops). J5 · G5 · S5 · N5 · A5
6
Communications, Signal & IT
All networks, radios, satellite comms, data links, IT infrastructure, cybersecurity, COMSEC (communications security), and information management. The military's IT department. J6 · G6 · S6 · N6 · A6
7
Training & Force Development
Exercise planning, readiness reporting, individual and collective training programs, force generation, leader development. Air Force A7 = installations & mission support. Usage varies by branch. J7 · G7 · A7
8
Financial Management & Resources
Budgeting, resource allocation, comptroller functions, program objective memoranda (POM), contracts oversight, cost analysis, financial reporting to higher commands. J8 · G8 · N8 · A8
9
Civil Affairs & Interagency
Civil-military operations, host-nation relations, NGO/IGO coordination, reconstruction, PSYOP (Psychological Operations) coordination, USAID partnerships, governance support in conflict zones. J9 · G9 · S9 · A9
🔭 Sub-Designators — The Third Digit (e.g., J63) BRANCH LEVEL ▶
Reference — Sub-Sections Within Directorates
Third Digit = Branch Within the Functional Directorate
Large headquarters (combatant commands, service HQs) further divide each directorate into branches. The third digit follows the same 1–9 logic: 1=Manpower, 2=Intel, 3=Ops, 4=Logistics within that function. Smaller units (battalions, brigades) rarely use sub-designators.
▸ UNIVERSAL SUB-DESIGNATOR LOGIC
Sub # Function Within the Directorate Example in J6
X1 Manpower & Personnel within that function — staffing, billets, HR for the directorate J61 — J6 manpower & workforce management
X2 Requirements, Architecture & Assessment — needs analysis, doctrine, policy J62 — Network architecture & requirements
X3 Operations — day-to-day execution, current operational support J63 — Network operations & comms ops center
X4 Logistics, Resources & Programs — budget, contracts, sustainment of the function J64 — IT programs, resource management
X5 Plans & Strategy — future development, long-range planning within the function J65 — Comms policy & interoperability plans
X6 Communications within the function — less common at sub-level J66 — COMSEC & crypto management
X7 Training & Exercises within the function J67 — Comms training & exercise support
X8 Financial management specific to the function J68 — IT budget & acquisition oversight
X9 Interagency / special programs within the function J69 — Coalition network integration

Code Full Meaning What They Do

J22 Joint Intelligence — Production Produces all-source intelligence assessments, threat reports, and finished intelligence
J23 Joint Intelligence — Operations Runs the Joint Intelligence Support Element (JISE), 24/7 intelligence battle tracking

⚖️ Branch Comparison — Same Number, Different Context SIDE-BY-SIDE ▶
Cross-Branch Reference
How Each Branch Uses the Same Numbers Differently
The number means the same function, but the scope, size, and tools differ dramatically between a battalion S-section and a combatant command J-directorate.
▸ FUNCTION 1 — PERSONNEL
Code Level Focus & Scope
S1 Battalion (400–1000 personnel) Leave requests, promotions, awards, strength reports, casualty notification for the battalion. Usually 2–4 people.
G1 Division (10,000–20,000 personnel) Same functions but manages policy across multiple brigades. Interfaces with Army HRC (Human Resources Command).
J1 Combatant Command (multi-service, global) Manages manpower for all services assigned to the command; joint manning documents; handles inter-service personnel policy conflicts.
N1 Navy HQ Total force management for all Navy personnel: recruiting, retention, career development, diversity programs.
A1 Headquarters Air Force Manpower & personnel for the entire Air Force: force structure decisions, officer/enlisted development, Air Force Personnel Center (AFPC) oversight.
▸ FUNCTION 3 — OPERATIONS (THE MAIN EFFORT)
Code Level Focus & Scope
S3 Battalion Plans and supervises all battalion training and combat operations. Runs the battalion Tactical Operations Center (TOC). Usually a Major.
G3 Division Synchronizes maneuver, fires, aviation, and combat support across the division. Manages the Division Main CP battle rhythm.
J3 Combatant Command Executes the commander's operational concept across all services globally. Runs the 24/7 Joint Operations Center (JOC). Often a 2-star billet.
N3 Navy Fleet Fleet operational employment; ship deployment scheduling; current fleet operations and readiness.
A3 Air Force Largest Air Force staff directorate. Oversees air operations, flying hour programs, readiness, and airpower employment globally.
▸ FUNCTION 6 — COMMUNICATIONS & IT
Code Level Focus & Scope
S6 Battalion Maintains radios (SINCGARS, SOCOM radios), tactical comms, NIPR/SIPR terminal at battalion level. Often a Warrant Officer or Captain.
G6 Division Division network (Tactical LAN), frequency management, satellite terminals, Signal Battalion oversight.
J6 Combatant Command Enterprise-level network operations. Manages the Joint Information Environment (JIE); classified and unclassified networks; cyber integration with USCYBERCOM.
N6 Navy Navy enterprise networks (NMCI/ONE-Net), shipboard comms systems, spectrum management, Navy COMSEC program.
A6 Air Force AFNET, Air Force IT infrastructure, C2 systems, spectrum, cyberspace capabilities integration into air operations.

6Signal / Communications / CyberS6, G6, J6

⚓Common Codes DecodedMilitary • Reference▶

🧒Reading Military Codes (Beginner)MIL • Start Here▶
BIG IDEA
Why the Letters and Numbers?
Militaries need to communicate fast and without confusion. So they standardize: a letter says which level/branch a staff section is, a number says its job, and a phonetic alphabet keeps spoken letters from being misheard over a noisy radio.
DECODE IT
Letter + Number
Read the letter, then the number. The letter is the echelon/service (S, G, J…), the number is the function (1 = people, 2 = intel, 3 = operations…). So J2 is Joint Intelligence and S4 is unit-level Logistics.
SPELL IT OUT
NATO Phonetic Alphabet
To avoid 'B' vs 'D' mix-ups, each letter gets a word: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta… 'CAT' becomes 'Charlie-Alpha-Tango.' Pilots, police, and IT support all borrow this trick for spelling things aloud.
CLOCK
24-Hour (Military) Time
No AM/PM confusion: the day runs 0000 to 2359. 1:00 PM is 1300 ('thirteen hundred'). Subtract 12 from afternoon hours to get back to a 12-hour clock.
NumberStaff Function
1Personnel (people / admin)
2Intelligence (information)
3Operations (the mission)
4Logistics (supply)
6Communications / Cyber
🎖️Ranks & Echelons (Very Basic)MIL • Start Here▶
THREE GROUPS
Enlisted, NCO, Officer
Most militaries have three broad tiers. Enlisted are the trained doers; NCOs (non-commissioned officers, like sergeants) are experienced leaders risen from the ranks; officers are commissioned leaders who plan and command. NCOs are often called ‘the backbone.’
SIZE LADDER
From Squad to Division
Units nest like Russian dolls, each led by a more senior person: a handful of troops form a squad, squads form a platoon, platoons a company, and so on up. Bigger unit = higher-ranking commander.
Unit (Army, roughly)SizeLed By (roughly)
Squad~8–12Sergeant
Platoon~30–40Lieutenant
Company~100–150Captain
Battalion~500–800Lt. Colonel
Brigade~3,000+Colonel
Division~10,000+Major General
📻 Military Communication Standards — Clear, Concise, Correct MIL • Foundation ▶
WHY MILITARY COMMS
When Miscommunication Costs Lives
Military communication standards were designed for high-stress, noisy, partial-information environments where a misunderstood message can have catastrophic consequences. These principles apply directly to IT operations, incident response, and emergency management — anywhere clarity under pressure matters.
SALUTE REPORT
Size · Activity · Location · Unit · Time · Equipment
A SALUTE report is a standardized format for reporting enemy contact or suspicious activity. Gives responders exactly what they need, in the right order, nothing extra.
LetterFieldExample
SSize3 individuals
AActivityMoving northbound along the road
LLocationGrid 123456, 500m east of checkpoint
UUnit/UniformCivilian clothing, no visible insignia
TTime0830 local
EEquipmentArmed, backpacks, one vehicle
IT application: Use SALUTE-style structured reporting for security incidents — "3 systems affected, lateral movement detected, VLAN 10, identified at 14:32 UTC, using PSExec and Mimikatz."
SITREP
Situation Report — Periodic Status Update
A SITREP (Situation Report) is a standardized periodic update on current status. Key elements:
Current situation — what is happening right now
What has been accomplished — progress since last report
Next actions — what you're about to do
Issues/requests — what you need from higher command
Format matters: be concise, use the same structure every time, report at agreed intervals (even "no change" is information).
RADIO PROCEDURE
Pro-Words (Procedural Words)
Pro-WordMeaning
OVERMy transmission is complete; I expect a reply
OUTConversation is finished; no reply expected
ROGERI received and understood your last message
WILCOI understand and WILL comply (includes Roger)
SAY AGAINRepeat your last transmission (not "repeat" — that has an artillery meaning)
BREAKShort pause in a long transmission
STANDBYWait, I'll get back to you
NEGATIVENo / incorrect
AFFIRMYes / correct
BREVITY IN ALL COMMS
Say It Once, Say It Right
Military communication demands brevity because radio time is shared, batteries die, and enemies can intercept. The principle: say everything necessary, nothing more. In IT: this same discipline makes incident bridge calls, escalation emails, and Slack channels dramatically more effective. State the problem, the impact, what you've tried, what you need — then stop talking.
🎯 OODA Loop — Decision-Making Under Pressure MILITARY • Decision Frameworks ▶
WHAT IS THE OODA LOOP
The Framework Behind Fast, Good Decisions
Developed by Air Force Colonel John Boyd after studying why American pilots won more dogfights despite flying inferior aircraft in Korea. The answer: they could cycle through decisions faster. Boyd codified this as the OODA Loop — Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. The fighter who gets inside the opponent's OODA loop wins. Directly applicable to incident response, red teaming, and any competitive situation.
THE FOUR PHASES
OODA — Breaking Down Each Stage
PhaseWhat HappensCybersecurity Application
ObserveGather information from the environment. Sensory data, signals, telemetry — raw uninterpreted facts.SIEM alerts, network telemetry, threat intel feeds, user reports
OrientMake sense of what you observed. Filter through mental models, prior experience, cultural tradition, analysis. This is the most important phase — your worldview shapes everything.Apply threat knowledge (ATT&CK TTPs), understand adversary motivation, contextualize the alert
DecideChoose a course of action from available options based on your orientation.Contain vs. monitor, escalate vs. handle, which remediation path
ActExecute the decision. Then immediately begin observing again — it's a loop.Block IP, isolate host, patch, notify stakeholders
IT APPLICATION
Incident Response Through the OODA Lens
The fastest incident responders have fast OODA loops — not because they skip steps, but because their Orient phase is automatic from experience and training. This is why tabletop exercises, purple team exercises, and studying past incidents matter: they pre-load the Orient phase.
GoalHow to Achieve It
Speed up ObserveBetter tooling: more log sources, better SIEM, endpoint visibility (EDR)
Speed up OrientTraining, experience, runbooks, tabletop exercises, threat intel
Speed up DecidePre-approved playbooks, clear authority (who can approve isolation?), escalation paths
Speed up ActAutomation (SOAR), prepared scripts, pre-staged remediation tools
Disrupt attacker's loopDeception (honeypots), rapid changes (rotate credentials), unpredictable responses
📋 Commander's Intent — Empowering Action Without Micromanaging MILITARY • Leadership ▶
THE CONCEPT
Two Levels Up, Two Levels Down
In military doctrine, every order includes Commander's Intent — a clear statement of the end state (what does success look like?) and purpose (why are we doing this?). When the plan breaks down (and it always does — "no plan survives first contact with the enemy"), subordinates can make independent decisions that align with the intent rather than freezing to wait for orders.
The rule: know your commander's intent two levels up (why your boss's boss wants this), and ensure your subordinates know yours two levels down. This creates adaptive, decentralized execution.
IT APPLICATION
How Commander's Intent Applies to Tech Teams
Military ConceptIT/Tech Equivalent
Commander's IntentBusiness goal behind a project — "why are we building this?" Engineers who know the why make better tradeoff decisions when specs change
Plan breaks downRequirements change mid-sprint, production incident during deploy, API partner goes down
Decentralized executionOn-call engineers making incident decisions without waiting for management approval
Two levels upDevelopers understanding the business context; analysts understanding org risk tolerance
Two levels downTeam leads ensuring ICs understand the outcome, not just the task
MISSION-TYPE ORDERS
Tell Them What and Why — Not Always How
The German military concept of Auftragstaktik (mission tactics): give subordinates the objective and constraints, then trust them to figure out the method. This produces faster, more adaptive results than prescriptive orders — because the person closest to the problem has the most relevant information.
Applied to IT: instead of "run these exact five commands in this order," a good manager says "we need the backup restored and the service healthy before 8am Monday — you have authority to make it happen." The engineer has context the manager doesn't.
📝 After-Action Review — Learning From Every Event MILITARY • Continuous Improvement ▶
WHAT IS AN AAR
The Army's Structured Debrief
The After-Action Review (AAR) is a U.S. Army practice for learning from any event — a mission, an exercise, a failure. It's a structured, honest discussion conducted immediately afterward while memories are fresh. The civilian tech world adopted it as the "post-mortem" or "retrospective." It's one of the highest-leverage habits a team can build: every incident becomes a lesson instead of just a scar.
THE FOUR QUESTIONS
The Core of Every AAR
QuestionPurpose
1. What was supposed to happen?Establish the plan/expectation
2. What actually happened?Establish the facts, honestly
3. Why was there a difference?Root cause analysis — the real learning
4. What do we do differently next time?Actionable improvements, assigned owners
THE BLAMELESS PRINCIPLE
Hunt for Causes, Not Culprits
The single most important rule: AARs (and post-mortems) must be blameless. The moment people fear punishment, they hide information — and you lose the lessons. The premise is that everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time. The goal is to fix the system (better tooling, clearer process, more training) that allowed the mistake, not to punish the person. This maps directly to IT incident post-mortems: when engineers can speak freely about what went wrong, the organization actually improves.
Blameless (Good)Blameful (Toxic)
"The deploy process let an untested change reach prod""Bob broke production"
"Our runbook was unclear about the rollback step""You should have known better"
People share mistakes openly → org learnsPeople hide mistakes → org repeats them
🧭 Troop Leading Procedures — A Framework for Planning Anything MILITARY • Planning ▶
THE 8 STEPS (BMNT)
How Small-Unit Leaders Plan and Prepare
Troop Leading Procedures (TLP) are the 8-step process small-unit leaders use to plan and execute a mission. The genius is in step 3 — issue a warning order early so the team can start preparing in parallel while you finish planning. This concept maps perfectly to running an IT project or incident response.
StepMilitaryIT/Project Equivalent
1. Receive the missionGet the order/taskReceive the ticket/project/incident
2. Issue a warning orderAlert the team early"Heads up team, big task coming — start prepping"
3. Make a tentative planInitial course of actionDraft approach, identify resources
4. Initiate movementStart positioningProvision environments, gather access
5. Conduct reconnaissanceRecon the terrainInvestigate the system/codebase/logs
6. Complete the planFinalize detailsFinalize the runbook/design
7. Issue the orderBrief the teamKickoff: assign roles, confirm understanding
8. Supervise & refineExecute, adjust, rehearseExecute, monitor, adapt as you learn
PARALLEL PLANNING
Don't Make Your Team Wait on You
The biggest lesson from TLP for civilian work: warning orders enable parallel work. A weak leader plans everything in silence, then dumps a finished plan on the team at the last minute. A strong leader gives early, partial information ("we'll be migrating the database this weekend — start reviewing the schema") so the team prepares simultaneously. This compresses timelines dramatically and respects your team's ability to contribute.
📡 PACE Planning — Redundancy by Design MILITARY • Resilience ▶
WHAT IS PACE
Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency
PACE is a military communications planning method: for any critical capability, you pre-plan four methods ranked by preference. If the Primary fails, you fall back to Alternate, then Contingency, then Emergency — no panic, no improvising, because the fallbacks were decided in advance. It's a discipline of building redundancy before you need it, and it maps perfectly to IT resilience planning.
LevelMeaningComms ExampleIT Example
PrimaryBest, normal methodEncrypted radioSlack / primary monitoring
AlternateNearly as goodSatellite phoneEmail / secondary tool
ContingencyWorkable but degradedRunner with written messagePhone bridge / SMS
EmergencyLast resortSignal flaresPersonal phones / physical meet
PACE FOR IT
Apply It to Anything Critical
The brilliance of PACE is that it forces you to ask "what if this fails?" three times — before the crisis. During a major incident, your primary tools may be down (what if the outage takes out Slack and the monitoring dashboard?). A PACE plan means the team already knows where to go.
CapabilityA PACE Plan Might Be
Incident communicationP: Slack → A: Email → C: Conference bridge → E: Personal cell phones
AuthenticationP: SSO → A: Local admin → C: Break-glass account → E: Console/physical access
Internet connectivityP: Primary ISP → A: Secondary ISP → C: Cellular failover → E: Manual hotspot
Backups/restoreP: Hot replica → A: Cloud backup → C: Offsite tape → E: Rebuild from IaC
RISK MANAGEMENT WORKSHEET
The Military's 5-Step Risk Process
The Army's Composite Risk Management (now Risk Management, ATP 5-19) is a simple, repeatable process used before any operation. It mirrors how IT teams assess change risk — and it's worth internalizing as a mental checklist before any risky action.
StepActionIT Parallel
1. Identify hazardsWhat could go wrong?Threat model the change
2. Assess hazardsHow likely × how bad?Risk = likelihood × impact
3. Develop controlsHow do we reduce risk?Mitigations, rollback plan, testing
4. Implement controlsPut them in placeApply guardrails, schedule maintenance window
5. Supervise & evaluateMonitor, adjust, learnWatch metrics, AAR afterward
🎖️ Leadership — Styles, Mission Command & Cohesion MILITARY • Leadership ▶
LEADERSHIP STYLES
Match the Style to the Situation
There's no single "best" leadership style — effective leaders adapt to the situation, the people, and the stakes. The military teaches this explicitly, and it maps directly to leading technical teams and incidents.
StyleWhen It WorksIT Example
Directive (autocratic)Crisis, no time to debate, clear dangerActive incident — "isolate that host NOW"
ParticipativeSkilled team, time to deliberateArchitecture decisions, planning
DelegativeHighly capable, trusted people"You own this project — keep me posted"
TransformationalNeed to inspire change/growthDriving a culture or major modernization
ServantDay-to-day team enablementRemoving blockers so the team can deliver
The skill is the switch: a leader who is directive during an outage but participative in planning earns far more than one stuck in a single mode. Reading which the moment needs is the art.
MISSION COMMAND
Decentralized Execution Through Trust
Mission Command is the modern military's core leadership philosophy: leaders provide clear intent and the "why," then empower subordinates to use disciplined initiative to achieve it — without waiting for detailed orders. It rests on mutual trust, shared understanding, and accepting prudent risk. In fast-moving situations (combat or a production incident), the people closest to the problem must be able to act. Micromanagement is too slow and doesn't scale.
PrincipleMeaning
Build cohesive teams through trustTrust is earned over time; it's the foundation
Create shared understandingEveryone knows the goal and the why
Provide clear commander's intentThe end state, so people can adapt the how
Exercise disciplined initiativeAct toward the intent without being told
Use mission ordersSay what + why, not every how
Accept prudent riskPerfect certainty never comes; act anyway
UNIT COHESION
What Makes Teams Perform Under Stress
The military invests heavily in cohesion because cohesive units perform dramatically better under pressure — and the research (e.g., Google's Project Aristotle) found the same for tech teams: the #1 predictor of high-performing teams is psychological safety — members feel safe to take risks, admit mistakes, and speak up. This connects directly to blameless post-mortems: people who fear punishment hide problems, and hidden problems compound. Leaders build cohesion by sharing hardship, being competent and fair, communicating honestly, and putting the team's welfare above their own ego. Take care of your people, and they'll take care of the mission.
Beginner OPSEC – Operational Security in Cyber & Real Life
Core Concept
What Is OPSEC?
OPSEC (Operational Security) originated in the military but now applies universally to anyone who needs to protect sensitive information or activities from adversaries.

The core question: "What information, if known by the wrong person, would allow them to harm me, my organisation, or my mission?"

The five-step OPSEC process:
1. Identify critical information — what do I need to protect? (credentials, plans, personnel, locations).
2. Analyse threats — who wants this information and why? (criminals, competitors, nation-states, insiders).
3. Analyse vulnerabilities — where could I accidentally expose this? (social media, email, public logs).
4. Assess risk — likelihood × impact for each vulnerability.
5. Apply countermeasures — reduce the vulnerability (encryption, access control, need-to-know, training).

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — if sensitive information belongs to your organisation, don't share it even with colleagues who don't need it. Need-to-know is a core OPSEC principle.
Digital OPSEC
Personal Digital Security Hygiene
Every IT professional is a target. Apply OPSEC to yourself:
PERSONAL OPSEC CHECKLIST ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CREDENTIALS [ ] Use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password) — unique passwords everywhere [ ] Enable MFA on every account that supports it (TOTP app, not SMS) [ ] Never reuse passwords — one breach = one compromised account, not many COMMUNICATIONS [ ] Sensitive work: use encrypted email (ProtonMail) or end-to-end encrypted chat [ ] Assume corporate email is monitored and archived [ ] Don't discuss sensitive projects on public Slack workspaces / Discord SOCIAL MEDIA [ ] Don't post photos that reveal physical security details (badge readers, screens) [ ] Job posting recon: attackers read your LinkedIn to map tech stack [ ] Don't announce travel dates publicly — burglars and social engineers note it DEVICE SECURITY [ ] Full-disk encryption on laptops (BitLocker/FileVault/LUKS) [ ] Screen lock within 2 minutes of inactivity [ ] VPN on untrusted Wi-Fi (coffee shops, hotels, airports) [ ] Webcam cover when not in use WORK HABITS [ ] Clear desk policy — sensitive docs face down or locked away [ ] Shred documents before disposal; don't put them in recycling [ ] Be aware of shoulder surfing in public spaces [ ] Verify caller identity before providing information (voice phishing = vishing)
Org OPSEC
Protecting Sensitive Information at Scale
Organisational OPSEC controls applied in enterprise security:

• Information classification: Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted — policies dictate how each is handled.
• Data Loss Prevention (DLP): software that blocks classified files from being emailed externally or uploaded to personal cloud storage.
• Privileged Access Workstations (PAW): a dedicated, hardened device used only for admin tasks — never for browsing or email.
• Air-gapped networks: classified systems with no internet connection; data moves via signed, approved media only.
• Red team deception: honeytokens — fake credentials or files planted in your system; if accessed, you know an attacker has them.
# Create a honeytoken file (plant it; alert if accessed) # On Linux: use inotifywait to alert when the file is read touch /home/admin/.aws/credentials_BACKUP_2023 inotifywait -m /home/admin/.aws/credentials_BACKUP_2023 -e access | while read path action file; do echo "HONEYTOKEN ACCESSED: $path$file at $(date)" | mail -s "ALERT: Honeytoken read" security-team@corp.example.com done # AWS honeytoken: create an IAM key that only fires CloudTrail events # Canarytokens.org generates free honeytokens for: # AWS keys, Word docs, PDFs, URLs, DNS names
Mindset
"Assume Breach" – The Modern Security Posture
"Assume" makes an ass out of you and me — but in security, the one assumption you should make is that you have already been breached.

The Assume Breach philosophy:
• Design systems as if an attacker already has a foothold — use micro-segmentation, least privilege, and mutual TLS between services.
• Invest in detection and response as much as prevention — because prevention eventually fails.
• Run red-team exercises to find gaps before real attackers do.
• Know your mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) — measure and improve them continuously.

You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards — an attacker who got in through a phishing email is not your fault; the speed and quality of your response is entirely within your control.
Beginner Leadership – Military Principles Applied to IT Teams
Core Concept
Why Military Leadership Models Translate
Military leadership doctrine has been refined over centuries under the highest-stakes conditions imaginable — and a surprising amount of it maps directly onto leading an IT team through an outage, a project crunch, or simply day-to-day operations.

Both environments share key features: high-pressure decisions with incomplete information, the need to coordinate people who can't all see the whole picture, and consequences that compound when communication breaks down.

You don't need a title to lead — the engineer who keeps a calm head during an outage and gets the team organised is leading, regardless of what the org chart says.
Commander's Intent
"Commander's Intent" – Goals Over Scripts
In the military, a leader gives Commander's Intent: a clear statement of the end goal and the "why" — not a rigid step-by-step script. This way, when the situation changes (and it always does), subordinates can adapt without waiting for new orders.

In IT, this looks like:
Bad delegation: "Run these five exact commands in this order."
Good delegation: "We need this service back online with zero data loss — here's what I know about the failure. Use your judgment; call me if you hit something I haven't covered."

Good intent-based delegation does two things: it grows your team's capability, and it means the mission survives even if the leader is unreachable — exactly when it matters most (3 AM incidents).
After-Action Review
The After-Action Review (AAR) Process
The military's After-Action Review is the direct ancestor of the modern "blameless postmortem." Four simple questions, asked after every significant event:
THE AFTER-ACTION REVIEW — FOUR QUESTIONS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. WHAT WAS SUPPOSED TO HAPPEN? "The deploy was supposed to complete in 10 minutes with zero downtime." 2. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED? "The deploy took 47 minutes and caused a 12-minute outage." 3. WHY WAS THERE A DIFFERENCE? "The database migration locked a table longer than expected because the table had grown 3x since the migration was last tested." 4. WHAT WILL WE DO DIFFERENTLY NEXT TIME? "Test migrations against a copy of production-sized data. Add a pre-flight check that estimates migration duration. Add an automatic abort if a migration runs longer than 5 minutes." RULES THAT MAKE IT WORK: - No rank in the room — the newest hire's observation counts as much as the senior engineer's - Focus on the SYSTEM, not the PERSON ("the process allowed this" not "Dave messed up") - Write it down — verbal lessons evaporate; written ones compound
Mission Mindset
Putting It All Together — Leading Through Chaos
These three phrases — central to this entire guide — are themselves leadership principles refined into short, memorable forms (the way good military doctrine often is):

"Not my circus, not my monkey" — a leader protects their team's focus. Shield people from drama and scope creep that doesn't serve the mission; redirect it to whoever owns it.

"Assume makes an ass out of you and me" — a leader verifies before committing resources. "I think the backup ran" is not the same as "I confirmed the backup completed and is restorable."

"You can't make someone make the right choice, yet you can pick up the pieces afterwards" — a leader's real value often shows after something goes wrong: staying calm, organising the recovery, protecting the team from blame spirals, and turning the failure into the team's next strength.

Master these three, lead with clear intent, and run honest AARs — and you'll out-perform leaders with twice your technical knowledge but none of this foundation.
Beginner

Translating Military Experience into IT Resume Language

Why this matters

The translation gap is real — and fixable

A hiring manager reading "Maintained communications equipment for a forward-deployed unit under field conditions" may not immediately connect that to "can troubleshoot hardware, manage inventory, and keep systems running with no backup support nearby." The skills transfer; the vocabulary doesn't, automatically. Translating your experience into civilian IT language isn't dishonesty or exaggeration — it's making sure the reader understands what you actually did.

Concept

Side-by-side: military experience to IT resume language

What you didHow it translates
Stood watch / monitored systems on shift rotations"Performed continuous system monitoring and incident triage across rotating shift schedules — directly applicable to SOC/NOC environments"
Maintained or repaired communications/radio/radar equipment"Diagnosed and resolved hardware faults under time pressure with limited resources — comparable to field/desktop support and infrastructure troubleshooting"
Managed property, parts inventory, or supply accountability"Tracked and reconciled asset inventories using accountability systems — transferable to IT asset management (ITAM)"
Trained junior personnel on procedures or equipment"Developed and delivered technical training to incoming team members — translates to documentation and knowledge-transfer responsibilities"
Operated under a clearance, handled sensitive information"Held [clearance level]; managed sensitive information per strict handling protocols — directly relevant to compliance-driven environments (GRC, government contracting)"
Followed and enforced strict procedures / checklists"Executed and audited compliance with documented standard operating procedures — maps to change management, runbooks, and audit readiness"
Concept

Lead with impact, not just duties

Civilian resumes reward quantified outcomes over lists of responsibilities. Compare:

# Weak — describes a duty, says nothing about the outcome
