Instance/Task roleEC2/ECS/Lambda auto-receive creds — no keys on disk
Permission boundaryA ceiling on the max perms an identity can ever have
IAM Identity CenterSSO for humans → short-lived console/CLI sessions
OIDC federationLet GitHub Actions assume a role with no stored secret
Policy evaluation: an explicit Deny always wins; otherwise you need an explicit Allow. Effective permission = intersection of identity policy, resource policy, permission boundary, and any SCP (org guardrail).
🔑 GCP IAM — Members, Roles & Hierarchy GCP ▶
How-To
Who (member) Can Do What (role) on Which Resource
GCP IAM binds a member (user, group, or service account) to a role (a bundle of permissions) on a resource. Because of the resource hierarchy, a binding at the project or folder level is inherited by everything beneath it — powerful and easy to over-grant.
Role typeDetail
BasicOwner/Editor/Viewer — broad, legacy, avoid in prod
PredefinedFine-grained, service-specific (e.g. roles/storage.objectViewer)
CustomYour own hand-picked permission set for true least-privilege
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-proj \
  --member="user:alice@example.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
Prefer predefined/custom roles over basic ones, and bind as low in the hierarchy as possible (project > folder > org).
🤖 GCP Service Accounts & Workload Identity GCP ▶
How-To
Machine Identity Without Leaking Keys
A service account (SA) is an identity for an app or VM rather than a person. The trap is downloaded SA key files — long-lived JSON secrets that leak and rarely rotate. Workload Identity is the modern answer: it lets workloads (GKE pods, or external systems like GitHub Actions and even AWS) obtain short-lived SA credentials automatically, with no key file at all.
ApproachVerdict
Downloaded SA key (.json)Long-lived secret — avoid; the #1 GCP credential leak
Attached SA (on a VM/pod)Metadata server issues short-lived tokens automatically
Workload Identity FederationExternal identities (GitHub/AWS) assume an SA keylessly
Rule: if you're storing a .json key, ask whether Workload Identity can replace it. Usually it can.
⚠️ Cloud IAM Pitfalls & Privilege Escalation Security ▶
Security
How Over-Permissive IAM Becomes a Breach
Most cloud compromises aren't zero-days — they're IAM misconfigurations an attacker chains into full control. Knowing the traps is how you avoid (and, on a red team, find) them.
PitfallWhy It's Dangerous
Wildcards (*:*)"Just make it work" grants admin — the classic root cause
iam:PassRole / actAsLets a low-priv identity hand a powerful role to a service it controls → escalation
Overbroad AssumeRole trustA role anyone can assume is a role attackers assume
Long-lived access keysLeak in code/logs/laptops; rarely rotated
SSRF → metadata serviceApp-layer SSRF steals the instance's role creds (IMDSv2 mitigates on AWS)
Public resource policiesA bucket/queue open to "Principal": "*"
Defenses: least privilege, no wildcards, IMDSv2, short-lived creds, and continuous scanning with CSPM tools (Prowler, ScoutSuite, Steampipe) that flag these exact patterns.
🌐 AWS VPC — Subnets, Security Groups & NACLs AWS ▶
How-To
Your Private Slice of the AWS Network
A VPC is an isolated virtual network you define with a CIDR block (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16). Inside it you carve subnets, control routing, and layer two firewalls. Getting the public/private split right is the foundation of a secure architecture.
PieceRole
Public subnetRoute to an Internet Gateway (IGW) — for load balancers, bastions
Private subnetNo direct inbound; outbound via a NAT Gateway — for app servers, DBs
Route tableDecides where a subnet's traffic goes (IGW, NAT, peering)
Security GroupStateful firewall on the instance — allow rules only; return traffic auto-allowed
NACLStateless firewall on the subnet — allow + deny; must allow both directions
Remember: Security Groups are stateful (the common case, instance-level); NACLs are stateless (subnet-level, coarse). Put databases in private subnets and never give them a public IP.
🔀 AWS Load Balancing & DNS — ELB, Route 53, CloudFront AWS ▶
How-To
Getting Traffic to the Right Place, Fast
ServiceDoes
ALB (Application LB)Layer 7 — routes HTTP(S) by path/host, WebSockets, target groups
NLB (Network LB)Layer 4 — ultra-fast TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme throughput
Route 53DNS + health checks + routing policies (latency, weighted, failover, geo)
CloudFrontCDN — caches content at edge locations near users; also DDoS/TLS termination
A typical web path: Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB → targets across multiple AZs. Route 53's failover routing + health checks is how you build multi-region resilience.
🌐 GCP VPC — Global Networks & Firewall Rules GCP ▶
How-To
One Network That Spans the Planet
GCP's big networking difference: a VPC is global, not regional. One VPC can hold subnets in every region, and instances in different regions talk over Google's private backbone without extra peering. Subnets are regional; the VPC that contains them is global.
PieceRole
VPC (global)The whole network; subnets are regional within it
Firewall rulesStateful; applied by network tags or service accounts, not per-instance objects
Cloud NATManaged egress for private instances (no per-VM NAT gateway)
Cloud RouterDynamic (BGP) routing for hybrid/VPN links
Firewall rules being tag-based is the mental shift from AWS: tag an instance web, write a rule "allow 443 to tag:web" — no security-group object to attach.
🔀 GCP Load Balancing & DNS GCP ▶
How-To
A Single Global Anycast IP
GCP's global load balancer is a standout: one anycast IP serves users worldwide, automatically routing each to the nearest healthy backend — no per-region IPs or DNS tricks needed. It scales instantly without pre-warming.
ServiceDoes
Global External LBOne IP, worldwide HTTP(S) routing to nearest backend
Regional LBL4/L7 within a region
Cloud DNSManaged, scalable DNS with 100% SLA
Cloud CDNEdge caching, enabled on the LB backend
🔗 Hybrid Connectivity — VPN, Interconnect & Peering Cloud ▶
Reference
Wiring the Cloud to Your Datacenter (and Itself)
Real deployments connect cloud networks to on-prem and to each other. The options trade cost against bandwidth and reliability.
NeedAWSGCP
Encrypted over internetSite-to-Site VPNCloud VPN
Private dedicated lineDirect ConnectCloud Interconnect
Connect two VPCsVPC Peering / Transit GatewayVPC Peering / Network Connectivity Center
Reach a managed service privatelyPrivateLink / VPC EndpointsPrivate Service Connect
VPN is cheap and quick but rides the public internet; Direct Connect / Interconnect is a private circuit — pricier, but consistent low latency and high bandwidth for production hybrid workloads. PrivateLink-style endpoints keep traffic to cloud services off the public internet entirely.
🖥️ AWS Compute — EC2, AMIs & Auto Scaling AWS ▶
How-To
Renting Virtual Machines That Scale Themselves
EC2 is AWS's virtual-machine service. You launch instances from an AMI (a machine image), pick an instance type (family + size), and — critically — put them behind an Auto Scaling Group so capacity follows demand instead of running fixed (and overpaying).
ConceptDetail
AMISnapshot template an instance boots from (OS + config)
Instance familyt/m = general, c = compute, r = memory, g/p = GPU
Auto Scaling GroupMin/desired/max; adds/removes instances on metrics
Launch templateThe blueprint an ASG uses to create instances
User dataBoot script to configure an instance on launch
▸ PRICING MODELS
ModelUse
On-DemandPay per second; spiky/unpredictable
Savings Plans / Reserved1–3 yr commit → ~30–70% off steady load
SpotSpare capacity ~90% off; can be reclaimed → fault-tolerant jobs
📦 AWS Serverless & Containers — Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate AWS ▶
How-To
Run Code Without (Managing) Servers
ServiceWhat
LambdaFunctions triggered by events; scale-to-zero, pay per ms
ECSAWS's own container orchestrator (simpler than K8s)
EKSManaged Kubernetes (when you need K8s portability)
FargateServerless container compute — runs ECS/EKS tasks with no EC2 to manage
App RunnerPush a container/repo → get a URL; simplest path
Decision: event-driven glue → Lambda; long-running services in containers → ECS/EKS on Fargate (no servers) or EC2 (cheaper at scale, more ops). Fargate is the "I don't want to manage nodes" answer for containers.
🖥️ GCP Compute — Compute Engine & MIGs GCP ▶
How-To
VMs on Google's Infrastructure
Compute Engine is GCP's VM service. Two nice differentiators: per-second billing with sustained-use discounts applied automatically (no upfront commit needed for savings), and custom machine types — pick exact vCPU/RAM instead of fixed sizes.
ConceptAWS Analog
Machine image / familyAMI / instance family (e2, n2, c3…)
Managed Instance Group (MIG)Auto Scaling Group — autoscaling + auto-healing
Instance templateLaunch template
Preemptible / Spot VMsSpot — deep discount, reclaimable
Sustained-use discountAutomatic; no reservation needed
🏃 GCP Serverless & Containers — Cloud Run, Functions, GKE GCP ▶
How-To
Cloud Run Is the Star
Cloud Run is GCP's standout: give it a container, get a scalable HTTPS endpoint that scales to zero and bills per request — serverless containers with almost no config. It's often the simplest way to deploy a web service on any cloud.
ServiceWhat
Cloud RunServerless containers (scale-to-zero, per-request)
Cloud FunctionsEvent-driven functions (like Lambda)
GKEManaged Kubernetes — the reference K8s experience (Google created K8s)
GKE AutopilotK8s where Google manages the nodes for you
Rule of thumb: a stateless web service or API → Cloud Run. Event glue → Cloud Functions. You genuinely need Kubernetes (complex microservices, existing K8s manifests) → GKE.
🧭 Choosing Compute — VM vs Container vs Serverless Reference ▶
Reference
A Decision Guide
Pick…When
Serverless functionsEvent-driven, spiky, short tasks; you want zero ops & scale-to-zero
Serverless containers (Cloud Run / Fargate)Web services/APIs you want managed, but with a real container & no cold-start-only limits
Managed KubernetesMany services, complex networking, portability, an existing K8s investment
Plain VMsLegacy apps, special OS/kernel needs, GPUs, or maximum control
The trend runs left-to-right toward more managed — start as serverless as the workload allows and drop down to VMs only when you need the control. Less to operate = less to break.
💾 AWS Storage — S3 Classes, EBS & EFS AWS ▶
How-To
Three Storage Types for Three Jobs
AWS storage splits into object (S3), block (EBS — a virtual disk for one EC2), and file (EFS — a shared NFS mount for many). Pick by access pattern; mixing them up is a classic mistake. (See the Object Storage topic for S3 fundamentals — here we focus on the AWS-specific pieces.)
ServiceTypeUse
S3ObjectFiles, backups, static sites, data lakes
EBSBlockBoot/data volume for one EC2 (like a disk)
EFSFileShared filesystem mounted by many instances
FSxFileManaged Windows/Lustre file systems
▸ S3 STORAGE CLASSES (cost vs access)
ClassFor
StandardHot, frequent access
Standard-IA / One Zone-IAInfrequent access, cheaper storage
Intelligent-TieringAuto-moves objects by usage
Glacier / Deep ArchiveCold archive — pennies to store, slow/paid retrieval
Use lifecycle rules to age objects into colder classes automatically. EBS volumes are AZ-locked — snapshot to S3 for backup/restore across AZs.
🗃️ AWS Databases — RDS, Aurora & DynamoDB AWS ▶
How-To
Managed SQL & NoSQL
ServiceWhat
RDSManaged relational (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MariaDB) — patching, backups, replicas handled
AuroraAWS's cloud-native MySQL/Postgres-compatible engine — faster, auto-scaling storage, Serverless v2
DynamoDBManaged key-value/document NoSQL — single-digit-ms at any scale, serverless
ElastiCacheManaged Redis/Memcached (caching, sessions)
Choosing: relational data with joins/transactions → RDS/Aurora. Massive scale with simple key-based access → DynamoDB (design around your access patterns — no ad-hoc joins). Always enable Multi-AZ for production databases (automatic failover).
💾 GCP Storage — Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk & Filestore GCP ▶
How-To
The Same Three Types, Google's Names
ServiceTypeAWS Analog
Cloud StorageObjectS3
Persistent DiskBlockEBS
FilestoreFile (NFS)EFS
Cloud Storage classes mirror S3: Standard → Nearline → Coldline → Archive, from hot to cheap-cold. A nice touch: one API/bucket namespace with a per-object storage class, and lifecycle rules to auto-tier. Persistent Disks can be resized live and snapshotted globally.
🗃️ GCP Databases — Cloud SQL, Spanner & Firestore GCP ▶
How-To
Including the One Only Google Has
ServiceWhat
Cloud SQLManaged Postgres/MySQL/SQL Server (≈ RDS)
SpannerGlobally-distributed, strongly-consistent relational DB that scales horizontally — unique to Google
FirestoreServerless document NoSQL (≈ DynamoDB), great for app backends
BigtableWide-column NoSQL for huge analytical/time-series workloads (≈ Cassandra/HBase)
Spanner is the standout — it breaks the usual "you can't have global scale AND strong consistency" rule (via TrueTime atomic clocks). Reach for it when you genuinely need both; otherwise Cloud SQL is the everyday relational choice.
📊 BigQuery — Serverless Data Warehouse GCP ▶
How-To
Query Terabytes With SQL, No Cluster
BigQuery is GCP's flagship analytics warehouse: fully serverless (no infrastructure to size), it runs SQL over terabytes-to- petabytes in seconds by massively parallelizing the scan. It's the OLAP counterpart to the transactional databases above (see the OLTP vs OLAP topic).
TraitDetail
ServerlessNo clusters; it scales compute (slots) automatically
ColumnarReads only the columns your query touches → fast + cheap
Cost modelPriced by bytes scanned (or flat-rate slots) — SELECT * on a huge table is expensive
BQ MLTrain ML models in SQL, in place
Cost tip: select only needed columns and use partitioned/clustered tables — you pay for data scanned, so pruning saves real money. AWS's equivalent is Redshift (and Athena for S3).
🛡️ AWS Security Stack — CloudTrail, GuardDuty & Security Hub AWS ▶
How-To
See, Detect, and Govern Your Account
AWS security starts with visibility. These services layer together: log everything, detect threats, check config, and aggregate it all. CloudTrail is non-negotiable — turn it on day one.
ServiceDoes
CloudTrailRecords every API call — the audit log of who did what
ConfigTracks resource configuration over time + rules for compliance
GuardDutyML/threat-intel detection on logs (crypto-mining, recon, exfil)
Security HubAggregates findings from all of them + CIS/AWS benchmarks
InspectorAutomated vuln scanning of EC2/ECR/Lambda
MacieFinds sensitive data (PII) in S3
Pattern: CloudTrail + Config feed GuardDuty + Security Hub, which stream findings to your SIEM/SOAR. This is the AWS-native version of the Blue Team stack.
🔐 AWS Data Protection — KMS & Secrets Manager AWS ▶
How-To
Encryption & Secrets, Managed
KMS (Key Management Service) creates and controls encryption keys; most AWS services integrate with it for encryption-at-rest with a checkbox. Secrets Manager stores credentials/API keys with automatic rotation, so secrets never live in code or env files.
ServiceDetail
KMSManaged keys; envelope encryption; per-key IAM policies + audit via CloudTrail
Secrets ManagerStore + auto-rotate DB creds/API keys; fetch at runtime
Parameter StoreCheaper config + secret storage (SSM)
Enable default encryption on S3/EBS/RDS with KMS, and pull secrets from Secrets Manager at runtime — the two habits that close the most common data-exposure gaps.
🛡️ GCP Security — Cloud Audit Logs & Security Command Center GCP ▶
How-To
The Google-Side Equivalents
ServiceDoesAWS Analog
Cloud Audit LogsAdmin/data-access API audit trailCloudTrail
Security Command CenterCentral posture + threat findings dashboardSecurity Hub + GuardDuty
Cloud Logging / MonitoringLogs, metrics, alertingCloudWatch
ChronicleGoogle's SIEM at scale—
SCC is the single pane for GCP security posture — it surfaces misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, and active threats across your projects, mapped to standards.
🔐 GCP Data Protection — Cloud KMS, Secret Manager & VPC-SC GCP ▶
How-To
Keys, Secrets & a Data-Exfil Perimeter
ServiceDetail
Cloud KMSManaged encryption keys (like AWS KMS); CMEK on most services
Secret ManagerVersioned secret storage with IAM + audit
VPC Service ControlsA security perimeter around services to stop data exfiltration — GCP-distinctive
DLP APIDiscover & redact sensitive data (PII)
VPC-SC is the standout: it draws a boundary so that even a stolen credential can't pull data out to the internet — mitigating the exact SSRF/exfil chains from the IAM Pitfalls card.
🔎 CSPM — Prowler, ScoutSuite & Steampipe Security ▶
Reference
Continuously Audit Your Cloud Posture
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools scan your accounts for misconfigurations — public buckets, over-broad IAM, unencrypted volumes, disabled logging — against benchmarks (CIS). This is the bridge between the Cloud and Blue Team domains: run them regularly to find gaps before attackers (using the same tools) do.
ToolDetail
ProwlerOpen-source AWS/GCP/Azure security assessments (CIS, NIST, etc.)
ScoutSuiteMulti-cloud config auditing → HTML report
SteampipeQuery your cloud with SQL (find issues with a SELECT)
Cloud-nativeSecurity Hub / SCC do continuous CSPM too
🏗️ Terraform on AWS & GCP IaC ▶
How-To
One Tool for Every Cloud
Terraform's superpower in the cloud is being provider- agnostic — the same HCL workflow (init/plan/apply) provisions AWS, GCP, Azure, and 100+ others. You declare a provider, then resources. (See the Terraform topic for the core workflow — here's the cloud-specific shape.) 
provider "aws"    { region  = "us-east-1" }
provider "google" { project = "my-proj", region = "us-central1" }

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "data"   { bucket = "my-data" }
resource "google_storage_bucket" "data" { name = "my-data", location = "US" }
Cloud essentials: store state remotely (S3 + DynamoDB lock, or GCS) so a team shares it; use modules for reusable stacks (a "VPC module"); and never edit cloud resources by hand once Terraform manages them (drift).
📜 AWS-Native IaC — CloudFormation & CDK AWS ▶
Reference
Terraform's In-House Rivals
CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC — YAML/JSON templates, deeply integrated, no state file to manage (AWS tracks it as a "stack"). CDK (Cloud Development Kit) lets you write infra in a real programming language (TypeScript, Python) that synthesizes to CloudFormation — loops, conditions, and abstractions instead of sprawling YAML.
CloudFormationCDKTerraform
LanguageYAML/JSONReal code → CFNHCL
ScopeAWS onlyAWS onlyMulti-cloud
StateManaged by AWSManaged by AWSYou manage
Rule of thumb: all-in on AWS → CloudFormation/CDK is tightly integrated; multi-cloud or tool consistency → Terraform. GCP's equivalents are Deployment Manager and Config Controller (Terraform is common on GCP too).
💸 Cloud Cost Control — Budgets, Tags & Rightsizing Cloud ▶
How-To
Keep the Bill From Surprising You
Cloud spend is variable and easy to lose track of. The practical controls (a hands-on companion to the FinOps topic) start on day one and run continuously.
ControlAWSGCP
Budgets + alertsAWS BudgetsBudgets & alerts
Cost analysisCost ExplorerBilling reports / BigQuery export
Attribute spendCost allocation tagsLabels
Anomaly detectionCost Anomaly DetectionBudget anomaly alerts
Biggest levers: tag everything (or you can't attribute spend), set budget alerts before you deploy, rightsize idle resources, and commit (Savings Plans / CUDs) for steady workloads. Watch data-egress — the sneaky line item.
🏛️ Landing Zones & Multi-Account Structure Cloud ▶
Concept
Don't Put Everything in One Account
Mature cloud setups isolate workloads across many accounts / projects — separate prod from dev, and each team/app in its own blast- radius boundary — governed centrally. A landing zone is the pre-built, secure, multi-account foundation you start from.
ConceptAWSGCP
Org hierarchyOrganizations + OUsOrganization + Folders
GuardrailsService Control Policies (SCPs)Org Policies
Landing zoneControl TowerCloud Foundation Toolkit
The win: a compromise or mistake in one account/project can't reach the others, and central guardrails (SCPs/Org Policies) enforce rules — "no public S3," "only these regions" — org-wide.
📦 GCP-Native IaC — Deployment Manager & Config Controller GCP · IaC ▶
Reference
Declarative Infrastructure the Google Way
Beyond Terraform, GCP has native declarative options. Google now steers most users toward Config Controller (managed Config Connector + Policy Controller) — you describe cloud resources as Kubernetes-style YAML and GCP reconciles them continuously.
OptionNotes
Config ConnectorManage GCP resources as K8s CRDs (GitOps-friendly)
Config ControllerManaged KRM stack: Connector + Policy Controller + sync
Deployment ManagerThe older Jinja/Python template engine (legacy; being retired)
Terraform (+ Blueprints)Google's actual recommended default for most teams
Takeaway: for greenfield GCP IaC, reach for Terraform or Config Controller, not Deployment Manager. The KRM model unifies app and infra config under one reconciliation loop (ties to GitOps in ops).
🚚 Cloud CI/CD — CodePipeline & Cloud Build AWS · GCP ▶
Reference
Managed Build-and-Deploy Pipelines
Both clouds offer first-party CI/CD so you don't run your own build servers. They slot in next to (or instead of) GitHub Actions when you want tight IAM and artifact integration with the platform.
AWSGCPRole
CodePipelineCloud Build (triggers)Orchestrate stages
CodeBuildCloud BuildRun build/test steps
CodeDeployCloud DeployProgressive delivery to targets
ECRArtifact RegistryStore container/package artifacts
Why native: pipelines assume an IAM role (no long-lived keys), and use OIDC to let external CI authenticate without stored secrets. Push signed images to the registry, then Cloud Deploy/CodeDeploy roll them out canary-style.
📊 AWS Observability — CloudWatch & X-Ray AWS · Ops ▶
Reference
Metrics, Logs, Alarms & Traces
CloudWatch is the central nervous system for AWS ops — it collects metrics, aggregates logs, fires alarms, and triggers automated responses. X-Ray adds distributed tracing so you can see a request hop across services.
PieceDoes
Metrics & AlarmsNumeric time-series; alarm → SNS/Auto Scaling/Lambda
Logs & Logs InsightsCentral log store with a query language
DashboardsSingle-pane views of a service's health
X-RayTraces & service maps for latency debugging
Modern path: instrument with OpenTelemetry (via the AWS Distro, ADOT) so your telemetry isn't locked in. Alarms on the golden signals (latency, errors, saturation) are what turn raw metrics into on-call signal.
📈 GCP Observability — Cloud Monitoring, Logging & Trace GCP · Ops ▶
Reference
The Operations Suite (formerly Stackdriver)
Google's operations suite mirrors CloudWatch/X-Ray with metrics, logs, and traces — and leans on the SRE practices Google literally wrote the book on (SLOs, error budgets are first-class in Cloud Monitoring).
ServiceAWS equivalent
Cloud MonitoringCloudWatch metrics/alarms/dashboards
Cloud LoggingCloudWatch Logs (with LogQL-like queries)
Cloud TraceX-Ray (distributed tracing)
Cloud Profiler / Error ReportingContinuous profiling & error grouping
Define an SLO right in Cloud Monitoring and it tracks the error budget and burn rate for you — the theory from the SRE card, operationalized. Also OpenTelemetry-native.
🏛️ Well-Architected & the Architecture Framework AWS · GCP ▶
Concept
The Pillars for Grading a Cloud Design
Both AWS (Well-Architected Framework) and GCP (Architecture Framework) publish a set of pillars to review any workload against. It's the rubric architects use in design reviews and the basis of the "Well-Architected Review."
PillarAsks
Operational ExcellenceCan you run & improve it (IaC, observability, runbooks)?
SecurityLeast privilege, encryption, detection in depth
ReliabilityRecovers from failure, scales to demand
Performance EfficiencyRight resources, evolve as tech changes
Cost OptimizationPay only for what delivers value (→ FinOps)
Sustainability(AWS) minimize environmental impact
Run a review before a big launch: score each pillar, log the risks, remediate the high ones. It's the cloud-specific companion to the engineering-domain system design cards.
🔷 Azure — Getting Started & Entra ID Azure ▶
Reference
The Third Major Cloud
Microsoft Azure is especially common in enterprises already on Microsoft 365. Its identity backbone is Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) — the tenant-wide directory that authenticates users and apps across Azure and M365.

TenantThe identity boundary (~ AWS Organization root)

Entra IDIAM Identity Center / Cloud Identity
az CLI / Cloud Shellaws / gcloud CLI
# Sign in and set the active subscription

Note the terms: Azure "subscription" ≈ AWS account, and RBAC is assigned on scopes (management group → subscription → resource group → resource) that inherit downward.

The Building Blocks
Everything in Azure lives in a Resource Group — a container for related resources sharing a lifecycle. Networking, compute, and storage map cleanly onto their AWS/GCP counterparts.

The Defensive Stack
Azure's security services close the loop with the Blue-team domain: Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR, and Defender for Cloud is the CSPM/CWPP posture engine.
ServiceRoleAnalog

🏛️ Software Engineering & Architecture
ARCH SWE
System Design · Architecture · Craft · Reliability · Career ▾
📈 Scalability 101 — Vertical vs Horizontal System Design ▶
Concept
Two Ways to Handle More Load
Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine — more CPU/RAM. Simple, but there's a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means more machines behind a load balancer — effectively unlimited and fault-tolerant, but only if your app is designed for it. The design requirement is statelessness: any server can handle any request, so session/state lives in a shared store (Redis, DB), not in one server's memory.
Vertical (up)Horizontal (out)
HowBigger boxMore boxes
CeilingHardware limit~Unlimited
FailureSingle pointRedundant
ComplexityLowNeeds LB + stateless design
Real systems do both: scale up the database (hard to shard) and scale out the stateless app tier. Shared-nothing architecture — nodes share no memory/disk — is what makes horizontal scaling clean.
⚖️ Load Balancing & Sharding System Design ▶
Concept
Spreading Requests, Then Spreading Data
A load balancer spreads incoming requests across servers; sharding spreads the data across databases when one can't hold or serve it all. Both are "divide the work," at different layers.
▸ LOAD-BALANCING ALGORITHMS
AlgorithmSends request to…
Round robinEach server in turn
Least connectionsThe least-busy server
WeightedBigger servers get more
IP hash / stickySame client → same server
▸ SHARDING STRATEGIES
StrategySplit byWatch out
RangeKey ranges (A–M, N–Z)Hot ranges
Hashhash(key) % NResharding pain
Consistent hashingRing of hashesAdding nodes moves few keys — the standard
The enemy is the hot shard — one key or range getting disproportionate traffic (a celebrity user). Choose a shard key with even distribution and no cross-shard joins on the hot path.
🧮 Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation System Design ▶
Reference
Numbers Every Engineer Should Know
Before designing, sanity-check scale with rough math. Knowing that memory is ~1000× faster than disk, and a cross-region round trip is ~150 ms, tells you where the bottleneck will be without building anything.
▸ LATENCY NUMBERS (orders of magnitude)
Operation~Time
L1 cache reference~1 ns
Main memory reference~100 ns
SSD random read~100 µs
Network round trip (same DC)~0.5 ms
Disk (HDD) seek~10 ms
Round trip across continents~150 ms
▸ CAPACITY MATH (worked)
1M daily active users, 10 requests/user/day = 10M req/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ ~115 req/s average. Peak is typically 2–3× average → design for ~300 req/s. Storage: 10M writes/day × 1 KB × 365 × 5 yr ≈ ~18 TB. These two numbers (QPS + storage growth) drive most of the architecture.
🛟 Designing for Failure System Design ▶
Concept
Everything Fails — Plan for It
At scale, hardware dies, networks partition, and dependencies time out constantly. Robust systems assume failure and stay up anyway. The core moves: eliminate single points of failure, contain damage, and degrade gracefully instead of collapsing.
TechniqueWhat It Buys
Redundancy (N+1)No single point of failure — replicate across AZs
Health checks + failoverRoute away from dead instances automatically
BulkheadsIsolate resources so one overloaded feature can't sink the rest
Graceful degradationServe a cached/limited response instead of an error (show stale prices, hide recommendations)
Blast-radius limitsCell-based / sharded design so an outage hits 5% of users, not 100%
Pair with the resilience patterns (circuit breaker, retry-with-backoff, timeout) at the call level. The mindset: "what happens when this dependency is down?" should have an answer for every dependency.
🧩 The System Design Interview — A Framework Career ▶
Reference
A Repeatable Structure for an Open-Ended Question
"Design Twitter" has no single right answer — interviewers assess how you think. A structure keeps you from freezing and shows senior judgment: drive requirements, estimate, sketch, then go deep where it matters.
StepDo
1. ClarifyNail functional + non-functional requirements. Who uses it? Read/write ratio? Consistency vs availability?
2. EstimateQPS, storage, bandwidth — back-of-envelope (previous card). Sets the scale.
3. APIDefine the core endpoints/contract — forces concreteness.
4. Data modelEntities, access patterns → SQL vs NoSQL choice.
5. High-level designBoxes & arrows: clients → LB → services → DB/cache/queue.
6. Scale & deepenFind bottlenecks; add caching, sharding, replicas, CDN, async queues.
7. Trade-offsName what you gave up. There is no perfect design — only fit-for-purpose.
The senior signal is talking trade-offs out loud and tying decisions back to the requirements — not memorizing one "correct" architecture.
🏗️ Monolith vs Microservices vs Modular Monolith Architecture ▶
Concept
The Most Consequential Architecture Choice
A monolith is one deployable unit — simple to build, test, and deploy, but hard to scale teams and selectively scale parts. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services — great for large orgs and independent scaling, but you trade code complexity for operational complexity (networking, data consistency, observability). The modular monolith is the underrated middle: one deployable, but with strict internal module boundaries — so you get simplicity now and can extract services later if you actually need to.
MonolithMicroservices
DeployOne unitMany, independent
ScaleWhole appPer service
Team fitSmall teamsMany teams
DataOne DB, easy joins/txnsDB-per-service, distributed txns
FailureAll-or-nothingIsolated (if done right)
Ops costLowHigh
Default advice: start with a (modular) monolith. Microservices solve organizational scaling problems you probably don't have yet — adopting them too early buys distributed-systems pain for no benefit.
📡 Event-Driven Architecture Architecture ▶
Concept
React to Facts, Don't Call in Lockstep
Instead of service A calling B calling C, components emit events ("OrderPlaced") to a broker, and interested services react. This decouples producers from consumers: add a new consumer (email, analytics, fraud) without touching the producer. It's the architecture behind responsive, extensible systems — at the cost of harder debugging and eventual consistency.
StyleHowTrade-off
ChoreographyEach service reacts to events independentlyLoose coupling; flow is emergent/hard to trace
OrchestrationA coordinator directs the stepsClear flow; the orchestrator is a coupling point
Watch for: event ordering, duplicate delivery (make consumers idempotent), and schema evolution (version your events). Pairs with the Message Queues topic and CQRS/Event Sourcing below.
⬡ Clean / Hexagonal Architecture Architecture ▶
Concept
Keep Business Logic Independent of Frameworks
Clean Architecture (and its cousin Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters) organizes code so your business logic sits at the center, knowing nothing about the database, web framework, or UI. Those outer concerns are adapters that plug into ports (interfaces) the core defines. Swap Postgres for Mongo, REST for gRPC, without touching the core.
The key rule is the dependency rule: dependencies point inward. The domain never imports the framework; the framework imports the domain. Concretely: the core defines a UserRepository interface; a PostgresUserRepository in the outer layer implements it. This makes the core trivially unit-testable (mock the ports) and resistant to framework churn — the business rules outlive the tech stack.
LayerContains
Entities / DomainCore business rules (no dependencies)
Use casesApplication-specific orchestration
AdaptersDB, web, external APIs — the replaceable edge
✂️ CQRS & Event Sourcing Architecture ▶
Concept
Split Reads from Writes; Store Events, Not State
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses separate models for writing (commands) and reading (queries) — so each can be optimized and scaled independently (e.g. a normalized write DB + denormalized read replicas). Event Sourcing goes further: instead of storing current state, store the full sequence of events that produced it. Current state is a replay of the log.
PatternGainCost
CQRSIndependent read/write scaling & modelsTwo models to keep in sync (eventual consistency)
Event SourcingFull audit trail; time-travel; rebuild any viewComplexity; schema/versioning; snapshots for speed
Powerful together, but not free — they add real complexity. Use them where audit, temporal queries, or extreme read/write asymmetry genuinely demand it (banking, ledgers), not by default.
1️⃣2️⃣ The Twelve-Factor App Architecture ▶
Reference
The Checklist for Cloud-Native Services
The Twelve-Factor methodology is a battle-tested set of rules for building services that deploy cleanly to modern platforms and scale horizontally. You don't need to memorize all twelve — internalize the handful that bite hardest.
FactorRule
ConfigStore config in the environment, never in code
Backing servicesTreat DBs/queues as attachable resources (via URL)
ProcessesStateless & share-nothing — state goes to a backing service
Port bindingExport services via a port; self-contained
DisposabilityFast startup / graceful shutdown (scale & recover fast)
Dev/prod parityKeep environments as similar as possible
LogsTreat logs as event streams to stdout — the platform routes them
Follow these and your app runs the same on a laptop, in a container, or across 100 nodes — the foundation for autoscaling, twelve-factor is why containers and PaaS "just work."
🗂️ Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Design ▶
Concept
Model the Business, Not the Database
DDD is an approach to complex software that puts the business domain at the center. Developers and domain experts build a shared ubiquitous language — the same words in conversation and in code — and split the system into bounded contexts where each term has one precise meaning ("account" means something different to Billing vs Auth).
ConceptMeaning
Bounded contextA boundary where a model & language are consistent (often → a service)
Ubiquitous languageShared vocabulary used identically by experts & code
EntityObject with identity that persists over time (a User)
Value objectDefined only by its attributes, immutable (an Address, Money)
AggregateA cluster of objects with one root that guards invariants
Bounded contexts are why DDD and microservices pair so well — a well-drawn context is a natural service boundary. Start with the language; the model follows.
🧱 SOLID Principles Design ▶
Reference
Five Rules for Maintainable OO Code
SOLID is five principles that keep object-oriented code flexible and testable. You don't apply them dogmatically — you reach for them when code becomes rigid or hard to change.
PrincipleMeans
SSingle ResponsibilityA class has one reason to change
OOpen/ClosedOpen to extension, closed to modification
LLiskov SubstitutionSubtypes must be usable as their base type
IInterface SegregationMany small interfaces > one fat one
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions, not concretions
The throughline is manage dependencies: isolate what changes, program to interfaces, and keep the direction of dependency pointing at stable abstractions (this is the engine behind Clean Architecture).
🔗 Coupling & Cohesion Design ▶
Concept
The Two Words That Describe Good Structure
Almost every design principle reduces to two ideas. High cohesion: things that change together live together (a module does one job well). Low coupling: modules depend on each other as little as possible, through narrow interfaces. Aim for both — you want tight-inside, loose-between.
PropertyGoodBad
CohesionHigh — focused moduleLow — grab-bag of unrelated code
CouplingLow — few, clean dependenciesHigh — change one, break many
The Law of Demeter ("only talk to your neighbors" — avoid a.getB().getC().doThing()) is a practical way to keep coupling low. When a change ripples across many files, that's high coupling telling you the boundaries are wrong.
📐 API-First & Contract-Driven Design Design ▶
Concept
Design the Interface Before the Implementation
API-first means the API contract (e.g. an OpenAPI or Protobuf spec) is written and agreed before anyone builds the backend. Frontend, backend, and consumers all code against the same contract in parallel, and you can generate clients, mocks, and docs from it. The interface becomes the source of truth, not an afterthought.
BenefitDetail
Parallel workTeams build against the spec + a mock, not a finished server
CodegenClients, server stubs, docs, validation from one spec
Consumer-driven contractsConsumers publish expectations; a broken change fails CI (Pact)
GovernanceConsistent conventions, versioning, and review across APIs
This is what makes microservices and public platforms manageable — the contract is a stable boundary that lets teams move independently without constant breakage (ties to the API Design topic).
🧮 Idempotency & Exactly-Once — Safe Retries Reliability ▶
Concept
The Property Distributed Systems Live and Die By
In any networked system, messages get lost, duplicated, and retried. An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once — the single most important property for correctness under retries. "Charge $10" is dangerous to retry; "set balance to $90" is safe.
TechniqueHow
Idempotency keyClient sends a unique ID; server dedupes and returns the original result
Natural idempotencyDesign ops as "set to X" (absolute) not "add X" (relative)
Dedup storeTrack processed message IDs; skip repeats
Outbox patternAtomically write state + the event to publish, so neither is lost
True "exactly-once" delivery is famously near-impossible; the practical answer is at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers = effectively-once processing. Build every consumer and API assuming it will see duplicates.
✍️ Clean Code & Naming Craft ▶
Concept
Code Is Read Far More Than It's Written
You write a line once; it's read dozens of times over its life. Clean code optimizes for the reader — clarity beats cleverness. The highest-leverage skill is naming: a good name removes the need for a comment.
PrincipleDetail
Intention-revealing nameselapsedDays > d; say what it is
Small functionsDo one thing; a screenful is a smell
Few arguments0–2 ideal; many args hint at a missing object
No surprisesA function does exactly what its name says, nothing hidden
Comments explain whyNot what — the code shows what; comments justify the non-obvious
The Boy Scout Rule: leave the code a little cleaner than you found it. Small, constant improvements beat big rewrites.
👀 Code Review — Doing It Well Craft ▶
Concept
The Highest-ROI Quality Practice
Review catches bugs, spreads knowledge, and keeps a codebase coherent — but only if done with care. Bad reviews (nitpicky, slow, ego-driven) poison a team; good ones make everyone better.
As reviewerAs author
Review promptly (unblock people)Keep PRs small & focused
Comment on the code, not the personExplain the "why" in the description
Distinguish must-fix from nit (label it)Respond to every comment
Ask questions, don't demandDon't take feedback personally
Approve when good enough, not perfectLet the machine catch style (linters)
Automate the boring parts (formatting, lint, tests in CI) so humans review what matters: correctness, design, edge cases, and clarity.
🧪 Testing Strategy — The Test Pyramid Craft ▶
Concept
Many Fast Tests, Few Slow Ones
The test pyramid guides how to balance test types: lots of fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of slow end-to-end tests on top. Invert it (mostly E2E) and your suite is slow, flaky, and brittle — the dreaded "ice-cream cone."
LevelTestsTrait
Unit (many)One function/class in isolationFast, precise, cheap
Integration (some)Components together (DB, API)Slower, more realistic
E2E (few)The whole system as a userSlow, flaky, high-value paths only
TDD (write the test first) drives better design and guarantees coverage; BDD frames tests as behavior ("given/when/then"). Aim to test behavior, not implementation, so refactors don't break the suite.
💳 Technical Debt — Recognize & Pay It Down Craft ▶
Concept
Borrowing Speed Now Against Effort Later
Technical debt is the implied future cost of a quick-and-dirty choice. Like financial debt, a little is a useful tool (ship now, fix later); too much, unmanaged, and the "interest" — slower changes, more bugs — eventually consumes all your capacity.
TypeExample
Deliberate"We'll hardcode this to hit the deadline" (fine, if tracked)
AccidentalLearned a better design too late; code lagging behind understanding
Bit rotDependencies age, the world changes, code decays
Manage it: make it visible (a backlog, not tribal knowledge), pay it down opportunistically (Boy Scout Rule) plus dedicated time, and prioritize debt in code you touch often. Debt in a stable, untouched corner rarely matters.
📝 ADRs & Design Docs Craft ▶
Reference
Write Down the Decision and the Why
Six months later, no one remembers why the team chose Postgres over Mongo, and the reasoning gets re-litigated. An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short doc capturing one decision: the context, the options, the choice, and the consequences. A design doc (or RFC) does the same before building something significant.
ArtifactPurpose
ADR1-page record of a single decision (context/options/decision/consequences)
Design doc / RFCPropose & get feedback before building; align the team
C4 modelDiagrams at 4 zoom levels: Context, Container, Component, Code
Keep them short and in the repo (version-controlled next to the code). The value is the trail of reasoning — it onboards new people and stops old debates from restarting.
🔌 Resilience Patterns — Circuit Breaker, Retry & Timeout Reliability ▶
Concept
Stop One Failure From Cascading
In a distributed system, one slow or dead dependency can drag down everything that calls it — threads pile up waiting, and the failure cascades. Resilience patterns contain that at every remote call.
PatternProtects against
TimeoutWaiting forever on a hung dependency
Retry + backoff + jitterTransient blips — but back off so you don't stampede
Circuit breakerA failing dependency — "trip open" and fail fast instead of hammering it
BulkheadOne overloaded feature sinking the rest (isolate resource pools)
FallbackDegrade gracefully — cached/default response over an error
Careful with retries: naive retries during an outage create a retry storm that keeps the dependency down. Always pair retries with backoff, jitter, and a circuit breaker; only retry idempotent operations.
💰 Distributed Transactions — Saga & Outbox Reliability ▶
Concept
Consistency Across Services Without 2PC
When a business action spans multiple services/databases (place order → charge card → reserve stock), you can't wrap it in one ACID transaction. Two-phase commit (2PC) technically can, but it's slow and fragile — so modern systems avoid it.
PatternHow
SagaA sequence of local transactions; on failure, run compensating actions to undo
OutboxWrite state + the "event to publish" in one local transaction, so the event can't be lost
2PCCoordinator locks all participants to commit atomically — avoided at scale (blocking, SPOF)
Sagas trade atomicity for availability: the system is briefly inconsistent, then converges (or compensates). "Charge failed → cancel the order" is a compensating transaction. Pair with idempotency (E3) so retried steps are safe.
🌊 Backpressure & Flow Control Reliability ▶
Concept
Don't Accept More Than You Can Handle
When work arrives faster than a system can process it, unbounded queues grow until memory runs out and everything crashes. Backpressure is the system signaling "slow down" upstream, so load is shed or throttled rather than silently piling up.
TechniqueDetail
Bounded queuesFixed size; reject/block when full instead of growing forever
Load sheddingDrop low-priority work under overload (protect the core)
Rate limitingCap intake at a sustainable rate (token bucket)
Reactive streamsConsumer signals demand to the producer (pull, not push)
The counter-intuitive lesson: a system that rejects excess load cleanly stays up; one that politely accepts everything falls over. Fail fast, shed early.
🎛️ Consistency in Practice — Quorums & Tunable Reads Reliability ▶
Concept
Dialing the CAP Trade-off Per Operation
The CAP theorem is abstract; in practice distributed databases give you knobs. With quorums, a value is written to/read from a majority of replicas — and by tuning how many must respond (W + R > N), you choose consistency vs latency per query.
TermMeaning
N / W / RReplicas / write acks required / read acks required
W + R > NGuarantees a read sees the latest write (strong)
Low W, low RFast + available, but reads may be stale (eventual)
Read repair / anti-entropyReplicas reconcile in the background
So a shopping-cart read can be fast-and-eventual (low R) while the final checkout uses a strong quorum — the same store, tuned per operation. This is how Dynamo-style systems make CAP practical (ties to the CAP Theorem topic).
🪜 The Engineering Ladder — Junior to Principal Career ▶
Reference
What Changes as You Level Up
Seniority isn't about writing more code — it's about the scope of impact and how much ambiguity you can absorb. The ladder describes a widening blast radius of responsibility.
LevelScope
JuniorCompletes well-defined tasks with guidance
MidOwns features end-to-end independently
SeniorOwns systems; mentors; handles ambiguity within a team
StaffImpact across multiple teams; sets technical direction
Principal+Org/company-wide technical strategy
The shift from senior → staff is the big one: from "I solve hard problems" to "I make other teams more effective" — via influence, not authority.
⭐ Staff+ Archetypes Career ▶
Reference
There's No Single "Staff Engineer"
Will Larson's Staff Engineer identifies four common shapes the role takes. Knowing them helps you play to your strengths and recognize the kind of senior leadership your org needs.
ArchetypeDoes
Tech LeadGuides a team's execution on a specific area
ArchitectOwns direction for a critical domain across teams
SolverParachutes into the gnarliest problems
Right HandExtends a senior leader's reach across the org
All four share the staff-level core: technical judgment, cross-team influence, and moving the org forward — not just shipping personal code.
🍴 Tech Lead vs Engineering Manager Career ▶
Concept
The Fork in the Senior Road
Around senior level, careers often fork into two tracks — both leadership, but different work. Good orgs value them equally; the mistake is assuming management is "up" and IC is "stuck."
IC / Tech Lead trackManagement track
Leads throughTechnical influence & designPeople, process, delivery
Spends time onArchitecture, hard problems, mentoring1:1s, hiring, coordination, careers
Measured byTechnical outcomes & leverageTeam health & throughput
You can switch tracks (and back) — many do. Choose based on what energizes you: solving technical problems, or growing people and systems. Neither is superior.
📣 Influence Without Authority Career ▶
Concept
The Skill That Defines Senior+ Engineers
Past a certain level, your impact depends on getting other people and teams — whom you don't manage — to align on technical direction. That's done through credibility, clear writing, and trust, not org-chart power.
LeverDetail
Write it downAn RFC/design doc scales your idea & invites input
Build credibilityShip, help others, be right consistently
Frame in their termsTie your proposal to what stakeholders care about
Disagree & commitArgue hard, then support the decision fully
Give creditTrust compounds; hoarding credit destroys it
The best technical idea loses to a well-communicated mediocre one. Learning to write and persuade is as much a "senior engineering skill" as system design.
🎓 Cert Roadmaps — Choosing a Path Career ▶
Reference
A Study Order for the Big Tracks
Certs won't make you an engineer, but they structure learning and clear HR filters. Pick a track that matches your goal and work up it.
TrackPath
IT foundationsA+ → Network+ → Security+
Blue teamSecurity+ → CySA+ → (GCIH/GCIA) → CISSP
Red teamSecurity+ → PenTest+ → OSCP → (OSEP/CRTO)
Cloud (AWS)Cloud Practitioner → Solutions Architect Assoc → Security Specialty
Cloud (GCP)Cloud Digital Leader → Associate Cloud Engineer → Professional Architect
ManagementPMP / CISM for leadership tracks
The whole site maps to these — this reference domain (Red/Blue/Cloud/Engineering) is effectively a study companion for the tracks above.
☁️ Cloud-Native & Serverless Architecture Patterns Architecture ▶
Concept
Designing for the Platform, Not Just on It
Cloud-native architecture assumes elastic, disposable infrastructure and managed services. Serverless takes it further — you write functions and the platform handles scaling to zero and back. Both change how you decompose a system.
PatternDetail
Managed-service-firstPrefer a queue/DB/auth service over running your own
Event-driven / FaaSFunctions triggered by events; scale per-event
Strangler FigIncrementally replace a monolith by routing slices to new services
BFFBackend-for-frontend: a tailored API per client type
Cold starts / limitsServerless trade-offs: latency spikes, timeouts, statelessness
Trade-off: serverless minimizes ops and cost at low/spiky load but can get expensive and awkward at steady high volume (and vendor lock-in rises). Match the model to the traffic shape — ties to the "Choosing Compute" cloud card.
🗃️ Schema & Data Modeling Patterns Data Design ▶
Concept
Model the Data to Match the Access
How you shape data determines what's fast and what's painful. Relational normalization optimizes for integrity; denormalization and NoSQL optimize for read patterns. Good design starts from how the data is queried, not an abstract ideal.
ChoiceTrade-off
Normalization (3NF)No duplication, integrity — but more joins
DenormalizationFast reads, fewer joins — but update anomalies
NoSQL single-tableModel around access patterns (DynamoDB style)
Polyglot persistenceRight store per job: relational + doc + cache + search
Star / snowflakeDimensional modeling for analytics warehouses
Rule: normalize until it hurts, denormalize until it works. In NoSQL you design the table around queries up front — the opposite of relational's "model entities, query later."
📐 Estimation & Planning Career ▶
Concept
Why Software Estimates Are Always Wrong
Estimation is hard because building software is discovering the problem, not repeating a known task. Mature teams estimate relative effort and manage uncertainty rather than pretending to predict exact dates.
IdeaDetail
Story pointsRelative size (complexity/effort/uncertainty), not hours
VelocityPoints/sprint historically — forecast, don't commit to it
Planning pokerEstimate together to surface hidden complexity
Cone of uncertaintyEstimates tighten as you learn — re-estimate
Ranges & buffersGive "2–4 weeks", not "3 weeks"; account for the unknown
Senior move: break big work into small, independently shippable slices — small things estimate accurately, and you get feedback early. Padding a giant estimate just hides the risk.
🧑‍💻 Career Ladders & Interviews Career ▶
Reference
Leveling Up & Getting Through the Loop
A career ladder makes expectations explicit per level; interviews test whether you meet the bar. Preparing deliberately for each stage beats raw talent for both getting hired and getting promoted.
Interview stagePrep
CodingData structures & algorithms; think aloud, test your code (LeetCode-style)
System designUse the framework: requirements → estimate → API → data → scale → trade-offs
BehavioralSTAR stories tied to the level's expectations (scope, impact)
Take-home / practicalClean, tested, documented — treat it like real work
For promotion: operate at the next level before the title — keep a brag doc of impact mapped to the ladder's criteria. The whole Engineering domain here is study material for the design & coding loops.
